<meta>Continuing from the discussion of light passing through apertures and the formation of inverted images. This page (377) of Kepler's 1604 work *Astronomiae Pars Optica* transitions into the practical application of these geometric principles to sundials (scioterics).</meta>

->**THE OPTICAL PART OF ASTRONOMY. 377**<-

The same is true concerning the extremities or "nodes" <note>original: "nodis"</note> of gnomons <note>A gnomon is the part of a sundial that casts the shadow; the "node" is a specific point or tip on the gnomon used to indicate the date or time.</note>: which take the place of the window. And just as in our camera <note>Referring to a *camera obscura* or darkened room experiment.</note> two cones of light met at their vertices, so in <term>Scioterics|The mathematical study or art of shadow-marking, specifically for sundials</term> the cone of light is joined to the cone of shadow at the common mark of the gnomon. I do not know whether this has been noticed by those who write on the subject of sundials.

And since in our climate all lines of this kind are hyperbolas <note>Kepler is describing the curved path the shadow of a gnomon's tip traces on a flat surface over the course of a day.</note>, (except when the Sun completes the equinox, for then the path of the ellipses is a straight line, the most obtuse of all hyperbolas) the relationship of the radiant ellipses to their own hyperbola must also be noted. It is known from the preceding sections that if a perpendicular line is dropped from the center of the window, the axes (or more commonly, the longer diameters) of all the ellipses stretch themselves toward that point on the floor where the perpendicular from the small window falls. For the perpendicular, the ray, and the axis of the ellipse are all in the same plane of the vertical circle. Indeed, the axis of the hyperbola created by the ellipses also tends toward that same point.

<summary>Kepler explains that the geometry of light passing through a window is identical to the geometry of shadows cast by a sundial's gnomon, noting that the sun's path usually traces a hyperbola on the ground.</summary>
<keywords>Kepler, optics, sundials, gnomon, scioterics, geometry, hyperbola, ellipse, equinox, camera obscura</keywords>

<meta>Kepler is continuing his discussion on the practical methods of observing solar eclipses using optical projections, specifically focusing on how to measure time and magnitude when standard instruments are unavailable.</meta>

->378 **OF JOHANNES KEPLER**<-

...drawn across, it measures the interval of time between noon and the phase <note>referring to a specific stage of the eclipse</note>.

You may also measure the duration of time and the minutes even without a clock in this manner: if you catch the right lateral edge of the projected ellipse (which is already marked) with a stylus <note>a pointed tool for marking or pointing</note>, and hold it there until the luminous ellipse passes the stylus and touches it with its left edge; at that moment, remember to mark the axis of the ellipse, and move the stylus to the right side, and so on. From the number of consecutive ellipses, you will determine the time. For the body of the Sun in <term>apogee</term> <note>the point in the Sun's orbit where it is furthest from the Earth</note> occupies precisely half a degree, which measures about two minutes of time. However, the shape of the ellipse on the plane is a little larger (due to the width of the aperture) than the shape that would be created by a hole the size of a point.

For example, in the year 1598, on February 25th (or March 7th) <note>Kepler provides dates for both the Julian and Gregorian calendars, which were both in use at the time</note>, when I lacked suitable instruments and the cloudy sky had almost made me despair of making an observation, I stayed under a roof and had opened a crack of uncertain shape and size, watching for any opportunity. When a notable portion [of the sun] was already missing, the shadow stood precisely to the right: it was one or two <term>digits</term> <note>a traditional astronomical unit representing one-twelfth of the diameter of the solar or lunar disk</note>. The ray on the paper was the size of a silver groschen <note>original: "grossi argentei"; a common European coin of the time</note>; I was unable to discern it accurately, for the Sun was hidden again in the blink of an eye. 

On the city clock, it struck one quarter past ten. After an hour, I caught another fleeting glimpse <note>original: "furtum aspectus", literally a 'theft of a sight'</note>. The crescent <note>original: "cornu", literally "horn"</note> was tilted downward, veering slightly toward the west in the projected ray, and was very thin—therefore, in the sky, it was tilted upward, and the eclipse was northern. The end was clear. At slightly less than 12 o'clock by the city time, 6 digits were in the shadow of the ray. The shadow was to the left and below, if you looked at the ray with your face turned toward the north. At a quarter past twelve in the city, there were about 4 digits. The inclination was about 23°. When there were about 3¾ digits, the inclination seemed to be 20°. When there were 3⅔ digits—the other clock now striking one quarter [past twelve]—the inclination was about 21°. A little later, 3¼ digits; the inclination was about 22. At half past one by the city clock, 1⅔ digits; the inclination about 25. A little later, about 1½ digits; the inclination, as it seemed most truly, was 21°. The cause of this discrepancy was that, following the instruction of Maestlin <note>Michael Maestlin, Kepler’s former professor and mentor</note>—

-> THE OPTICAL PART OF ASTRONOMY. 379 <-

Not being well-mindful of the instructions, I neglected to bring the circles drawn on paper—with their diameters divided into <term>inches</term><note>The "uncia" or inch here refers to a twelfth part of the diameter used for measurement on his projection screen.</note>—to the observation. Therefore, while I was marking both circumferences with points, the Sun meanwhile moved away, and I could not discern whether the ray fell perpendicularly onto the paper. Thus, the diameter of the Moon appeared for the most part smaller, yet sometimes larger than or equal to the solar diameter. Furthermore, this was lacking: there was no other indication of the <term>vertical</term><note>The "verticalis" or zenith line, used to orient the image relative to the horizon.</note> than the length of the paper. I already recognized these obstacles; therefore, turning to improvised plans, I began to note the end of the eclipse through ellipses, having no doubt that through calculation—which I am now teaching—both the inclination and the time could be obtained from this. From this moment, therefore, I recorded nine ellipses up to the end of the eclipse at six o'clock, which certainly did not touch one another. Thus, more than twelve minutes remained until the end. Indeed, when it had ceased, a little

With this, therefore, I took the distance of the Sun from the <term>zenith</term><note>The point directly overhead.</note> after the third quarter had sounded; it was slightly less than 54 degrees. At noon that day, the position of the Sun according to Tycho <note>Tycho Brahe, the famous Danish astronomer and Kepler’s predecessor.</note> was 16° 49' of Pisces ♓, and the southern declination was 5° 14'.

...would be the whole sine <note>original: *sinus totus*; in early trigonometry, this refers to the radius of the circle, typically set at 100,000 units to allow for integer-based calculations of sines</note>. But because the path itself is a curved and hyperbolic line, while the Sun’s path is a minor circle, therefore $PR$ applied as an ordinate is the tangent of angle $PBR$ when $BR$ is the radius, and of angle $PAR$ when $AR$ is the radius or whole sine. Let it be proposed to us to continue the calculation for these moments:
0 hours, 15 minutes;
0 hours, 30 minutes;
0 hours, 45 minutes;
1 hour, 0 minutes
after noon.

Let the meridian be represented by $\beta \gamma$. On it, let the south pole be $\beta$. Let the Sun be at $\delta$, and let the portion of the great circle be $\gamma \delta$. And because time measures the angles at the pole, the angles $\gamma \beta \delta$ will therefore be:
3° 15' | 7° 30' | 11° 15' | 15° 0'.

Furthermore, the angle $\beta \gamma \delta$ is a right angle, and $\beta \delta$ is the complement of the Sun’s southern declination, namely 84° 46'. From these known values, the side $\beta \gamma$ is sought from the base and the adjacent angle. This results in:
*   In the first moment: 84° 45 1/3'
*   In the second moment: 84° 43 1/3'
*   In the third moment: 84° 40'
*   In the fourth moment: 84° 35'

Let $\beta \epsilon$ be the depth of the pole <note>The "depth" or altitude of the celestial pole, used here to define the observer's latitude</note> at 47° 2'. The remainders $\epsilon \gamma$ or $BRA$ will be:
37° 43 1/3' | 37° 41 2/3' | 37° 38' | 37° 33'.

Their complements $BAR$, increased by the parallax <note>The displacement in the apparent position of the Sun as viewed from different points</note>, are:
52° 18 2/3' | 52° 20 2/3' | 52° 24' | 51° 19'.

Therefore, the values for $BR$ are:
129437, 129603, 129853, 130244.
Previously, $BC$ was 129385. Therefore, $CR$ is:
52, 218, 468, 859.
Since $HC$ is 39870, and half of $NC$ is 19935, $NR$ will become:
19987, 20153, 20403, 20794.

...of the city's mechanical clocks <note>original: "automaton vrbicum"</note>, two minutes after the end [of the eclipse], rang the third quarter toward one o'clock <note>12:45 PM</note>. The altitude of the Sun—though measured somewhat unreliably as it was midday and I used a small quadrant—observed about three minutes after the end, indicates 58 1/4 minutes <note>Kepler likely means 58 degrees and 15 minutes of altitude</note>. This agrees quite well with my hyperbolic angle. Indeed, in the next diagram, let **α β** be 1 37. 2., **β δ** 84. 46., and **δ α** 53° 50'. This produces an angle **α β δ** of 14° 34'. It is most certain that this was in the afternoon, for by then the ellipses <note>The projected shapes of the Sun through a pinhole</note> were already moving away from the aperture.

If we trust the city clock’s consistency over such a short span of time—which I believe we safely can—the duration of the eclipse will now be clear. For at the precise moment I saw the eclipse lacking one <term>digit|A traditional unit for measuring eclipses, representing one-twelfth of the diameter of the celestial body</term> or slightly less, the clock rang exactly the first quarter past ten <note>10:15 AM</note>. Therefore, since it rang three quarters past twelve <note>12:45 PM</note> two minutes after the end of the eclipse, the total duration was more than 2 1/2 hours. In the final thirteen minutes of time, the eclipse decreased by 1 2/3 digits; thus, one digit decreases or increases every eight minutes. Consequently, if one digit was missing at the first sighting, the duration becomes 2 hours and 36 minutes. If the missing portion was smaller than that, the duration will also be shorter.

Since by these two indications the end of the eclipse falls at 12:55, and we subtract 2 hours and 36 minutes, the beginning must fall at 10:19 or later. Shall we find confirmation for this from observation? Let us see. When my quadrant showed the Sun’s distance from the <term>vertex|The zenith, or the point directly overhead</term> was 59 degrees, there was not yet any trace of a "failure" <note>Kepler uses "defectus" to refer to the eclipse</note>. Calculation shows this was eight minutes before ten o'clock <note>9:52 AM</note>. After that, the Sun went behind the clouds, and indeed remained hidden for about half an hour, until it emerged appearing to lack one digit.

At Hven in Denmark <note>The island of Ven, where Tycho Brahe built his observatories</note>, a certain student of Tycho’s who was on the island for the purpose of this observation reported the beginning at 10:03 and the end at 12:32. This gives a duration of 2 hours and 29 minutes, with a magnitude of 9 2/3 digits. However, the duration ought to have been longer there than at Graz <note>original: "Gratij"</note>. Since the Moon is to the north, it is natural that at that northern latitude <note>original: "poli eleuatione," the elevation of the pole</note>, which exceeds mine by 9 degrees, the Moon should appear 5 minutes deeper into the Sun's body and should have traveled a path that much longer across the Sun.

Consider, then, the optical illusions discussed above in chapter six. Tycho himself, as he wrote to Maestlin <note>Michael Maestlin, Kepler's former professor</note>, observed the beginning at Wandsbek near Hamburg using <term>armillary spheres|An astronomical instrument composed of a nested framework of rings representing the great circles of the heavens</term> at 9:52 AM. This would be 10:04 1/2 AM at Hven, because according to Hondius <note>Jodocus Hondius, a Flemish cartographer</note> the difference in meridians <note>longitude</note> is 3° 8'. Therefore, the middle of the eclipse at Hven...

->384 JOHANNES KEPLER<-

<margin>Again, the difference of meridians between Uraniborg and Graz, though without considering the difference in parallax.</margin> ...[the eclipse ended] at Hven <note>The island where Tycho Brahe's observatory, Uraniborg, was located.</note> at 11 hours, 17½ minutes. At Graz, it was 11 hours, 37 minutes, or more. Therefore, the difference of the <term>meridians</term><note>In historical astronomy, the "difference of meridians" refers to the difference in longitude expressed as a difference in local time.</note> is about 20 minutes, or 5 degrees of longitude—provided that all the measurements used were correctly established. Nor does the map by Hondius <note>Jodocus Hondius (1563–1612), a famous Flemish cartographer.</note> differ much, as it places the difference of the meridians at just over 4 degrees.

Now I will also explain Problem 17 using this example, and I will show what inclinations result from my ellipses. First, I will seek the proportions of the diameters to one another at solar altitudes of 37° and 36°, which were the altitudes shortly before and after the end of the eclipse, at the time I marked the ellipses. With an arc of 52° 45' | 53° 0' | 53° 15', the differences of the <term>tangents</term><note>Kepler is using trigonometric tables to calculate how a circular light source projects as an ellipse when hitting a surface at an angle.</note> come out to 1197 and 1212. Therefore, the longer diameter is 2409, while the shorter one, drawn through the axis of the cone (by multiplying the <term>secant</term> of 53 degrees by the tangent of 15 minutes), is 1450. Again, with arcs of 53° 45' | 54° 0' | 54° 15', the differences of the tangents come out to 1255 and 1271. Thus, the longer diameter is 2526 and the shorter one through the axis of the cone is 1486. This is a ratio of roughly 17 to 10, the former being slightly less.

The proportion in my own diagrams—which were very rough and made in great haste—comes out smaller, and is therefore faulty for the reasons stated in Problem 17. This is why I am undertaking to correct them according to the rule of Problem 17 in this manner. The longer diameter in the second of my ellipses was exactly this one, expressed by the letters AB; one <term>horn</term><note>The "horns" (cornua) are the pointed tips of the crescent shape formed by the sun during a partial eclipse.</note> was at the lowest point D, and the other on the line GL perpendicular to AB. Therefore, having divided BA at the midpoint E, let a circle BG be described from E. Let the line LG intersect this circle at G. Then let the arc DG between the horns be bisected at H. DH will be the inclination, which now comes out to 22½ degrees.

Pardon me, Reader, that I present these observations to you which are not everywhere consistent with one another. For it was a remarkable eclipse <note>Kepler refers to the solar eclipse of July 10, 1600, which he observed in Graz, Austria.</note>, which had been eagerly awaited by certain astronomers for many years; yet it was seen in only a few places due to a cloudy sky. Therefore, I think it better that these records, such as they are, should exist, rather than have the event go entirely unobserved. Nor is there such great uncertainty in them that they should be rejected. That I disclose all my doubts is a mark of my candor. But a warning was not necessary everywhere: for near the end of the eclipse, two things which are slippery to observe—and about each of which I might separately doubt whether I was attentive enough—coincide at almost the same moment, most sincerely and without any prejudice, from the proposed observation, before they were examined: the altitude of the Sun, and the angle between the ellipse and the hyperbola. And this agreement itself is not accidental, but they agree with observations in Saxony and Denmark, and with Tycho's <note>Tycho Brahe, the Danish nobleman and astronomer whose precise data Kepler used.</note> own renewed calculation. I do not know what can be objected against four agreeing witnesses. Furthermore, concerning the inclination, I shall inquire into this same matter in the following problems, to see if they agree with these times.

->### Problem XXVI.<-

*From given visible longitude and latitude at certain moments, and assuming from elsewhere the distances of the Moon and the Sun from the center of the earth, to establish the true longitude and latitude, and thus the hourly motion and the moment of true conjunction; or conversely, by assuming the hourly motion, to moderately investigate the distance of the Moon from the earth.*

Parallax <note>The apparent shift in position of a celestial body when viewed from different locations</note> mixed with true motion constitutes the visible motion; when separated, it leaves the true motion. Indeed, parallax is caused by the proximity of a celestial body to the center of the earth. This problem is thus sufficiently clear from the reversal of the instructions for computing Eclipses. I only repeat it here to declare the use of the instruction brought forward above in Chapter 9 in its proper place, and at the same time so that the use of observed inclinations in establishing the true location of the Moon may be clear. This is also so that Solar Eclipses may be freed from false accusation <note>original: "calumnia". Kepler refers to scientific errors or the "reproach" that solar eclipse data was less reliable than lunar eclipse data</note>, by demonstrating that they contribute more to investigating the Moon's motions than Lunar ones <note>Kepler argues that solar eclipses actually provide more precise data for mapping the Moon's orbit than lunar eclipses do</note>. Let the distance of the Sun and the earth be assumed as 1150 semi-diameters <note>Earth radii</note>, as it pleases Tycho <note>Tycho Brahe (1546–1601), the Danish astronomer whose data Kepler refined</note>, about which I have written elsewhere. This sum, when sought at the head of our parallax table, offers a horizontal refraction <note>The bending of light as it passes through the atmosphere at the horizon</note> of approximately 3'. Let the Moon’s distance from the earth be assumed, as above, as 55 semi-diameters. Its horizontal parallax, proportionally excerpted from the head of our table, will be 62' 30''. From this, the solar parallax of 3' being subtracted leaves a horizontal parallax of the Moon from the Sun of 59' 30''.

Now let there be a first moment when the distance between the nonagesimal <note>The highest point of the ecliptic above the horizon</note> and the zenith <note>The point directly overhead</note> was 56° 4'. With this value, under the heading of precisely 59 minutes, 48' 57'' are excerpted from the table; under the heading of 30, 24'' 53''' are excerpted. The sum is 49' 22'' for the parallax of latitude of ☾ <note>The Moon</note> from ☉ <note>The Sun</note>.

Therefore, at the end of the 12th hour and 55th minute, the Moon had surpassed the true position of the Sun by 53' 49''. If 32' 50'' minutes make one hour, what does 53' 49'' make? The <term>Rule: the mathematical "Rule of Three" used to find an unknown value by comparing proportions</term> will show 1 hour, 38 minutes, and 20 seconds. Therefore, the moment of true conjunction at Graz <note>Kepler was living and teaching in Graz, Austria, when he performed these observations.</note> would have been at 11 hours and 17 minutes. If the timing of the end is correct, we are certain of the midpoint of true conjunction within nearly one minute.

If you wish to return from the assumed hourly motion to investigate the parallaxes, the way is not so straightforward, but rather crab-like or by looking backward. For fortune must be invoked so that you might assume right at the start the very parallax you desire—that is, the one that leads you to the desired position and the assumed hourly motion, using the method already explained. If you wander from the true parallax, the labor must be repeated, and the truth must be felt out by comparing errors with the differences in parallaxes through a blind reasoning, as if by the <term>rule of false: also known as the "Rule of False Position," a trial-and-error method where you guess a number and adjust it based on how wrong the result is</term>.

## Problem XXVII.

*Given the elevation of the pole <note>The latitude of the observer.</note>, the visible start and end times or specific moments of an eclipse, and the known position of the Sun; having also assumed the hourly motion and the diameters of the luminaries <note>The Sun and the Moon.</note>, the nature of the movement in latitude roughly calculated <note>original: "crassiori minerua," a Latin idiom for a rough or plain approximation.</note>; and finally the distances of the luminaries from the center of the earth: to investigate the exact moment of true conjunction and the true latitude: and from there, to determine the difference in Meridians <note>By comparing local observation times to a reference meridian, astronomers calculated longitude.</note>.*

     Let us play. For no reward for this labor is more certain than this pleasure. And if it pleases us, let us even solace our labor with a song. I desire to know at what moment the true conjunction occurred in Denmark, so that a more certain difference of the meridians may be obtained; at the same time, I also desire to know whether the observer, hindered by optical illusions <note>original: "visus fallaciis." Kepler was deeply concerned with how the human eye and the camera obscura distorted astronomical measurements.</note>, noted the beginning too late or the end too slowly. For that will easily become clear if we elicit a latitude greater than our own. Nor shall we be unmindful that in our own latitude, there exists an uncertainty of two minutes at the end of the Eclipse. 
     The altitude of the pole at Hven <note>The island of Hven, site of Tycho Brahe’s observatories, Uraniborg and Stjerneborg.</note> is 55° 54' 45". The sum of the <term>semidiameters</term> <gloss>half the width of the celestial discs</gloss> is 31' 40". We know the Moon is truly to the North and is moving away from the ascending <term>node</term> <gloss>the point where the Moon's orbit crosses the ecliptic</gloss>. Let the horizontal <term>parallax</term> <gloss>the apparent shift in position when viewed from different locations</gloss> of the Moon from the Sun be, as before, 59' 30".

At the end of the eclipse, the right ascension <term>Right Ascension: The celestial equivalent of longitude, measured along the celestial equator from the vernal equinox.</term> of the Sun (at 16° 50' Pisces ♓) is 347° 54'. Add 8° for the time distance of the Sun from the meridian, and the right ascension of the Midheaven <term>Midheaven (Medium Coeli): The point of the ecliptic that is at its highest on the meridian.</term> becomes 355° 54', at which 25° 32' Pisces ♓ is at the meridian. And its declination is 1° 47' South, namely the segment **MA**. Therefore, **MV** is 57° 43'. At that moment, 27° 43' Cancer ♋ is rising, and point **N** is at 27° 43' Capricorn ♑. Therefore, **MN** is 32° 11' and **NV** is 50° 44'. And its complement is 39° 16', from which I extract the Moon's parallax <term>Parallax: The apparent shift in the position of a celestial body when viewed from different points on Earth.</term> from the Sun: 46' 3'' in latitude and 37' 39'' as the nominal <note>original: "titularem," referring to a preliminary or placeholder value before correction.</note> longitude. And since the Sun is at 16° 50' Pisces ♓, the nonagesimal <term>Nonagesimal: The point on the ecliptic 90 degrees from the horizon; the highest point of the ecliptic above the horizon.</term> is at 27° 43' Aries ♈. Therefore, **SN** is 40° 53'. I subtract about 25 minutes, by which the Moon visually follows the Sun, so that it becomes 40° 28'; with this value and the nominal values already found (37' 39''), I extract the true parallax of the Moon's longitude from the Sun as 24' 26'' toward the west. Let these values again be ready for use.

Now, because the elapsed time is 2 hours 29 minutes, and the hourly motion of the Moon from the Sun is 32' 50'', the motion of the Moon is 1° 21' 32''. By how much the latitude varies along the arc near the nodes <term>Nodes: The two points where the Moon's orbit crosses the ecliptic (the Sun's apparent path).</term> at a distance of ten degrees from the node: by 6' 57'' (assuming a latitude angle of 4° 58' 1/2''). And because the Moon is ascending toward the north, the true northern latitude at the end will be 6' 57'' greater. But the visible latitude also increases because of parallax. For in the beginning, the parallax of the Moon's latitude from the Sun was 56' 22'', and at the end, it was 46' 3''. The difference is 10' 19'', which is added to the difference of the visible latitudes. Therefore, I add it to 6' 57'', which produces 17' 16'' as the excess of the visible latitude at the end over the initial latitude. In the same way, since both parallaxes of longitude delay the Moon, I subtract the smaller (0' 48'') from the larger (24' 26''), leaving a delay of 23' 38''. This, in turn, is subtracted from the true motion of the Moon, which was 1° 21' 32'', leaving 57' 54'' as the visible motion of the Moon from the Sun during the given duration. On the line AC, let an isosceles triangle AFC be constructed, so that each leg has a length of 31' 40'' <note>31 minutes and 40 seconds of arc</note>, which is the sum of the <term>semidiameters</term> <note>The radii of the Sun and Moon added together.</note>. From points A and C, let the circles of the Moon's diameter be drawn, and from F, the circle of the Sun's diameter, touching the diameters of the Moon. Through F, let the straight line DE be drawn parallel to BA, and let CB be extended to D, with AE made equal to it. Then DE will be the **visible ecliptic**, and AE and CD will be the **visible latitudes**, from which the true latitudes are afterwards easily obtained by means of <term>parallaxes</term> <note>The apparent shift in position of a celestial body when viewed from different locations on Earth.</note>.

It is necessary to apply to CB some line BD so proportioned that, when the squares of CD and BD (or AE) are subtracted from the squares of FC or FA, two squares remain whose roots, when joined, equal ED. If anyone wishes to derive the answer through **Algebra**, they will arrive at an equation where the cube and a constant are equal to the squares and the linear terms <note>original: "vbi cubus & numerus æquatur quadratis & poſitionibus." Kepler is describing the structure of a cubic equation.</note>. For us, the **Geometric** path lies open. For as AB is to BC, so is the <term>total sine</term> <note>In historical trigonometry, the "total sine" refers to the radius of the circle used for calculation, equivalent to the modern sin(90°).</note> to the tangent of angle BAC, which becomes 16° 36' 1/2. Conversely, as the total sine is to AB, so the secant of angle BAC is to AC, which becomes 1° 0' 25'', half of which (AG) is 30' 12'' 1/2. Therefore, as AF is to AG, so the total sine is to the sine of angle AFG, 72° 33', whose complement, angle FAG, is 17° 27'. From this, subtracting angle BAG (16° 36' 1/2) leaves angle FAB (or AFE) as 0° 50' 1/2. Finally, as the total sine is to the sine of angle AFE, so is AF to AE (or the sought-after BD), which is 0' 28''.

Therefore, the **visible latitude** at the beginning of the eclipse is 0' 28'' North. At the end, once the parallaxes of the latitudes are added, the **true Northern latitude** there comes out to 56' 50'', and here at the end, 1° 3' 47'' North. See how much greater this result is than the one observed by **Gratius** <note>A contemporary observer whose data Kepler is scrutinizing.</note>, who recorded 51' 20'' at the beginning and 56' 30'' at the end (or at most 58' 20''). And since our calculation agrees more correctly with the calculation of **Tycho** <note>Tycho Brahe, the famous Danish astronomer whose precise data Kepler inherited.</note>, who shows a true latitude of 54' 11'' at the middle of the eclipse, we plainly conclude that a common error crept in for the observer: he did not mark the actual beginning and end, but rather the moments closest to them when his vision failed in the bright light of the Sun.

Nor should it disturb you that I attribute an error of 5 1/2 minutes to him in the true latitude. It is as if the two "little moons" <note>original: "lunula," referring to the lunar crescents or positions in his geometric diagram.</note> of our diagram, as if their bonds were loosened, were sinking deeper into the body of the Sun.

And this was what needed to be investigated at this time.

Therefore, if a solar eclipse has been properly observed with all its circumstances in at least one single location, and only the specific moments of the beginning and end were recorded in other places, the difference of meridians can be determined most reliably by this method.

<meta>This page continues the mathematical analysis of a solar eclipse observation, specifically focusing on correcting the tilt or inclination of the observing instrument to determine the Moon's exact position relative to the Ecliptic.</meta>

### THE OPTICAL PART OF ASTRONOMY. 401

...we said that the plane of the instrument was parallel: thirdly, imagine that it is touched at the center of the Sun by a third plane. Therefore, the intersection of this and the plane of the horizon falls outside the sphere. However, the intersection of the plane of the instrument with the plane of the horizon falls within the sphere.

[A geometric diagram showing a triangle and several intersecting lines labeled with letters S, T, V, A, X, Y.]

Let **AXY** be the plane of the horizon, **STV** the plane of the instrument, **SXY** the third plane, **A** the center of the sphere, **S** the Sun, and **TV** and **XY** the intersections. In the plane **TSV**, let another line **SV** be compared to **TS**, making an angle **TSV** of 19°, and let **AV** be continued into **XY** and **SY** be connected. And because **ATV**, **ATS**, and **AXY** are right angles: **TS** will be the sine of the altitude of the Sun, 60,529. <note>Kepler is using a standard trigonometric scale where the radius is 100,000. 60,529 corresponds to the sine of roughly 37° 15'.</note> But **TSV** was found to be 19°. Therefore, **TV** is 20,842. Moreover, **AT** is the sine of the complement of the altitude <note>This is what we now call the cosine.</note>, 79,600. Indeed, the angle **TSX** is equal to the altitude of the Sun, 37° 15'. Therefore, **TX** is 46,027. Thus, the whole **AX** is 125,627. Now, as **AT** is to **TV**, so **AX** is to **XY**, which therefore becomes 32,893. And because **STX** is a right angle, and **TSX** is 37° 15', therefore as the whole <note>The "whole" refers to the radius or total sine.</note> is to **ST**, so the secant of **TSX** is to **SX**, which becomes 76,051. Therefore, because **SXY** is a right angle (for **SX** is in the vertical plane, and **XY** in the horizontal plane), as **SX** is to **XY**, so the whole is to the tangent of the sought angle **XSY**, which becomes 23° 23', the larger value.

Thus, at the end of the eclipse, when the altitude of the Sun was 41° 15' and the inclination on the instrument was 30°, the angle **XSY** on the circumference of the sphere itself is found by a similar process to be 37° 31'. And in this way, both of these inclinations have been corrected.

Since, therefore, in the third moment, the upper angle to the right between the Ecliptic <term>Ecliptic: the apparent path of the Sun across the sky</term> and the vertical is 32° 35', as was proved above from the time, and the lower angle to the left is equal to it; and the angle of the vertical and the circle through the centers <note>The line connecting the centers of the Sun and Moon.</note> is likewise 23° 23' lower and to the left. Therefore, when this is subtracted from that, there remains 9° 12' between the circle through the centers and the Ecliptic. The Moon is in the South. <note>original: "Luna in Austro"</note>

In the fourth moment, the former angle above was 34° 15'; the latter of the same conditions was 37° 31' and larger. Therefore, when that is subtracted from this, there remains 3° 15' between the Ecliptic and the line through the centers. The Moon is now northern. <note>original: "boreali"</note>

Furthermore, in Problem 14, I warned that this method is slippery, 
<margin>Eee</margin> 
due to the wavering... <note>The text cuts off mid-word "titubationem," likely referring to the instability of the measuring instrument or the difficulty of the calculation.</note>

->402 **JOHANNES KEPLER**<-

due to the unsteadiness of the hands. <note>original: "titubationem manuum"; Kepler refers to the manual errors inherent in holding or adjusting observational instruments.</note> How much this was possible on this occasion will not remain hidden in the result.

Now, having found these angles, we will establish the visible <term>longitude</term><note>The angular distance of a celestial body along the ecliptic.</note> and <term>latitude</term><note>The angular distance of a celestial body north or south of the ecliptic.</note> for all four moments. For in the small triangles **L S E** from problem 24, the bases **LS** and the angles are given: therefore the sides **LE** of latitude and **SE** of longitude are also given. However, the bases in the first and second moments are equal, because on both sides the <term>semidiameter</term><note>Half the diameter, or the radius, of the celestial body's disk as seen from Earth.</note> appeared to be missing. The distance, or **LS**, was therefore found above to be 14 minutes and 55 seconds. In the third moment, because a fourth part of the <term>enlarged radius</term><note>original: "radii ampliati"; Kepler is accounting for the optical effect where the image in a pinhole camera appears slightly larger than the actual light source.</note> seemed to be missing, this should therefore be subtracted from the sum of the semidiameters. For instance, since the semidiameter of the Sun is 24 and the Moon 23, the sum is 47. A fourth of the Sun's diameter is 12; the remainder is therefore 35 in the enlarged radius. Yet the centers remain in their place according to problem 12. And by however much the Solar semidiameter is increased, the Lunar one is decreased by the same amount: thus the sum of the semidiameters remains the same, as also in problem 28. Therefore, the ratio of the sum to the distance of the centers is the same. But because the sum of the semidiameters is truly 30 minutes and 27 seconds, then as 47 is to 35, so is the sum to the distance of the centers, which is 22 minutes and 40 seconds. At the end, however, the distance of the centers equals the sum of the semidiameters, 30 minutes and 27 seconds. I treat this refined detail only for the sake of the example. For as far as the matter itself is concerned, I remember that the <term>apertures</term><note>original: "foramina"; the holes in the pinhole camera used for the observation.</note> were changed during the observation: therefore a slightly different quantity might have existed in the later ones, and everything might not correspond exactly <note>original: "ad amussim"; literally "by the mason's rule."</note> to this calculation. But I proceed with the example.

Having now recognized the bases as differing very little from straight lines, we will multiply them by the sines of the angles, and having rejected the last five digits, the latitudes will be produced, along with the visible longitudes of the Moon from the Sun using the sines of the complements.

| | First Moment | Second Moment | Third Moment | Fourth Moment |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| | **before the Sun** | **after the Sun** | | |
| **Longitude** | 7' 10'' | 12' 21'' | 22' 23'' | 30' 24'' |
| **Latitude** | 13' 3'' | 8' 22'' | 3' 37'' South | 1' 44'' North |

The same result will be produced if you follow the shortcut added to problem 24.

Thus far we have conducted the example through problem 24. Now, so that we may also fully satisfy problem 25, let us also treat the <term>parallaxes</term><note>The apparent shift in the position of a celestial object when viewed from different locations on Earth.</note>.

And because Tycho Brahe <note>Tycho Brahe (1546–1601) was a Danish nobleman and astronomer whose precise planetary observations provided the data for Kepler’s laws.</note> assigns the Moon a distance of 56 1/2 earth-radii at its average distance, therefore, by an eccentricity <note>In astronomy, eccentricity describes how much an orbit deviates from a perfect circle.</note> of 4336 (which I judge to be more probable), the Moon will be at a distance of 58 2/3 from the earth during the anomaly of this eclipse. Therefore, the horizontal parallax <note>Parallax is the apparent shift in position of an object when viewed from two different locations; horizontal parallax is used here to calculate the Moon's distance.</note> is 58' 54'', while that of the Sun is 2' 58''. 43' 15'' | 41' 31'' | 37' 45'' | 37' 7''.

50' 25'' | 29' 10'' | 15' 22'' | 4' 43''. 
It followed, therefore, that the true conjunction <note>Conjunction occurs when two celestial bodies have the same longitude; in a solar eclipse, this is the moment the Moon is directly between the Earth and Sun.</note> occurred after the end of the eclipse. There is little reason to doubt this true longitude, but no small reason to doubt the latitude. For within an hour and a half, the true latitude can scarcely vary by 4 minutes; here, there are nearly 13. Even if we use the final inclinations in the corrected versions of 19° and 30°, there would still be 9 minutes in the variation of latitude. Therefore, I attribute this to a trembling of the hands and an unreliable <note>original: "lubrico," meaning slippery or uncertain</note> method of observing. Tycho’s calculation for the meridian <margin>The difference between the meridians of Tübingen and Uraniborg.</margin> of Hven <note>Hven was the island where Tycho Brahe's observatory, Uraniborg, was located.</note> places the moment of true conjunction at 9:02 AM. Therefore, the difference between the meridians would be 1 degree—quite small. Let us therefore consult the Uraniborg observation, so that we may also have something more certain regarding the Moon's latitude. At 6:53 AM the deficit was already recognized; at 9:00 AM the Sun shone in its entirety. The observers judged that the eclipse began at 6:50 AM and ended at 8:58 AM, so that the duration was 2 hours and 8 minutes. Illustrations were also added, the first of which represents the Moon slightly higher than the Sun. But at 7:05 AM...

404

**The Discovery of the Philippines**

In the year 1521, the navigator **Ferdinand Magellan** <note>original: Fernando de Magallanes</note>, while seeking a westward route to the Spice Islands <note>the Moluccas</note> for the Spanish Crown under Emperor Charles V, reached the archipelago. On March 16, the expedition sighted the island of Samar and anchored at the island of Homonhon. Magellan named the region the **Archipelago of Saint Lazarus** <note>original: Archipiélago de San Lázaro</note> because they arrived on the feast day of that saint.

On the island of Limasawa, the first Mass was celebrated, marking the introduction of the Catholic faith to the region. The expedition then traveled to the island of Cebu, where Magellan formed an alliance with the local sovereign, **Rajah Humabon**. The Rajah and his people were baptized, and a wooden cross was erected to commemorate the event.

The peace was short-lived. A local chieftain named **Lapu-Lapu**, the leader of Mactan, refused to acknowledge Spanish sovereignty. In the ensuing conflict on April 27, 1521, Magellan was killed. Following this defeat, the remaining crew members, eventually led by **Juan Sebastián Elcano**, continued to the Moluccas and then back to Spain, completing the first circumnavigation of the world.

The islands did not receive their current name until 1542, when the explorer **Ruy López de Villalobos** named them *Las Islas Filipinas* in honor of the Spanish Prince, later **King Philip II**.

that an inequality lies hidden in the motion of the Moon, unnoticed by previous authors, and that it reveals itself especially around the time of Eclipses, when the Moon crosses the Ecliptic <note>The Ecliptic is the apparent path of the Sun across the sky; when the Moon crosses this path, eclipses can occur.</note>.

   And so, I thought it worthwhile to warn others—should any happen to navigate this sea—to beware of this reef.

   Such a person will therefore note, first, that Ptolemy, in the final chapters of Book 6 <note>Referring to Ptolemy's *Almagest*, the foundational Greek astronomical text.</note>, openly testifies that he would not pursue the highest precision in this business; for which reason he also judged that these inclinations toward the regions of the winds <note>original: "ventorum plagis"; a reference to the cardinal directions or quarters of the sky.</note> need not be recorded with extreme exactness. But that table of latitude is constructed from a constant angle of 5 degrees. Therefore, it would be necessary for the parallax of latitude to vary not at all from the beginning to the end, if the visible latitudes could truly be extracted by Reinhold's method. But Ptolemy himself affirms, and the tables testify, that the parallaxes of latitude change significantly at every moment. Therefore, it is not plainly a "visible" latitude, but a "quasi-visible" one, which is extracted through Rule 64. For a parallax of latitude is indeed applied; but it is not the proper one, but one transferred from the middle of the eclipse to the boundaries of the disappearance. Nor is the diagram of the Eclipse constructed truly according to Rule 65 of the <term>Prutenic Tables</term> <note>A set of astronomical tables published by Erasmus Reinhold in 1551, based on Copernicus's theories.</note>, but only nearly true. For the most part, the visible path of the Moon is twice, thrice, or four times more oblique to the Ecliptic, which is why the maximum obscuration also differs more from the point of visible conjunction in longitude, and the times of entry and exit vary.

Bernhard Walther <note>Bernhard Walther (1430–1504) was a German humanist and astronomer who continued the work of Regiomontanus</note> therefore reports that on January 12, 1482, in the morning, two and a half hours before sunrise, he saw the Moon—then nearly half-full—moving toward Saturn, which it later covered as it moved toward the meridian. The description is as follows: *When the Moon was in its last quarter <note>original: "vltima quadratura"; the phase where the Moon is half-illuminated before becoming a New Moon</note>, or thereabouts, it was indeed dark on its western side. Later, clouds intervened, so that I could [not] see the beginning. However, I judged for certain that the Moon's southern horn <note>original: "cornu auſtrali"; the pointed tip of the lunar crescent</note> was about to capture Saturn. But when I saw Saturn again, it was at a distance of about two digits <term>digit: an astronomical unit representing one-twelfth of the diameter of a celestial body's disk</term> from the northern horn: and then it began to reappear; they had already passed the midheaven <note>the point where a celestial body crosses the observer's meridian</note>. At that time, which I judged to be the middle of this eclipse, I measured the altitude of the Moon as it was almost on the meridian line, and found it to be 32 degrees.*

What I stated above—namely, that the Moon would first capture Saturn with its southern horn—**DOES NOT SEEM POSSIBLE, CONSIDERING THE PATH OF THE MOON.** But this indeed appeared clearly: that Saturn was about two digits from the Moon’s northern horn. The author is distinguished and the observation diligent, and we bring this case forward primarily so that we may apply no less diligence in weighing the evidence.

Let E be the darkened part toward the western parts of the Ecliptic <note>the Sun's apparent path across the sky</note> (or the great circle through the Sun and Moon), and D be the eastern parts toward the Sun. And the arcs of those circles near this quadrant position will be nearly parallel; it cuts AL and the line AC at right angles. Therefore AC is in a certain way parallel to both the Ecliptic and the circle through the lights. Here, therefore, even though the Moon is not carried with such a rapid motion in latitude as it is at the nodes <note>The nodes are the two points where the Moon's orbit crosses the path of the Ecliptic.</note>; yet because it is simultaneously moving toward the descending node, and at the same time Sagittarius, Capricorn, and Aquarius <note>Original symbols: ♐, ♑, ♒</note> are rising—signs through which the angle between the Ecliptic and the horizon decreases, and in turn the parallax <note>Parallax is the displacement or difference in the apparent position of an object viewed along two different lines of sight.</note> of latitude increases—hence, by both true motion and the illusion of sight, it is carried toward the South. This is why such a thing happened even to Walther, an experienced astronomer, which seemed not only wonderful to him but even led him to doubt the reliability of his own eyes.

**THE OPTICAL PART OF ASTRONOMY. 411**

**Problem XXXI.**

*Whether it is possible for the beginning of a certain solar eclipse to incline toward the east, and the end of another toward the west: while for a moon in eclipse, the beginning [is] in the west, and at another time the end [is] in the east.*

This is among the paradoxes proposed by Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman naturalist whose works often listed astronomical marvels</note>. For it is agreed that in the ordinary way, the Sun begins to fail from the west and is filled again from the east; the Moon, conversely, begins from the east and finishes in the west. Let us begin with the Moon. Around center A, let the circle of the Earth’s shadow BCDE be drawn. Through A, let the straight line FG be drawn, representing the vertical line: through

[A geometric diagram showing a large central circle representing the Earth's shadow. A vertical line FG and an oblique line HI (the Ecliptic) intersect at the center 'a'. Two paths, KM and LN, show the Moon passing near the shadow at different angles.]

the same point, let the arc of the <term>Ecliptic</term> <note>The apparent path of the Sun across the sky; eclipses only occur when the Moon is on or very near this line</note> HI be drawn very close to the west, so that FAH is the angle between the Ecliptic and the vertical. And let KL be drawn at right angles to HI. Now, if the center of the Moon is at K or L, that will be the moment of true <term>conjunction</term> <note>The instant when the Moon and the Sun (or the Earth's shadow) reach the same celestial longitude</note>. Then, let the sum of the radii of the Moon and the shadow equal the true latitude of the Moon—decreasing toward the south at K, so that the Moon's path is KM toward the Ecliptic; and increasing toward the north at L, so that the Moon's path is LN away from the Ecliptic. On both sides, therefore, some small part of the Moon will be eclipsed (for authors require this little correction in this matter as well), for the Moon a little after K and a little before N is closer to center A because of the slant of the Moon’s path relative to the Ecliptic: and at that point of its path where the perpendicular from A falls, the eclipse is greatest.

And for the sake of measurement: Just as the <term>secant</term> <note>A trigonometric function representing the ratio of the hypotenuse to the adjacent side of a right triangle</note> of 5 degrees (the maximum latitude) is 100,382 to the radius, so the sum of the radii—which we shall assume to be 60 <term>minutes</term> <note>Kepler uses the term "scrupula," a traditional unit for minutes of a degree</note>—is to the distance of the centers at the maximum eclipse, 59' 46''. Thus, 14'' <note>seconds of arc</note> fall into the eclipse: a very small part indeed, not even a hundredth. However, we are here following the extreme tips. Nothing prevents the same thing that we are demonstrating here from happening even when the Moon at K has grazed the shadow somewhat. The mark of the eclipse <note>original: "nota defectus"</note> will incline toward the west <note>the setting point</note> to the right, as will the entire duration; but the end will incline toward the east <note>the rising point</note>. Both can also occur in the eastern arc. Then in that case, the eclipse at the beginning will incline toward the west to the right; but at D, the final eclipse will incline toward the east.

      Such an eclipse of the Moon was seen most recently on November 18, 1603. Since it had begun at approximately 65° from the zenith <note>the point directly overhead</note>, counting to the left, it ended without the shadow quite reaching the zenith, but still inclining to the left, toward the east. For in the eastern quadrant there was a southern obscuration, with the Moon descending toward the south.

      It began ten minutes after the **right shoulder of Aquarius** <note>the star Sadalmelik</note> had culminated <note>reached its highest point in the sky</note>, although a pale light had already been noted in that very part half an hour before, or a little lower toward the left.       It ended three minutes after the **head of Andromeda** <note>the star Alpheratz</note> had culminated. Therefore, at 8:17. The duration was 1 hour and 56 minutes. Tycho’s <note>Tycho Brahe, Kepler's predecessor</note> calculation predicts 2:10. To me, certainly, near the middle, it was thought that less than a fourth part was missing; but others contended that more than a fourth part was hidden. Regarding the circumference, it was judged that less than 1/3 but more than 1/4 was gone. However, these points agree: that the eclipse was smaller and the duration shorter than in the calculation, and that the shadow did not reach the zenith. The middle was at 7:19; this is the very minute that Tycho's calculation shows for the Hven meridian <note>the location of Tycho's observatory, Uraniborg</note> for the true conjunction in longitude, which differs somewhat from the middle of the eclipse.

      The darkened circumference was visible; even when the very bright Pleiades, a few degrees away, were scarcely seen: so clearly was the Moon illuminated even in the shadow; refer this to the previous discussion <note>Kepler often discussed how sunlight refracted by the Earth's atmosphere illuminates the Moon during total eclipses, giving it a reddish hue</note>.

If the sum of the semidiameters, 60' 16" (for Tycho makes the semidiameter of the shadow 44' 6", concerning which see in its proper place), is multiplied by the sine of this angle, it shows the latitude at this moment to be 53' 40".

the axis of latitude decreases the most, and the Moon—no matter which sign it is in above the horizon—is visibly carried toward the North, more than its true motion toward the South, and much more so if it is also ascending by its true motion. Therefore, when the Sun is near its setting during a small southern eclipse, it is possible for what was proposed to happen: that the Sun begins to be eclipsed from the east <note>Kepler is explaining a paradox where the Moon's parallax makes it appear to move "backward" relative to the Sun's disk.</note>. Conversely, a small northern eclipse occurring toward the east could be "filled in" from the west.

On the other hand, when Capricorn is rising from Libra toward Aries, the angle of the horizon is diminished, the parallax increases, and the Moon is carried toward the South by its visible motion. Therefore, northern eclipses occurring in the eastern quadrant will begin to fail from the east; southern eclipses in the eastern quadrant will end from the west. However, this cause is so evident that it remains valid almost at midday, with the help of other factors. For at midday, the Moon is quickly driven backward by a **visual illusion** <note>original: viſus phantaſiam; Kepler refers to the effect of parallax, which creates a perceived shift in position based on the observer's location on Earth</note>. Thus, it seems to ascend almost entirely toward the North, at least in the appropriate signs.

In the year 1599, on July 12 or 22, in the morning at the very rising of the Sun, a small defect <note>An eclipse or "bite" taken out of the Sun's disk.</note> was seen in Prague by Tycho <note>Tycho Brahe, the famous Danish astronomer whose data Kepler inherited.</note> at almost the very top of the solar body.

Therefore, although the Moon had descended toward the **descending node** <note>The point where the Moon's orbit crosses the ecliptic moving from North to South.</note> by its true motion, it was instead carried very far to the North by the visual illusion of parallax, the minutes of latitude being affected because Leo was rising. Therefore, the smallest inclination of the end of the eclipse looked toward the east. In southern climates, therefore, where the eclipse was smaller, it must be that the defect stood from the west from beginning to end. In the year 1593, on May 20, at Zerbst <note>original: Serueſtæ</note>, the Sun was observed to be eclipsed by two **digits** <note>A "digit" is an astronomical measurement representing one-twelfth of the diameter of the Sun or Moon.</note> from below; at the beginning, the defect turned slightly to the left, and at the end, more so. It began, therefore, from the east, with the Moon striving toward the North by its motion in latitude. At Hven <note>original: Huennæ; Tycho Brahe’s observatory on the island of Hven.</note>, nothing was seen to be eclipsed, as the calculation showed the time to be 2:40.

### The First Example

In the year 1600, on June 30th (or July 10th by the new calendar), in Graz, Styria, I was outdoors under the open sky with a wooden instrument—the description of which appears clearly in Problem 1—with a screen set up around it. Since the instrument had not yet been graduated into its smaller divisions, I carved 15 marks into it with a small knife and marked them in order with their own numbers. Whatever was seen on the tablet at each individual mark, I recorded separately on paper. 

However, I will present the series of observations to you quite honestly, transcribed directly from my record sheet. For I loathe unskillful and unreliable "additions and subtractions" <note>original Greek: τὰς προσθαφαιρέσεις ἀτέχνους (tas prosthaphaireseis atechnous); Kepler is referring to the practice of "fudging" or adjusting raw data to fit theoretical models</note>, and I only wish such things did not haunt the primary observations of Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer whose data Kepler often scrutinized for accuracy</note>. I, for my part, write these things as if I were convinced...

It is clear, therefore, that regarding the movement of the crossbar—since the hinge of the small post was sticking somewhat firmly—the instrument followed after being pulled back by force as the stays gave way, and this occurred after the fifth moment. Yet the error in time was very slight. In contrast, during the final moments, the beam from which I had suspended the screen <note>Kepler likely used a "camera obscura" setup where the sun's image was projected onto a screen or paper to observe the eclipse safely.</note> slightly hindered the moving rod, preventing it from keeping up with the Sun's descent through its elevation. 

If at the end you calculate the time from the altitude, and again from the azimuth <term>azimuth: the horizontal angle or direction of a celestial object, measured clockwise from the north or south</term>, you will find a difference of 4 minutes. For the altitude gives the hour as 2:59:36, while the azimuth gives the hour as 2:55:23. And since it is certain that both are slightly in error—the azimuth and the altitude—the midpoint of 2:57 ½, taken as the true value, will not deviate by even a single minute from the truth itself. In other matters, I stand by the altitudes, with the azimuths providing supporting evidence from a distance. 

I record these things so diligently both because the foundations of lunar demonstrations can be placed upon this eclipse as if upon a cornerstone, and because I had some dispute with Tycho Brahe (of blessed memory) <note>original: "p. m.", an abbreviation for *piae memoriae*, a traditional way to honor a deceased colleague</note> regarding the time of the start; he, seizing upon a trivial occasion, called the reliability of all the timings into doubt. But I do not doubt that if he had lived long enough for me to show him this agreement, he would have yielded his position.

The times, therefore, are as follows, together with the necessary data from the primary motion <term>primary motion: the apparent daily rotation of the heavens around the Earth</term>, according to the problems discussed above. The Sun's declination <term>declination: the angular distance of a celestial body north or south of the celestial equator</term> is 22° 17'. And due to parallax, 16'. The altitude of the pole <note>This refers to the latitude of the observation site.</note> is 47° 2'.

Therefore, the mid-point estimated from the beginning and end by me at Graz was 1:47:30 PM. The duration was 2 hours and 20 minutes. Tycho’s observers at Benátky Castle <note>Benátky nad Jizerou, Tycho Brahe's observatory in Bohemia</note>, which is 5 German miles <note>approximately 37 kilometers or 23 miles</note> north-east from Prague: the mid-point was 1:46:30 PM. The duration was 2 hours and 1 minute. The digits <note term="digits">A "digit" is an ancient measurement for eclipses, representing one-twelfth of the diameter of the celestial body</note> themselves were judged to be about 5; whereas to me, they appeared as 6 1/2 on the radius <note>referring to the scale of his projection device</note>, which after clarification <note>mathematical refinement of the optical data</note> were 7 1/2.

Yet Tycho Brahe ought not to have feared that his observations would be overturned by mine, nor should he have argued against mine based on his own, or thought it absurd that the beginning was seen by me (who am further east) at 12:37:30, and by him (who is further west) at 12:46:00. For I was also 3 degrees further south, and I saw the Sun covered by almost as many minutes <note>arc-minutes</note> more; therefore, for me the beginning was earlier and the end later. Furthermore, the darkness under the "stage" <note>Kepler likely refers to the interior of his camera obscura or darkened viewing tent</note> assisted me in discerning the beginning and the end: the optical principles explained above deceived their own eyesight somewhat, both in duration and in the magnitude of the eclipse. Nor were they able to use a compass <note>dividers for measuring the projected image</note> as I did, relying instead on fallacious estimation alone.

->428 OF JOHANNES KEPLER<-

Others also noted this at Wittenberg, which is 2 degrees further north. This is certainly due to the diversity of viewpoints <note>original: "diuersitate visuum," referring to parallax, where an object appears in a different position when viewed from different locations</note>.

Concerning the estimation of the Moon’s diameter through this eclipse, see Problem 12 above.

Now, as you see, both from this table and from the digits <term>digits|a traditional unit for measuring eclipses, representing one-twelfth of the diameter of the celestial body</term>, the maximum obscuration was between 2:00 and 2:03:30. It was closer to the latter; therefore, around 2:03 was the visible conjunction according to longitude, occurring half an hour closer to the end of the eclipse than the beginning. For the increments of the longitudinal parallaxes <term>parallax|the apparent displacement of a celestial object when viewed from different points on Earth</term> decrease after midday.

And because the Sun is in 18° of Cancer, its semidiameter will be 15' 1". The Moon's simple anomaly <term>anomaly|the angular distance of a planet or the Moon from its furthest point from Earth (apogee)</term> in Leo at 14° 30', with an eccentricity of 4336, shows a semidiameter of 16' 10", whereas at its apogee <term>apogee|the point in an orbit where the Moon is furthest from the Earth</term> it is 15' 15". Therefore, the sum of the semidiameters is 31' 11". This is the distance between the centers of the Sun and Moon at the beginning and end of the eclipse.

To ensure this same distance is determined for the other moments as well, note what has been repeated more than once in these problems from Chapter 2: that the missing digits in the enlarged radius measure the true approach of the centers. Indeed, the missing digits in the radius are twelfth parts of that enlarged radius. And the enlarged radius of the Sun, as indicated above in Problem 2, was 105 1/2, or more accurately 106. Therefore, in the second moment and the remaining ones where digits are noted, these small parts are provided. When subtracted from the 53 parts of the semiradio <note>the half-radius</note>, together with the 8 1/4 semidiameter of the window <note>Kepler refers here to the aperture of the camera obscura used to project the eclipse image</note>, there remain the parts extending to the center of the Sun. How many minutes these are worth can be found from the "enucleated" <note>refined or extracted</note> radius, which is 89 1/2. For if 89 1/2 units are equal to 30' 1", how many minutes will the remainder to the center produce? Whatever result is produced here, when added to the Moon’s semidiameter, constitutes the true distance between the centers. 

But if the sum of the parts gathered from the semidiameter of the small window and the digits exceeds the parts of the semidiameter of the radius, the excess—converted into minutes of a degree—must be subtracted from the Moon’s semidiameter so that the true distance of the centers is again obtained.

With these things thus established, and by applying the angle which we found last, the visible longitude and latitude are established for all moments that I use in this table.

You see at the beginning how beneficial it is to have several moments recorded, besides just the start and the end. For if the second moment (and the rest following from it) had not immediately supported the first by their agreement, I would have been left in doubt by about 5 minutes regarding the initial <term>latitude</term> <note>The angular distance of a celestial body north or south of the ecliptic.</note>—an error I fell into due to a careless calculation of the <term>inclination</term> <note>The angle between the orbital plane and the ecliptic.</note>, having skipped over ten degrees.

You also see, secondly, how easily an error is exposed in the eleventh moment. For in the observation notes, it is stated that the <term>deficiency</term> <note>the amount of the sun or moon obscured during the eclipse</note> was less than 5 <term>digits</term> <note>a standard unit of eclipse measurement equal to 1/12th of the diameter</note>. Here, therefore, if we had assumed exactly 5 digits, the visible latitude would have appeared to move backward and decrease. Therefore, it is well that more is required from this latitude according to the scale of the observation.

Hhh 3 <note>printer's signature mark</note> Thirdly

430 JOHANNES KEPLER

**Thirdly**, it is clearly evident that the maximum obscuration occurred at moments 7 and 8, when the Moon was not yet visibly conjoined with the Sun in terms of longitude. The <term>digits</term><note>A "digit" is a historical unit for measuring eclipses, representing 1/12th of the diameter of the celestial body.</note> measured $6\frac{1}{3}$ in the radius and $7\frac{1}{10}$ in the sky after calculation.

**Fourthly**, the visible angle of latitude is significant, as is clear from the certain first and thirteenth moments. Indeed, the difference in latitudes is $12' 6''$, while the Moon visibly covers $47' 38''$ of longitude. Therefore, the angle of visible latitude is $14^\circ 16'$. For the <term>parallax</term><note>The apparent displacement of an object when viewed from different points; in astronomy, this helps determine distance and relative position.</note> of latitude was increasing, while at the same time the Moon was descending toward the South in its true motion. The reason this angle was not greater is due to the altitude of the <term>sign</term><note>The zodiac sign/constellation the Sun was occupying.</note>, in which the parallaxes are small and the increments themselves are modest.

**Fifthly**, the visible path of the Moon was curved, which is evident from the 1st, 8th, and 13th moments. For if the 1st and 8th are compared, the Moon, through $28' 16''$ of visible longitude, was visibly carried upward by $7' 49''$. Therefore, the angle of latitude was $15^\circ 27'$, which is greater than before from the 1st and 13th moments.

To what end this eclipse may be useful to us in proving the motions of the Moon—the cause for which we have put so much effort into analyzing it—will follow in the second part, where the parallaxes of this eclipse are also recorded.

->*Another example.*<-

In the year 1601, on the 14th and 24th of December<note>Kepler provides both the Julian (14th) and Gregorian (24th) dates, as Europe was divided on calendar usage at this time.</note>, at Prague in Bohemia, we observed a northern afternoon eclipse of the Sun in the following manner:

I had brought my tablets from Styria<note>Kepler lived and taught in Graz, Styria (Austria) before moving to Prague to work with Tycho Brahe.</note> with me, along with a foot-measure, with which I compared the length of its ruler to the Styrian standard. The room was exceptionally dark. The ruler with the tablet rested on a transverse support and was raised into a vertical plane, as described in Problem 15; since the thickness of the wall would not support the whole instrument, I first described the apparatus. Indeed, the window had to be changed near the end, as the Sun was striking the southern wall too obliquely.

The times were recorded not from the altitude of the Sun, but more conveniently by means of a **Tychonic clock**<note>A high-precision clock designed by Tycho Brahe, featuring indices for minutes and seconds.</note> with an indicator for minutes and seconds. We had tested this clock the previous night to see if it was of the correct speed by observing the transits of the fixed stars; and on the preceding noon, with the indicator fixed at the 12 o'clock point, we held its motion back until the center of the Sun reached the meridian according to Tycho's quadrants. Furthermore, using a small brass quadrant of one and a half feet, we noted the <term>Azimuths</term><note>The horizontal angle of a celestial object measured from the North or South point of the horizon.</note> of the Sun at the beginning, by a rougher estimate.

Regarding propositions 24 and 25 on page 23. That light is not colored in reflection is established by a easy experiment, if you expose to the Sun several dishes in a row containing liquids of various colors (yet equally pure); positioned so that the reflection is directed into a shaded place and onto a white surface. By these experiments it becomes evident that colors are not on the surface, but in the depth: hence they shine out, and therefore they reside within transparent matter to a certain extent. Colors require a body <note>original: *corpus*; Kepler argues that color is a physical property of matter, not just an optical illusion</note> entirely, no less than light does below in Chapter 6. However, the fact that reflecting bodies nonetheless mix their own shared light (scattered spherically) with the reflected light is clear in weaker radiations or illuminations: for instance, certain metallic mirrors represent the face as reddish, because they illuminate and tint the <term>retiform</term> <note>original: *retiformem*, referring to the *tunica retiformis* or the retina of the eye, which Kepler was the first to correctly identify as the light-sensitive screen of the eye</note> with a simple ray of their own color. This is not much weaker than the "double ray" of the face, or the reflection from the mirror. From this, according to proposition 28, a mixture is made from both, and a new color is formed in the eye.

Accordingly, in proposition 25, color on a surface is established no differently than density was above in proposition 13. This is the meaning: that hitherto indeed light, as if it were a certain surface, has been affected by the density of the surface alone, because the density of the body's volume had nothing in common with it. But now every color, throughout the entire depth of the body, is partly related to light, on account of "potential light," and partly contrary to it, on account of the intermingled darkness. Therefore, through the entire volume of a transparent thing, light is affected by color, not only in the passage through the surface when it is refracted.

To page 24. Proposition 31 with its corollary is properly referred to Chapter 5 and the explanation of the cause of color in the retiform coat <note>The retina</note>.

To page 32, line 34. I say a case is given never in actuality, but by fiction; namely, assuming that only the Sun shines. To page 37. The word "Ray" <note>original: *Radius*</note> is now henceforth almost always used for a portion or shape of light falling upon and shaped by a surface through some window or opening.

Regarding page 79, line 19; and regarding page 83, from line 23 to 27; and regarding Proposition 9, from page 116 to 120. There are two distinct states for every kind of vapor <note>In 17th-century science, "vapor" or "exhalation" referred to any substance rising from the Earth into the atmosphere, which was thought to influence weather and optical phenomena.</note>. The first occurs when it rises from the bowels of the earth, carried upward by a certain subterranean heat. In this state, it possesses a natural tendency to ascend, bubbling up from mountainous regions like a spring. From the peak of this "ebullition" <note>original: "ebullitionis"—the process of bubbling or boiling over</note>, it spreads out in a circle toward the lower slopes as soon as it encounters the cold of the mountains; in this way, it generally produces winds. In this particular state, the vapor is transparent, much like water. Because of this, the light of the stars appears enlarged and twinkles intensely. By this sign, it is known that winds—and in winter, a breaking of the frost <note>A "resolution of the cold" refers to a thaw or a warming trend.</note>—are imminent.

The second state is that of settled and chilled vapor, which hangs motionless in one place and is mixed with thicker smokes. Through this medium, the light of the stars appears dim and reddish—or as *Virgil* says, "rusty" <note>original: "ferruginea" from Virgil’s *Georgics*. This refers to a dark, murky, iron-red color often associated with the sun or moon seen through thick haze.</note>. This type of vapor is by no means transparent.

The former kind of vapor is rare and fleeting, while the latter is an everyday occurrence.

### 438 JOHANNES KEPLER

...magnitude, they are so much smaller and cease so much sooner, as was demonstrated above.

Hence, below on line 34, in Hesse <note>A region in Germany; Kepler is likely referring to observations made at the observatory of Wilhelm IV of Hesse-Kassel</note>, which is at a high elevation, the refractions are said to be smaller—specifically those occurring at higher altitudes—and those are the ones in which the stars can be observed. For they observed the horizontal refraction elsewhere to be immense, and they rarely captured stars exactly on the horizon with their instruments.

For these two things must be carefully distinguished: first, that in some region or time, refractions can be smaller due to the thinness of the air. In such cases, the reduction of refractions occurring at a certain altitude of the stars is indeed followed by a reduction in the "total refraction"—namely, that which occurs in a ray grazing the sphere of the air. Secondly, however, in that same region and time, the horizontal refraction can nonetheless appear larger. This is because, due to the high altitude of the region, the observer is closer to the outer surface of the air and experiences the ray grazing the sphere of the air at its most refracted point; this is a ray which would have passed far above his head if the observer had been situated in a lower place. For it is not the case in every location that the setting Sun experiences the maximum possible refraction, as I have carefully emphasized.

And it is self-evident that a part of a smaller quantity, if it is closer to the whole, can be larger than some part of a larger quantity that falls further short of its own total. Therefore, even if the total refraction of a grazing ray is sometimes smaller in one place than in another, the portion of it that the setting Sun has can still be larger than the portion measured in another place.

Regarding **page 191, Proposition 16, first corollary**. If you desire a demonstration of the corollary, examine the diagram for **Proposition 13**. Suppose the radiating point <note>The source of light</note> is in AD toward D, at an effectively infinite distance; it will therefore illuminate nearly an entire hemisphere MBG. The rays KB and LG will be nearly parallel, according to the postulate in the second chapter. Therefore, by Proposition 13 of this book, I is the intersection point closest to the globe that can exist.

But the other limit of the intersections, F, is also the closest of all. Transfer your thoughts to the upper part of the diagram and imagine the radiating point approaching from an infinite distance; its rays will always, without exception, meet with the axis until the point comes near F, according to **Proposition 13**. Now, from F, certain rays no longer meet. But when parallel lines are formed from secant <note>lines that cross or cut through</note> lines, the intersection point moves out toward infinity before it ends in parallels. Therefore, as the radiating point approaches the globe until it is near F, the final intersection point escapes to infinity. Previously, however, when the radiating point was infinitely distant, the final intersection above F was a little more than the radius of the globe away—no further. Therefore, since the causes increase continuously from the infinite distance of the radiator to the shortest distance, the effect—the proximity of the final intersection—must also increase continuously from the shortest distance to infinity, without being interrupted.
