<meta>This page continues the geometric analysis of light rays refracting through a glass sphere (representing the eye's lens). Kepler is concluding a proof from the previous page and moving into corollaries regarding the focal points (intersections) of these rays.</meta>

# THE OPTICAL PART OF ASTRONOMY. 443

...be broken. Thus, at the start, it will be the closest of all to the sphere, which was the point to be demonstrated. <note>original: "quod erat demonstrandum," the classic mathematical conclusion Q.E.D.</note>

The second corollary has already been partly explained regarding the final limit of the intersections. What remains can be seen most clearly in the diagram on page 192. For the closer $\alpha$ <note>a designated point in Kepler's geometric diagram</note> approaches, the further $\nu$ flees. And in the diagram on page 189, with the light source <term>radiante: the "radiant" or point from which light rays originate</term> placed at the limit at $F$, all the rays converge; as it moves below $F$, only the outer rays converge, which mark the nearest limit by their intersection behind the sphere. Finally, with the light source at $I$, even the furthest rays cease to intersect, and the point of intersection flees to infinity. But if the light source is at an infinite distance on the other side of the sphere, the nearest limit is right next to the sphere at $I$. Thus, once again, while the light source moves from the shortest distance to an infinite one, this nearer limit decreases from an infinite distance to the shortest distance.

It cannot happen that as causes continually increase, the effect sometimes increases and then decreases again. Therefore, it must be smallest at the beginning and largest at the end. Thus, when the light source is placed near $F$, the nearest limit is indeed at some point and distant from the sphere, yet it is even further—indeed infinitely distant—from the final limit, which is no longer a "limit" since it does not bound anything when the intersections run off into infinity. However, this corollary does not mean that when the light source is at $F$, the nearest limit is further away than when it is at $I$. For at $I$, both the nearest and furthest limits go off to infinity; whereas at $F$, while the furthest limit vanishes, the nearest still remains at a certain distance. Therefore, the corollary here compares point $F$ not with points $F$ and $I$, but with those points above it of the third kind.

The third corollary follows from what has been said and can be shown visually in the diagram on page 192. If $\delta \mu$ and $\epsilon \zeta$ are parallel, then $\lambda \alpha$ and $\lambda \nu$ will be equal, because the bases $\delta \epsilon$ and $\eta \zeta$ of the isosceles <term>isosceles: a triangle with two equal sides</term> triangles $\lambda \alpha \epsilon$ and $\eta \nu \zeta$ are equal, and the angles at $\alpha$ and $\nu$ are equal due to the same refractions <term>refraction: the bending of light as it passes from one medium (like air) into another (like glass or water)</term> at $\delta, \epsilon$ and $\eta, \zeta$. In that case, $\lambda \gamma$ will also be equal to $\lambda \theta$ (if $\lambda$ and $\theta$ are the nearest limits) and $\lambda \beta$ to $\lambda \mu$ (if $\beta$ and $\mu$ are the furthest), and finally $\gamma \beta$ and $\theta \mu$ will be equal.

...the intersections of non-parallels, and the intersections of parallels, which I designate according to Proposition 15, or the boundaries of both. Therefore, note this carefully: The boundaries of the intersections of parallel rays always maintain the same position relative to the sphere, whereas the boundaries of non-parallel rays wander back and forth even unto infinity.

Regarding page 192, line 20: understand the corollary immediately following.

Regarding Corollary 1, page 192: Whatever is perceived by the radiations from the <term>cap <note>original: "pileolus"; Kepler uses this term to describe the central, "polar" section of a sphere or lens resembling a small skullcap.</note></term> (which we introduced in the notes for Proposition 13) will appear upright; whatever is perceived through the <term>rim <note>original: "limbum"; the outer edge or periphery of the lens.</note></term> or <term>zone <note>original: "zonam"; the area between the center and the edge.</note></term> will appear inverted. Whatever is perceived through the circle that forms the boundary between the rim and the cap will appear circular (that is, a single point—for example, the black pupil of the eye—will be stretched out into a circular fringe).

Regarding Corollary 3: Geometrically, it is the same whether the eye radiates toward the object or the object radiates toward the eye; in both cases, an interposed sphere produces the same effect. However, when the eye is placed between β and γ, the radiations are divided into the polar or "cap" rays, the circle, and the zone. The radiations of the zone, such as α δ η ν and ε ζ, intersect each other between θ and μ. Therefore, an object placed here is presented to those rays, and it flows into the eye inverted if it is between ν and μ; yet at the same time, it appears upright because it also meets the polar radiations which do not intersect each other. Indeed, the whole object will be seen as upright because it is too small to meet the radiations of the circle. However, the images will differ in their perceived location. For the upright image, being large, will be thought of as distant behind the sphere, while the inverted image will appear to stick to the convex surface of the sphere itself.

Corollary 4 occurs when the visible object is so large that it also meets the radiations of the circle: this should be judged based on Corollaries 1 and 3.

Regarding page 196, line 20: Even without the obstruction of a perforated tablet, much light is accumulated near the K boundary of the final intersection, according to the preceding Proposition 15.

Regarding page 197, line 4: ...they are bounded by the obstruction of a piece of paper at the KN location where the rays converge.

Regarding page 198, line 2 and following: I use the words "converge" and "diverge" for the sake of brevity to describe straight lines which, if extended in either direction, would all meet at the same point.

Regarding page 214, line 10: Archimedes <note>Archimedes of Syracuse (c. 287–212 BCE), who attempted to measure the apparent diameter of the Sun in his work "The Sand Reckoner."</note> aimed only at this: to find an angle that was certainly smaller than the angle by which the Sun is seen.

->Regarding the direction of the eyes<- the Sun certainly illuminates the earth and the air more clearly from the middle of the sky and produces a greater brightness of day than when it rests upon the Horizon, which has been shown up to this point. *Thus, so far, we have dealt with the deceptions of sight; the matter has been conducted through methods and precautions for observing, and we have remained almost entirely within the limits of Books 4, 5, and 6 of Ptolemy’s **Great Work** <note>original: "Opere Magno," referring to the Almagest, the most influential astronomical text of antiquity</note>. It is time, therefore, to sound the retreat <note>a military metaphor meaning to finish the current task</note>, lest we try to do "everything in all things."*

*Furthermore, if GOD grants me life and strength, I shall reveal the use of these observations in another small book—which you may call either the second part of this Work or an Appendix. There, I will interpolate the three aforementioned books of Ptolemy with new, ingenious, and most delightful problems regarding the **secondary moving bodies** <term>secondary movables: a term for the planets and the Moon, which move independently of the fixed stars</term>; and I will teach how to investigate, more briefly and concisely, and with fewer and easily comparable observations, the same things that Ptolemy investigated. This seems all the more necessary because Tycho Brahe’s works on the Moon were published without the full apparatus of demonstrations, in the form of his book **Introductory Exercises** <note>original: "Progymnasmatum," referring to Tycho Brahe's "Astronomiae Instauratae Progymnasmata"</note>, as was warned in its appendix, since the entire matter was squeezed into only a few pages. And because the primary goal of that little book will be to investigate the sizes and distances of the three Bodies—the Sun, the Moon, and the Earth—Hipparchus himself pursued the same material (as is clear from Theon) in a specific book with this very title. Therefore, may it be happy and auspicious: let the title of the book be **HIPPARCHUS**. Farewell, reader, and follow my endeavors with your prayers, remembering that:*

...around this [the Earth, labeled $a$] let there be the air $\delta \epsilon$ <note>Kepler uses the Greek letters delta ($\delta$) and epsilon ($\epsilon$) to mark the boundaries of the atmosphere.</note>. And let $\delta \epsilon$ be the **circle of illumination of the air**: and let the rays $\xi \delta$ and $o \epsilon$ from the extremities of the Sun meet at $\tau$, defining the shadow of the air, which causes the **Eclipse of the Moon**. Indeed, the rays touching the sphere of the air at $\delta$ and $\epsilon$ are refracted <note>Refraction is the bending of light as it passes from the vacuum of space into the denser medium of the Earth's atmosphere.</note> at $\delta, \zeta, \eta$; and having exited there, they are refracted again into $\zeta \omega$ and $\eta \omega$. Therefore, $\alpha \omega$ will be the **nearest boundary of the shadow**. For as pertains to the parts of the Sun within the $\xi \delta$ and $o \epsilon$ rays, they do not reach as far as $\delta$ and $\epsilon$; however, those rays touching the sphere of the air higher up toward $\kappa$ and $\lambda$ make the same angles of refraction, and having entered at a higher place than $\delta$ and $\epsilon$, they also exit at a higher place than $\zeta$ and $\eta$. Thus, they become further out than $\zeta \omega$ and $\eta \omega$.

<margin>Complete the outermost refracted line to the left.</margin>

Again, let $\rho$ and $\sigma$ be locations on the opposite semicircles of the Earth's meridian, in which places—the center of the Sun being positioned on the line $\alpha \omega$—the whole Sun is **perceived through refraction**, with its lowest edge grazing the horizon: so that $\mu \kappa$ and $\nu \lambda$ are refracted into $\kappa \theta$ and $\lambda \iota$, and from there into $\theta \chi$ and $\iota \chi$, intersecting $\zeta \omega$ and $\eta \omega$ at $P$ and $Q$. It is necessary, by those things which were demonstrated in Chapter 5, Number 3, Proposition 9 <note>Kepler frequently cites his own earlier proofs regarding the physics of light and lenses.</note>, that even if $\xi \delta$ and $\mu \kappa$ had been perfectly parallel (and likewise $o \epsilon$ and $\nu \lambda$), nevertheless $\xi \delta \zeta \omega$ and $\epsilon \eta \omega$ would meet nearer at $\omega$ than $\mu \kappa \theta \chi$ and $\nu \lambda \iota \chi$ would meet at $\chi$. This is now much more the case when those lines are inclined, because $\xi \delta$ and $o \epsilon$ are assumed to come from the **upper margin of the Sun**, while $\mu \kappa$ and $\nu \lambda$ come from the **lower margin**. Thus $\chi$ <note>The point chi ($\chi$)</note> will be more remote than $\omega$, and $\theta \chi$ and $\iota \chi$ will be the boundaries of the other refracted radiations. ...will strike the Earth; since $\mu, \kappa, \nu, \lambda$ are the last rays not striking the Earth, but rather touching it at $\beta, \gamma$ after refraction has occurred. With these things so arranged, let $\zeta \omega, \eta \omega, \theta \chi, \iota \chi$ be extended until they intersect each other at $\phi, \psi$ and further until they intersect $\delta \pi$ at $Q, T$ and $\epsilon \pi$ at $\sigma, \upsilon$ when joined. There will therefore be in the middle of the shadow a double-vertex conical region $\phi \chi \psi$ in which the incoming refracted rays are collected in a circular fashion, at a height of about 43 semidiameters <note>A "semidiameter" refers to the radius of the Earth.</note> from the Earth. Again, in the shadow of the Earth there will be a certain slanted crown <note>original: *corolla*</note>, ending in a sharp edge, represented in two places by the spaces $\zeta \theta P, \eta \iota Q$. In this region, the refracted light of the Sun is scattered circularly, yet it is more concentrated in the circle $P, Q$ where a hollow conical region begins again, represented by $P \omega \phi, Q \omega \psi$. In this region, the refracted light of the Sun is scattered again, but more weakly, because the openings <note>Kepler uses "chasmata" to refer to gaps or atmospheric phenomena</note> spread through a wider region. Whether either of these serves to illuminate the "chasms" <note>This likely refers to auroras or "gaping" light phenomena in the night sky.</note>, which almost always face the north, let the Physicists <note>In Kepler's time, "Physici" referred to natural philosophers who studied the physical causes of phenomena.</note> judge. Finally, there remains a conical region hollowed out on both sides of the shadow, represented by $\rho \sigma \chi \tau$ and $\sigma \psi \chi \upsilon$, through which the refracted light of the Sun is dispersed much more widely; it is much higher than 43 Earth semidiameters, and in the middle it is hollowed out by the pure shadow $\tau \chi \upsilon$. This, then, is the place which the Moon passes through.

To measure this region, note first that above in Chapter 4, number 6, proposition 9, the refraction of a ray coming from the ether <note>The "ether" was the substance then believed to fill the vacuum of space.</note> and touching the air (assuming that the ray which touches the Earth after refraction undergoes a refraction of 34 minutes) was $1^\circ 1' 30''$. # THE OPTICAL PART OF ASTRONOMY. 281

If the thickness of the air $\alpha \zeta$ is 1, then $\alpha \sigma$ becomes 46 1/2 <term>Earth radii|The distance from the center of the Earth to its surface, used as a standard astronomical unit</term>. Here, therefore, begins the region illuminated by the refracted rays of the Sun. <note>Kepler is calculating the distance from Earth where the atmosphere begins to "bend" sunlight into the shadow.</note>

Again, because the upper arc $\beta \gamma$, based on what has been established (and by Chapter 6, number 8), ought to have been 179° 23' if the Sun’s rays had arrived without being refracted; however, since each observer at $\beta$ and $\gamma$ sees the Sun 34' higher than its true position <note>34 minutes of arc is the standard value Kepler used for atmospheric refraction at the horizon</note>, this arc is increased by 1° 8', becoming 180° 31'. Consequently, the lower arc $\beta \gamma$ is 179° 29'. Half of this, 89° 44' 30'', is the angle $\beta \alpha \chi$. Therefore, the line $\beta \theta$, when extended, forms an angle of 15' 30'' with $\alpha \chi$; and the exterior angle $\theta \chi \alpha$ equals that sum plus the complement of $\theta \beta \chi$, which is 34'. Thus, $\theta \chi \alpha$ is 49' 30''. And since the extension of $\chi \theta$ cuts $\alpha \delta$ between $\beta \delta$, very close to $\beta$, it matters little whether we take $\alpha \beta$ or something slightly larger (though much smaller than $\alpha \delta$) as our measurement. Therefore, since $\beta \alpha \chi$ is 89° 44' 30'' and $\alpha \chi \theta$ (let it now be $\alpha \chi \beta$) is 49' 30'', $\alpha \beta \chi$ will be 89° 26'. If we take a value close to $\alpha \beta$ as 1, then $\alpha \chi$ results in 70. Thus $\chi$ would be 70 Earth radii away from the Earth, which is much further than $\rho$ or $\sigma$. However, the rays are not refracted from all parts of the Sun all the way to 70 Earth radii; they are only refracted from the very edge. It was proven above that the point where the rays from *all* parts of the Sun begin to be refracted is at a height of 43 Earth radii. Since $\rho \sigma$ are at a distance of 46 radii, and $\tau \upsilon$ are much more than 70 radii, and the region $\rho \tau$ and $\sigma \upsilon$ becomes illuminated by the refracted rays of the Sun, and since the Moon passes between these boundaries at altitudes between 54 and 60 Earth radii (as Astronomy testifies), it is therefore evident that while the Moon is within the shadow of the air, it is nonetheless somewhat illuminated by the Sun.

Again, while the pure shadow $\tau \chi \upsilon$ ends at the apex $\chi$ at a distance of 70 Earth radii, the Moon would not pass through the "pure" shadow because it passes lower than that; and yet, if $\tau \chi \upsilon$ is understood as the region lacking even a single particle of the Sun’s light (even refracted light), it ends at the apex $\chi$ at a distance of 43 Earth radii. The Moon, therefore, which passes higher than this, will certainly cross through the "spike" of $\tau \chi \upsilon$ (taking it in the second sense). Thus, when it first enters the shadow of the air, it still enjoys a refracted view of the entire Sun; but when it falls into the middle of the air's shadow, it no longer enjoys the sight of the whole Sun, but only a very small portion. From this, it is entirely consistent...

<meta>This page continues Kepler's investigation into the optical phenomena observed during lunar eclipses, specifically focusing on the coloring of the Moon and the effects of atmospheric refraction on the Earth's shadow.</meta>

282 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; JOHANNES KEPLER

It is well known from Gemma <note>Cornelius Gemma (1535–1578), a physician and astronomer who wrote on the "Cosmographic Divine," often cited by Kepler regarding atmospheric phenomena.</note> that the colors of the **Rainbow** are sometimes seen on the Moon. For in a watery globe <note>Kepler is likely using a water-filled sphere as a model for the Earth's atmosphere to study refraction.</note> it is most certain that where a particle of the Sun shines by refraction, and is hidden by the very lack of refracted rays, colors arise one after another, depending on how much or how little of the solar body has shone through. You see, therefore, an admirable agreement of almost all the things that have been set forth; anyone who wishes to tear this down through false claims <note>original: *per calumniam*</note> must necessarily employ great art.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; There remains a single doubt <note>original: *scrupulus*, literally a small sharp stone; used here to mean a difficulty or nagging concern</note> proposed in this very context, and indeed now almost removed, but it befits a lover of truth to conceal nothing. When the Moon was distinguished into three parts, as it were, by the previous experiments—the **shining**, the **reddish**, and the **hidden**—the shining part was distinguished from the reddish by a manifest line, but the reddish from the obscured part not by a manifest line or boundary, but rather the reddish faded gradually <note>original: *successive*</note> into the obscured. It seems altogether consistent that the part which was perfectly red was illuminated by the whole body of the Sun through refraction, while the part that was perfectly dark (as far as it happens to be dark) clearly lacked any sight of the Sun, and the doubtful part placed between them saw only a small portion of the Sun. Therefore, the pure shadow <term>umbra</term> <note>The "pure shadow" refers to the umbra, the darkest part of the shadow where the light source is completely blocked.</note> $\gamma \chi \upsilon$ and its apex $\chi$ ought not to arise only from the seventieth diameter of the earth, but far lower, so that in the place of the Moon’s transit some small part can be in the pure shadow. 

It is asked how this may be obtained? The response is easy if a greater horizontal refraction is assumed; for then $\theta \chi$ and $\iota \chi$ will meet more quickly. Thus, in the year 1598 in August, if **A G** is the Ecliptic and **A C G** is the shadow of the earth, and **C D** is the southern part, then the boundary **F** of the refracted rays will come from a smaller refraction, and **E** from a larger one. In the North, therefore, the refraction was greater than in the west (because **A** is part of the eastern shadow).

<meta>This page continues the discussion of celestial shadows, moving from the Earth's shadow (the cause of lunar eclipses) to the Moon's shadow (the cause of solar eclipses). ->THE OPTICAL PART OF ASTRONOMY. 285<-
->CHAPTER VIII.<-
->On the Shadow of the Moon and Daytime Darkness.<-

**P**ertinent as this question is to what we are to say below concerning the size of the Moon’s diameter—and placed here for the sake of easier understanding—the elegance of the systematic method does not allow the shadow of the Moon to be separated from the shadow of the Earth.

->1. The occasion for this question.<-

When Tycho Brahe—the <term>Hipparchus of our age</term> <note>Hipparchus was a Greek astronomer (c. 190–120 BCE) considered the father of trigonometry; Kepler is calling Tycho his modern successor</note>—noticed that Solar Eclipses always showed the diameter of the Moon to be much smaller than it appeared during <term>oppositions</term> <note>the Full Moon phase</note>, whether the light rays were let in through a tube <note>original: "per canalem," referring to a pinhole camera or camera obscura setup</note> or received by the eyes, he first conceived a suspicion which he finally defended as a settled opinion. In the first volume of his *Progymnasmata* <note>Tycho Brahe's "Introductory Exercises" to his astronomical work</note>, he openly declared that the Moon does not retain the same visible diameter during <term>conjunctions</term> <note>the New Moon phase, specifically during an eclipse</note> that it had during oppositions. Instead, he claimed that by the power of the solar light, the Moon's edges are thinned out, as suggested by some optical reasoning.

Because of this, as if it were a universal rule, he published a special table of <term>semi-diameters</term> <note>half the width of the celestial body as seen from Earth</note> specifically for New Moons. And when he wrote to Clavius <note>Christopher Clavius, a leading Jesuit astronomer and mathematician</note> in the year 1600, he mentioned he was amazed that Clavius had seen a total Eclipse in Portugal in the year 1560, with "nighttime darkness" occurring during the day. For Tycho's own observations did not allow the Sun to be totally covered by the Moon, no matter how low the Moon might be.

However, the Solar Eclipse that followed in December 1601, immediately after Tycho’s death—concerning which a warning was added in the appendix to the *Progymnasmata*—taught that one should not rely on this table of semi-diameters. As for the opinion itself: first, it must be granted entirely that the Full Moon appears larger than is right; though this varies from person to person. Indeed, the main purpose of Chapter 5 was to show, from the very structure of vision, the reasons why the edges of bright objects are amplified, especially in the dark. Thus, in this case, the Moon's edges are not thinned by the power of the Sun's light, but are instead amplified by the power of the Moon's own light, which is received from the Sun. Therefore, the Astronomer should diligently note from this passage that unless vi- <note>The text cuts off mid-word, "vires" or "vision," continuing on the next page.</note>

Kepler counters this by suggesting the Moon actually looks larger during a Full Moon due to optical "irradiation" (amplification of bright edges) rather than shrinking during an eclipse.</summary>

unless one is endowed with the sharpest and strongest sight, it is unsuitable for measuring the diameter of the Moon at full moon without error; indeed, this is something that hardly any human can achieve.

Next, this must also be granted: during a solar eclipse, the boundaries both around the Sun and toward the entering Moon appear dilated <note>original: "dilatari"; Kepler is referring to the optical effect where bright objects appear larger than they are, a phenomenon now known as irradiation.</note> to the eye, as was demonstrated above at the end of the fifth chapter, likewise based on the structure of the eye and the nature of vision. But when the question is whether it will be day or night during a solar eclipse, and in general, what portion of daylight will be lost, it is useless to look to the defects of vision; for even if vision should fail completely in one particular man, it does not thereby extinguish the light of day for other men. Therefore, astronomers will now note this second point: the eye is not to be trusted, neither regarding the <term>number of digits</term> <note>A "digit" was a traditional astronomical unit representing one-twelfth of the diameter of the Sun or Moon, used to measure the magnitude of an eclipse.</note>, nor regarding the narrowness of the interior and hollow circle bounding the Sun, which is the circle of the lunar body. Therefore, one must not argue from this accident of vision to that which happens without consideration of vision; nor should tables be constructed for the sake of vision which represent neither the thing itself nor the defects of all visions. For the Astronomer ought not to provide anything except those things which truly happen. We leave the correction of vision to the Physicians.

->ASTRONOMY: THE OPTICAL PART. 287<-

Having premised these things, we must demonstrate at the beginning with many examples that the diameter of the Moon is indeed so great that it has at times covered the Sun entirely and enveloped certain regions in deep darkness. Then, I shall assign the optical causes by which it can happen that, even when the Moon intercepts the entire Sun, the Sun nonetheless appears to protrude all around <note>Kepler is describing an annular eclipse, where a ring of light remains visible.</note>.

### 2. *Historical examples where the Moon’s shadow brought night during the day.*

That the shadow of the Moon is conical—on account of both the Sun and Moon being round, and the Moon being smaller than the Sun—is evident from the same principles by which we pronounced the Earth’s shadow to be conical above in Chapter 7, Number 1.

Now, if the diameter of the Moon is not perceptibly larger than the diameter of the Sun, but equal to it, the tip of the Lunar shadow fails <note>reaches its end</note> at our very sight, and involves only a very thin region of the air. In this case, therefore, total darkness can by no means occur. For even if the Sun is turned away from at least one point on Earth by the intervention of the Moon, the Sun still most brightly illuminates all the surrounding parts of the Earth with some portion of itself; these parts vibrate the light received from the Sun upward into the air from all sides, even where the air is in the Moon's shadow, and thus they provide brightness to it nonetheless.

It is necessary, therefore, whenever nocturnal darkness rushes in during the day under a Solar Eclipse, that the Moon is seen at a larger angle than the Sun: so that the Sun lies well hidden and stored away behind the Moon, and so large a portion of the horizon is covered by the shadow that the air of the spectator cannot be illuminated by the neighboring air. In a word, it is necessary to extinguish even that <term>matter<note>Kepler refers here to the "crepuscular matter," a physical substance he believed existed in the atmosphere to catch and scatter sunlight, creating twilight.</note></term> which is accustomed to lighting the twilight torch for us.

If, to mention this in passing, the height of that matter reaches 12 miles <margin>On the matter of the twilights.</margin>, then for this to be deprived of the Sun's light by the Moon, it would be necessary for the Moon's shadow near us to have a thickness of 300 miles.

A digit is a measurement of an eclipse's magnitude, representing one-twelfth of the diameter of the celestial body</note>, it could easily happen that a corrected calculation (for it does need correction) would reveal one or the other as a total eclipse.

Herodotus <note>Known as the "Father of History," a Greek writer from the 5th century BCE</note> in Book 2, concerning the war between the Lydians and the Medes: *In the sixth year a pitched battle occurred; during the conflict, the day was suddenly turned into night. Thales of Miletus <note>An early Greek philosopher often credited with the first scientific prediction of an eclipse</note> predicted this change of day to the Ionians, adding the time—this very year in which the change occurred.* However, since Herodotus makes no mention of the Moon, being unskilled in astronomy, lest anyone think it was some other omen, Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman author and naturalist</note> confirms it for us. In Book 2, Chapter 2, he ascribes this doctrine first among the Greeks to Thales of Miletus for the predicted failure of the Sun, which occurred under King Astyages in the 4th year of the 48th Olympiad <note>A 4-year period used by the Greeks for dating; the 48th Olympiad began around 588 BCE</note>. Bunting <note>Heinrich Bünting, a Protestant pastor and chronologer</note>, therefore, found the eclipse of the New Moon in the indicated year to be eleven and a half digits according to the Prutenic index (which is not yet certain), with the Moon approaching its perigee <note>The point in the Moon's orbit where it is closest to Earth</note> in the 1st degree of Gemini, in that summer from the middle of which the 4th year of the 48th Olympiad began.

The same Herodotus in Book 7: *When Xerxes <note>The Persian King who invaded Greece in 480 BCE</note> was setting out from Sardis to Abydos with his army, the Sun, leaving its seat in the sky, became invisible, though there were no clouds, but rather a great serenity; instead of day, it became night.* Since the passage of Xerxes into Europe fell in that year in whose summer the 75th Olympiad was celebrated (for some reported this to Xerxes when he had already entered Greece: that the Greeks were watching the Olympic games without a care), and yet the astronomical calculation for that year shows no eclipse of the Sun...

<meta>This page continues Kepler’s investigation into historical solar eclipses, comparing ancient and medieval accounts with the "Prutenic Tables" to verify the precision of astronomical calculations.</meta>

->294             OF JOHANNES KEPLER<-

At the first rising of the dawn, even until noon (I mean its position in the sky, not the time), stars shimmered continuously. Added to these terrors was the fact that when the heavenly light was covered and light was **UTTERLY** snatched away from the world's sight, the fearful minds of men judged that the Sun had failed for a long time—first thinned into the <note>original: "corniculant. effigiem"</note> crescent shape of the moon, then increased into the appearance of a half-circle, and afterwards restored to its whole. For this reason, here too the Sun failed entirely, even though the <term>Prutenic calculation</term> <note>These were astronomical tables published in 1551 by Erasmus Reinhold, based on Copernican theory.</note> uselessly leaves a ring around the Moon, with the Moon being at its <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in the Moon's orbit where it is furthest from the Earth, making it appear smaller.</note>. For the author, after explaining the causes, also adds these words: *Sometimes the sky is overwhelmed by thicker shadows, as if the air were thickened, so that we cannot see even the closest and opposite things.* This very eclipse undoubtedly taught this, as his own eclipse previously taught Plutarch. It was the Year of Christ 360, August 28.

Since histories over several centuries mention only the rarest of eclipses, it is believable that no others were recorded except those that struck the eyes by the conversion of day into night and were total. Such were those that Lichtenberger recorded in the time of Saint Martin; Jordanes and Marcellinus in the year 418, July 19; the Constantinople Annals in the year of Christ 592, March 19; and Bede in the year 664, May 1. It is credible that these were total; nor indeed does the Prutenic calculation much disagree, which shows the former at 10½ and the latter at nearly 12 <term>digits</term> <note>A "digit" was a unit of measure for eclipses, representing one-twelfth of the diameter of the Sun or Moon.</note>. In the year 787, a very great eclipse of the Sun occurred. The calculation of Cedrenus shows September 16, 11½ digits. But that it was total is gathered from the words.

In the year 840, May 5, an anonymous author says the eclipse of the Sun was so powerful that even stars were seen because of the darkness of the Sun, and the color of things on earth was changed. Another author says it was total; Aimoin says it was "The Greatest." The Moon was at its <term>perigee</term> <note>The point in the Moon's orbit where it is closest to the Earth, making it appear larger.</note>. Concerning this eclipse, these notable words are inserted in the *Life of Louis the Pious*: *An eclipse of the Sun occurred on the third day of the Greater Litanies in an unusual manner. For in such a withdrawal of light, darkness prevailed so much that nothing seemed to differ from the reality of night. For the fixed order of the stars was so perceived that no (note this) star suffered the dullness of the Sun’s light; rather, the moon, which had presented itself in opposition to it, by gradually seeking the east, first restored the light to it in a crescent shape <margin>note</margin> from the western part in its own manner, as when it is seen on its first or second day, and thus through increases the whole wheel of the Sun received back its entire beauty.* The author is worthy of trust because he had skill in astronomy and exactly [noted] all the stars.

Yet, these very words of the author demonstrate that Clavius recorded this phenomenon with sufficient care, having weighed the circumstances well. Therefore, let us discuss this as a matter that is quite certain.

And first, indeed, I do not deny that the hypotheses of certain astronomers are so arranged that the Sun at perigee <note>The point in an orbit where a celestial body is closest to the Earth.</note> can be covered by the Moon at apogee <note>The point in an orbit where a celestial body is farthest from the Earth.</note> in this manner, leaving a protruding rim of light. For the one whom we suspected above was being criticized by Cleomedes under the general term "the multitude"—namely Sosigenes—is openly credited with this view by Proclus Diadochus <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on astronomy.</note>, after first mentioning the opinion of Ptolemy. Ptolemy had said that, through the use of Hipparchus's *dioptra* <note>An ancient portable sighting instrument used for measuring angles and diameters of celestial bodies.</note>, it is held for certain that the Sun's diameter does not sensibly vary from apogee to perigee, but is seen at the same angle. He claimed, however, that the Moon's diameter is only seen to be equal to the Sun's diameter when the full Moon is located at the apogee of its epicycle; but at its perigee, the Moon appears larger. Proclus, therefore, adds to this: *If this is true, then what Sosigenes the Peripatetic <note>A follower of Aristotle's school of philosophy.</note> relates is not true in those works he titled "On Revolutions": that when eclipses occur while the Sun is at perigee, the Sun is seen not entirely running forward into the front (I understand this as the Sun placing itself behind the Moon), but at its extreme edges, it escapes the circle of the Moon and gives off a very small amount of light.* <note>original: "Hoc si verum, non est verum quod Sosigenes narrat... minimè impeditum lumen dare."</note> It appears that Hipparchus said the same thing that Ptolemy said regarding the diameters of the lights; but Sosigenes added this interpretation: if the lights at apogee are seen at the same angle, certainly the Sun at perigee will be seen as larger, even if this is not detected through the *dioptra* because of its smallness. It is possible, therefore, that the Moon at apogee <note>original Greek: ἀπόγειῳ</note> is placed in front of the Sun at perigee, and thus being at a smaller angle, the Sun is not totally covered throughout all its extremities. Because of this, Proclus adds: *For if anyone were to admit this, the Sun will make a difference in its apparent diameters.* Indeed, Sosigenes will reply to Proclus that because it is altogether necessary for the Sun to make a difference in its apparent diameters (for it approaches and recedes), I have therefore thought this must be admitted. Thus Proclus teaches us that Sosigenes established that such eclipses are altogether seen, just as Clavius recorded one for us. In this very place, Proclus brings an interpretation of what he had said at the beginning of the book of *Hypotheses*, in the fifth of the "Wonderful Questions." *When also, he says,*

### THE OPTICAL PART OF ASTRONOMY. 299

Certain differences are observed regarding the Moon during perfect solar eclipses: for sometimes the entire Sun appears to be hidden from our sight; at other times, at the very moment in which the two centers <note>The center of the Sun and the center of the Moon</note> and the eye of the observer fall upon the same line, the Moon is seen within the perimeter of the Sun. I say that in the place previously cited, Clavius shows he is speaking here not from his own experience, but from the traditions of Sosigenes <note>Sosigenes of Alexandria was the astronomer who advised Julius Caesar on the calendar.</note>. For if he had possessed his own, or at least certain, experience of those things he said here, he would never have added those remarks we cited in the first place in such a manner; he would never have called into doubt the things Sosigenes had handed down, as they would have been confirmed by experience itself.

Can this eclipse reported by Clavius be excused by the Ptolemaic hypotheses <note>The traditional Earth-centered model of the universe</note> taken up by Hipparchus and Sosigenes? Not at all. First, the Moon was at its mean longitude, and the <term>diameter</term> <note>The apparent width of the celestial body as seen from Earth.</note> of the Moon was even larger <note>original: "μείζων" (meizōn)</note> than the solar diameter. Furthermore, the Sun itself was moving toward <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in the Sun's apparent orbit where it is farthest from the Earth, making it look smaller.</note>, and was seen at nearly its smallest angle.

Therefore, another cause for the phenomenon must be sought. And I do not know whether Plutarch, in that book *On the Face in the Moon* which I have already cited so many times, clearly uncovered it. When starting from an eclipse he had seen himself, he weaves a discourse on the subject in general: *The Moon,* he says, *even if it sometimes hides the whole Sun, nevertheless that eclipse lacks breadth and time (he makes a rule from his own example, though you have seen different in the examples mentioned), but a certain splendor shines out around the orbit, not allowing the shadow to become too deep or excessive.* It is clearly so: although the whole Sun is covered, the air surrounding the Sun is brighter the closer it is to the Sun. Therefore, if the air should be thicker, and some small part of it—as much as is intercepted by the <term>cone</term> <note>The cone of shadow or vision</note> of the seen Sun—is obscured, the surrounding air will appear to shine in a circular shape. 

Other experiences support this. Indeed, Dr. Jessenius <note>Johannes Jessenius, a physician and friend of Tycho Brahe and Kepler.</note>, of whom I made mention in Chapter 5, confirms to me that on February 25 or March 7, 1598, he saw an eclipse of the Sun in the court at Torgau through the clouds, with a splendor clearly encircling the Moon; and that he pursued that form of the "laboring Sun" in epigram and allegory. However, that eclipse could not have been total according to the <term>Brahean calculations</term> <note>Calculations based on the highly accurate observational data of Tycho Brahe.</note>, not even by the legitimate diameter of the Moon as it moved away from <term>perigee</term> <note>The point in the orbit closest to the Earth, where the Moon appears largest.</note>. Therefore, Jessenius could not have seen the Sun from all sides, but what he did see surrounding the Moon on all sides was the splendor of the air.

But if those things which Clavius <note>Christopher Clavius (1538–1612), a leading Jesuit astronomer and mathematician who helped calibrate the Gregorian calendar.</note> saw in the Eclipse of the Year 1567 are of this kind of condition: it must follow that Clavius also saw his own bright rim <note>original: "limbum lucidum"</note> gradually becoming thinner toward the outside, and not marked by a precise boundary on its outer edge.

For, because above in chapter 6, number 9, we proceeded to such a point of boldness with Plutarch <note>Kepler refers to Plutarch’s "On the Face which Appears in the Orb of the Moon," a classical text suggesting the Moon is a world like Earth.</note> that we dared to ascribe continents, seas, mountains, and valleys to the Moon, such as this earth of ours has: how much is left but that we also surround the Moon with air, just as air is poured around this earth of ours? 

For then (though not frequently) that will happen which we demonstrated in chapter 7, number 5, regarding the terrestrial air; so that the rays approaching from the extremities of the Sun might go around the Lunar body by a certain winding path, through <term>refractions</term> <note>The bending of light as it passes through a medium like air.</note> in the lunar air, and thus be terminated at our sight in a shorter cone. As in the diagram, which is the first one in chapter 7, number 5; if the eye were to stand between points χ and ω. In this way, therefore, it would not be the Moon's diameter that appeared smaller than it should, but the Sun's diameter that appeared larger than it should.

Indeed, a certain great patron of these arts suggested this very thing to me in a single word: *that the outermost parts of the Moon appear transparent.* <note>original: "videri partes Lunae extremas pellucidas"</note> But this could not be defended as lightly as it is easily said. For what does it help for them to be transparent, if they are of a denser substance than the ethereal breeze, and the Moon is round? For if this happens, there is no direct path for the solar rays, nor can anything certain be demonstrated without that diagram in the seventh chapter. Furthermore, it could be asked: if the edges of the Moon are always transparent, why does a circle of the Sun not always remain? 

Therefore, I prefer to attribute air to the Moon—not of great depth, so that only occasionally, and indeed most rarely, it can proceed far enough to produce this effect. But I much prefer that the cause cited in the second-to-last place should prevail, while this one should not be in common use, but remain in the "storehouse" <note>Kepler means he is keeping the "lunar atmosphere" theory as a backup hypothesis rather than his primary explanation.</note> of possibilities.

# THE OPTICAL PART OF ASTRONOMY [Right aligned] 303

### 4. Several corollaries regarding solar eclipses.

To ensure we conclude this chapter with some profit <note>original: "fœnore," literally "interest" or "usury," here meaning intellectual benefit or "with interest" on the reader's time</note>, we shall note these following rules based on what has been previously discussed.

1. Whenever any eclipse of the Sun spreads a darkness similar to night over the lands during the day, it is certain that the entire Sun was hidden by the Moon.

2. However, an <term>astrologer</term> <note>In this period, the terms "astrologer" and "astronomer" were often used interchangeably for those who studied the heavens.</note> should not therefore predict that darkness will occur, even if he sees that the entire Sun is going to be covered, unless the Sun is also near its <term>perigee</term> <note>The point in an orbit where the celestial body is closest to the Earth, making it appear slightly larger.</note> and the air is pure. You have the cause of this matter above in Chapter 6, number 11.

3. Nor does it follow that if the stars appear, the eclipse was total. For we read of stars being revealed during many partial eclipses.

4. But this is certain: if a total eclipse is to occur in a clear sky, the stars will be revealed.

5. Morning eclipses are always more prone to darkness before midday, and evening eclipses after midday; the former occur when the <term>nodes</term> <note>The two points where the Moon's path crosses the Sun's path (the ecliptic).</note> and the semicircle of the <term>Zodiac</term> are descending, the latter when they are ascending. For they extinguish that portion of the air illuminated by the Sun which brings the most light to us from above our heads.

6. The color of things is truly changed, not so much by eclipses near the horizon as by those that are vertical, occurring in summer and in a very clear sky. For the clearer the air is, the more forcefully a sudden darkening of light strikes the eyes, as they were previously strongly imbued with light and were retaining strong "species" <note>An optical term of the era referring to the visual images or "impressions" retained by the eye.</note> of light. On the contrary, if rain and clouds occupy the sky and cause darkness beforehand, nothing unusual will strike the eyes, even if the darkness is increased by the eclipse. Thus, in the year 1590, on July 21 or 31, an eclipse in Swabia presented a yellow color everywhere to the harvesters, and a reddish color in Styria; yet this eclipse was not so great. But an eclipse much larger than this one, occurring in the year 1598 on February 22 or March 4, in a sky that was troubled, rainy, and wintry, with the Sun lower in the sky, excited no complaint about colors, even though it inclined the light of day toward the darkness of evening.

7. There are many eclipses that are not entirely total which induce a greater darkness on the lands than total ones do when the Moon is at its <term>apogee</term> <note>The point where the Moon is furthest from the Earth, appearing smaller and sometimes leaving a ring of sunlight visible.</note> or the air is shining; this is because when the Moon is at apogee, the Sun is not deeply hidden all around. But if almost the whole Sun is covered near the horizon by a Moon that is slightly higher, yet with a bit of the Sun protruding below, [Right aligned] the air

## CHAPTER IX.
### On Parallaxes. <note>original: "De Parallaxibus." Parallax is the apparent change in position of a celestial object when viewed from different points on Earth, or from Earth's surface versus its center.</note>

**C**onsequently, the bodies whose appearances and diameters astronomy considers are, as we have said, the Sun, the Moon, and the stars: to which are added the shadows of the Earth and the Moon. Furthermore, what we chiefly seek in these bodies are their movements, which are so admirable. So that the astronomer might be able to "fish out" these movements through geometric demonstrations, it is necessary that he first measure their position with instruments. 

For just as in Geometry, when we are unable to describe a spiral or a conic section <note>Curves like ellipses, parabolas, and hyperbolas.</note> in a single continuous action, we fix certain points through which the line passes, from which the entire path of the line may be discerned: so in astronomy—and I say this for the benefit of those less experienced—we do not see the actual movements of the stars with our eyes. Rather, we compare various positions with one another, and from there we seek the *form* of the motion, by which all those positions noted before, and those similar ones yet to come, might be produced in a regular order. When this is achieved, we have fully performed the duty of the astronomer. Thus, the various positions of the stars at specific times are like certain elements, or rather the "results" <term>apoteleśmata: the final effects or outcomes of a process</term> of their movements.

And "position" is a matter of relationship; it concerns, as we are now considering it, the locations of the stars. For we are enclosed within the same outermost sphere of the world along with all the stars. And since there are three regions of this worldly edifice, arising from the nature of the spherical shape it has attained—the center, the surface, and the space between—the center...

<summary>Kepler uses an ancient observation of Mars by Aristotle to fix a historical date and then introduces Chapter 9, explaining that astronomers must use discrete observations of "positions" to calculate the true geometric forms of celestial motions.</summary>
<keywords>Aristotle, Mars, Occultation, Eudoxus, Chaldeans, Parallax, Geometry, Celestial Motion, Sphere of the World</keywords>

308 [space] JOHANNES KEPLER

...whether we occupy ourselves with the center truly, or according to our senses: therefore, two remaining regions are left for the stars, according to which their position is considered in a double respect: namely, either in respect to the middle or <term>diameter of the World<note>Kepler refers here to the physical distance from the center of the universe to its edge.</note></term>, or in respect to the outermost surface.

### 1. *On the visible or estimated position or place of the stars among the fixed stars.*

Indeed, the position of a star in respect to the diameter of the world concerns the physical reality itself more closely; however, the position in respect to the surface concerns almost only our vision.

For since everything that is seen is encompassed and viewed by a certain angle of light rays flowing together from the edges of the thing seen to the center of the eye: we only think we have correctly "seen" a star—that is, observed it—when we have accurately measured that angle of vision. Now, angles are measured by a circle drawn from the point where the angle originates. And that massive circle, or the spherical surface of the outermost world, is described from this point of our visual angles—that is, from the Earth. This is because the tiny distance by which our home, the Earth's surface, stands apart from the very center of the world effectively vanishes within such vastness. It follows, therefore, that the spherical surface of the outermost heaven is used by us to measure the visual angles formed within our eye: and conversely, that our visual angles sufficiently prove the position of the stars in respect to the surface of the world.

For this consideration is also twofold. First, it will be said in what follows that stars cannot be perceived by the eyes with their specific distance from us being clear. Therefore, between the stars very near to us and those <term>fixed<note>The "fixed stars" are what we call stars today; to Kepler, they were "fixed" because they do not move relative to one another, unlike the "wandering" planets.</note></term> in the most remote sphere, we do not distinguish a difference in place unless one is covered by the other. In this way, we note with our eyes the <term>conjunctions<note>A conjunction occurs when two celestial bodies appear to be in the same place in the sky from our perspective.</note></term> of the <term>planets<note>original: "errantium" or "errones," literally "wanderers," the term used for planets because they move against the backdrop of the stars.</note></term> with the fixed stars. Therefore, at whatever angle two fixed stars are seen to be joined with two planets, we say that the planets themselves are distant in respect to the surface by that same angle and by that same arc of a <term>great circle<note>A circle on the surface of a sphere that has the same circumference as the sphere itself, used here as a measuring tool for the sky.</note></term> which measures the visual angle. Thus, the angle at which the outer edges of the Sun or Moon are seen to be apart is said to be the "magnitude" of the Sun or Moon. And so, from this perspective, the Sun and Moon are thought to be equal, although the Sun [is larger than] the Moon by many...

<summary>Kepler explains that because we cannot visually perceive the actual depth or distance of stars, we must measure their positions using the angles they form on the "surface" of the sky as seen from Earth.</summary>

<margin>Even with a single eye long accustomed, there remains a small ability to discern very close distances, due to the width of the eye and the movement of the opening in the iris <note>original: "tunica uvea"</note>, and especially due to the movement of the head; but those factors do not hinder us here. I will therefore explain how something similar happens to us in the observation of the stars, so that it may be fully clear what Astronomers mean by parallax.

In this way it happens that we think the Moon and all the Planets are located just beneath the <term>sphere of the fixed stars</term> <note>The outermost shell of the universe in the traditional model, where the stars were thought to be embedded.</note>, with the distance between our eyes providing us no help in depth perception. Nature, in turn, relieves this defect of the sense of sight by an admirable mechanism. For it was entirely the will of God the Creator that man, made in His image, should lift his eyes from these earthly things toward those celestial ones, and diligently contemplate such great monuments of His wisdom. The entire distribution of the world’s machinery tends toward this goal: to make this will of the Creator known to us, as if proclaimed by a living voice. For this reason, the proportion of the terrestrial globe relative to the orbit of the Moon was made perceptible. Thus, what was lacking for the eyes of a single person might be supplied by the collective diligence of all people living across the entire surface of the Earth, aided by the planet's vast size. In this way, man might learn the positions of the wandering stars <note>The planets</note> along the diameter of the world through those previously mentioned distances relative to the surface, or by means of angles <note>Kepler is describing the concept of parallax, where an object's position appears to shift when viewed from two different points.</note>.

the line of sight from the center, while *BH* is the line of sight from the surface. Therefore, from both locations of sight, the same position *D* among the fixed stars would be marked. Consequently, astronomers choose this limit for the arcs in which **parallaxes** <term>parallax: the apparent shift in the position of an object when viewed from two different locations</term> are measured, because it is from this common limit that parallaxes first begin to exist in all directions. For example, if a celestial body is now at *G*, it will appear at *E* when seen from *A* <note>Point A represents the center of the Earth</note>, and at *F* when seen from *B* <note>Point B represents the observer's location on the Earth's surface</note>. Thus, *DE* (or the angle *DAE*) is smaller than *DF* (or the angle *DAF*). Or, to put it another way, the position *F* seen from the surface *B* is further removed from the zenith <note>original: "vertice", the point directly overhead</note> *D* than the position *E* seen from the center *A*, which they otherwise call the **true place**. For it is an optical axiom that things which are farther away appear smaller; that is, they are perceived by a smaller angle of vision. Let *HG* be the arc of the celestial body's distance from the zenith in its own orbit, which, since it is perceptibly closer at *B* than at *A* (because the semi-diameter *AB* <note>The radius of the Earth</note> is established as being perceptible compared to the distance of the body *AG*). Therefore, the angle *HAG* will be perceptibly smaller than the angle *HBG*. For this reason, its measurement *DE* will be perceptibly smaller than the measurement *DF* of the latter. And the difference between these, *EF*, is what astronomers call the **parallax** of this celestial body located at *G*.

However, *EF* is the measure of the angle *EGF* or *BGA*. This is because the ratio of *BA* to *AE* <note>The ratio of the Earth's radius to the distance of the fixed stars</note> is imperceptible, while the ratio of that same *BA* to *AG* <note>The Earth's radius compared to the distance to the planet/body at G</note> is perceptible by assumption; therefore, the ratio of *GA* to *AE* is also imperceptible. Consequently, the angle at *G* is equivalent, for all practical purposes, to the angle that can be formed over *EF* at the center *A*. The same point is also clear in this way: since *DF* is the measure of the angle *DBF* for all practical purposes, but the angle *DBG* is equal to the internal and opposite angles *BAG* and *AGB* joined together. Therefore, the measure *DF* is the measure of the angles *BAG* and *AGB* taken together; thus, the remainder *EF* is the measure of the remaining angle *AGB*, or is equal to *EGF* for all practical purposes.

It follows from these points that the angle *BGA* is likewise called the **parallax** of the celestial body at *G* by astronomers.

Therefore, the use of this parallax in astronomy is **divine**. <note>Kepler uses the word "divine" to emphasize the profound importance and elegance of this mathematical tool for understanding the heavens.</note> For whenever the arc *DE*—the true distance of the celestial body from the zenith—can be obtained for a certain moment from astronomical theory (which is done in various ways), and the arc *DF*—the visible distance from the zenith—is obtained at that same moment using suitable instruments and the necessary precision...

*4. A very easy and most brief derivation of daily parallaxes in longitude and latitude through the new Parallactic [Method].*

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The theory of parallaxes creates a particular trouble for astronomers regarding Solar Eclipses. To such an extent that, because of this labor alone, it is no wonder if astronomy is neglected. Therefore, practitioners have always considered it a point of pride to help everyone with a shortcut. Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the influential Greco-Roman astronomer.</note> performed excellent work, having described a clear outline <note>original Greek: ὑποτυπώσει (hypotypōsei)</note> of the variations that exist in parallaxes. Reinhold <note>Erasmus Reinhold (1511–1553), who calculated the Prutenic Tables based on Copernicus’s work.</note>, with tables most laboriously constructed for most elevations of the pole, thought he was assisting the less experienced. But he overwhelmed the ardor of the ingenious with the boredom of searching for the proportional part. Thus, Tycho Brahe <note>Kepler’s mentor and the greatest observational astronomer of the era.</note> recalled astronomers to triangles, showing some shortcuts for solving them. However, even here the labor is immense. Therefore, I think that if, following the examples of these authors, I finally roll this Sisyphian stone <note>A reference to the mythological Sisyphus, condemned to push a boulder up a hill forever; Kepler uses it to describe the endless, heavy burden of manual astronomical calculations.</note> over the ridge so that it falls back no further, I ought to hope for some gratitude from astronomers.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*I say first: All parallaxes of latitude, in whatever degree of the Ecliptic the Moon or Sun is positioned, are equal: provided that the same point of the Ecliptic is at the horizon <note>original: "in ortu," literally "in the rising"</note> at the same altitude of the pole, and the Moon is equally distant from the sight...*

For because CDG is a right angle, the Moon C will be on the horizon, or slightly below. And because CB or CA is 5,400,000 where BD is 70,711, the angle BCD will be 45' 1''. Therefore, the difference from BGD is 37'', which is the maximum it can possibly be.

## 5. On Parallax due to the distance of the Sun and Earth, or the Annual Parallax.

But the most wise Architect of the World did not even then cease to instruct the human race. For just as the distance between a person’s eyes was not sufficient for him to recognize the true distance of the Moon from the Earth (which is the lowest heavenly body), and the vastness of the globe of the earth had to come to the aid of the weakness of sight; so also, when even this departure of the earth's surface from its center <note>i.e., the Earth's radius.</note> vanished when compared to the incredible height of the superior Planets: lest these too should wander through the circuits of the heavens in vain and unobserved—or rather, so that the human mind might reach even to these—God designed another and much more ample kind of parallax. This was done in case there should ever be a man among humans who desired to follow this reasoning with unoffended piety <note>Kepler frequently argues that studying the Copernican system is a form of worship, not heresy.</note> and without slandering His works. Copernicus and Reinhold, in the *Prutenic Tables* <note>Technical tables used for astronomical calculations, based on the Copernican model and published by Erasmus Reinhold in 1551.</note>, call this the parallax of the annual orbit. Tycho Brahe, however, transferred this reasoning from the mobility of the earth to the mobility of the Sun; so that the Optical scientist <term>Opticus: a scholar of optics and perspective</term> has no grounds by which to choose one reasoning or the other. I shall explain both in the previous diagram, no. 3, beginning with the Copernican view.

-> [A geometrical diagram showing a small circle at the bottom with points 'a', 'b', 'c'. From this circle, lines extend upwards. One line goes straight up to point 'd'. Another line goes up at an angle to point 'e'. There is a horizontal line segment 'h-g' connecting the two vertical/angled lines. The angled line also has a point 'B' on it.] <-

Let **A** be the body of the Sun, the common center; **B C** the annual orbit which carries the earth; and **D F** the sphere of the fixed stars; and let the proportion of **B A** to **A D** be imperceptible <note>meaning the distance to the stars is so vast that the Earth's orbit seems like a point in comparison.</note>. Let the heavenly body <note>original: "Sidus"; here referring to a planet.</note> be at **G**, and the proportion of **B A** to **A G** be perceptible. Therefore, with the Earth situated at **C**, in the middle position between the Sun **A** and the heavenly body **G**, the lines **A G** and **C G** will coincide, and both, being continued, will reach a single point **E** among the fixed stars. Therefore, whether seen from the Sun **A**, or from the Earth **C**...

If Earth is positioned at C as the eye, the star will be seen in the same place among the fixed stars. Here, then—specifically when the Sun and the star are in opposition <note>In astronomy, "opposition" occurs when a celestial body is on the opposite side of the Earth from the Sun.</note>—there is no <term>parallax</term> <note>Parallax is the apparent displacement or difference in the apparent position of an object viewed along two different lines of sight.</note> of the star arising from the annual orbit. Keeping everything else the same, let the Earth be at B, away from the line GA. Therefore, the location of the star will appear from Earth at F among the fixed stars, but from the Sun (A) it appears at E; this is because the ratio of the line BA to AG is perceptible, and thus the inclination of lines BG and AG is also perceptible. 

Since B is just as much the center of the arc DE to our senses as A is in truth, the arc EF will again be the measure of the angle EGF or BGA. Both this angle and that one represent the parallax of the annual orbit when Earth is positioned at B. Thus, once the location of the star E—which the line drawn from the Sun determines among the fixed stars—is known through other astronomical rules, and the location of the star F—which the sight coming from Earth determines among the fixed stars—is also known, and thus the parallax EF or BGA is known, the ratio of the distance AG (the distance of the star from the Sun) to the distance AB (the distance of the Sun from the Earth) cannot remain unknown, no matter how immense that distance might be. 

Thus it appears it was not fitting that man, as an inhabitant and future observer <note>original: *speculator*</note> of this world, should reside in its very center as if in a closed bedroom; in such a way, he would never have arrived at the contemplation of stars so remote. Instead, in this most magnificent building, he walks about and wanders through the annual movement of the Earth, his own home, so that he can more correctly perceive and measure the individual members of the house. <term>Geometric art</term> <note>Kepler compares the Earth's orbit to the "baseline" used by surveyors to measure distances to objects they cannot physically reach.</note> imitates something similar in measuring inaccessible things. For unless a surveyor moves from one station to another and takes a sighting from both sides, he cannot arrive at the desired measurement.

In the **Tychonic system** <note>The model proposed by Tycho Brahe where the Earth is stationary at the center, the Sun orbits the Earth, and the other planets orbit the Sun.</note>, A becomes the Earth, the center of the Sun's orbit BC, and DF becomes the sphere of the fixed stars. Let the star be at G, and let the ratio of the three lines BA, AG, and AE be perceptible. First, let Earth be at A, the Sun at C, and the star at G on the same straight line; there will be no parallax, because lines CG and AG, drawn from the Sun and Earth to the star, will coincide. 

Now let the Sun be not at C, but at B, and let line AB show the location of the Sun at D among the fixed stars. And because the Sun at B is the point to which Tycho refers the <term>eccentricities</term> <note>The deviation of an orbit from a perfect circle.</note> and <term>apogees</term> <note>The point in an orbit farthest from the center.</note>, as well as the simple motions of the planetary orbits, let it be known from astronomy how great the angle DBG is between the line from the Sun through the Earth and the line from the Sun through the star. And for that very purpose...

### 6. *A brief appendix on the curved tails of Comets.*

Those who have argued concerning the curvature of the tail in the Comet of the year [15]77 <note>The Great Comet of 1577 was famously observed by Tycho Brahe and helped prove that comets were celestial objects, not atmospheric phenomena.</note> from the doctrine of parallaxes, as if this illusion of curvature consisted in the different parallaxes of different parts of the tail and was not truly present in the tail itself: they do not sufficiently weigh the business of parallaxes. Nor do they correctly cite the Optical writers, who in those passages are not dealing with the error of sight regarding curvature, but with the true and legitimate vision of obliquity. But if parallax truly showed straight things as curved, then it would no longer be true that every straight line, however extended, when perceived from the perceptible center of the world, would appear in all its parts as some <term>great circle</term> <note>A great circle is the largest possible circle that can be drawn on a sphere, like the equator on Earth or the path of the ecliptic on the celestial sphere.</note>

# CHAPTER X.
## Optical foundations concerning the motions of the stars.

**S**ince we are presented in astronomy with the celestial motions to contemplate, and because everything we learn comes first to the senses, it is worth the effort to weigh carefully whether the motions of the heavens strike the sense of the eyes directly, and what deceptions of vision might occur in these celestial motions. Let us begin thus.

Every thing that moves, moves in a place, for motion is a change of place. Yet "place" <term>Locus (Place): In Aristotelian physics, "place" is defined as the inner boundary of the containing body in contact with the contained body.</term> is attributed to the surface which contains the moving body. Indeed, that which encompasses is larger than that which is encompassed, and that which provides the place is larger than that which occupies the place. For the whole is greater than its part; and that which encompasses and holds, together with that which it holds, is a certain "whole."

<summary>Kepler concludes a discussion on the reliability of physical measuring tools before beginning a new chapter on the optical perception of motion, arguing that we must understand how the eyes are deceived to truly understand astronomy.</summary>
<keywords>Johannes Kepler, optics, celestial motion, sensory perception, philosophy of space, astronomical instruments, place and space</keywords>

--- Page 147 ---
<meta>This page continues a discussion on optical illusions and the perception of motion, specifically how the eye focuses on objects and how our frame of reference dictates what we perceive as moving or stationary.</meta>

# THE OPTICAL PART OF ASTRONOMY 325

...both obliquely and confusedly. See Chapter 5 regarding these matters. From this, it happens that the thing which is perceived as larger occupies more of the eye, while that which is smaller occupies a smaller part of the ocular surface. When, therefore, a separation occurs—as, for example, between a cloud and a star shining through it—the smaller object to the sight (namely, the star) becomes more conspicuous by the very act of separation, and it draws the keenness of the eye toward itself. The eye, therefore, gazes directly at the star, as it is perceived at a small angle; <note>In optics, "angle" refers to the "visual angle," or how much of our field of vision an object fills. A small angle means the object is tiny or far away.</note> the eye views the cloud obliquely, as it is seen at a larger angle that occupies almost the entire eye. The eye then ascribes the act of separation to the thing it is gazing at directly—the star. In this way, the vision errs regarding the moving object. For if a cloud moves with a swift motion from the east toward the west, the star—even if it is also moving toward the west, though more slowly—will seem to be carried toward the east, moving against the cloud.

The most evident cause of all such errors <term>aberration; <note>original: "aberrationis"</note> a wandering away from the truth or a distortion in perception</term> lies in this: the eye, being fixed into the head at its rear part, perceives nothing at a larger angle than the protruding parts of the face. These facial features maintain the same position relative to the eye; therefore, everything else will seem to move if someone, unaware, is turned by some machine, provided they are not the one calculating the motion they are making. And just as the eyes are fixed to the head, so through the head they are fixed to the body, through the body to a ship or a house, or to the entire region and its visible horizon. Since these things are nearby, appear large, and are seen at a great angle—and because they maintain the same position relative to the eye—it is inevitable that everything else, whose position changes relative to that which contains the observer (whether it be a ship or the flat expanse of the earth), appears to move by itself. For those nearby things are regarded as the place <note>the stationary frame of reference</note>, while those things immediately surrounding the eye are likened to the "location" and the "container."

From these facts it follows that even if someone were transported to the Moon or another of the wandering stars <note>the planets</note>, and even if the motion of the Moon were extremely sensible <note>perceptible</note> because of its speed (of which we shall speak later), the Moon would nonetheless appear to us to be at rest. The Sun, however, and whatever stars were at a proper distance, would all be thought to move—in addition to their own motions—with those motions which actually belong only to the Moon itself. Therefore, the Opticians have nothing they can bring forth from their armory <note>Kepler suggests that those who study the physics of light and vision cannot use their science to disprove the Earth's motion.</note> against Copernicus, when he declares that the Earth, our dwelling place, is in motion.

And so that I may also add this in passing, the supposed absurdity of the <term>triple motion</term><note>Critics of Nicolaus Copernicus argued that it was physically impossible for the Earth to have three distinct movements (daily rotation, annual orbit, and the "wobble" or axial tilt maintenance) simultaneously.</note> is exaggerated through misrepresentation. For the motion that Copernicus attributes to the Earth is of no other form than that of a wheel on a carriage traveling in a straight line. First, the wheel turns; then, by that very turning, the axis is moved forward; thirdly, the axis points toward the same regions of the sky and remains parallel to itself. Who would conceive of this as a "third motion," considering that it is actually a state of rest?

For as for the fact that the Earth's axis eventually tilts over the course of centuries, that does not fall into this account; it would be a "fourth motion," if one were inclined to continue the misrepresentation. Astronomers know this is of the same kind as that by which the <term>Apogees</term><note>The point in an orbit farthest from the center.</note> and <term>Nodes</term><note>The two points where an orbit crosses the ecliptic (the sun's apparent path).</note> of all the Planets are shifted—not by a motion of its own, but by a certain difference, as it were, between two other acknowledged motions.

But now the students of Optics will have much less to say against Copernicus if I point out that the speed of the stars is not even perceptible. Aristotle, in Section 15, Question 12, takes this as a confessed fact, pronouncing that **the sun's movement is unapparent** <note>original Greek: ἄδηλον τὴν μετάβασιν ἡλίου</note>. And Cleomedes in Book 2 says, **since it appears to stand still** <note>original Greek: ἐπεὶ ἑστὼς φαίνεται</note>. For it is agreeable to reason that between two motions, the one which is slower is more closely assimilated to rest. Therefore, since those animal motions and the turnings of the body, neck, and eyes are, to our senses, many times faster than the celestial motions, it is clear that the motions of the heavens are more likely to be likened to rest by our sight. This is even more so because any visible thing must have a certain quantity and speed, and a sensible proportion to the eye and its movements.

Whatever is beyond this cannot be grasped by sight, as Optics testifies (see Book 4, Theorems 3 and 110 of <term>Vitellio</term><note>Witelo, a 13th-century friar and physicist whose work on optics Kepler is here "supplementing" or commenting upon.</note>). Now, the speed of the stars is in no perceptible proportion; this will be apparent if you consider that your sight is carried by the Sun around the center—whether of the eyes or the head—in a space of twelve hours, through no more than 180 degrees. We are otherwise accustomed to turn our eyes through that same space faster than in one second of an hour's <term>scruple</term><note>A "scruple" here refers to a small division of time, a second.</note>. But in one hour there are 3,600 seconds; in 12 hours the sum is 43,200 seconds. And what is the proportion of one to fifty thousand? It is clearly imperceptible. The same follows from Theorem 112 of the fourth book of Vitellio, since
