<meta>This page continues Kepler’s discussion on the psychology of vision and how our eyes can be deceived by celestial movements, bridging the gap between optical science and biblical interpretation.</meta>

### OPTICAL PART OF ASTRONOMY 327

When an object remains in the same perceptible location for a perceptible amount of time, it is thought to be at rest. This is certainly true of the stars. For a "moment," or one second of an hour <note>original: "vnum ſecundum horæ ſcrupulum"</note> (which is usually about equal to the beat of a pulse), is a perceptible length of time. However, a location—or rather an arc in the eye—with the width of a single degree cannot be perceived without the use of an instrument. Yet a star remains within any given degree for four minutes, which is to say 240 seconds <note>The "seconds" Kepler refers to here are "scruples," a historical term for small divisions of time or measurement.</note>; it stays in a space that essentially has the character of a single point. Therefore, whatever we grasp of the motions of the heavens through our senses, we have actually gathered through the benefit of intervening reasoning: "Previously the Sun was there, now it is here; therefore, it has moved from there to here."

Just as sight erroneously attributes motion in general to things that are at rest, so too does it invent specific types of motion for itself. From this comes "rising" and "setting"—that is, the sight attributes ascent and descent to the stars. Ovid, imitating this appearance, attributed it to Phaethon in that most charming fable in the second book of the *Metamorphoses* <note>Ovid was a Roman poet; in this myth, Phaethon tries to drive the sun-chariot and struggles with the steep "climb" of the morning and the "drop" of the evening.</note>. This happens because sight finds these differences of location in relation to the human observer and their upright position relative to the visible horizon, even though no such thing exists in the heavens themselves. Hence, Vitello <note>Witelo (or Vitellio) was a 13th-century Polish friar and a major authority on optics whose work Kepler is updating here.</note> in Book 4, after showing in Proposition 10 that a series of continuous objects makes the furthest point seem more distant than if the space were empty, shows in Proposition 13 why the horizon of the earth seems to join the sky. He explains why that part of the sky seems further away from us, and the distances of the stars appear greater, than those which are at the Zenith <term>Zenith: the point in the sky directly above an observer's head</term>. These are, therefore, necessary ways of speaking based on sight, which we could not do without, even if we were truly being carried around on the globe of the Moon.

For this reason, we should not be surprised that Copernicus dared to distinguish between those things which are correctly said in Holy Scripture according to the method of explaining sight, and those things which, when examined astronomically, are found to be otherwise. For the Scriptures do not speak falsely; rather, they most truly assert that the sense of sight says this, or rather, they adapt what is suggested by sight to their own purpose. The astronomer—or more accurately, the student of Optics—proves the fallacy of the sense of sight without any intended insult. Indeed, when we read in a thousand places mention of the "ends of heaven" <note>Kepler refers to biblical phrases describing people being scattered to the "four corners" or ends of the earth/sky.</note> to which the Jewish people are scattered and from which they are recalled, everyone sees that these must be explained through the 13th proposition of Vitello’s fourth book.

<summary>Kepler explains that we perceive the stars as moving through reason rather than direct sensation and defends Copernicus by arguing that the Bible describes the world as it appears to human eyes, not as it is physically structured.</summary>

328 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; JOHANNES KEPLER

Since indeed, according to the third book of the fourth volume of Vitello <note>Witelo (c. 1230–1285) was a Polish friar and philosopher whose work on optics was a primary source for Kepler.</note>, motion itself is judged from the space over which a visible object moves, and because all motion occurs along a line—whether that be straight or circular—it is evident that if any error happens to the sight regarding the lines of motion, the same error happens regarding the motions themselves. These types of errors, or rather <term>illusions<note>original Greek: φαντασίαι (*phantasiai*); refers to appearances or mental images that do not correspond to physical reality.</note></term>, are of two kinds among astronomers, based on the two primary circles they assign to a single planet: the <term>Eccentric<note>A circular orbit where the Earth (or Sun) is not at the exact center.</note></term> and the <term>Epicycle<note>A small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger one; used in ancient astronomy to explain the complex paths of planets.</note></term>. But Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the Greco-Egyptian astronomer who refined the Earth-centered model.</note> saw this one way, Copernicus <note>Nicolaus Copernicus (1473–1543), who proposed the Sun-centered system.</note> (whom I follow) another, and the most recent Tycho Brahe <note>Tycho Brahe (1546–1601), a Danish nobleman known for his precise astronomical observations; he proposed a system where the Sun orbits Earth while other planets orbit the Sun.</note> yet another. For, according to Copernicus and Tycho, the planet itself travels the **Eccentric** circle with its own body; for Ptolemy, it is not the body of the planet that travels it, but the center of the **Epicycle**. Conversely, for Ptolemy, the planet itself travels the **Epicycle** with its own body, each planet on its own; for Copernicus, the single circuit of the Earth removes all epicycles; for Tycho, the one and the same circuit of the Sun and the entire planetary system, common to all parts, likewise removes all epicycles.

Therefore, for Ptolemy and Tycho, the motion of a planet is not simple—neither an epicycle for the former nor an eccentric for the latter—around some immobile point, but is in reality a spiral composed of both the Eccentric and the Epicycle. Only for Copernicus is that Eccentric, which he assumes, in reality the simple motion of the planet itself around a fixed point or the Sun (except insofar as I am about to bring a certain *minor correction* regarding this opinion, pertaining to all authors, in my commentaries on the motions of Mars <note>Kepler is referencing his groundbreaking work, *Astronomia Nova* (1609), where he proved orbits are elliptical rather than circular.</note>). Nor is it varied by epicyclic motion, since in that author's work <insert>Copernicus</insert>, this is nothing other than an **illusion of motion**: while the single motion of the Earth is concealed from us on Earth and is instead attributed to each of the individual planets.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; However this difference in hypotheses is arranged, there exists, as I said, a double perception of motions that is prone to error. One is common to all authors, which comes from the Eccentric; the other arises from the Epicycle. In Copernicus, this second one is a mere hallucination of sight regarding the planet; in the other authors, it involves something of the planet’s actual motion.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; The causes of an eccentric planet appearing either slow or fast are partly physical and partly optical. The physical part of the cause does not provide the sight with a reason to err, but reflects what truly happens; even to the sight...

represents, about which [I wrote] in the *Commentaries on the Motions of Mars* <note>original: *Commentarijs de motibus Martis*; this refers to Kepler's work *Astronomia Nova*, which he was writing concurrently with this volume.</note>: The ancients represented it through an **equant circle** <term>equant: a mathematical construction used by ancient astronomers like Ptolemy to account for the observed changes in a planet's speed</term>. There isn't one single "correct" phrase, but depending on the context (acting, psychology, or general literature), here are several ways to describe the ability to translate internal states into outward physical expressions using an **"X to Y"** structure:

### Most Common/Literal
*   **Internal to external:** The most direct way to describe moving a feeling from the inside to the outside.
*   **Thought to expression:** Focusing on the transition from a mental state to a visible look.
*   **Emotion to action:** Often used in acting to describe how a feeling triggers a physical movement.

### Idiomatic & Evocative
*   **Inside out:** As in "He knows his character from the inside out," or "She expresses her grief from the inside out."
*   **Heart to sleeve:** Derived from the idiom "to wear one's heart on one's sleeve," implying that one’s internal emotions are easily visible.
*   **Mind to muscle:** Frequently used in dance and physical acting to describe the neurological and artistic connection between a thought and the body’s movement.

### Poetic & Literary
*   **Soul to surface:** Suggests a deep, spiritual connection that is visible to an observer.
*   **Spirit to skin:** A more tactile way of saying the person’s essence is visible in their physical presence.
*   **Feeling to feature:** An alliterative way to describe how an emotion changes the features of the face.

### Technical/Academic
*   **Affective display:** (Not "X to Y") The psychological term for the external expression of emotion.
*   **Intent to inhabit:** Used in performance theory to describe the process of a person fully occupying a physical space with their mental intention.

**Which one should you use?**
*   If you are talking about **acting technique**, use **"Inside out"** or **"Mind to muscle."**
*   If you are talking about a **transparent person** who can't hide their feelings, use **"Heart to sleeve."**
*   If you are writing **prose or poetry**, use **"Soul to surface."**

# THE OPTICAL PART OF ASTRONOMY. 331

Planets in their epicycles <note>In the older Ptolemaic system, an epicycle was a small circle on which a planet moved, while the center of that circle moved along a larger path called a deferent. This was used to explain why planets sometimes appear to move backward.</note>, while they traverse their lower semicircle: since, as Aristotle teaches in his *Mechanics*, a circle may move in opposite directions with one and the same motion, but in different parts; and this retrograde <note>Backward-moving</note> motion of the parts exceeds the slower forward progress of the center in speed. The same thing happens in Tycho’s <note>Tycho Brahe (1546–1601), the Danish astronomer whose data Kepler used to revolutionize planetary theory.</note> system, with the planet indeed progressing somewhat in the eccentric <note>An orbital path where the Earth is not exactly at the center.</note>, but being driven backward by the Sun’s motion together with its whole eccentric, it is carried in the opposite direction much more swiftly. Since indeed, according to the 4th proposition of Witello’s <note>Witello was a 13th-century physicist; Kepler's book is written as a "supplement" to Witello's work on optics.</note> fourth book, a straight line appears as a point when it is extended directly away from the sight, almost the same judgment will apply to the apsides <note>The points in an orbit where the planet is closest to or farthest from the center of motion.</note> of the epicycle’s circle or the points of contact. These arcs, tending almost directly upward from our sight into the depths of the sky, appear if not as a point, then certainly as a very small quantity; therefore, they are perceived as slowest around those parts. Thus it can happen, even with a faster epicycle than the eccentric, that the forward motion of the eccentric and the contrary motion of the epicycle nevertheless become equal to the senses; and so, with one subtracted from the other, the planet appears to stand still, and in the sky itself, with respect to the sphere of fixed stars, remains in the same place of longitude: although meanwhile it either attempts an ascent in a nearly straight line from the sight into the ether, or lowers itself from the deep ether toward the earth.

As for what concerns Copernicus, this entire phenomenon <term>phantasia</term> <note>original: "φαντασία". Kepler uses this Greek term to describe the "appearance" or visual illusion of planetary stations and reversals.</note> of stations and retrogradations is most beautifully demonstrated from Optics. And although these things are more properly learned from the author himself; yet, lest nothing be said here that might interest the reader, I will repeat the foundations in three words from Euclid himself. Indeed, I think that if we had no other arguments by which the antiquity of this Copernican opinion was proven, this passage alone could have sufficed to reclaim Copernicus for Pythagoras <note>Kepler often linked the sun-centered system of Copernicus to the ancient Greek philosopher Pythagoras, who believed the universe was structured by numbers and geometry.</note> in earnest. First, it is established both by itself and from Proclus <note>An ancient commentator on Euclid.</note> the interpreter, that Euclid’s entire Geometry is Pythagorean and directed toward the knowledge of the five regular shapes, which they called "mundane" <note>The five Platonic solids, which Kepler believed formed the blueprint of the solar system.</note>: Euclid, therefore, was a Pythagorean. Next, look for me at the bundle of Euclidean propositions in his *Optics*, namely 53, 54, 55, 56, 57, 58, which Witello transferred into his 4th book as propositions 134, 135, 136, 128, and 132.

On the other hand, the fixed stars joined to the Sun (such as at point E) will seem to be abandoned by the Sun and to accompany the Earth in this region toward the same direction. In this instance, the term **lagging behind** <note>original Greek: ὑπολείπεσθαι (hypoleipesthai)</note> came to be used in common speech, although later writers used it more strictly in astronomy to describe motion in the order of the signs <term>motion in the order of the signs: movement from West to East, following the sequence of the zodiac constellations</term> from B to A, without regard for the Earth's position—a context in which it does not apply to the fixed stars. Astronomers might give this reason for these names: that in the combination of the primary motion <term>primary motion: the apparent daily rotation of the heavens from East to West</term> and the secondary motions, those which are driven by **retrograde** <term>retrograde: appearing to move backward or "against the grade"</term> motion reach the meridian <term>meridian: the imaginary line in the sky that a star crosses at its highest point each day</term> earlier than they did the previous day, thereby getting ahead of their position among the fixed stars. Thus, they are said to **lead the way** <note>original Greek: προηγεῖσθαι (proēgeisthai)</note>. However, those things which move with **direct motion** reach the meridian or the horizon later than the locations they held among the fixed stars on the previous day. In this way, they are understood to be **lagging behind**, just as if two runners were heading toward the same goal, but the slower one complained of being left behind by the other. Thus, an optical cause gave birth to these names. For although, as has been said, not even the primary and daily motion of the stars is obvious to the naked senses, the eyes—aided by a bit of reasoning—easily notice this primary and daily motion from east to west; but they notice the secondary motions only through the differences in the daily ones.

The fallacy that fathered these names is no different than if someone on the shore were to see a ship going down a favorable river current, and on that ship two men, one of whom stood still at the bow, while the other walked from the bow to the stern, against the ship's course. A spectator, ignorant of the situation, might think those two men were being carried by two distinct ships, one of which was slower. He would be in error, for he would wrongly attribute the motion belonging to the man on the ship to the ship itself, but in the opposite direction. And those who first introduced these names into astronomy erred in a similar way, thinking that the primary motion in the Moon, for example, was slower than in the Sun; they were unaware that the Moon, by its own proper motion, actually struggles against the common primary motion (to use the common hypotheses currently in use).

And...

### THE OPTICAL PART OF ASTRONOMY. 335

And these are roughly the things that sight—and the careless reasoning that follows it—falsely attributes to the stars, and which must be clarified through the laws of optics.

#### Appendix on the motion of Comets.

*Those who demonstrated the motions of the comet of the year 1577 using circles undertook a very difficult task; yet they did not entirely succeed, because they did not think they needed to investigate more diligently. They will experience much greater difficulties if they take it upon themselves to demonstrate the same for other comets. For me, in several cases where I have obtained recorded observations, the following path succeeded more easily: if I attributed straight lines to them, as the nature of things suggests, which they would for the most part cross equally in equal times, being slightly slower only at the beginning and end, and closer to rest, as other trajectories usually are. For the whispering-in <note>Kepler uses the term "insinuans," suggesting how the Earth's own movement "sneaks" into our observations of other bodies.</note> motion of the Earth easily grants them a circular appearance. For instance, the comet of 1577: if it had risen in a straight line from the plane of the Tropic of Capricorn toward the North Pole, or even at a slightly more inclined but still straight line; then the Earth, as it circles the resting Sun, imparts the appearance of circular motion to the comet. In the same way, as the Earth circles a comet that is nearly stationary (for the comet itself moves almost entirely sideways in this hypothesis), it bestows that same appearance of circular motion upon it. Thus, the comet of Regiomontanus <note>Johannes Müller von Königsberg (1436–1476), a celebrated Renaissance astronomer.</note>, carried in a straight line from the deepest ether past the Earth, and passing it very closely, will find a beautiful opportunity to complete 40 degrees of a great circle in a single day at the midpoint of its appearance, and very little before and after. Here also the cause will be clear why the tail, at that moment in time when the comet was so fast, equaled 50 degrees in length. According to Theorem 22 of the fourth book of Vitello.* <note>Vitello (Witelo) was a 13th-century scientist whose work on optics was the standard text before Kepler's.</note>

*Using this aid, some have claimed regarding the star of the year 1572 <note>This refers to the famous supernova observed by Tycho Brahe in Cassiopeia.</note> that it was withdrawn into the deep ether by a straight-line motion, using the argument of its decreasing size; for this, Theorems 4 and 132 of the fourth book of Vitello served them. Indeed, they reasoned correctly from an optical perspective, if you grant them their assumptions. However, you may see in the author <note>Referring to Tycho Brahe.</note> what he argued against them in Book 1 of his "Introductory Exercises" <note>original: "Progymnasmatum"</note>, based solidly and with great evidence from other sciences.*

## On the ingenious observation of the diameters of the Sun and Moon, and of their eclipses.

### Problem I.

**I**Nstrumentum Eclipticum <term>Ecliptic Instrument (a specialized camera obscura used for solar and lunar measurements)</term> to construct. Let a stage be erected under the open sky, with many layers of black cloth, lest any light break in. If this convenience is lacking, let a room be chosen facing the region from which the solar eclipse will be viewed. Let this room have a wall that is not thick, which provides a window; and let it be possible for both this window and all cracks to be blocked against the entry of light—

...entry. Then, a **Rule** <term>Rule (Latin: *Regula*); a long, straight sighting rod or ruler used for alignment</term> should be fashioned of the greatest possible length, with all its lines perfectly straight. Its thickness should be that of a planed board, and its width half a foot. It should be fitted in such a way—since wood is flexible—that it rests upon a support or "back" and is supported at a point midway between its ends to prevent it from bending. However, it should not be perforated through the middle of its width, lest it be weakened and break under its own weight. Instead, a small beam should be joined to the line of the back where it will rest, so that the center of the hole or socket <note>original: *matricula*</note> can be placed exactly along the line of the joint.

The socket should have its own small axle. Next, let a swiveling little column be made upon the axis; it should be bifid <note>split into two parts or "forked"</note> at the top, so that it can receive the thickness of the rule in its slit. It must be perforated so that it can be passed through by the same axle as the rule. The small beam, in which the socket receives the column, should be supported by equal timbers rising transversely on either side; these should set the column perfectly upright <note>original: *perpendiculo*</note>, enclosing the rounded column in a hollow embrace at the top. To this small beam, three others should be joined, so that a rectangular frame <note>original: *parallelogrammum rectangulum*</note> is formed from them all, serving in place of an **Azimuthal circle** <term>Azimuthal circle; a graduated circle used to measure the horizontal angle (azimuth) of a celestial body</term>.

At the head of the column, where the axis exits into the beam, a crossbeam <note>original: *transtrum*</note> should be attached and joined to one of the flat faces of the column which has the slit above. This crossbeam must also be pinned to the transverse column so that the column remains at a right angle to the crossbeam. Thus, if the crossbeam resting on the rectangular frame is moved, it will turn the column. The crossbeam should be of a suitable length and hollowed out in the middle so that it can hold the thickness of the Rule within this slit; in this way, the rule may be carried around together with the crossbeam and the column.

At the same time, it must be possible to raise the rule toward the zenith <note>original: *verticem*</note> or lower it toward the horizon, as much as the altitude of the Sun demands near the beginning and end of the eclipse. For this reason, it is proper for the column to be tall enough so that the rectangular frame never hinders the rule. Furthermore, the crossbeam and the rule itself must be long enough so they do not slip apart when the Sun is setting. The slits on both sides must be aligned, and the square itself raised high enough so that the rule, when lowered, does not strike the floor. The horizontal plane can be easily checked by a plumb line <note>original: *perpendiculum*</note> hanging from the column. Truly, this design cannot be universal unless either a geometric square is made from the crossbeam and column, or a proper quadrant is used. However, for these sudden needs, this makeshift structure was sufficient for me.

### THE OPTICAL PART OF ASTRONOMY. 337

Now, concerning the **Rule** <note>original: "Regula"; here meaning a long measuring staff or rod</note>, which is of primary use in this situation. On this rod, measure a certain length from the point of the pinning <note>original: "infibulationis"; the point where components are joined or hinged</note> downward, not exceeding the height of the small column. There, make notches <note>original: "crenas"</note> in both sides of the width, perpendicular to the length. At the head of the rule, which will be at the top, across the axis, make similar notches, separated from the lower ones by about 12 feet. Next, prepare two matching small boards <note>original: "tabellas"</note>, a palm's width or slightly more; the length should be composed of its own width and that of the pole, and the thickness should be such that it fits into the notches of the rule. In the middle of the width, cut out a section from one side of the length, so that the height of the slots equals the width of the rule, and the width of the rule's thickness—after the notches are made—fits snugly. Thus, the boards inserted into the notches will be both parallel to each other and perpendicular to the rule in both length and width. On each board, draw a line along the length, rising from the middle of the slot and the thickness of the rule; and at the midpoint of that line, at the point of intersection, let another line be drawn perpendicularly across the entire width of the board.

Afterward, in the board that is to be the **upper** one, remove the middle parts where the lines intersect, creating a square window <term>aperture|a small opening for light to pass through</term> two fingers wide. However, let the remaining parts of the straight lines stay on the margins of this window. Then, on a very thin plate of bronze <note>original: "lamina ænea"</note>, well-flattened and not stiff, let two lines intersect at right angles. At the center of this intersection, make a small hole the size of a pea, ensuring that this diameter is smaller in proportion to the distance between the boards than the diameters of the luminaries <note>The Sun and the Moon</note> are to their own distances, according to **Chapter 2, Proposition 6** <note>Kepler refers to his earlier geometric proofs regarding how light behaves when passing through small apertures</note>. Let it be filed so that the hole is accurately circular and centered between the crossed lines. The width of the bronze plate should be slightly larger than the small window. This plate is to be fixed to the perforated board so that its lines align with the lines on the board, and the hole is positioned in the very center of the window.

On the other board, which is to be the **lower** one and positioned with its surface facing upward, describe a circle from the center of the intersection of the lines, as large as the width of the board allows. Divide this from the top to the middle parts into 90 degrees each, and the same on both sides from the bottom. Or, if you prefer, use another series of numbers. Then, let the board hold a very short stylus <note>a small pin or pointer</note> in the middle, at the center or intersection. Around this stylus, fit a revolving disk <note>original: "rotula"</note>, upon which we will later describe small circles from the point of attachment. From the other side of the disk, there should project—

Once these things are constructed, measure everything with the greatest precision, just as I did with my own instrument. Let the window that allows the rod to pass outside be well-fortified all around against the light.

**Problem II.**

*To measure the diameter of the Sun with the instrument. This could generally be done according to the 8th and 9th propositions of the second chapter with any ray, admitted through any window, even a square one; however, the senses here do not follow mathematical subtlety. Instead, according to the 29th proposition of the first chapter, the edges of the image—where only a few parts of the Sun radiate—are not perceived, due to the brightness of the central parts of the image where all parts of the Sun radiate. This happened in the practice of the <term>Tychonics</term> <note>The followers or assistants of the astronomer Tycho Brahe.</note>, while they used a ray indeed, but with a square opening that was larger than what would allow for a complete intersection according to the 6th proposition of the second chapter.*

Therefore, let the instrument be prepared, and let the rod be directed toward the body of the Sun. This is done by a double rotation: one of the rod upon its column, the other of the column and the cross-bar upon the Azimuthal quadrant <note>A device used to measure the horizontal angle (azimuth) of a celestial object.</note>. Thus the Sun, striking the upper tablet directly, will send its rays through the small window of the plate and the channel, into the darkened room and onto the lower tablet. It will create a round image of the illuminated surface, according to the eighth proposition of the second chapter. When you see this image (which we shall henceforth call the <term>Ray</term> <note>original: "Radium"</note>), first take its diameter with a compass as accurately as you can. But because trembling may hinder you, using half of what you took with the compass, draw a small circle from the center of the tablet (which acts as the wall); then draw others, some slightly narrower and others wider, as many as you **need** <insert>to use</insert>.

->**What the Abacus actually was among the Ancients.**<-

It is a well-known fact that the ancients, especially the Greeks and Romans, used so-called *counting boards* for calculating, which they called <term>abacos</term> <note>The Latin plural of abacus; a flat surface or board used for arithmetic</note>.
<margin>Pliny, Book 35, Chapter 18.
Cicero in the Paradoxes.</margin>
There were various types of these. Some were simply sprinkled with sand, upon which one drew <term>characters</term> <note>original: "Characteres"; numbers or letters</note> with a stylus, as can be read in the works of *Martianus Capella*.
<margin>Martianus Capella, Book 7.</margin>
Others, however, had certain grooves or furrows in which one could slide counting-pennies <note>rechen-pfennige; these were metal jetons or tokens moved across a board to perform sums</note> back and forth.
The form of such a Roman <term>abacus</term> <note>original: "Abaci"</note> can be found in the works of *Pignorius* <note>Lorenzo Pignoria (1571–1631), an Italian antiquarian who illustrated ancient Roman life</note>, as it is included here.

In the year 1600, in the month of June, the parts of the ray <note>meaning the image of the Sun projected through the aperture</note> at Graz in Styria <note>original: "Gratii Styriæ"; Graz is the city in Austria where Kepler taught before moving to Prague</note>, viewed through the same small window and at the same distance, appeared to me to be 105 1/2. Moreover, that there is no more than a one-minute difference between the summer and winter diameters is marvelous, and how aptly it fits with the true and geometric eccentricity of the Sun (if you set aside the fallacy arising from a physical cause, which is discussed in chapter 10). Tycho Brahe and the Landgrave <note>original: "Landgrauiani"; referring to William IV, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel, a prominent astronomer</note> demonstrate by a unanimous calculation that the Eccentricity <note>the amount by which an orbit deviates from a perfect circle</note> is 3,600 out of 100,000. **Problem III.**
*To observe the diameter of the Sun through a narrow opening.*

I found this in the observations of Tycho, to which was added a eulogy stating that the Right-angle is the master of all Mathematics. Let AB be a plane equidistant to the Horizon, and AE a wall perpendicular to AB, in which there is a narrow opening <term>rima: literally a crack or slit</term> GE and a light source DF. From its highest part F, a ray descends through G, the bottom edge of the opening, and extends to point C, nearest to the perpendicular A. 

<margin>Restore the letter E, which is broken above the G.</margin>

[Diagram: A geometric diagram showing a vertical wall AE with an aperture GE. Rays from a light source DF pass through the aperture to a horizontal plane AB at points C and B. Point A is at the base of the wall.]

Conversely, from the lowest edge of the light source D, through the top of the opening E, the ray DE extends to the most distant point B. Therefore, as CA is to the total sine <note>original: "totum sinum"; a trigonometric term for the radius of the circle used in calculations, usually 100,000</note>, so AG is to the tangent of the angle GCA, which measures the altitude of the highest edge F above the horizon. Again, as BA is to the total sine, so AE is to the tangent of the angle EBA, which measures the altitude of the lowest edge D above the horizon.

By subtracting the smaller arc from the larger, the angle is left which the body of the luminary occupies here on Earth. This method is also good, if care can be taken that in some building EA is precisely perpendicular to AB, and sufficiently high. Tycho, on March 15, 1578, observed the diameter this way; it resulted in 30' 40" | 30' 06" | 30' 44" | 30' 50" | and on June 14, 30' 04" twice | 29' 30" once.

There exists among Tycho’s astronomical letters an epistle from Mästlin <note>Michael Mästlin, Kepler's university professor and mentor</note>, my Teacher, to the consul of Augsburg, if I am not mistaken, in which he makes the diameter of the Sun nearly the same, except that by the hypothesis of a simple Eccentric—

...inherent in the eccentricity, he expands it; and indeed at the **apogee** <note>The point in an orbit where a celestial body is farthest from the Earth.</note> he says he found it to be 30' 36". In the mean longitude, 30' 11"; and in the **perigee** <note>The point in an orbit where a celestial body is closest to the Earth.</note>, 31' 45". Nor does Gemma <note>Gemma Frisius (1508–1555), a Dutch mathematician and instrument maker.</note> differ much using his **radius** <term>Cross-staff: an early astronomical tool used to measure the angle between two celestial bodies.</term>, if anything certain can be sought with such a crude instrument.

Indeed, the ancients agree entirely with me. Archimedes testifies concerning Aristarchus <note>Aristarchus of Samos (c. 310–230 BCE), the first known proponent of a sun-centered universe.</note> that he said the diameter of the Sun was 1/720th part of four right angles <note>original: "quatuor rectorum". A full circle is 360 degrees; 1/720th of that is 0.5 degrees, or 30 arcminutes.</note>, which is 30 minutes. Hipparchus, however (whom Albategnius <note>Al-Battani (c. 858–929), a pivotal Arab astronomer whose work influenced Europe.</note> complains that Ptolemy followed in his calculations), denied that the Sun varied its size to any perceptible degree from apogee to perigee. This was surely because the change is no more than one minute; and it is gathered (as seen above in Chapter 8) that he himself assumed it to be 30 minutes, as is clear from Ptolemy and his commentator, Theon. Proclus seems to testify the same regarding Sosigenes <note>An Egyptian astronomer who helped Julius Caesar design the Julian calendar.</note>.

Ptolemy was the first to depart from the ancients' modes of observation as well as from the very truest quantity of the diameter of the **luminaries** <note>A traditional term for the Sun and the Moon.</note>. He used an absurd and even incredible method of measuring, which authors—and even Copernicus himself—have followed until now. For this reason, I used that measure in Chapter 7 without much risk. But the matter is certain and open for anyone to explore: the diameter of the Sun is 30 minutes at apogee and 31 minutes at perigee.

### Problem IV.
***To observe the diameter of the Moon by an instrument.***

This is a difficult task. For the Moon's brightness is not so great as to suffice for our eyes to have certainty of vision. And if it shines through an instrument into a **chamber** <note>A reference to the "camera obscura," where light enters a dark room through a small hole.</note> and into darkness, it is very difficult to distinguish between the ray of light and the neighboring dark edges of the paper. You shall attempt the matter this way, however: describe several small circles on paper, very close to each other in size but increasing slightly in order. Fill the enclosed surface with ink, especially around the edges, so that the blackness occupies either the entire surface or at least some width from the edges toward the center. You will apply these in order to the tablet on the instrument, considering which of them the Moon's ray surrounds in such a way that the illuminated whiteness of the paper around the black circles catches the eye. For whichever is first found to be narrower than the ray, most closely...

In the year 1600, July 15/25, <note>Kepler often provides dates in both the old Julian and new Gregorian calendars.</note> at Graz, I found the particles of the radius <note>These "particles" refer to units or divisions on his measuring instrument, likely a cross-staff or a scale within a camera obscura.</note> to be more than 105 1/2 and fewer than 110. So easily does it elude one who is nodding <note>Kepler suggests that even a small lack of attention or poor conditions can lead to significant errors.</note>. Therefore, other methods must be tried for observing the diameter of this luminary.

### *On judging the proportion of the visible diameter of the Moon to the diameter*
### *of the Sun from the horn of the Moon in its first*

Above, in chapter 6, number 11, I mentioned the rising of the Moon which I saw on March 4/14, 1603, at Prague at the 6th hour, when the Sun was in 23° 49' Pisces and the Moon was in 14° 41' Aries, moving along the Ecliptic. The arc through the visible place of the Moon and through the Sun intersected the horizon at an angle of about 78°. For the horns of the Moon clearly pointed very nearly to the left of the zenith. For this [the horn] was evidently lacking from a semicircle, according to the senses. I say that from this, it is demonstrated that the visible diameter of the Moon to the diameter of the Sun...

...the visible center of the Sun was notably larger, even though the Sun was seeking its <term>mean distance</term> <note>The average distance in an elliptical orbit.</note>, being closer to its <term>perigee</term> <note>The point in an orbit where a body is closest to the Earth.</note>, and the Moon had not moved even two signs of the zodiac away from its <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in an orbit where a body is furthest from the Earth.</note>. ### PROOF

Let the <term>great circle</term> <note>A circle on the surface of a sphere that has the same circumference as the sphere itself.</note> of the body of the Moon be drawn from center **A**, labeled **B C D**. In this circle, let **B A C** be the diameter, and let **E A** be at a right angle to it. Let **E** be the center of the Sun; therefore, the circle of illumination will be parallel to **B A C**. Let this be **F G**. Now, let a point **H** be taken outside the line **E A**, which represents a location on the surface of the Earth—for instance, Prague. Since **H A** is the axis of the circle of vision, this circle will be at a right angle to **H A**. Let this circle be **K M L**, cutting off a small portion of the Moon that is illuminated by the Sun, or a <term>horn</term> <note>Kepler uses the term "cornu" (horn) to describe the thin crescent shape of the visible illuminated portion of the Moon.</note>, the true width of which is **L G**. 

And since this horn falls short of being a semicircle, the "half-horn" will fall short of a quadrant; it will therefore not reach as far as **M**. Let the circle of illumination **F G** therefore intersect the circle of vision **K L** at a point beyond **M**, toward **L**; let that point be **I**. Indeed, let the axis of vision **H A** intersect **F G** at **N**, and let the axis of illumination **E A** intersect the same at **R**. Therefore, if the horn had reached plainly as far as **N**, the circle which passes through **N** parallel to **K L** itself (representing the vision) would have been smaller than the illumination **F G**. For **A N**, being the <term>hypotenuse</term> <note>original: "subtensa"</note> to the right angle **A R N**, is longer than **A R**. Therefore, a circle through **N** would have been further from the center **A** than the circle **F G**; for this reason, it would be smaller, since only the circle passing through the center is the largest of all.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Now, indeed, the half-horn <note>The "horn" refers to the pointed end of the lunar crescent.</note> did not extend all the way to *N*, so that it might be seen at the length of a quadrant <note>A quadrant is 90 degrees, or a quarter of a circle.</note>, but it fell short at *I*. Therefore, *KML* stood further away from *A* than *N*; it was, therefore, much smaller than *N*. But even the one through *N* was smaller than the illuminating circle *FG*; therefore, the visual circle *KL* was much smaller than the illuminating one. Truly, by the 24th Theorem of Euclid’s *Optics* <note>original: "Theorema Opticorum Euclidis"; Euclid's Optics was a foundational text for Kepler's work on vision.</note>, the less of a sphere that is seen, the larger its diameter appears. And as demonstrated above in Chapter 6, number 3, if the visual circle *KL* and the illuminating circle *FG* had coincided, both luminaries <note>The Sun and the Moon.</note> would have been seen at the same angle. Therefore, because *KTL* is now smaller than *FTG*, the apparent diameter of the Moon is larger than that of the Sun—and that quite perceptibly, although it is near its apogee <note>The point in the Moon's orbit where it is farthest from the Earth and should appear smallest.</note>.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Now, so that the theorem may be complete, let the proportion of the horn to the rest of the body's circumference be known from visual estimation without error, which is indeed quite difficult. And I myself could not estimate anything more precisely than that the horn was midway between a third and a half of the visual circle, that is, between 120 and 180 degrees. Let it be our purpose to investigate the visible diameter of the Moon from this calculation. Therefore, *LI*—the horn—will be half of the estimation. Let *D* be the pole of vision and let arc *DI* descend, intersecting *BC* at *Q*. Therefore, in triangle *DQC*, the angle *QDC* is given as the length of half the horn. *DCQ* is truly a right angle. And side *DC* is given. For because the Sun is at mean longitude, and the Moon is 5 or 6 degrees past its apogee, the ratio of *HE* to *HA* will be given from the hypotheses of the authors. But the angle *AHE* is known from the visible position of both lights; therefore, with *EA* extended to *T*, *TAH* will be given, the measure of which is *TD*, and its remainder to the quadrant is the sought *DC*. In *DQC*, therefore, let *DQ* be sought from the givens, and then *DQC*. Then, from *I*, let a perpendicular arc fall on *BC*, which shall be *IS*. In triangle *IQS*, therefore, angle *S* is a right angle, *Q* is given, and side *IS* is 15 minutes—which is the distance of the circle of illumination from the great circle, as seen above in Chapter 6, number 3. Therefore, *QI* will be given, to be subtracted from *QD* so that the arc between the pole and the circle of vision may be obtained; the complement of this to the quadrant indicates the visible semidiameter, through the demonstrations in Chapter 6, number 3. It must not be hidden that the apparent diameter of the Moon becomes immense from this, if you say that even the smallest perceptible amount is missing from the semicircle of the nascent horn.

### APPENDIX.

***Other methods of measuring the Moon’s diameter compared with those previously mentioned.***

Although the most certain and safest measurement of all will finally be determined later through observations of solar eclipses: here, meanwhile, the remaining methods are to be examined. Indeed, Hipparchus’s <term>dioptra</term> <note>A sighting instrument used by ancient astronomers, consisting of a rod and movable markers, to measure the angular diameters of celestial bodies.</note> is known from the writings of Ptolemy; though Ptolemy used it himself, he despaired of determining a certain quantity from it. He found only this: that the Moon at its <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in the Moon's orbit where it is farthest from the Earth.</note> appears equal to the solar diameter, and at its <term>perigee</term> <note>The point in the Moon's orbit where it is closest to the Earth.</note> it appears larger, which is also what Hipparchus had said.

In the year 1598, on the evening of March 29 (or April 8) at 8 o’clock in Graz, I saw the Moon joined with the western stars in the quadrilateral of the <term>Pleiades</term> <note>A prominent star cluster in the constellation Taurus, often called the "Seven Sisters."</note>, such that its edge was no more than a sixth part of the lunar diameter away from the nearest star. At its outer edge, it was as far from a bright star of the third magnitude as the width of its own body. At that position, the two stars on the western side of the quadrilateral were further apart than the Moon could have covered both at once, even if it had passed directly over them. The Moon was three days old, past its mean longitude and moving toward apogee; being very close to its maximum northern latitude, its whole body could be seen very clearly <note>This likely refers to "Earthshine," where the dark portion of the Moon is faintly illuminated by light reflected from the Earth.</note>.

On the following July 17 (or 27) in the morning, between 2 and 3 o’clock, the Moon—again ascending toward apogee and closer to it, and near its northern limit—stood with its horns turned toward the Pleiades. A perpendicular line drawn from the bottom horn would have grazed the upper stars of the Pleiades. It had passed the Pleiades and was further from the brightest star than <term>Palilitium</term> <note>An ancient name for the bright red star Aldebaran, the "Eye of Taurus."</note> is from the neighboring <term>Hyades</term> <note>original: *Sucularum*. A V-shaped star cluster in Taurus near Aldebaran.</note> toward the "nostrils" of Taurus, but less than the distance from those stars to the lowest star in the nostrils. The distance between the two bright transverse stars in the Pleiades seemed to equal the Moon's diameter. ### CHAPTER III.
### Of the Commanding and Obeying Power.

The **Practical Intellect** <note>The 'Practical Intellect' refers to the mind's ability to apply knowledge to action, as opposed to the 'Theoretical Intellect' which seeks knowledge for its own sake.</note> is called "Commanding" insofar as it does not rest in the mere contemplation of truth but moves further to direct and order an action.

<margin>What is Command?</margin>
**Command** (*Imperium*) is an act of the reason, presupposing an act of the will, by which one moves and directs something toward the performance of an action.

<margin>In what does it consist?</margin>
Regarding this act of command, there is a famous dispute among the Scholastics. **St. Thomas Aquinas** <note>A 13th-century philosopher and theologian who shaped much of Western thought.</note> (1a 2ae, q. 17. a. 1.) teaches that command is essentially an act of the **Reason**, because to command is to put things in order, and ordering is the proper task of the intellect. However, it presupposes an act of the **Will**, for the reason only moves to command because the will has already desired the end. Others, such as **Scotus** and **Suárez**, argue that command is an act of the will, as the will is the primary mover of the soul's faculties. In this work, we follow the Thomistic view: the will provides the impulse, but the reason provides the "command" or the specific direction.

<margin>Which is the obeying power?</margin>
The **Obeying Power** is that faculty which is moved and directed by the command of the higher part of the soul (the reason and the will). This includes both the internal and external powers of man, but in different ways.

<margin>The two-fold subjection of the lower powers to reason.</margin>
**Aristotle** (in *Politics*, Book 1, Chapter 3) teaches that there is a two-fold way in which the lower parts of a human being obey the higher:

1.  **Despotic Rule** (*Principatus despoticus*): This is like the rule of a master over a slave. The slave has no power to resist the master's will. In the human person, the soul rules the body and its limbs (like the hands or feet) with this kind of absolute power. Unless there is a physical disability, the limbs immediately obey the mind's command.
2.  **Political or Royal Rule** (*Principatus politicus & regalis*): This is like the rule of a king over free citizens, who have their own will and can sometimes resist. This is how the **Reason** rules the **Sensitive Appetite** <note>The 'Sensitive Appetite' refers to our irrational desires and emotions, such as anger, fear, or lust.</note>. Our emotions and passions do not always immediately obey reason; they can "rebel" or pull us in a different direction, requiring the reason to persuade or govern them more gently.

Therefore, the **Sensitive Appetite** is truly an "obeying power," but because it possesses its own natural inclinations, it must be brought into harmony with the **Rational Appetite** (the Will) through habit and virtue.

<summary>This chapter explores the hierarchy of the human soul, specifically how the "Practical Intellect" issues commands and how the body and emotions ("Sensitive Appetite") respond to those commands through either absolute or persuasive control.</summary>

<keywords>Practical Intellect, Command, Thomas Aquinas, Aristotle, Despotic Rule, Political Rule, Sensitive Appetite, Will, Psychology, Scholasticism</keywords>

->Problem VI.<-

*To estimate the quantity of a defect in an Eclipse of the Moon, or even of the Sun.*

This is commonly done without an instrument, through an imaginary division of the diameter into 12 parts <note>original: "digitos" or digits. Astronomers divided the disk of the Sun or Moon into 12 equal parts to measure the "magnitude" of an eclipse.</note>.

In this way we use it most safely when the obscured part and the illuminated part are nearly equal. Thus <term>Maestlin</term><note>Michael Maestlin, Kepler's university professor and mentor.</note> in the year 1572 on the 25th of June estimated the maximum defect to be precisely half of the diameter. (But <term>Gemma Frisius</term><note>A Dutch mathematician and instrument maker.</note> writes in book 2 of his *Cosmocritice*, folio 233, that 8 digits were missing at Leuven.)

An observer is helped even more when the shadowed circumference is in view at the same time. But outside of these cases, the method is fluid and dangerous.

In the year 1601, on November 29 or December 9, a good portion of the Moon's body indeed remained, but exactly how much it was could not be discerned by anyone with confidence. <term>Ambrose Rhodes</term><note>Ambroshius Rhodius, an assistant who worked with Tycho Brahe.</note>, who for some time assisted Tycho with calculations, estimated the defect at 10 digits at Wittenberg.

In the year 1603, on November 8 and 18, others contended that more than a fourth part was in defect; to me it seemed to be something less than this: and yet the shadowed part of the circumference was conspicuous.

Since it is of great importance to astronomy that partial eclipses <note>A "partial defect" or partial eclipse occurs when only a portion of the celestial body is obscured.</note> are correctly recorded, Tycho Brahe—following the instructions of Cornelius Gemma—was accustomed to using a <term>radius</term> <note>The "radius" here refers to a cross-staff or "Jacob’s staff," a graduated rod used to measure angles between celestial bodies or the angular diameters of the sun and moon.</note> to measure both the diameter of the Moon before the eclipse and the remaining part at the moment of maximum eclipse.

Furthermore, the difficulties by which this method is hindered have been explained at great length in the preceding sections.

On June 14, 1592, Tycho Brahe observed the diameter of the Moon while it was still whole to be 32 minutes <note>A "minute" in this context is a minute of arc, a unit of angular measurement equal to 1/60th of a degree.</note> by means of the radius. Then, around the middle of the eclipse, he found 14 minutes remaining, such that 18 minutes had been eclipsed. Yet this quantity differs greatly from his own calculation, which claims 26 1/4 minutes for the portion of the lunar body within the shadow. Therefore, I attribute this to the difficulty of observing. For even if someone were to call the Tychonic calculation or the diameter of the shadow into doubt (which I discuss elsewhere), he would never succeed in making this eclipse fit into a consistent rule with the others at this quantity.

Therefore, so that I might rely on somewhat firmer supports here as well, I have been accustomed to estimate the missing arc of the lunar circumference. For if this is given, and the proportion of the diameters of the Moon and the shadow is moderately well known, the quantity of the eclipse itself is also given. Let the circle of the shadow, **FEG**, be drawn with center **D**, and the circumference of the lunar disk, **FAG**, with center **B**, cutting the shadow at **F** and **G**. Let the centers be connected to each other and to **F**; likewise, connect the points of intersection with lines **FB**, **FD**, **BD**, and **FG**, which will intersect each other orthogonally <note>Intersects at right angles (90 degrees).</note> at **C**. Let **FAG**, for example, be a sixth part of the circumference; then **FA** will be half, namely 30 degrees. This is the angle **FBC**. Therefore, angle **BFC** is 60 degrees, and the <term>secant</term> **BF** is 200,000, of which **FC** is 100,000. <note>Kepler is using early trigonometric tables where the radius was often set to 100,000 or 1,000,000 to avoid decimals.</note> But let the proportion of **BF** to **FD** be given, which is 1 to 3; thus **FD** will be 600,000, the secant of angle **DFC** 80° 24'. The tangents of these same angles are also given: **BC** as 173,205 and **CD** as 591,236. When these are subtracted from **BA** (200,000) and **DE** (600,000), they leave **CA** as 26,795 and **CE** as 8,764. Therefore, in the system where **BF** is 200,000, the missing part **EA** is 35,559.

### Problem VII.

*Given the true appearance of the eclipsed Sun, to find the true proportion of the diameters of the Sun and Moon, and the true Ecliptic digits.*

This is a problem from Maestlin <note>Michael Maestlin (1550–1631), Kepler’s university professor and mentor</note>, my teacher. We used to go up under the roof of a church, and with the doors secured against the light, someone would climb up onto the high beams to remove a tile in a suitable spot so that a very narrow crack was open to the light—now this one, now that one, depending on whether the beams intercepted one ray or another. Thus, the convenience of the building's height provided us with a ray much longer than my instrument or measuring rod, which was no longer than 12 feet. This ray, while the Sun was being eclipsed, he captured on paper (following the principles in Chapter 2, Section 9). And because the entire beam of light is a "right cone" <term>Right cone: A geometric cone where the tip is directly above the center of the base</term> whose vertex is at the hole, it is clear that unless the paper is placed perfectly perpendicular to the beam, the shape formed on the paper will not be a circle (according to Proposition 9 of the first book of Apollonius <note>Apollonius of Perga, a Greek geometer known for his work on conic sections</note>). Therefore, he drew several circles of various sizes on the paper, roughly matching the size he saw the ray occupy—

...occupied, and he would divide the drawn diameters into 12 equal parts or digits <term>digits: a traditional astronomical unit representing 1/12th of the diameter of the Sun or Moon, used to measure the extent of an eclipse</term>. Then he would catch the ray of light upon the marked circles from the opposite side, so that the edge of the ray coincided exactly with the circumference of one of the circles, by switching circles or by moving toward or away from the aperture until this was achieved. Let A B C D be the ray of the eclipsed Sun <note>original: "Solis deficientis"</note> and its true appearance; let its exterior surface A B C match the circle drawn from center E. Therefore, the circle A D C with center F represents the lunar body, and the proportion found mechanically between the radius F D and the radius E B is the proportion of the visible diameter of the Moon to the visible diameter of the Sun.

However, the diameter of the Moon observed by this method usually appeared smaller than that of the Sun. Yet, through Proposition 11 of the second chapter, it is clear that unless the aperture is extremely small—like a mere point—the proportion of the diameters is always distorted; the Moon appears smaller than it truly is, and according to Proposition 12, fewer digits are shown. Therefore, this method is unreliable when used so simply. ### Problem VIII.
### To capture with points the appearance or ray of the eclipsed Sun, as it is shaped in the instrument.

This is done as in the preceding section, but with slightly greater certainty. For the instrument ensures that I do not need to change the circles, nor move closer or further away. Indeed, on the day the eclipse is to occur, the size of the Sun's ray is noted accurately in the instrument, and a circle of that size is described. This circle, applied to the tablet, is moved around everywhere, and throughout that entire day it will certainly match the ray of the Sun. Regarding the marking of the points, however, the same complaint remains as before. For the Sun's ray is moved at every moment; therefore, both the crossbar and the ruler on the crossbar must be moved together during the marking. 

Nevertheless, use this caution: Mark one point when the outer circumference of the ray exactly fits into the circle. Then, by moving the instrument, anticipate the ray; while the ray follows, you will note with your eyes the place for marking the second point. It will be helpful to have a spectator present who, while you are intent on the other edge <note>original: "limbum"</note>, may signal to you when the edge from the other side falls again upon the point already marked. Then you will apply it again for the sake of proof; and do so quickly, before the eclipse increases or decreases perceptibly. However, this appearance is **adulterated** <note>Kepler uses 'adulterated' to describe how the image is blurred or distorted because the aperture (the 'window') has a physical size, rather than being a single mathematical point. ### Problem XI.
### To deduce the true appearance of the eclipse from the transverse ruler.

Let **C D E F** be the appearance of the eclipsed ray, whose center is **G** and the marked diameter is **D F**. Let the line of the index be **I D H**. And let line **C H E** touch the obtuse horns **C** and **E**, and cut the marked diameter at **H**; and let it cut the same segment **C F E** at **F**. [A geometric diagram showing a circle and arcs with labels A, b, c, d, e, f, g, h, i, k, l, m, n, o, p, q, s. A horizontal bar represents the 'regula' or ruler.]

Then, with center **G** and distance **G L**, let circle **N L O** be written, which will represent the correct appearance of the Sun, as shown in Problem 9 of this book. This will cut the line **N P O**; let it cut at **N** and **O**. Therefore, through the three points **N**, **M**, and **O**, let a circle be described whose center is **K**. The demonstration of this lies in the fact that the two slits of both the cross-bar and the small column place the rule in the plane of the vertical circle; the line of length on the tablet follows this same plane, and from this line the division of the outer circle on the tablet begins.

If the whole instrument is not always at hand—for instance, if nothing is present but the rule with the tablets—you will direct the rule into the vertical plane in this way: join a transverse piece two feet long (or more) to the base of the rule at right angles, and then allow the rule with the transverse piece to lie upon a level floor parallel to the horizon. For the transverse piece will raise the rule onto its back so that it fits into the vertical plane, exactly as the same thing was achieved before through the slits of the cross-bar and the small column.

**Problem XVI.**
*To also designate inclinations on the floor.*

It was stated in the second chapter that a ray of this kind in a dark room <note>Kepler is describing a *camera obscura* setup</note> forms a **right cone**, provided that the circular opening is perpendicular to the light; its vertex is above the opening, and its base is on the illuminated surface. If this surface is presented directly to the window <note>meaning the surface is parallel to the window or perpendicular to the central axis of the light</note>, the base of the cone, or the illuminated portion, will be a **circle**, according to Proposition 8 of the second chapter. But if the surface is presented obliquely to the ray, the base of this cone, or the tilted portion of the illuminated surface, will be a **conic section**, specifically an **ellipse**: provided that the surface intercepts the entire ray, according to Proposition 13 of the first book of Apollonius <note>Apollonius of Perga was an ancient Greek mathematician known as "The Great Geometer" for his work on conic sections</note>. Therefore, since in our climate the plane of the horizon or the floors always receive the Sun's ray at an angle, the shape of the ray will always be elliptical; this remains true for almost all window shapes, provided that a full intersection occurs. For, according to Proposition 6 of the second chapter, the window then contributes very little of its own shape to the cone, while the Sun contributes the most. Since the Sun is circular in appearance, it will nevertheless produce a nearly right cone, even if the shape of the window happens to be something other than circular.

   Therefore, if you lack an instrument—as happened to me on February 25 or March 7 in the year 1598—trace ellipses on paper placed on the floor, just as the Sun portrays them; and because they move their position quickly, make three or four marks

[A geometric diagram on the left side of the text shows an ellipse inscribed within a larger circle, with various intersecting lines and points labeled with letters: A, B, C, D, K, g, n, m, h, f, s.]

at the highest point **A** and the lowest point **B** of the ellipse's vertex, as well as at the tips of the two horns <note>the points of the crescent shape formed during a partial solar eclipse</note>. For the length of the ellipse **AB** extends itself along the <term>vertical circle: an imaginary circle passing through the point directly overhead (zenith) and the point directly below (nadir), perpendicular to the horizon</term>. Wherefore, by means of knowing the ellipse, the inclination of the eclipse **CD** <note>the line representing the orientation of the obscured part of the sun</note> to the vertical line **AB** will be given by its position. This is especially useful at the beginning and end of an eclipse, where the points **C** and **D** become one. Likewise, it helps in discerning whether the shadow stands precisely at **A** or **B**, or at the "squared" locations <note>90-degree points</note>. Outside of these cases, it is a bit more precarious.

### Problem XVII.

***To determine the inclination of the eclipse from the description of the ellipse.***

First, the mechanical method is as follows. In the preceding diagram, draw the longer diameter **AB**, and let it be bisected at point **E**. With **E** as the center and the distance **EA** or **EB** as the radius, let a circle be drawn. From the corners <note>original: "cornubus"; likely referring to the 'horns' or tips of the eclipsed solar image.</note> **C** and **D**, drop perpendicular lines onto **AB**, extending them to that part of the circumference; let these points be **CG** and **DF**. Let the arc of the circumference **GF** be bisected at **H**, and let the line **EH** be drawn. Therefore, the angle **HEB** is the angle of inclination, which is determined from the arc **HB**, assuming the semi-circle **AHB** is divided into 180 degrees. Since this cone is extremely acute—as its angle is no greater than half a degree—the center of the ellipse deviates by a completely imperceptible amount from the axis of the cone. For this reason, from whatever point on the circumference of the ellipse a perpendicular is dropped onto the longer diameter, it cuts off the versed sine <term>versed sine: a trigonometric function (1 - cosine) used historically in astronomy to measure distances along the radius</term> of that arc starting from the vertical point in the circle of which **BA** is the diameter.

But if you have also marked two points for the shorter diameter, or if you have calculated the ratio of the shorter diameter to the longer diameter from the altitude of the Sun: for the sake of proof, you shall draw a circle from center **E** with the width of the shorter diameter. From points **C** and **D**, draw lines parallel to **AB** so that they intersect the smaller circle at **I** and **K**. If the midpoint of that arc falls upon the line **EH**, the description is certain. For again, the shorter diameter of the ellipse is imperceptibly longer than the line perpendicular to the axis at that point of the axis which lies in the plane or base. Therefore, a perpendicular drawn from any point of the elliptical circumference to the shorter diameter cuts off the right sine <term>right sine: the standard sine of an angle (the vertical distance from the diameter to a point on the circle)</term> between itself and the center, of that arc which is intercepted in the circle (having the width of the shorter diameter) between the vertical point (or that which is on line **AB**) and the given point.

However, lest those skilled in the elements of conics find something lacking in my work, I shall also add the precision <note>original: "ἀκρίβειαν" (akribeia); Greek for exactness or mathematical rigor.</note> from Apollonius <note>Apollonius of Perga (c. 240 – 190 BC), the "Great Geometer" known for his work on conic sections.</note>. Let **N** be the point upon which the axis of the cone falls. We shall then obtain **NA** and **NB** in this manner. Increase and decrease the distance of the Sun from the zenith by 15 minutes, or by however much the semidiameter of the Sun is, and of all three...

However, the shorter semi-diameter, originating from point N (which in the work of Apollonius is the <term>ordinate</term> <note>a line segment drawn from a point on a curve to its axis, perpendicular to that axis</note>), is obtained as follows: As the total sine is to the secant of the Sun's distance from the zenith <note>the point in the sky directly above the observer</note>, so is the tangent of fifteen minutes to the value of the shorter semi-diameter, using the same scale by which AN and NB are determined from the tangents. Therefore, this ordinate represents the more accurate width of the smaller circle.

And because there is a risk that you might not mark points A and B exactly in the middle of the circular edges—especially since, because of the time it takes, the edges of the light rays might move away from A and B before you have marked points C and D, which would ruin the measurements of CL and DM—you should therefore note, according to Proposition 21 of the first book of the <term>Conics</term> <note>referring to *The Conics* by Apollonius of Perga, the foundational Greek text on ellipses, parabolas, and hyperbolas</note>: just as the longer diameter AB (which Apollonius calls the axis of the figure) is to the shorter diameter (generally, as the transverse side of the figure... <note>the text cuts off mid-sentence at the end of the page</note>

...craftsmen should fix a quadrant, suitable for the vertical plane, onto a tripod, and place the quadrant into a circle with an open socket; they should then attach the circle to the same tripod at two opposite points on a line parallel to the horizon. This instrument is particularly useful.

This method should be used during a Lunar Eclipse, when our Ecliptic instrument <note>An "Ecliptic instrument" was a device designed to measure positions relative to the path of the sun (the ecliptic).</note> does not provide a sufficiently clear ray of the fading Moon in the dark, and the ray itself cannot withstand the presence of a lit candle for the purpose of counting the degrees of inclination on the measurement tablet; or if the frequent switching between candles and darkness hinders the eyesight in discerning the faint ray. ->**Problem XIX.**<-
<note>original: "Problema XIX."</note>
**To record certain inclinations of either eclipse in a common way.**
<note>original: "Populariter quasdam utriusq; deliquii inclinationes annotare." By "either eclipse," Kepler refers to both solar and lunar events. "Popularly" here means using simple, visual methods rather than complex mathematics.</note>

Look carefully at those moments when the shadow is precisely at the top, or at the lowest part of the luminary <note>The "luminary" refers to the body being eclipsed—the Sun or the Moon.</note>, or on either side. That is, when the horns <note>The "horns" or cusps are the pointed ends of the visible crescent during an eclipse.</note> are precisely upturned and supine, or prone and facing downward, or stand perfectly upright and perpendicular. For in these instances, visual estimation does not easily fail. Record these moments diligently in the following ways. Many examples of this rule are supplied from the observations of Tycho <note>Tycho Brahe (1546–1601), the Danish nobleman and astronomer whose precise data Kepler used to derive the laws of planetary motion.</note>; and also from those observed by me, which I will join immediately below.

**Another way to record the inclinations of a Lunar eclipse without an instrument.**
<note>original: "Alio modo sine instrumento deliquii Lunaris inclinationes annotare."</note>

Almost as before, note the times when the horns of the Moon coincide with any of the fixed stars or Planets in the same straight line, or are turned perpendicularly toward them. But then, in the final calculation, remember the <term>parallax of the Moon</term> <note>Parallax is the displacement or difference in the apparent position of an object viewed along two different lines of sight. Because the Moon is close to Earth, its position against the stars looks different depending on where on Earth you are standing.</note>, especially if it was compared to a nearby star. For the horns would appear in a different alignment if they had been viewed from the center of the earth. If you keep this one thing in mind, for the rest, this method offers a shortcut. For until now, the inclinations of the circle through the centers [of the Sun and Moon] relative to the vertical line were recorded, not indeed because...

### Problem XX.
### To record the times of the phases in a common manner.

Long ago, Regiomontanus <note>a famous 15th-century German mathematician and astronomer</note>, following Albategnius <note>original: "Albategnio," referring to the 9th-century Arab astronomer al-Battani</note>, taught to record the altitude of the Sun. At night, the altitude of some bright fixed star is most correctly taken. If the sky is cloudy and the stars are hidden, the altitude of the Moon itself is recorded. The recording of the <term>Azimuths</term> <note>the horizontal angle or direction of a celestial object</note> of all these also helps.

How the time is obtained from this is taught abundantly in the <term>doctrine of the first motion</term> <note>the branch of astronomy dealing with the daily rotation of the heavens from east to west</note>. I hear that the most distinguished man, Melchior Jöstel, has in hand an outstanding work of four hundred problems of the <term>prime mobile</term> <note>the outermost moving sphere of the heavens</note> through simple <term>prosthaphairesis</term> <note>a mathematical method using trigonometric identities to simplify multiplication into addition and subtraction, common before the invention of logarithms</note> of arcs and chords; this kind of calculation has been familiar to Tycho <note>Tycho Brahe</note> for many years, and was refined not insignificantly by Clavius, and is now finally being perfected by Jöstel. I therefore refer the reader there. For these are observational problems; those that follow in the second part will serve the <term>secondary mobiles</term> <note>the individual orbital motions of the planets and the Moon</note>, namely the motions of the Moon, not the prime mobile.

Tycho Brahe teaches how to use clocks <note>original: "horologiis"</note> more efficiently. The first trial of a clock is made over several preceding days. Then, having started from any known mark at the beginning of its run, notations are made in it—not only of the phases, but also of the <term>application</term> <note>the arrival or transit</note> of the Sun, Moon, or fixed stars to the <term>meridian</term> <note>the imaginary north-south line in the sky</note>, or another identical and certain circle. In this way, the phases are connected with the specific moments of the day through certain time intervals indicated by the clock. Examples are in Problem 21 and those following.

I will demonstrate some of the methods through examples. In the year 1595, April 13/23, at Graz in Styria, when the beginning of the eclipse was observed, the altitude of Arcturus <note>a very bright star in the constellation Boötes</note> was 44° <term>roughly</term> <note>original: "ὁλοχερῶς" (holocherōs), meaning in a general or rough sense</note>, measured with a paper <term>astrolabe</term> <note>an ancient astronomical instrument for solving problems relating to time and the position of the stars</note> three-quarters of a foot in width and a pendulum; the altitude of the Moon, however, was 15 1/2°. Since now no...

This is more of a piece of advice regarding those things which are usefully observed during Eclipses of the Moon, lest they perhaps be neglected; and it has some relationship with the preceding Proposition 19. Indeed, it can happen in various ways. It is best if the Eclipse occurs at the beginning of Cancer or Capricorn, and its midpoint coincides with the Moon’s arrival at the meridian <note>The meridian is the imaginary line passing through the north and south poles and the observer's zenith; an object "on the meridian" is at its highest point in the sky.</note>: or in whatever sign, provided that the Moon stands near the ninetieth degree <note><term>Nonagesimo gradu</term>: The highest point of the ecliptic (the sun's path) above the horizon at a given time.</note> around the middle [of the eclipse], and is not far removed from some fixed star in terms of longitude. But if it should be outside these points, provided that attention is paid to the middle of the eclipse, the other advantages can be supplied through the treatment of lunar parallaxes.

Direct a plane perpendicular to the horizon toward the south, or the ninetieth degree, or entirely toward the region of the Moon near the middle of the eclipse. From there, carefully note on a clock indicating minutes and seconds the moments at which the western and eastern limbs of the Moon, and a nearby fixed star, arrive at the meridian. For from the interval of times, the difference in the culminations <note>original: "mediationum"</note> of the heavens is obtained. If the Moon stands in the ninetieth degree at the very middle of the eclipse, the matter does not require a longer circuitous route, and the Right Ascension <note><term>Ascensio recta</term>: The distance of a point east of the First Point of Aries, measured along the celestial equator.</note> of the centers of both the Moon and the shadow is obtained, counted from a nearby fixed star; therefore, also the distance of the star from the center of the Sun. However, other aids lacking these conveniences are not to be despised.

Tycho <note>Tycho Brahe (1546–1601), the Danish nobleman and astronomer whose precise observations provided the foundation for Kepler’s laws.</note>, throughout the entire duration, before and after the middle, frequently took the distances of the unaffected limb <note>original: "marginis illęsi"</note> from nearby fixed stars using sextants and armillary spheres <note><term>armillas</term>: A model of objects in the sky consisting of a spherical framework of rings, used here as an observational instrument.</note>. It will also be useful to record the drawing of lines, as Maestlin <note>Michael Maestlin (1550–1631), Kepler’s former professor and a key defender of the Copernican system.</note> was accustomed to do in observations of the other stars.

It is believable that Hipparchus <note>A Greek astronomer (c. 190–120 BCE) often called the "father of astronomy."</note> used these methods in some way; who, as reported by Ptolemy in Book 3, Chapter 2, when he had discovered in the 32nd year of the third Callippic cycle <note>A 76-year period used by ancient Greeks to reconcile the solar year and lunar months.</note> that the vernal equinox occurred on the 27th day of the month of Mechir <note>A month in the ancient Egyptian calendar.</note> in the morning: later, from the observation of a coinciding lunar eclipse (in which the position of the Sun from the equinox—and therefore in the Zodiac—was given from the time; from the position of the Sun, the opposite position of the shadow; from the position of the shadow at the beginning and end of the eclipse, the position of the Moon) he reported the star Spica in the Virgin at 23° 30' ♍.

Regiomontanus and Peuerbach <note>Two influential 15th-century astronomers whose work laid the foundation for the Copernican Revolution</note> recorded a Lunar Eclipse at Vienna in these words: *In the year 1460, on December 27, at the beginning of the Eclipse, the star which they call Alramech* <note>original: "Alramech"; this is the star Arcturus</note> *had a morning altitude of 7°. From this, they derive the beginning at 11:42. The beginning of the delay <gloss>totality</gloss> at 12:47; the end of the delay at 1:55. Tycho Brahe added this note to this record: *if these were exact, the locations of the stars could be verified from them.*

We also employed large quadrants to note the arrival of stars at the meridian. The location of the Sun was 17° 48' of Sagittarius.
