->### Problem XXII.<-

<note>Small brown stain on the original manuscript page</note>

->**To record times quickly using an ecliptic instrument.**<-

I offer nothing new here, except that I am explaining the use of the instrument and demonstrating how all the observations that have occurred so far can be performed by a single observer.

The observer, therefore, stands at the table, moving the crossbar <note>original: "transtrum"</note> with his arm to follow the motion of the Sun, while either raising or lowering the ruling-arm <note>original: "regula"</note>. Whenever he wishes to record a specific moment with all its circumstances, and the index of the small wheel is correctly aligned with the ray, he makes a mark on the Azimuthal square <term>Azimuthal square: a component of an instrument used to measure the horizontal angle (azimuth) of a celestial body</term>, on the crossbar, and on the ruling-arm where they intersect each other. He applies the same mark to these three signs. Afterward, without moving the instrument, he transcribes the number or the mark of the signs, adding what the index showed, what the transverse showed, and what the shadow showed on the divided diameter. Once that is done, he returns again to wait for another moment to capture. In this way, all things are performed in the same place, by the same hands, and without hesitation—which must be considered a great advantage when skilled assistants are lacking. For those unaccustomed to the work cause more confusion than help.

Therefore, on the Azimuthal square, the tangents of the Azimuths will be found; on the ruling-arm, the secants of the distance of the light-source from the zenith; and on the crossbar, the tangents of that same arc, provided that the legitimate measurement of the parts has been applied. These three are used for the sake of verification to determine the exact moment of time. An example will follow at the end of the chapter.

**That the path of the Ellipse which the Sun paints on the floor, when admitted through a crack, is a conic section.**

For the path of the Sun in the heavens is a circle; at the equinoxes <note>The two times of year (March and September) when the Sun crosses the celestial equator and day and night are of equal length.</note> it is at its greatest, and is almost a circle (for the connection of one day’s path to the next somewhat disrupts a perfect circularity in every way); at the solstices <note>The times of year when the Sun reaches its highest or lowest point in the sky at noon, marking the longest and shortest days.</note> it is at its smallest magnitude in the tropics, and in the intermediate places, it is intermediate. Now indeed, both our little window <note>original: *fenestella*</note> and the entire globe of the Earth are, to our senses, located on an axis perpendicular to all those circles of the natural days. Therefore, the lines connecting the little window with all points of the circle which the Sun traverses each day—that is, the rays of the Sun having entered through the same hole during one entire day—when joined together from all the Sun's positions, form a <term>right cone: a cone whose tip is perfectly centered above its circular base</term> according to the 1st, 4th, and 8th definitions of the first book of *Conics*. <note>Kepler is referencing the classical work on geometry by Apollonius of Perga.</note> But by that same first definition, these same rays of the Sun also form another cone inside the Room or the fene[unclear] <note>likely *fenestellam*, or "little window"</note>, similar to the exterior one, since the angles **at the vertex** <note>original Greek: *κατὰ κορυφὴν*; these are "vertical angles" formed where two lines cross at a single point</note> are equal. The floor, meanwhile, is placed parallel to the plane of the horizon. And the rays of the Sun, having entered through the hole in whatever position, are continued onto the floor. Let us imagine many continuous bodies of the Sun throughout the entire daily circle; therefore, the rays from all of them will enter at once—that is, a conical surface will enter through the hole. And that surface is cut by the plane of the floor. Therefore, the common section—that is, the path which the solar ellipse <note>The projected circular image of the Sun's disk, which appears slightly elongated</note> describes throughout the day—is a **conic section**. When, therefore, the Sun does not set, but grazes the horizon of the little window, the plane of the horizon is parallel to the lowest line of that cone; wherefore the section here is a **parabola**, according to the 11th theorem of the first book of the *Elements*. <note>Refers to the geometric proofs for cutting a cone.</note> But where the Sun clearly does not set, and all the rays fall upon the floor all around during the 24 hours, the section is an **ellipse**, according to the 13th theorem of the same. Except beneath the pole itself, where this section is a **circle**, according to the 4th theorem of the same.

Where indeed the Sun sets, the plane of the horizon does not receive all the rays of the entire circle (for it does not receive those that are below the horizon) and is parallel to some plane which, drawn through the vertex of the cone, cuts its base—namely, the circle of the natural day. Therefore, according to the 13th theorem of the first book of *Conics*, this section is a **hyperbola**; and to avoid confusion, I repeat to you that the continuation of the ellipses on the floor throughout the entire day creates the figure of a hyperbola.

...angle at an altitude of thirty degrees, even then a sixth part would be horizontal refraction, <note>original: "horizontalis refractionis"</note> which Tycho himself would reject, as he had measured these angles differently through experience: and thus, some refractions would occur even near the zenith <note>The point in the sky directly overhead.</note> itself. Therefore, regarding his own opinion, he proposed another method which established vapors as the cause for refractions; he held it as certain that there is a specific distance for the rays of the stars through which they can pass undisturbed by vapors. Thus, if they reach a place on the Earth's surface by a shorter path through the vapors than this distance, they are not refracted at all. But where the transition from the side exceeds the established distance, they are entirely bent. In this way, he hoped he had satisfied the requirements of the matter.

Many things were said for and against this; the dispute is so entangled that I can hardly extricate myself from it. In what opinion Tycho remained after this discussion with Rothmann, you may find in the first volume of his *Progymnasmata*, <note>Tycho Brahe’s "Introduction to the New Astronomy," published posthumously in 1602.</note> on page ninety-two. 

Furthermore, as often happens when establishing the principles of things, both men were at a standstill. <note>original: "vtrique aqua hæſit," literally "the water stuck for both," an idiom meaning they were both stuck or at a loss.</note> For if they had applied the genuine measure of Refractions, Tycho would not have needed to allege a dual cause of refraction—namely, two distinct bodies, one of air and another of vapors—nor would Rothmann have denied that light is refracted by some imperceptible amount even toward the zenith. Finally, it would have become clear that the surface which bends the rays belongs neither to vapors wandering about at random, nor to some celestial body near the borders of the Moon, but plainly to that very air <margin>The nature of our air.</margin> in which we humans draw our breath in the same way that fish draw in water. 

Tycho would therefore have established, not a successive thinning of the air into the ether and a fading away of atmospheric density, but a manifest and evident distinction—one which, if someone were standing above it, would strike their eyes no less than the surface that separates air from water strikes our eyes now. Rothmann, on the other hand, would not have stumbled over optical principles <term>optical principles</term> <note>The fundamental laws governing how light behaves, which Kepler was working to formalize in this book.</note> by claiming that the surface of a denser medium is struck by light and yet suffers no change nor refraction; or that what is not present in individual parts exists in the combined whole; or that rays are refracted by the depth of the media rather than by their surfaces—all of which are absurdities.

80 JOHANNES KEPLER <note>Johannes Kepler (1571–1630) was a pivotal figure in the Scientific Revolution, best known for his laws of planetary motion. This text is from his 1604 work on optics, *Astronomiae Pars Optica*.</note>

## II. *Various methods of others for measuring Refractions refuted.*

The discovery of the single method and measure of Refractions <term>Refraction|The bending of light as it passes from one transparent substance, like air, into another, like water or glass.</term> cost a great deal of effort: and you, reader, are not to be let off so easily; rather, you must first be led through the same thickets of inquiry that I myself crawled through. Since you are to share in the common fruit of this labor, you should also have a taste of the work itself. Although this turns out to your advantage: because even though there is still something left to be desired regarding the cause of refractions, you may nevertheless know for certain that no other measure remains hidden after all the recesses have been surveyed. Thus, you may have the method of inquiry before your eyes, the very sight of which serves as the strongest proof that this method of measuring was not chosen arbitrarily. For it is of such a kind that it might seem contrived <note>original: "affectatus"</note>, rather than offered by the nature of things, unless you are warned.

First, in this matter, it is easily established by experience alone that the density of the transparent medium is the cause of Refractions, which we also demonstrated above from first principles <note>original: "a priori" — reasoning from theoretical causes to observed effects.</note> in Proposition 14 of the first chapter.

Next, it is also certain that if light falls perpendicularly onto the surface, it is not refracted; but it is refracted all the more evidently the more obliquely it falls. Therefore, the incidence <term>Incidence|The arrival of light at a surface; the 'angle of incidence' is the angle at which the light hits the boundary between two substances.</term> also contributes to the cause, which I also attempted to deduce above from first principles in Proposition 20 of the first chapter.

It is clear, then, that both causes are mixed together, so that density accomplishes nothing if you mentally remove the incidence; because that type of incidence—specifically, that which occurs at right angles—plainly strips the dense body of its refraction. This is an evident proof of what I deduced above from first principles on pages 10 and 14 of the first chapter: that light is not affected by the "body" <note>original: "corpore"</note> of the dense material, but by the surface alone. For incidence is the termination of motion, and motion is in a straight line. The ends of a line are points, and the boundary of infinite contiguous lines is a surface (which consists of infinite continuous points), but not physical bulk <note>original: "corpulentia"</note>.

Therefore, the cause of refraction does not reside in the bulk of the dense medium, but in its surface. Let these be our certain principles for judging measures.

Therefore, any measure of refraction that follows only one of these causes is not correct.

...it falls at angles to the bottom of the water, which is parallel to the surface. Here there is no difference in incidence, yet there is some refraction.

Let us proceed to those modes that join both causes: density and incidence.

The first to present itself is the one that was raised by Rothmann against Tycho in the beginning. He says: if the refraction at the horizon is only 3 <term>minutes <note>original: "scrupulorum"; Kepler uses the term "scrupula" to refer to minutes of arc in astronomical measurement</note></term>, then at an elevation of 45 degrees, the refraction will be one and a half minutes. The reasoning would be thus: that the maximum horizontal refraction is determined by the density of the medium, and that this is spread gradually through all degrees of incidence, so that as much as the light is elevated in the arcs of a circle, the remaining refractions decrease from the maximum in that same proportion, until they are wiped out at the <term>zenith <note>original: "vertice"; the point directly overhead</note></term>. Later, both Tycho and Rothmann recognized that this model contradicts experience. For in <term>Vitello’s <note>Witelo (c. 1230–1285/1314) was a Polish natural philosopher whose treatise on optics was the standard text Kepler is here "supplementing" (Paralipomena)</note></term> table in Book 10, Proposition 8, even in water, the refractions plunge <note>original: "praecipitantur"; meaning they increase sharply or change rapidly</note> toward the horizon, and the vertical (or nearly vertical) refractions do not correspond to the horizontal ones in this proportion of the arcs of incidence. In the refractions that occur in air, they lean much more toward the horizon, as can be seen in the tables found within Tycho's *Progymnasmata* <note>Tycho Brahe’s "Astronomiae Instauratae Progymnasmata" (1602), a foundational work of observational astronomy</note> on pages 79, 124, and 280. 

Furthermore, neither of them thought this sudden increase near the horizon existed because of the form of the measurement itself; to both it seemed likely that either the refractions were proportional to the inclinations, or that a new cause intervened from elsewhere—namely, a new body of vapors. But I say that a measurement must be established from which these things follow by necessity, with nothing else intervening. For the analogy from water to air makes us confident enough to state that the single surface of the air bears this entire burden. For if in water, which is quite dense, refractions sensibly yield toward the horizon, and the maximum refraction at the horizon is about 37 degrees, and nothing intervenes here except the surface of the water: then the refractions will verge much more toward the horizon where the density of the medium is slight and the horizontal refraction is seen as small and thin.

And thus far, even that last opinion of Tycho Brahe on pages 95 and 96 of the *Progymnasmata*, although the closest of all to the truth, has been refuted; it is truly of this kind: that the measure [of refraction] is established by the length of the passage...

measures of refraction, from which a proportional part might be taken based on the quantity of the inclinations. This would result in infinite refraction at the horizon of water; it would arise from the density <note>original: *corpulentia*, referring to the "body" or thickness of the substance</note> and increase with the depth of the medium. Finally, it does not even agree with the data for air. For Tycho <note>Tycho Brahe (1546–1601), the Danish astronomer whose precise observations Kepler used to revolutionize astronomy.</note> sets the horizontal thickness of the air at 142 miles, and at an altitude of 60°, at 14 miles. Therefore, 1/10th of the horizontal refraction should be owed to the 60° altitude—specifically 3½ minutes—of which 1 minute should be owed to an inclination of 30° (because the altitude is set at 60°). Brahe denies that this occurs.

I did not leave this untried either: whether, once the horizontal refraction was established from the density of the medium, the rest would correspond to the sines of the distances from the zenith? But neither did the calculation approve it, nor indeed was there a need to inquire. For refractions would grow in the same way in all media, which contradicts experience.

For this reason, that cause of refractions alleged by Alhazen and Witelo <note>Alhazen (Ibn al-Haytham) and Witelo were the primary medieval authorities on optics; Kepler spent much of this book updating or correcting their work.</note> is criticized. Light, they say, seeks a compensation for the loss <note>original: *compenfationem damni*</note> sustained from an oblique impact. For by as much as it was weakened by encountering a denser medium, it gathers itself by approaching the perpendicular, so that it may strike the bottom of the denser medium with a more direct blow. For they claim those blows which are perpendicular are the strongest. And they add some subtle point or other: that the motion of light incident obliquely is composed of a perpendicular motion and a motion parallel to the surface of the dense body, and that this <term>composite motion</term> <note>The idea that a single movement can be analyzed as the sum of two different directions, like "down" and "sideways."</note> is not destroyed by the encounter with a denser transparent body, but only hindered. Therefore, the whole motion, as it is composed, fortifies itself again—meaning that there reside in the motion through the dense surface, though now altered, traces of the original composition, so that it becomes neither entirely perpendicular nor entirely parallel. It deflects toward the perpendicular rather than the parallel because the perpendicular motion is stronger. They explained the matter hardly any better than Macrobius <note>A 5th-century Roman writer; his *Saturnalia* was a popular source of encyclopedic knowledge in the Renaissance.</note> in the 7th book of his *Saturnalia*, who attributed a "hesitation" to the vision and a "recoil into itself" upon offense. It is as if the species of light were endowed with a mind, by which it might estimate the density of the medium and its own loss, and by its own will—not by an external force; by acting, not by being acted upon—it would refract itself.

If this reasoning were true, the measurement of refractions would be straightforward.

Since density is clearly the cause of refractions, and refraction itself seems to be a certain compression of light (namely, toward the perpendicular), it occurred to my mind to inquire whether the same proportion of the mediums on account of density might be the proportion of the spaces at the bottom which the light strikes—first entering an empty vessel, and then one filled with water.

This method is multifaceted. For it is conceived either in straight lines—as if someone were to say, regarding the next diagram, that the line *EQ*, illuminated by refraction, is to *EH*, illuminated directly, as the density of one medium is to the other. Or, if someone says the refracted line *FC* is to *FH* (the continuation of part *AF*) as the density of one medium is to the other. Or it is conceived in surfaces—as if the power <note>In 17th-century geometry, "power" (*potentia*) often refers to the square of a line's length, representing an area.</note> of *EQ* were to the power of *EH* in this proportion of densities, or a circle or any figure whatever to a similar one. For thus, whatever the proportion of *EQ* to *EP*, its double would be *EH* to *EI*. Or this method is conceived in the volume of truncated pyramids *FHEC* and *FQEC*, so that just as one measure is to another <note>original: *modium ad modium*, referring to the "modius," a Roman dry measure similar to a peck or bushel, used here to represent a unit of density.</note> in density, so are these pyramids: the empty one to the one full of liquid. Finally, because the proportion of mediums is a threefold consideration—since they receive density in length, width, and depth—I even proceeded to seek a cubic proportion between the lines *EQ* and *EH*. Nay, I even consulted other lines. Let a perpendicular *GY* be dropped to the bottom from one of the points of refraction, for instance from *G*. The question will be whether the triangle *GIY*—that is, the base *IY*—would be divided by the refracted ray *GP* in the proportion of the density of the mediums. I have grouped all these methods together because they all share the same <term>Elenchus: a logical refutation or cross-examination</term>.

For by whatever ratio the line, plane, or pyramid *EI* to *EP* (or the shortened *YI* to *YP*) maintains the same proportion everywhere (namely, that of the mediums), certainly *EI*—the tangent of the distance of point *A* from the vertex—will become, at a horizontal distance, infinite—

Fifthly, do images rise in the proportion of the sines of the inclinations? Not at all. For the ratio of the ascent would be the same in all media <note>Kepler is testing if a single law of sines could apply to all materials regardless of their density, which he finds impossible</note>.

Generally, we consult the image or the location of the image in vain, for the very reason that it *is* an image. For it has nothing to do with the density of the medium, nor the real physical <term>affection</term> <note>original: πάθος (*pathos*); in this context, a physical change or property of the light itself</note> of light itself, nor the <term>refraction</term> <note>original: ἀνάκλασιν (*anaklasis*); an ancient term used for both reflection and refraction</note> itself; rather, it concerns what happens to the sense of sight, from whose error the image results.

### 3. Preparation for the true measurement of refractions.

Up to this point, we have followed a nearly blind method of inquiry and have called upon luck. From now on, we were opening the other eye, insisting upon a reliable method.

For when I considered that the image of an object seen under water is so close to the legitimate measurement of refractions that it almost measures them—it is low if the object is viewed from the perpendicular, and gradually becomes higher as the eye leans down toward the horizon of the water—on the other hand, the reasoning just mentioned denied that the measurement should be sought in the image. This is because the image exists not purely from the nature of the thing, but simultaneously from a deception of vision, which is <margin>accidental</margin> <note>The original Latin catchword "accidens" at the bottom of the page indicates the sentence continues onto the next page, likely describing the "accidental" nature of visual errors.</note>

...is an accidental property of the thing itself. From the comparison, I say, of these conflicting arguments, the idea finally occurred to me to investigate the actual causes of an image formed in water, and within these causes, the measurement of refractions. This opinion was confirmed in me all the more when I saw that the cause of the image—appearing in both mirrors and water—had not been correctly explained by the <term>Opticians</term><note>Kepler refers here to traditional optical writers like Euclid, Ptolemy, and Alhazen.</note>. And this is the origin of that labor which we undertook above in Chapter 3.

Nor indeed was it a small task; while dealing with principles in such a complex matter, I followed other false opinions in place of the false traditions of the Opticians. Three or four times I set out on a different path, repeating the whole business from scratch; and as many times, as often happens, I embraced in my mind that very thing I was searching for with such passion, rashly convinced it was already discovered.

And indeed I finally cut this knot of <term>Catoptrics</term><note>The branch of optics dealing with reflection and mirrors.</note>, more difficult than the Gordian knot, by analogy alone, in the manner I described above. I did this while I considered what happened in mirrors, and what would be consistent to happen in water following their likeness. For in mirrors, it is not any physical matter that places images outside the location of the object seen, but only the reflection from a polished surface. Therefore, it followed that in water as well, images rise and approach the surface, not due to the laws of greater or lesser density in the water—depending on whether the gaze was more direct or more oblique—but because of the refraction alone of the light-ray gliding from the object to the eye.

Once this was established, everything I had previously attempted regarding the image and its elevation in the measurement of refractions completely collapsed. This was even more certain after I found the genuine cause for why the image is located on the same perpendicular line as the object itself, both in mirrors and in denser <term>mediums</term><note>A "medium" is any substance light travels through, such as air, glass, or water.</note>.

Since, therefore, this kind of analogy had succeeded so well in that most difficult demonstration regarding the location of the image, I began to pursue this analogy further, drawn by the desire to measure refractions. For I hoped to grasp a measure of refractions, however obscure it might be, provided I had some measure at all; I held the certain hope that once the measurement was correctly known, the cause would also become clear. Thus I proceeded.

Just as in convex mirrors the image of an object becomes smaller, so also in <term>rarer mediums</term><note>In this context, "rarer" means less dense materials, like air compared to water or glass.</note>; and as in concave mirrors the image becomes larger, so

At the same time, it was clear that a flat surface of water takes on a certain quality of curvature. I proceeded, therefore, to the measurement. Since there are many types of media differing in density, it was necessary to establish something <term>analogous</term><note>A corresponding or similar relationship.</note> for this variety in concave mirrors. Therefore, just as the image becomes larger in a concave mirror, the eye must be within the center; the closer it is to the center (and thus further from the surface), the larger the image will be. And so, since denser media likewise create a larger image, different media corresponded to different positions of the eye along the diameter of the mirror.

I was therefore fitting the extremes: in a concave mirror, the locations of the eye are the surface and the center; in media, the densest medium and a medium exactly equal to that in which the eye is located. If the eye were placed at the center, the same things would happen as occur when looking at an object in a medium of <term>infinite density</term>.

For in all other media, the denser any medium is, the more closely the refracted rays approach their perpendiculars.

### 4. On Conic Sections.

Cones are of various kinds: right-angled, acute-angled, and obtuse-angled; likewise, there are Right Cones (or regular) and Scalene Cones (or irregular and compressed), about which see Apollonius and Eutocius in their commentaries. The sections of all these indiscriminately fall into five species. For a line established on the surface of a cone by a section is either a straight line, a circle, a Parabola, a Hyperbola, or an Ellipse. Among these lines, there exists an order based on their properties; and speaking analogically rather than Geometrically: there is a transition from a straight line through infinite hyperbolas into the Parabola, and from there through infinite ellipses into the circle. For the most "obtuse" <note>Kepler uses "obtuse" to mean the flattest or most spread out.</note> of all Hyperbolas is the straight line, while the most "acute" <note>Meaning the most curved or pointed.</note> is the Parabola; likewise, the most acute of all Ellipses is the Parabola, and the most obtuse is the Circle. Therefore, the Parabola has on one side two shapes that are infinite in nature—the Hyperbola and the Straight Line—and on the other side two finite shapes that return into themselves—the Ellipse and the Circle. It [occupies] the place <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence; "It" refers to the Parabola acting as the boundary or bridge between the infinite and finite shapes.</note>

In the middle position, it [the parabola] possesses a middle nature. For it too is infinite, but it seeks a boundary from the other side; for the further it is extended, the more it becomes parallel to itself, and—if I may put it this way—it does not expand its *arms* like the *Hyperbola*, but draws them in from the embrace of the infinite, always embracing more indeed, yet always desiring less: whereas with the *Hyperbola*, the more it actually embraces between its arms, the more it also desires. 

Therefore, the circle and the straight line are the opposite limits: there we find pure curvature, here pure straightness. The *Hyperbola*, *Parabola*, and *Ellipse* are placed between them, and participate in both the straight and the curved; the *Parabola* equally so, the *Hyperbola* more in straightness, and the *Ellipse* more in curvature. For this reason, the further the *Hyperbola* is extended, the more it becomes like its straight line or <term>Asymptote</term> <note>A line that a curve approaches closer and closer but never actually touches.</note>. The further the *Ellipse* is continued beyond its middle, the more it affects circularity, and finally it meets with itself again. 

The *Parabola*, in its middle position, is always more curved than the *Hyperbola* if they are extended by equal intervals, and always straighter than the *Ellipse*. And just as the circle and the straight line close the extremes, so the *Parabola* holds the middle: thus, just as all straight lines are similar, and likewise all circles, so also all *Parabolas* are similar, and they differ only in size. <note>original: "quantitate differunt." Kepler is observing that while ellipses can be "skinny" or "fat," all parabolas have the exact same shape, just scaled differently.</note>

There are, moreover, certain points in these lines of special consideration, which have a certain definition but no name, unless you use a definition or some property as a name. For from these points, straight lines drawn to the <term>tangents</term> of the section and the points of contact form equal angles with those lines that are formed if the opposite points are connected with the same points of contact. For the sake of light, and with our eyes fixed on Mechanics, we shall call these points **Foci** <note>original: "Focos." This is a landmark moment in science. Kepler adopts the Latin word for "hearth" or "fireplace" to describe these geometric points because, in optics, light rays reflect through them to create heat.</note>.

Therefore, in the circle there is one **Focus**, *A*, and it is the same as the center; in the *Ellipse* there are two **Foci**, *B* and *C*, equally removed from the center of the figure, and further apart in the sharper ellipses. 

In the *Parabola*, one focus, *D*, is inside the section; the other must be imagined either outside or inside the section on the axis, removed by an infinite distance from the first, so that a line drawn—*HG* or *IG*—from that <term>blind focus</term> <note>original: "caeco foco." overlaps. Let the length of the string be double the distance AC, and let the ends of the string be tied in a knot. Now, insert the stylus <note>original: "Graphium," a writing or drawing tool</note> D into the same loop of string along with points A and B. Let focus A be proposed, and vertex C, so that AC is the axis; let it be continued from point A toward infinity, or as far as you wish to draw the Parabola. Let it go as far as E. Hold the other end of the string E in one hand, and the stylus in the other; extend the string as far as C. Also let EF be erected perpendicularly to CE. Therefore, move the stylus C and the other hand E at equal intervals away from the line AE, so that the other hand and the end of the string always remain on line EF, and the string segment DG is always parallel to the axis AE itself; the path CD, which you will have marked with the stylus, will be a **Parabola**.

ADDITIONS TO WITELO. 97

In the preceding parts, it was demonstrated that the dimension of the angles of refraction <note>The bending of light as it passes from one medium, like air, into another, like water.</note> through different incidences of light into denser media must be sought by an inviting analogy from the angles of reflection <note>original: "repercuſſuum"</note> through various incidences of light into concave mirrors. One extreme in the analogy fits well: namely, the densest medium corresponds to the position of light at the focus of a Parabola. This is because, just as in the densest medium the rays become parallel after refraction, so do rays from the focus of a parabola become parallel after reflection.

But regarding the subsequent media in order of decreasing density, it was not yet clear where they should be assigned: whether to different positions of light within the same parabola below the focus—so that the medium in which there is no refraction would belong to the position of light on the very concave surface or vertex of the parabola—or whether, instead, because the parabola is the most acute among both Hyperbolas and Ellipses, the media differing in degrees from the densest should be assigned either to various hyperbolas or various ellipses, so that the position of light always remains at the focus of the section. In this way, for that medium which lacks refraction, a straight line or plane mirror would be required in the first case, and a concave spherical mirror in the second. Therefore, I did not leave it unattempted to inquire whether each medium might have its own hyperbola. For if you mark the locations of images in water through all inclinations with points, a hyperbola will be roughly outlined, which increases confidence in this idea. For example, for the refractions of water, let an angle of refraction of 30° be taken at an inclination of 80° (leaving a refracted angle <note>Kepler defines the "refracted angle" as the angle relative to the surface or the remaining angle, resulting in 50° here.</note> of 50°) according to Witelo. And let B be the focus opposite to A; at point B, let an angle of 80° be compared to the line BA, which shall be CBA. Likewise, at point

And in general, because BA represents the perpendicular line into the water, and the line raised from B at right angles to BA represents a ray parallel to the surface of the water (or the horizon): it should be known that in a hyperbola, near the vertical incidences, the angles of reflection increase suddenly, but near the horizon they increase very little and quickly become maximal. In refractions, it is otherwise: for both the angles of refraction and the very increments of those angles increase toward the horizon. Therefore, we seek the measurement of refractions between the <term>foci</term> <note>The two central points that define the shape of a curve like an ellipse or hyperbola.</note> of hyperbolas in vain.

Let $A$ be the opposite <term>focus</term> <note>In an ellipse, the focus is one of two central points that define the curve's shape.</note>, and $D A B I$ be the axis. Let $I B F$ again be 80° and $B A F$ be 50°. Here, $A F B$ will be 100,000 <note>Kepler uses a standard trigonometric scale where the radius is 100,000 units.</note>. Therefore, $A F$ will be 197,962 and $B F$ 153,208. According to Proposition 52 of the third book of <term>Apollonius</term> <note>Apollonius of Perga was a Greek mathematician known for his work on conic sections like the ellipse.</note>, the sum of both will be 351,170, which is the length of the axis $D I$. Thus, $A D$ or $B E$ is 125,585. Having established the Ellipse in this way, let $I B C$ now be 70°. I know that $B C$ and $C A$ must equal the axis, 351,170.

Suppose then, as <note>original: "Vitellio"</note> Witelo <note>Witelo was a 13th-century monk whose "Perspectiva" was the standard textbook on optics until Kepler wrote this book.</note> posits, that the <term>refraction</term> <note>The bending of light as it passes from one medium, like air, into another, like water.</note> is 24° 30' for the angle $B C A$. This results in $A C$ being 202,485 and $B C$ being 171,996. The sum is 374,481. This is too large; it ought to have been only 351,170. Therefore, the angle $B A C$ is too large, and $B C A$ is smaller than it should be. Let it then be larger, namely 27°, and $B A C$ 43°. This results in $A F$ 206,985 and $B F$ 150,244. The sum is 357,229, still a little larger than it should be. Therefore, the angle $B C A$ must still be increased slightly. It will thus become larger than Witelo's recorded refraction. For this reason, the measurement of refractions is **not** to be sought in the focus of an Ellipse. In general, this shape also increases the said angle by great increments from the <term>vertex</term> <note>The "tip" or highest point of the curve.</note>, but where the light exits the focus perpendicular to the axis, the increments of the angles are small, almost as they are in the hyperbola itself.

Therefore, let another method be consulted, so that for the sake of all <term>media</term> <note>The substances light travels through, such as air, water, or glass.</note>, the measures of refraction are placed solely in the **Parabola**. Let the measurement for the densest medium be established by lines drawn from the focus; whereas for the thinnest medium (or that which lacks refraction), let the measurement be taken (speaking analogically) by lines drawn from the point that is at the very bottom (or geometrically, the vertex) of the Parabola, at its deepest point. Let the other intermediate media be assigned to intermediate points on the axis. 

For example, in the refractions of water, let $A$ be the focus in the following figure, $A B$ the axis, and below $A$ let point $C$ be taken. Let $D C$ be inclined toward $A B$ at an angle $D C B$ of 80°. At $D$, let the line $F D$ touch the section, cutting $A B$ at $E$. Let $F D G$ be made equal to angle $E D C$, and let $G D$ be continued until it meets $A B$ at $I$. 

We ask first: how great is the height of point $C$ from the bottom or vertex $B$, so that $G I A$ becomes 50°? (This is the refracted angle Witelo posits for an 80° inclination). Therefore, in triangle $C D I$, the angle $D I C$ is 50° and $I C D$ is 80°. Thus $I D C$ is also 50°; therefore $C D$ and $C I$ are equal. In units where $C I$ or $C D$ is 100,000, $D I$ is 128,558. And since $E D C$ and $F D G$ are set as equal, and likewise $I D E$ and $F D G$ are vertical angles, then $I D E$ and $E D C$ are equal. Therefore, as $C D$ is to $D I$, so is $C E$ to $E I$, by Proposition 3 of the sixth book <note>Referring to Euclid’s "Elements," the foundation of geometry.</note>. Thus $C E$ will be 43,753 and $E I$ 56,247. Now let a perpendicular line $D K$ be dropped from $D$ onto $E C$. Angle $K D C$ will be 10°; therefore $D K$ is 98,481 and $K C$ is 17,365.

### Conditions
under which the undersigned enters into service as a servant in the household of **Dr. Schuberth** <note>Likely Gotthilf Heinrich von Schubert (1780–1860), a renowned German natural philosopher and educator who resided in Nuremberg during this period.</note> here.

1. Punctuality, cleanliness, and orderliness in dress and person.
2. Loyalty, obedience, and devotion toward the **master** <note>The original uses *Principal*, a traditional term for an employer or head of a household.</note> and his family.
3. Diligent attendance at public worship services and **religious instruction** <note>Original: *Christenlehre*, a form of catechetical instruction.</note>.
4. Management of household duties, namely: opening and closing the house, providing wood and water, cleaning boots and clothes, as well as all tasks in general assigned to him by the **family** <note>Original: *Herrschaft*, referring to the employers or heads of the household.</note>.

For the hyperbola, anatomical experience spoke—of which we shall speak below in the consideration of the eye.

->**SUPPLEMENT TO WITELO. 111**<-

...ends, or rather here affects the infinite motions of infinite points of light; indeed, in this respect, let it consider density no less than the physical body itself. Therefore, it will have a greater effect if, in some respect, it encounters a denser medium for the light. Now, it encounters a denser medium when the light arrives from an oblique <note>original: "ex obliquo," meaning at an angle rather than straight on</note> direction. Let A be the light and BC the denser medium. 

->[A geometric diagram showing parallel light rays, labeled S-K-M and A-B-L, as well as b-m-n and p-o, incident on a vertical interface labeled M-L-n-c. A triangle BLM is formed with a right angle at L.]<-

Let KM be parallel rays, or nearly so, coming from the Sun; their distance is measured on the perpendicular line ML. Since the angle BLM is a right angle, and LBM is assumed to be an acute oblique angle, LBM will therefore be smaller than BLM. Consequently, the side LM, which is opposite the smaller angle B, will be smaller than the side BM, which is opposite the larger angle L. But LM measures the width of the medium encountering the light falling directly on it, because BLM is a right angle; whereas BM measures the width encountering the light from an oblique angle. Therefore, there is "more" density <note>Kepler argues that because the path BM is longer than LM for the same "width" of light, the light "feels" more resistance from the medium.</note> in BM than in LM. Thus, there is greater resistance in this respect.

**PROPOSITION III.**
*The angles of refraction increase by larger proportional increments than the obliquity of incidence.*

For according to the corollary of the first proposition, even if density alone were considered, the angles of refraction would be proportional to the angles of incidence. Now, however, through the second proposition, the ratio of LM to MB also enters the mix. Therefore, the angle of refraction is composed of one part that is proportional to the incidences, and another part that is proportional to the lines BM. But the lines BM increase only a little at first; however, at a low incidence <note>meaning an angle closer to the horizon/surface</note>, they increase significantly, as the **table of secants** <term>secant: a trigonometric function representing the ratio of the hypotenuse to the adjacent side; as the angle increases toward 90 degrees, the secant value grows toward infinity</term> shows, where increasingly larger secants always correspond to equal degrees. Therefore, one part of the refraction angle is proportioned to the incidences, while the other part increases by larger proportional increments. Thus, the total angle increases by larger increments.

**PROPOSITION IV.**
*There is no difference in refraction between faint light and denser light, all other things being equal.* 

For if faint light were more easily overcome by a denser medium, refraction would be an effect caused by the essence of the light itself rather than an effect of motion. But refraction is only the lessening or inhibition of the motion of dispersion; and this motion receives no "ailments" from the density or thinness of light—that is, from its strength or weakness, its proximity or remote— <note>The text cuts off mid-word ("remotione") at the end of the page.</note>

<summary>Kepler uses geometry to demonstrate why refraction angles do not increase linearly with incidence angles, attributing the change to the increased "resistance" light encounters at oblique angles. He also asserts that the intensity or brightness of light does not change its refractive properties.</summary>

### PROPOSITION VI.

Since $B M$ can be considered in two ways, according to whether it forms various angles with rays that have undergone refraction in either a thinner or a denser medium, it must be understood that *the secants of those angles of incidence which are formed at the surface within the denser medium contribute to the measurement of refractions.* This is evident from the <term>absurdity</term> <note>a logical proof (reductio ad absurdum) where one shows that the opposite premise leads to an impossible result</note> of the alternative. For since the secant becomes infinite near the horizon, if the thinner medium were considered, its effect would also have to be infinite, and all horizontal radiations would be refracted by an infinite angle. This is an absurd thing to say. Therefore, the secants of the angles in the thinner medium are not to be used as a measure—that is, not the proportion of $B M$ to $M L$—but rather the proportion of $B M$ to $B R$. Furthermore, even if only a full right angle (and no more) were produced by an infinite secant, a single ray emerging perpendicularly from the depths of water or any other medium into a single point on the surface would be scattered into the entire hemisphere in the open air. For the path is the same for a ray entering as for one exiting. But here, two paths would be assigned for an entering ray: one from the perpendicular, and the other parallel to the surface of the water, and that in every direction. Regarding the genuine cause of this matter, which ought to be demonstrated directly and <term>a priori</term> <note>derived from theoretical principles rather than just observation</note>, I am stuck. <margin>Tell me in what lands, and you shall be my great Apollonius. <note>original: "Dic quibus in terris, & eris mihi magnus Apollonius." This is a playful adaptation of Virgil’s Third Eclogue, substituting the name of the great geometer Apollonius of Perga for the god Apollo.</note></margin> Perhaps the cause is this: since the angles of refraction occur within the dense surface, and the cause resisting the dispersion of light is also there, it is fitting to seek the measurement within as well.

*In the densest possible medium, all refractions occur along the perpendiculars themselves, and they are equal to the inclinations. In less dense media, which have less refraction, they cast the ray more toward the horizon, and they begin to be perceived later. For the highest density, by reason of its infinity, is the cause—*

### PROPOSITION VIII. Problem I.

*From a known composite refraction of any inclination, to hunt for the elements of refraction and the composite or whole refractions of other inclinations.*

Having obtained the simple refraction of the 80th degree, let a distribution be made into the other inclinations, because simple refraction is proportional to the inclinations, angle to angle. For example: For an inclination of 50° of a ray entering through the air, there resulted 12° 4' for the simple refraction, according to the distribution of simple refraction. Therefore, the previous value was too high when it was 3° 14'.

116          JOHANNES KEPLER

Do not let such a tiny discrepancy disturb you; believe me, experimental observation in such an unrefined medium does not reach such a high level of precision. You see that a great inequality exists between the differences in my values and those of <note>Witelo (Latinized as Vitellio) was a 13th-century friar whose work "Perspectiva" was the standard textbook on optics until Kepler’s time. Kepler is arguing that Witelo "fudged" his data to make it look more mathematically perfect.</note> Witelo. My refractions, however, proceed from equality and order. Therefore, the fault lies in Witelo’s refractions. You will believe this all the more if you look at the "increments of increments" in Witelo’s work. For they increase by 30' <note>30 minutes of arc, or half a degree.</note> minutes. It is certain, therefore, that Witelo adjusted his experimentally captured refractions by hand, so that he could force them into an orderly pattern by making the second increments equal. For with lines drawn from a circle—or from anything of a circular nature, as <term>refraction</term> <note>The bending of light as it passes from one medium (like space) into another (like the Earth's atmosphere).</note> is—their increments vary infinitely and are never perfectly equal.

*Given two refractions of the stars arising from the air at a certain altitude above the earth, to investigate the refractions of other inclinations.*

This business is involved in many perplexities. Let A be the center of the globe of the earth BC, and let the same point be the center of the sphere of air DE.

If both the surfaces BC and DE were flat and parallel...

...and with the refraction of <term>angle GEF</term> <note>referring to a diagram on a previous page</note> removed, there would remain the inclination of <term>FEH</term>, where the unrefracted ray <term>FE</term> sits above the <term>tangent EH</term>. However, the height of the air that causes refraction—represented by <term>EC</term>—is unknown. While optical writers demonstrate that the height of the matter creating twilight is equal to 12 miles, it does not immediately follow that this is the same matter that causes refraction. 

For let us now suppose <margin>The matter of twilight.</margin> that the substance which refracts the rays of the stars is liquid, moist, and heavy, differing from the substance of water only by degrees. It would follow, then, that if anything dry, smoky, or fiery exists here on Earth, it would struggle upward above this moist body in the same way that air escapes from water. Once this is achieved, the fumes would occupy higher places than this refracting matter. Being located there, and because they consist of physical matter, they would be illuminated to the brightness of twilight, yet they would produce no refraction. For according to Proposition 11 of the first chapter, the definition of "transparent" does not apply to fumes, and therefore neither does refraction.

Beset by these difficulties, let us attempt an approach—not the elegant <term>geometric</term> ones we might prefer, but those possible <note>original: "ἀτέχνως" (atechnōs) - meaning simply, without formal art, or empirically</note> **simply and empirically**, by comparing the refractions of two different pairs of inclinations. At the start, let us establish certain inclinations of the same ray in the air and on the Earth that do not differ in any way perceptible to the senses. For the smaller the proportion of the height of the air (<term>EC</term>) to the radius of the Earth (<term>AC</term>), the smaller this discrepancy of angles will be, and the more slowly it is perceived. For example, let <term>EC</term> be 95 units where <term>AC</term> is 100,000 units. The incidences would be as follows:

# 118 JOHANNES KEPLER

Thirdly. Now, therefore, let us descend to the consideration of the remaining inclinations. For at an altitude of 1°—that is, an inclination of 89°—the Sun is refracted by 26 minutes <note>original: "26' prima"</note>, as it appears on the same page. The question is: what is the refracted altitude of the Sun above the air? We seek a number of degrees which, if multiplied by 43 thirds <note>Kepler uses "thirds" (''') and "fourths" ('''') as subdivisions of a degree, smaller than seconds</note>, and if the product is multiplied by the <term>secant</term><note>The secant is a trigonometric ratio representing the length of a line from the center of a circle through a point on its circumference to a tangent line.</note> of that number of degrees (discarding the last 5 digits), results in 26 minutes.

Let us try 84° 16'. Multiply 1° 24' 16'' by 43'''; the proportional refraction produced is 1' 0'' 23''' 28''''. The secant is ten times the radius. Therefore, the refraction is 10' 3''. It should have been 26'.

Let it then be 87° 8'. Multiply 1° 27' 8' by 43'''; the simple result is 1' 3''. The secant is twenty-fold. Therefore, the refraction is 20'. It should have been 26'.

Let us try again with 87° 48'. Multiply 1° 27' 48' by 43'''; the simple refraction produced is 1' 3''. The secant is twenty-six-fold. Therefore, the refraction is 27' 20''. It should have been 26'. Therefore, in the air, that ray is inclined by refraction through 87° 47'.

If both refractions were correct here, we would have already hit the mark. But because such a small refraction as 1' 26''—which we adopted from Tycho <note>Tycho Brahe (1546–1601), the Danish astronomer whose precise data Kepler used to derive his laws.</note>—at an altitude of 30° very easily allows for an error of observation, which is not large in itself but later becomes intolerable during multiplication; we must now see if the others also correspond.

Therefore, in the diagram, since angle EBA is set at 91° because BE is 89°, and the angle found in the air corresponding to it is 87° 47', the difference BAE is therefore 1° 13'. Wherefore BEA is 87° 47'; and as the <term>sine</term> of BEA 87° 47' (99925) is to AB, so the sine of EBA (99985) is to AE (100060). 

If we now search from this for the horizontal refraction on the Earth, and let EBA be 90°, then the secant 100060 produces an angle BAE of 2°. The secant is 63''. Therefore, the total refraction comes to 30' 5''; according to Tycho's inclination, it should have been 34'. Even if we have not quite hit the mark this time, the light has nevertheless been opened to us, so that we may discern whether the value should be decreased or increased. Indeed, the increments of the refractions are not large enough. We must therefore move toward steeper secants. But as soon as we do this, the refraction at 89° will be increased too much. Therefore, the simple refraction, which we derived from the altitude of 30°, must be decreased.

**ADDITIONS TO WITELO. 119**

The measurement on Earth varies by one degree, while in the air it varies by barely 13 minutes. And if 43 thirds <note>A "third" is 1/60th of a second</note> are assigned to one degree, then barely 10 thirds will be assigned to 13 minutes. Therefore, the proportional refraction remains essentially the same for all practical purposes, being so tiny. And this value must be multiplied by two secants <term>secant: a trigonometric function that grows rapidly as an angle approaches 90 degrees</term>, so that one results in 26 and the other in 34 <note>These numbers (26 and 34 minutes) refer to Tycho Brahe's observed refraction values at 1° and 0° altitude respectively</note>. 

But since the proportion of equal multiples is the same: find two secants, separated from each other by about 13 minutes, so that one is to the other as 26 is to 34. Such a case is found roughly from 88° 54' to 89° 10'—a span of 15 or 16 minutes. See now whether the inclinations in the air, corresponding to inclinations on Earth of 90° and 89°, are distant by 16 minutes.

If angle BAE is 0° 50', then side AE is 10001058, where B is a right angle. But if EBA is 91°, then as EA is to EBA, so BA is to BEA. This results in 88° 45' for BEA. Previously it was 89° 10'; the difference is 25. They are distant by 25 minutes, and the secant of 88° 45' already shows a smaller refraction at 89° than 26 minutes. Therefore, we have already passed the mark. The truth lies between the secants of 88° and 89° 10' for a refraction of 34'; likewise between 87° 47' and 88° 45' for a refraction of 26'.

I will test 89° in the air, corresponding to 90° on Earth. Therefore, angle BAE is 1°. DE is 10001524. As this is to 9998477, so 10,000,000 is to the sine of BEA. This gives BEA as 88° 35'. The secants there are 573, etc. This is 404 1/2. If 34 gives 573, what does 26 give? It gives 438; it should have been 404 1/2. We have come closer, but nevertheless the secants, as you see, are still too steep <note>Meaning the rate of change in his mathematical model is still not matching the observations perfectly</note>.

We shall descend by another 10 minutes, so that angle BAE is 1° 10'. AE will be 10002074. As this is to 9998477, so the whole sine <note>the radius of the calculation circle, usually 10,000,000 in this era</note> is to the sine of BEA, which is 88° 28'. However, the secant of the composite angle BAE is 49.10. The secant of BEA is 37 1/2. The proportion of 34 to 26 required it to be 37 1/2. Therefore, we have come as close as possible; yet we are still slightly off, which will be overcome by a descent of a few more minutes, enough to satisfy the refractions of 26' and 34'.

But because the refractions provided by Tycho could not have attained such extreme precision from observation as is required here—as you see, they are expressed in round numbers: 34 precisely at the first altitude of 0°, and 25 <note>original: "25 prima"</note> at the first altitude of 1°. Tycho himself does not hide this fact on pages 79 and 124. Therefore, before a final measure is established, other refractions at slightly higher altitudes, which are clearly perceptible to the senses, must also be consulted.

Above, a difference of 2° between the angles on Earth and in the air satisfied a refraction of 1' 26" at an altitude of 30° and a refraction of 26' at an altitude of 1°. Again, a difference of 1° 15' between the angles satisfied the refractions of 26' and 34' at an altitude of 1° and 0°. The text explores the philosophical concept of **individuality** and its relationship to the **totality of humanity**. It posits that every individual should be a unique representation of the human race, rather than a mere carbon copy. While every person possesses the potential for all human traits, the reality of life requires a specific "mixture" and focus. The author argues that true education and self-development (<term>Bildung: a German concept of self-cultivation and holistic education</term>) involve discovering one's specific place and purpose within the greater whole, thereby contributing a unique perspective to the collective human experience.

### On the Nature of Individuality and the Whole

Should not every person be a unique representation of humanity? If in everyone there were a special mixture of elements, so that through their own peculiar form and through the specific combination of their powers, the whole of humanity would be represented in a distinct way? 

Certainly, the capacity to be everything resides in every person. Yet, no one can actually *be* everything at once. Therefore, each person must choose a specific path, a specific "measure," through which they express the universal. This is not a limitation, but rather the fulfillment of one's destiny. 

We must recognize ourselves as a specific point in the universe. Our task is to bring our own inner "harmony" into accordance with the "great harmony" of the world. In doing so, the individual does not lose themselves in the mass; rather, they become a necessary and irreplaceable part of the whole. 

<note>The text likely reflects the influence of Friedrich Schleiermacher or Wilhelm von Humboldt, focusing on the Romantic ideal of "Palingenesis" or the continuous rebirth of the self through culture and education.</note>

To truly become an individual, one must not only look inward but also outward, engaging with others to see how their own "partial" existence fits into the "total" existence of mankind. Only through this relationship between the self and the other can the "Idea of Humanity" be fully realized.

<meta>This page continues Johannes Kepler’s mathematical derivation of atmospheric refraction, specifically focusing on how to construct a table that aligns with the observations of Tycho Brahe. 126          JOHANNES KEPLER

### The construction of the table for simple refractions adapted to free inclinations in the air is completed as follows. 

The total refraction of the preceding degree is subtracted from the following degree; the secants <note>The secant is a trigonometric function, the reciprocal of the cosine.</note> of the remainder are extracted (discarding the last 6 digits when the total sine <note>original: "sinus totus"; in Kepler's time, this referred to the radius of the calculational circle, here set to 10,000,000.</note> consists of 7 zeros), and they are multiplied by the seconds of the simple refraction of that degree. The product should be divided by 600. If a large result is produced, differing significantly from the prior refraction, the operation must be repeated a second time, and sometimes a third, etc.

Suppose at 60° the total refraction is 1' 28''. Subtract this from 61°; there remains 60° 58' 32''. The secant [of this remainder] 206 etc., multiplied by the 44'' of simple refraction for the 61st degree, produces 9064. This, divided by 600, gives 1' 31'', which is the total [refraction] for the 61st degree. When this is subtracted from 62°, it leaves 61° 58' 29'', the secant of which is 21 etc. This, multiplied by the 45'' refraction of the 62nd degree, leaves a refraction of 1' 35'' for the 62nd degree. Again, let the refraction at 84° be 9' 43''. Subtract this from 85°; the secant of the remainder, 111 etc., multiplied by the simple refraction of 63'' and divided by 600, shows 11' 39''. This differs from the previous 9' 43'' by nearly 2 minutes in a place where the secants are now increasing rapidly. Therefore, repeat the operation: instead of 9' 43'' for the prior degree, now subtract 11' 39'' from its own degree of 85°. The secant 110 1/2 multiplied by 63'' produces 11' 36'', the correct refraction.

To ensure the inclinations of the refracted rays are adapted to the Earth, always multiply EA (10005578) by the sine of BEA, or the inclination of the refracted rays in the air.

I therefore conclude this tedious inquiry with the explanation of this small table, in which we come as close as possible to Tycho's <note>Tycho Brahe (1546–1601), the Danish astronomer whose precise observations Kepler used to derive his laws of planetary motion.</note> solar refractions—differing by only four minutes around a solar altitude of 15°—while in the meantime we satisfy those observations made by Tycho within the same day. Perhaps they would not differ even by that small amount if the things stated in Proposition 6 of this work had been correctly handled. 

<margin>An Apology</margin> Therefore, I beg the reader not to misuse this scrupulous inquiry of mine into the refractions published by Tycho to tear down the entire business of refractions, which I have instituted to confirm it. If I judge well of these matters, I have confirmed it greatly; for while Tycho thought [refraction] arose from the unequal thickness of the air at different altitudes, I have shown that very thing—or something not much different—from the [matter] itself <note>The text ends mid-sentence as a catchword for the next page.</note>

He concludes by defending his rigorous methods, arguing that his theoretical work confirms Tycho's observational findings regarding air density.</summary>

Therefore, let them cease for now to boast of the silence of others, which is surely born of their own obscurity.

->PROPOSITION X. Problem: III.<-
*To investigate the proportion of media to one another based on the quantity of refractions—for instance, air to water—according to their density.*

In Proposition 6 of this chapter, it was indicated that simple refraction <note>The bending of light as it passes from one substance to another.</note> is multiplied from the inclination <note>The angle at which the light ray hits the surface.</note> of the ray in the thinner medium over the common surface, by the secant <term>Secant: A trigonometric function; in Kepler's time, this was calculated as the ratio of the hypotenuse to the adjacent side of a triangle related to the angle of incidence.</term> of that inclination which the refracted ray makes in the denser medium over the common surface. Therefore, let the simple refractions of the same inclinations be compared, so that the different positions of each medium do not deceive us regarding the same incident ray. As in Proposition 8 of this chapter, at an inclination of 80°, the simple refraction of a ray from air into water is 19° 17'. At the same inclination of 80° in Proposition 9 of this chapter, the simple refraction of a ray from the ether into air is 59". <note>The "ether" was considered the extremely thin, weightless substance filling space beyond the atmosphere.</note> Therefore, from the ether into water, the simple refraction would be 19° 18'. Thus, the proportion is the same as that of Unity...

Now, refraction of this kind is caused only by that density which is considered in a straight line, because the surface of refraction (called so by optics), in cutting the surface of the denser medium, forms a line at the intersection. And even if that same surface, in cutting the denser body, forms a surface at the intersection, it was nevertheless demonstrated in the first chapter that no refraction occurs within the dense body, but all of it occurs at the surface. I myself doubt, however, whether it is not sufficient to square the terms of the proportions, or rather to multiply them by their own roots, because the density of the substance itself is represented on the surface of the medium, according to Proposition 13 of the first chapter. But this proportion is not constant: nor is it to be assigned to any part of the air except that which, in the clear sky, occupies the highest spaces. Indeed, the vapor that boils up from bubbling pots, and likewise that which provides the material for imminent rain, <margin>The source of rain.</margin> coming forth from the caverns of high mountains and overspreading the sky with darkness, is much closer to water: and it is immediately condensed back into it.

I am not unaware—lest you think otherwise—that I will run into the censure of the Physicists <note>Natural philosophers of the time, typically adhering to Aristotelian views.</note> for establishing here and previously that air is heavy or has weight. <margin>Air is by nature cold and heavy.</margin> But the contemplation of all nature has taught me so: indeed, along with Cardano <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), a prominent Italian polymath.</note> and many other most excellent Philosophers of this age, I even ascribe coldness to it. Nor do I see what remains for Aristotle by which he might defend the idea that air is absolutely light and hot by its own nature, if you take away from it one combination of qualities. Neither Medicine nor Physiology is put at risk, provided that air remains *relatively* light and more suited for heating. But there will be a more convenient place to speak of these things elsewhere: and something has been said in my *Astrological Theses*.

<meta>This page continues Kepler's investigation into the optical properties of the atmosphere. Having established geometric proofs for refraction in the preceding pages, he now calculates the physical height of the air and engages with the theories of his contemporaries, Tycho Brahe and Christoph Rothmann.</meta>

->SUPPLEMENT TO WITELO. 129<-

Since the matter of the air is fluid—as proven by the nature of the winds, which are, in my opinion, nothing other than a copious bubbling up <note>original: "ebullitio"</note> from the highest mountains, from which the matter, seeking the lower regions again by its own nature (a concept not foreign to Aristotle in Section 25, Problem 13), is poured around the mountain in a circle—and since from that first impulse one circle arises after another, just as in stagnant waters: it follows therefore from this (as was employed in the ninth proposition of this chapter) that the matter of the air encircles the globe of the Earth in a circular fashion. Therefore, to investigate the measurement of atmospheric refractions, it was plainly necessary to assume a specific height for the sphere of air. That height will therefore be the one which, when assumed, brings us closest to the observed measurement of refractions. Now, the value for the line EA <note>referring to a diagram on a previous page</note> was 10,055,578 units, where the distance from the center of the earth (A) to its surface was 10,000,000 units. Therefore, by the rule of proportions, if 10,000,000 units are equal to 860 German miles <note>A German geographical mile was roughly 7.5 kilometers or 4.6 miles.</note> according to the accepted tradition of geographers, then the 5,578 units representing the height of the air will give $\frac{4,797,080}{10,000,000}$ of a mile. This means that at the fortress of Uraniborg <note>The observatory of Tycho Brahe on the island of Hven.</note>, where the observations of the stars were taken, the height of the air was half of a German mile, and no more.

Here the reader should also be reminded of that debate which Tycho [Brahe] had with [Christoph] Rothmann concerning the substance of the air and the ether in Volume 1 of the *Letters*, which Tycho concludes on folio 92 of the *Progymnasmata* <note>Tycho Brahe's "Introduction to the New Astronomy."</note>. Rothmann and Pena <note>Jean Pena, a French mathematician who argued the air reached all the way to the stars.</note> said that from the earth to the heavens there is nothing but air, except for a little bit of vapor. Tycho, together with them, eliminated the Aristotelian [element of] fire, and recognized that the vapors around the earth were distinct from the air; but he extended the air to the borders of the Moon, and said that there, it gradually fades into the ether. I, moved by these experiments, hold a middle ground. <margin>What exists in the space between the earth and the Moon.</margin> First, what they called "vapor," I call "air"; I terminate it at the peaks of the mountains. Above these consist smoky exhalations, the "lamps of the twilights" <note>This poetic phrase refers to the matter in the upper atmosphere that reflects sunlight during twilight.</note>, and immediately thereafter the ether succeeds it.

136 

### Section VI: On the Distinction between Souls and Spirits

It is therefore quite different for **Spirits** or **Souls**. It can be said that they are the true **Atoms of Nature** <note>Leibniz uses this term to contrast his metaphysical units with the physical atoms of materialist philosophy.</note> and, in a word, the very elements of things. They can neither begin nor end but all at once; that is to say, they can only begin by *creation* and end only by *annihilation* <margin>Creation and Annihilation</margin>. On the other hand, that which is composite <gloss>the material body</gloss> begins or ends through its constituent parts.

As for what concerns ordinary souls <note>The "sensitive" souls of animals</note>, they do not perish. There is no such thing as a total death, consisting in the separation of the soul from the body. What we call "generations" <note>birth or coming-into-being</note> are in truth developments and growths, just as what we call "deaths" are enfoldings <term>Involution: the process of a complex organism shrinking back into a microscopic or seminal state</term> and diminutions.

There is, therefore, a **metamorphosis** <note>original: "metamorphose"</note> occurring here. There is no such thing as the transmigration of souls <note>original: "metempsychosis"</note>, for the soul never leaves its body all at once, nor is it ever entirely stripped of an organized body. Thus, there is no soul without a body, nor a body without a soul, unless one speaks of God, who is entirely separate from matter.

But the **Human Soul**, which we specifically call **Mind** or **Spirit**, is of a much more sublime nature. While the ordinary soul is a living mirror of the universe of creatures, the Mind is also an image of the Divinity <note>original: "Imago Divinitatis"</note>. This is why it is capable of knowing the system of the universe, and of imitating something of it by its own architectural <insert>and artistic</insert> constructions, each mind being like a little deity in its own realm.

-> This reveals the **System of Pre-established Harmony** <-

so that the distance **AB** appears to be **DE**. Indeed, **DE** will be smaller than **AB**. But because the arcs **AD** and **BE** <note>These represent the vertical displacement caused by atmospheric refraction at the horizon.</note> do not exceed 34 minutes, to our senses **AB** and **DE** will appear equal. For suppose **ACB** is exactly a quadrant <note>A 90-degree angle.</note>, a distance that is rarely captured by instruments—never indeed by Tycho's Sextants, nor by astronomical radii or staffs <note>The "Jacob's Staff" or cross-staff used for measuring angles.</note>—lest the eyes be strained too much and the observation be rendered unreliable. Therefore, having dropped the perpendicular **CF**, **CFE** will be a right angle and **FCE** 45°, because **DCE** is isosceles and **CE** is 89° 26'. And as the sine of **CFE** is to the sine of **CE**, so the sine of **FCE** is to the sine of **FE**, the double of which is **DE**. Thus, instead of the 90° that **AB** had been, the distance **DE**—distorted by refractions—will be 89° 59' 43": a difference of 17". This difference is even smaller where the distance **AB** itself is taken as smaller.

<margin>The distance of stars stretched from the zenith toward the horizon is notably smaller than it should be.</margin>

Regarding what is found in Proposition 53—that the distances of stars or the diameters of celestial bodies stretched from the zenith <note>The point directly overhead.</note> toward the horizon are smaller than they should be, especially if one end is near the horizon—I say these things are both true and evident to the senses, and are highly necessary for the Astronomer to know. Indeed, I do not believe this proposition has been read by those "accusers of Tychonic Refractions" <note>Scholars who doubted Tycho Brahe’s revolutionary data on how the atmosphere bends light.</note> about whom I spoke above in the conclusion of Proposition 9 of this chapter; I therefore refer them to this proposition.

<margin>Against those who deny the refraction of the stars.</margin>

<margin>The Sun is not round near the horizon.</margin>

Therefore, what Vitello <note>A 13th-century authority on optics whom Kepler is correcting.</note> teaches in the following Proposition 54—that all stars near the horizon appear smaller than they should be—is true. However, his claim that they also appear round is false. For it is not true that all their diameters appear equally smaller; since the diameter that is stretched toward the zenith becomes smaller to our senses, while the one parallel to the horizon is diminished by an imperceptible amount. Hence, refracted shapes take on an **oval form**, just like the shape of coins thrown into water if they are viewed from a very oblique angle. And this is the only proposition in which those who deny refractions have placed their *optical apprenticeship* <note>original: "tyrocinium optices"; meaning their basic training or primary argument.</note>, thinking there is no other power in refractions except to dilate or contract bodies seen through them. Therefore, the argument they build upon this—regarding the direction of sight toward the center of a star—cannot be any firmer than this very proposition of Vitello’s. Suppose the lower edge of the Sun touches the horizon; its refraction will be 34'. For the upper edge, which has an altitude of half a degree, the refraction will be 29'. Thus, instead of a 30' diameter, the Sun will appear to have a height of 25 minutes, while its transverse <note>Horizontal.</note> diameter, parallel to the horizon, will remain 30'. The semi-diameter of its altitude would be 12 1/2...

<margin>Against the <term>Tychomastigas</term> <note>From Greek: "Scourges of Tycho"; those who aggressively attacked Tycho Brahe's findings.</note> who deny refractions.</margin>

<summary>Kepler explains how atmospheric refraction causes celestial bodies near the horizon to appear squashed or oval-shaped rather than perfectly circular. He uses this to defend Tycho Brahe's observations against critics, proving that vertical diameters are contracted more than horizontal ones.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Kepler’s critique of traditional optical theories, specifically addressing the phenomenon of why celestial bodies appear larger under certain atmospheric conditions. He is responding to theories found in the works of Vitello (Witelo).</meta>

->SUPPLEMENT TO VITELLO. 133<-

[The author] asserts that when the East Wind blows, everything appears larger. Since this happens so frequently, it cannot simply arise from the accidental placement of vapor between us and the stars. Furthermore, all the stars in the entire hemisphere are seen this way at the same time; yet if some transparent and secluded vapor in one location were the cause, this phenomenon would sometimes be perceived in only one part of the sky. Then, by what force, I ask, could a transparent vapor remain suspended in the air when it is much heavier than air—so that, like spectacles <note>original: *perspicillorum*—Kepler is referring to magnifying lenses or eyeglasses, which were well-known by 1604</note> made of glass or crystal, it could magnify the stars? 

Nor does the example of clouds hold weight. For clouds hanging in the air <margin>Why clouds hang in the air.</margin>, as well as mists and things of this sort, bring about darkness and are not transparent. Since they seem to be of a somewhat drier nature once they have finished raining (for those heavy with moisture do not hang, but fall drop by drop), it is no wonder they float in the air like wood in water. But how would a moist, transparent, fluid, thick, and heavy vapor be held suspended in air that is much lighter than itself? 

Rather, when this happens, it is an indication that moist matter is ascending from the deepest bowels of the earth, and the lower regions—contiguous both to the earth and to our eyes—are filled first. The same thing happens to us as to those who are weeping; in both cases, the eye is touched by moisture. Add to this that the same things usually happen in refraction, affecting both the diameters of lights and the distances between them. But this phenomenon does not extend to distances. For it has never been observed that distances appear greater than they are; they are always either correct or smaller than they should be. 

Finally, this phenomenon occurs with stars at the zenith <note>original: *in vertice*—the point in the sky directly overhead</note> no less than at the horizon, which is contrary to how refractions behave. Therefore, it is necessary that this does not belong to that type of refraction about which we have spoken so far. It will not, therefore, be a phenomenon of quantity or of visual angles, but of light alone; of the sort that includes halos, rainbows, twinkling <margin>Halos, Rainbows, Twinkling; see the end of the chapter.</margin>, and similar things. The causes of these meteorological phenomena <note>Kepler uses "Meteororum" in the Aristotelian sense, meaning any atmospheric phenomenon, including weather and optical effects like rainbows</note> do not yet seem to have been sufficiently explained; but since they are of little necessity for astronomical considerations, I have not yet bestowed any particular care upon them.

The third cause, by which Vitello <margin>Why stars appear larger near the horizon.</margin> <note>Witelo (c. 1230–1275) was a Polish scholar whose work *Perspectiva* was the standard medieval text on optics. It harms neither the light, as the second cause does; nor the visual angle and the quantity of the appearance itself, as the first does; nor
