Because of this, the size of the thing seen (whether it be the distance between two stars or the diameter of a single star) appears quite large, even though the angle remains the same. For among those things perceived at the same angle, those which are further away are larger, and those which are closer are smaller. Nor does this cause concern astronomers much, because observations made through instruments do not contract any error from it. This fact only serves to show that when we read that the ancients performed their observations not with instruments but by the estimation of distances, we know they could have been deceived in this matter, since the estimating faculty itself is greatly deceived for this reason; a point which both Tycho Brahe emphasized, and Ptolemy himself in Book 9, Chapter 2 <note>Original: "lib.9.cap.2." of the *Almagest*.</note>.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*8. Are refractions the same in all places and times?*

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Refractions in maritime places are more constant; in inland regions they are sometimes almost non-existent, and sometimes prodigious. For in maritime places, the air retains almost the same height, and a height deep enough that even if something is added to its altitude, it is not so noticeable. But in inland regions, the air is lower, so much so that on certain mountains it is not even possible to live unless a sponge is applied to the nostrils, which Aristotle testifies regarding Mount Olympus in his *Meteorology* <note>Original: "Meteoris." Aristotle believed the air atop Olympus was too thin and dry for breathing without a moist sponge.</note>. And Bodin <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596), a French philosopher and historian.</note>, from Indian history, reports that very many Spaniards perished from the cold when they crossed the highest ridges of the mountains under the equator, even though the plains were parched with heat. # SUPPLEMENT TO WITELO. 135

Places near the sources of rivers, because of their height above the sea coasts—which encourages the downward flow of rivers—correspond to some extent to the short distances seen in the sea. From this comes the common opinion that the air in the Alps is healthier because it is thinner and more purified, while the thicker air settles down into the valleys. Therefore, <term>refractions</term><note>The bending of light as it passes through the atmosphere, which makes stars appear higher in the sky than they actually are.</note> will be non-existent in some places, very small in others, and almost entirely restricted to the horizon itself. For it is consistent that there are many places which are elevated half a mile <note>Kepler likely refers to the "German mile," roughly 7.5 kilometers; thus, half a mile is about 3.75 km, which he considers the limit of the dense, refractive atmosphere.</note> above the surface of the sea, which is the thickness of the air layer in the Danish straits according to Proposition 11 of this chapter.

Vitruvius, in Book 8, Chapter 7, requires a <margin>The leveling of rivers.</margin> <term>slope</term><note>original: "libramento"</note> of one-two-hundredth of the distance traveled for aqueducts. There is no doubt that such a great height [gradient] would be destructive to navigation. Therefore, if you attribute one hundred miles to the bends of the Elbe <note>original: "Albis"</note>, it falls much less than half a mile from the height of the Noric lands <note>The region of the Danube, roughly modern Austria and Bavaria.</note>, from where it rises and flows into the Ocean: because it flows gently and is often stagnant. But the Danube, carried through nearly another 100 miles, marks a higher elevation in Swabia than in the Noric lands. 

Thus it will happen that the Vosges <margin>The height of the Vosges.</margin> and the continuous Rhaetian Alps almost exceed the height of the air that produces refractions. Perpetual snows confirm this; for they indicate the nakedness of those peaks from the vaporous air. For this reason, there will generally not be any refractions there either. But if storms gather, and sudden vapors arise from neighboring mountains; before they flow down and spread themselves into the uniformity of the atmospheric sphere, it is consistent that they also do their part in the business of refraction, and that this varies greatly because of the uneven surface during their "boiling" <note>Kepler uses the term "ebullitione" to describe the turbulent, bubbling motion of rising vapors.</note>. 

Then, the closer a place is to the boundary of the air, the greater the refractions it perceives, because the air is circular and (as follows from this) it refracts the rays of the sun, which strike it most obliquely, at the greatest angle—as was just shown in Proposition 9, at 61 1/2 minutes. Those rays so refracted only pass through the highest parts of the air; however, those which penetrate to the lower parts are refracted at a smaller angle, because they also strike the air more directly. See the diagram in Chapter 7, Number 5.

This same point is confirmed by the testimonies of learned men and by experience. Certainly Rothmann <note>Christoph Rothmann (died c. 1600), a prominent astronomer who worked for Landgrave Wilhelm IV of Hesse-Kassel.</note> in Hesse, which is near the sources of the Weser <note>original: "Visurgis"</note>, constantly affirms that the refractions of the stars generally appear smaller than those which Tycho Brahe <note>The famous Danish astronomer (1546–1601) whose precise data Kepler used to derive his laws of planetary motion.</note> recorded in Denmark.

-># SUPPLEMENTS TO WITELO. 137<-

As the [eclipse] was beginning, we saw the Moon already fading in the South by several inches <note>original: "digitis," a term used to measure the extent of an eclipse in 12ths of the diameter</note>, raised nearly two degrees high; and conversely, as the center of the Moon was descending toward its setting, we noted the Sun at an altitude of two degrees above its rising. However, the Moon set before it had reached its maximum obscuration. From these observations, it is concluded that the horizontal refraction <term>refraction: the bending of light as it passes through the atmosphere, making objects appear higher than they actually are</term> of that day was much greater than two degrees, half of which was due to the Sun and the remainder to the Moon. For when the center of the Sun was rising, it was expected that the center of the Earth's shadow would be setting; and since the Moon had already then begun to enter the shadow—and usually enters from the western side—the center of the Moon was therefore further west than the center of the shadow. As the shadow's center set, the Moon's center had already set. And yet it was seen raised up by two degrees. Therefore, the total refraction of both the Sun and Moon together was more than two degrees—not to mention that the horizon at Tübingen is not without mountains, whose peaks are a little higher than the water-level <note>a horizontal baseline used for surveying</note>; thus while half the Sun is visible, if the mountains were absent, the whole would be visible. Therefore, the refraction of a single celestial body was greater than a whole degree. Moreover, that part of Swabia is not far from the sources of the Neckar and the Danube; <margin>Hoeberg Mountain in Swabia.</margin> and the Hoeberg mountain near Horb is infamous for sorcery and the gathering of witches—the common people's gullibility interpreting the ingenuity of Nature and the frequent eruptions of storms as magical illusions.

As for the fact that refractions are different at different times even in the same place, Rothmann stubbornly contends this on pages 85 and 86 of Tycho’s *Astronomical Letters*, and Tycho Brahe himself readily grants it in his *Introductory Exercises* <note>original title: *Progymnasmata*</note> on pages 79 and 280. And in Volume 1 of the *Letters*, page 64, he requires the air to be very pure and clear when he conducts a trial of refractions. Thus, in the *Observations* for the year 1587, I found it noted in the month of January that refractions appear larger around the Solstices. Although, in my opinion, the cause of the increased refraction on the day mentioned should not be attributed to the winter solstice, but to the air having become warmer due to a square <note>An astrological aspect where two planets are 90 degrees (one quarter circle) apart</note> of Jupiter and Mars, which occurred then. <margin>Why are the refractions of fixed stars smaller?</margin> For as to why a smaller refraction was found by Tycho in the fixed stars than in the Sun, no other cause seems likely than this: that solar refractions are most correctly observed in summer, and those of the fixed stars in winter; yet the air is more vaporous <note>thick with moisture or haze</note> and the Sun is higher in summer than in winter.

138 ->JOHANNES KEPLER<-

higher. For on page 64 of the first book of *Letters*, it appears, and in the *Progymnasmata* <note>Tycho Brahe’s *Astronomiae Instauratae Progymnasmata*, a foundational work on the "restitution" of astronomy.</note> on page 93 it is clearly instructed, that **refractions** <term>refraction: the bending of light as it passes through the Earth's atmosphere, which causes stars and planets to appear higher in the sky than they actually are.</term> are to be observed most especially at those times when the Sun would be quite high even at noon, and its **declination** <note>The angular distance of a celestial body north or south of the celestial equator.</note> would perceptibly change not at all within the same day, which occurs during the **summer solstice**. For in the winter time, the Sun does not rise above the height where refractions occur. Conversely, the refractions of the fixed stars are observed with difficulty in summer, partly due to the night-long clarity of the air in Denmark, and partly because the thick air near the horizon intercepts the sight of the stars. Therefore, they are best observed in winter and on the clearest nights, when the air is more settled. And why should refractions not increase when the easterly winds blow, since Rothmann <note>Christoph Rothmann, a prominent astronomer who corresponded with Tycho Brahe.</note> asserts on page 122 of the *Tychonic Letters* that he himself often saw the stars refracted through the vapors of the **heated room** <note>original: "hypocausti"; refers to a room heated by an oven or underfloor system.</note> while he was standing in the middle of the heated observatory?

Therefore, to conclude this section, let it be certain that there are different refractions in different places and times, and unusual ones in unusual conditions. Thus, if the altitude of a place is great, there will be no refraction; if there is an extraordinary release of vapors, the refraction will be prodigious. But if the places and times are moderate, the refractions will be nearly the same.

### *9. On the observation of the Dutch in the far North.*

The travel journal of the **Dutch** <note>original: "Batauorum", referring to the inhabitants of the Netherlands.</note> is in everyone's hands—the description of the voyage through the Northern Ocean into the deserted regions called **Novaya Zemlya** <note>An archipelago in the Arctic where the explorer Willem Barentsz and his crew were famously trapped in the ice during their search for the Northeast Passage.</note>, to seek a strait which would provide a passage into the Scythian and Eastern Ocean. In this little book, among other memorable things, they report this: when they were stuck in the ice and night had overwhelmed them, and they had seen the Sun for the last time on November 3, 1596, according to the **New Style** <note>original: "St. N." (Stilo Novo), referring to the Gregorian calendar.</note> calendar. From the altitude of the pole, which they calculated to be 76°, they held it as certain from astronomical principles that the Sun would not return before February 11, 1597. Nevertheless, it happened that on January 24, seventeen days before the legitimate time, they saw the Sun again by its top edge exactly at the point of noon. Indeed, at this time, a few hours later, they noted a **conjunction** of Jupiter and the Moon in the 2nd degree of Taurus, so that no one should think the date had been neglected...

...and a commonly encountered cause for this phenomenon is sufficient: namely, the refraction of light from both luminaries <note>The Sun and the Moon</note> in the surface of the air that surrounds the Earth. Therefore, refractions also occurred in Italy in ancient times, and this testimony admits no exception. Weaker conjectures follow.

Ptolemy, in the third book of his *Great Work* <note>Known as the *Almagest*, the most influential astronomical text of antiquity.</note>, asserts that he often observed the equinox twice on the same day using the Alexandrian armillary spheres <term>Armillary sphere: An astronomical instrument composed of graduated metal rings representing the great circles of the heavens, used to track the movement of the stars and Sun.</term>. He blames the faulty positioning of the instrument, which had supposedly shifted since its initial setup. However, Ptolemy levels the same blame against Hipparchus <note>A Greek astronomer from the 2nd century BCE whose work Ptolemy often relied upon.</note>, who lived closer to the time of the original setup and who testified that he had observed the equinoxes with those same armillary spheres. *For in the 32nd year of the third Callippic period* <note>A 76-year cycle used in ancient Greece to synchronize the solar year and lunar months.</note>, *on the 27th day of the month of Mechir, according to Ptolemy's report, Hipparchus observed the equinox in the morning; but in fact, the Alexandrian armillary spheres were equally illuminated on both sides at the fifth hour of the day.* Ptolemy therefore concludes that *the two observations do not agree within five hours.* Indeed, Hipparchus emphasizes that *the best observation is that which is made through the Alexandrian armillary spheres, for that is the hour of the true equinox in which both surfaces of the ring are equally illuminated.*

Therefore, while it is indeed possible that this discordant observation of the equinoxes arose from a defect in the instrument—and Ptolemy’s accusation may have been true—it is also true that in our time, Tycho Brahe <note>The Danish astronomer and Kepler's mentor, known for his high-precision instruments.</note> very frequently recorded the same thing using the most corrected and exquisitely positioned instruments: namely, that the equinox occurred twice on the same day. For in the morning, when the moment of the vernal equinox <note>The spring equinox, when day and night are of equal length.</note> is not yet imminent, the rising Sun appears higher due to refraction and closer to the celestial pole, so that it seems to already be on the equator while it is still to the south. In the afternoon, when the Sun is free from refraction—even if it has by then truly completed its winter semi-circle—it will then be on the equator once again, both truly and to the sight. The opposite must be thought regarding the Autumnal equinox. It is therefore uncertain whether the cause of why authors persuaded themselves they had seen the same equinox twice should be attributed to a defect in the instrument or to refractions.

I shall say something that is not strictly proper to this place, but should rather be deferred to a discussion on the calculation of the Year. What if <margin>Whether the eccentricity was truly greater in the past.</margin> this entanglement of refractions alone is the reason why Hipparchus long ago found a greater solar eccentricity <term>Eccentricity: In this context, the measurement of how much the Sun's apparent orbit around the Earth deviates from a perfect circle.</term> than we find today?

# ADDITIONS TO WITELO. 147

...as does Tycho <note>Tycho Brahe (1546–1601), the preeminent Danish observational astronomer whose precise data Kepler used</note> today, and Al-Battani <note>Albategnius (c. 858–929), a major Arab astronomer who refined the measurements of the solar year</note> eight hundred years ago. Ptolemy, however, in such a subtle matter, seems to have carefully adapted his own observations to the proofs of Hipparchus (which he fully retained). If this is established regarding the former, it is also settled regarding the latter: for there is such a great agreement between the two in calculating the length of the quarters of the year that it was clearly impossible to detect such precision with Ptolemaic or Hipparchian instruments. 

Therefore, the reason I raise this suspicion about Hipparchus is this. It is known from Ptolemy and Proclus Diadochus <note>A 5th-century philosopher and mathematician who wrote on astronomy</note> that Hipparchus and others were accustomed to measuring the diameters of the luminaries <note>The Sun and the Moon</note> using **water-clocks** <term>Clepsydrae|Ancient timekeeping devices that measured the passage of time by the regulated flow of water from one vessel to another</term>. When the very top edge of the Sun rose, water began to flow from an open hole of the water-clock into a separate small vessel; then, once the entire Sun had emerged, the remaining water was collected in another vessel throughout a continuous day and night, until the edge of the Sun was seen to rise again in the same place. 

Since they used this method of observation in measuring the Sun's diameter, what is more likely to be believed than this: that Hipparchus defined the day of the equinox as that day on which the Sun, on the visible horizon, would reach two diametrically opposite points—one while rising and the other while setting. Once these points were established by observation, he held them forever after as the markers for the equinoxes, provided he remained in the same location. 

If I have guessed correctly here, I will easily obtain the rest. For as long as the Sun is in the southern semicircle of the Zodiac, it cannot perform what we said was observed by Hipparchus—namely, that while rising it reaches a point on the horizon diametrically opposite to the one it reaches when setting. For both points still incline toward the south. Therefore, on the horizon where we assume the observation is made, because the Sun appears higher than it truly is due to **refractions** <term>Refraction|The bending of light as it passes through the Earth's atmosphere, which makes celestial bodies near the horizon appear higher than their actual physical position</term>, it will seem to have entered the equator <note>The celestial equator, marking the start of spring</note> earlier than it truly did, and in autumn it will seem to have descended into it later than is true. 

Thus, the time of the summer semicircle <note>The period between the spring and autumn equinoxes</note> will seem longer, with both ends of the period extended; therefore, the **Eccentricity** <term>Eccentricity|In the astronomy of Kepler's time, this referred to the offset of the Sun's circular orbit from the center of the Earth</term> will appear greater than it truly is. Therefore, anyone who is willing to believe that the Sun's eccentricity is the same today as it was in the past has here a clear argument based on the effects of refraction as observed by Hipparchus.

**The Civil Hospitals and Care Homes.**

The Christian love for the poor, which stirred in the hearts of the citizens shortly after the founding of the St. James <note>German: *St. Jakobi*</note> parish, led to the establishment of the hospital named after it. It was among the oldest charitable institutions in our city.

<margin>1227</margin> According to a report from the Council in the year 1227, Count Adolf IV <note>Adolf IV of Holstein (1203–1244), a key figure in the history of Hamburg and Holstein</note> granted a field for the construction of a hospital, which was called the *Hospital for the Poor* <note>original: "Hospitale pauperum"</note>. Initially, it stood outside the city gates, near where the *Spitalerthor* <note>Hospital Gate</note> once was, from which the street *Spitalerstraße* still derives its name today. It was originally intended for the "leper folk" <note>People suffering from leprosy, who were historically quarantined outside city limits</note>. 

However, because it was located too far from the church, and since the city had expanded significantly in that direction, the hospital was moved in 1260 to the *Mönckeberg*. It remained there until the year 1618, at which point the site was used for the later-built *Spinnhaus* <note>A "spin house" was a house of correction or workhouse, often where inhabitants were tasked with spinning wool or flax</note>. 

The administration and oversight of this hospital were entrusted to the *Provisoren* <note>Lay administrators or overseers responsible for the financial and operational management of church properties and charities</note> of the St. James Church. During the great plague years of 1605 and 1606, the building served as a *Lazareth* <note>A quarantine station or infirmary for those with infectious diseases</note> for the sick and dying.

In the year 1489, on the 6th of March, around sunset—specifically while the **Midheaven** <note>The point of the ecliptic that is highest in the sky at a given time.</note> was at 25° of Gemini <note>original: ♊</note>—the **Sun** was found via the **armillary sphere** <note>An astronomical instrument composed of rings representing the great circles of the heavens.</note> to be at 25° 15' of Pisces <note>original: ♓</note>. **Venus**, measured through another circle with the Ecliptic dividing the Sun, was found at 27° 15' of Aries <note>original: ♈</note>. However, when measured using the circle of latitude with the Sun in the middle (as is customary near the horizon), she was found in another place, namely at 25° 30' of Aries; I will add the reason for this later. These things are explained shortly thereafter; what follows is:

On the 7th of March, the **Sun**, by the appearance of the armillary rings, was at 26° 15' of Pisces. **Venus**, from the Ecliptic, was at 28° 15' of Aries; from the circle of latitude, she was at 27° 38' of Aries. Immediately following these observations, the author adds these words:

"Furthermore, lest it remain hidden from readers for too long how I proceeded, or why the position of Venus was found to be so inconsistent at almost the same moment, it must be noted that **stars appear near the horizon because of refracted rays** above the horizon, when in truth they are below it."

And this was clearly required by the logic and doctrine of <term>refractions</term> <note>The bending of light as it passes from one medium, like space, into another, like the Earth's atmosphere.</note> as handed down until now, rather than the opposite. For the rays of the Sun, falling obliquely onto the surface of water, proceed at a less inclined angle to that surface where they hide themselves within the water, just as if the Sun were higher. In the very same way, if those same rays of the Sun falling upon the surface of the **air**—which completely covers us humans like a flood—were to continue along the same path by which they struck the surface of the air, they would never strike our eyes, but would be carried far above our heads. 

But having been refracted at the surface of our air, they now descend more steeply toward us and appear to us to be higher up. And indeed, if we speak of water, the Sun can never be below the surface of the water, but always above it, because the portion of the water's surface in which we experience this refraction is so small that it appears entirely flat to us. 

However, since the air is round, a significant portion of it interposes itself between our sight and the Sun—a portion so great that it already begins to curve toward the Sun. Therefore, even if a certain ray of the Sun touches the surface of the air at some point that hangs over our heads (as when the Sun is right on the horizon), or at a point that is now closer to the Sun than what is above us (as when the Sun has already set), the parts of the aerial sphere which stretch toward the Sun after 그 point of contact will, due to the <term>conglobation</term> <note>The rounding or spherical gathering of the atmosphere around the Earth.</note> of the air, drop themselves below that tangent line. Thus, that which has already set for us is still elevated for those points in the atmosphere.

<meta>This page continues Johannes Kepler’s discussion on optical refraction from his 1604 work "Ad Vitellionem Paralipomena" (Supplement to Witelo). He is describing a method for observing the Sun's position near the horizon using an astronomical instrument to demonstrate how atmospheric refraction "lifts" the visible Sun above its true geometric position.</meta>

# SUPPLEMENT TO WITELO. 155

...[the instrument], by a clever device where the plumb line represented the vertical circle <note>The vertical circle is an imaginary circle passing through the zenith and nadir, perpendicular to the horizon.</note>, by considering that the point whose image is refracted—represented in this case by the intersection of the circle of latitude with the Ecliptic—the center of vision (represented by the aforementioned aperture), the point on the surface of the air where refraction occurs, and the perpendicular line from the point of refraction, are all in one surface, which we imagine here as the plane of the vertical circle. And I saw, while the intersection of the Ecliptic and the circle of latitude representing the true position of the Sun had reached the contact of the horizon—a position corresponding to the true sunset—that the Sun still illuminated the thread of the plumb line through the aperture of the other <term>pinnule</term> <note>pinnule: a small sighting vane on an astronomical instrument with a hole or slit for alignment.</note> facing the Sun, which I otherwise used only for the stars. I took care, that is to say, so that the Sun would equally illuminate not the circle of latitude, nor the Ecliptic, but the thread of the plumb line suspended from the aperture of one pinnule through the aperture of the opposite pinnule across the diameter. Thus, the aforementioned things were in one surface <note>original: "superficie" — in this context, Kepler means a geometric plane.</note>: namely, the center of the true Sun (that is, the point whose image is refracted), the center of vision (in this case the aperture from which the thread is suspended, or rather the lower point of the thread where it is illuminated by the Sun), the point of refraction in the air, and the perpendicular; and similarly both the true position of the Sun in the Ecliptic of the instrument, and finally the position of the image, or the visible Sun.

For because the apertures are diametrically opposite and the thread is suspended from the other aperture, the plane passing through the thread and the apertures therefore bisects the instrument. And because the visible Sun illuminates the thread through the other aperture, the visible Sun is therefore also in the same surface which, because of the plumb line, is perpendicular to the horizon; it is therefore in the plane of the vertical circle. Consequently, the true position of the Sun is in that same plane, since the true position of an object and the position of its image are always in the same surface. When this occurs in the instrument (provided that the other aperture or the intersection of the Ecliptic and circle of latitude represents the very true position of the Sun, as is posited), it is proof that the instrument has been so directed that the center, the apertures (or the said intersection), and the very true position of the Sun in the sky fall into one straight line; nor can it be positioned otherwise for this to happen. It is truly an ingenious shortcut for determining refractions by means of an instrument, without the need for calculation from longitude and latitude.

Furthermore, if anyone is so diligent that they do not wish to trust instruments blindly in such a subtle matter, they have a method for distributing the parallaxes and refractions that occur in altitude into longitude and latitude, found in Tycho Brahe’s *Progymnasmata*, especially volume 1, folios 93, 94, and 96, where he also teaches how to investigate the total refraction or the altitudes. In which study <note>original: *pragmateia*</note> you will find a most useful summary below in Chapter 9.

      I believe it has been sufficiently proven, by going through each instance, that refractions have been noticed by astronomers in every age. I am waiting, therefore, to see how those who deny the whole business of refractions—except for thinking it consists only in the enlargement of [apparent] diameters—wish to excuse their own rashness. I have shown above, however, that this phenomenon is quite distinct from the usual business of refractions. Indeed, it is true that everyone thinks they are allowed to rise up against those who seem to profess something new. When this happens without reason, it degenerates into detraction. It is much more shameful, however, that through such efforts, these men openly betray their own ignorance and their reckless contempt for others. They should have read at least the disputation of my teacher Maestlin <note>Michael Maestlin (1550–1631), Kepler’s professor at Tübingen who famously taught him the Copernican system.</note>, which appeared very recently. Since he is the most recent authority and, by God's grace, still living, I have chosen to append his words from Thesis 58 as a finishing touch <note>original: *coronidis loco*</note> to this chapter; so that this man’s findings may be compared with those of Tycho, and thus the authority of this doctrine may be greater, supported by more votes, so that the mouths of the critics may finally be stopped. He writes as follows, after citing the testimonies of Witelo <note>A 13th-century Polish friar and physicist known for his influential work on optics.</note> and Walther: *“If credit is to be given to our observations made with the astronomical radius <note>Also known as a Jacob's staff or cross-staff, used to measure the angle between two stars.</note>: we have found not infrequently (and sometimes in my presence) that the distance of Venus—when it is higher above the horizon—from the Sun—when the Sun is positioned near the horizon—is notably smaller than if the distance from the Sun were taken on the same day when the Sun is higher and freer from vapors <note>“Vapors” refers to the thick atmospheric air near the horizon that causes greater refraction.</note> (about which opinion on the cause enough has been said above). Therefore, the Sun's altitude through...”*

<summary>In this passage, Kepler defends the historical validity of atmospheric refraction, citing Tycho Brahe and his own teacher, Michael Maestlin, against contemporary skeptics. He argues that refraction significantly affects the measured positions of planets like Venus, especially when observed near the horizon.</summary>

SUPPLEMENTS TO VITELLO. 157

...vapors even along the surface of the air, [the object] appeared higher than is right. From this, we do not consider it impossible, but conclude for certain, that both this and other stars can similarly appear above the horizon when they are still below it. Furthermore, this is one of those ways by which **Tycho** <note>Tycho Brahe (1546–1601), the Danish nobleman whose precise astronomical observations provided the data Kepler used to calculate the laws of planetary motion.</note> very frequently investigated refractions, as will eventually be revealed, God willing, from the books of his observations. Moreover, **Mästlin** <note>Michael Mästlin (1550–1631), Kepler’s professor at Tübingen, known for his exceptionally keen eyesight.</note> is also very experienced in observing **Venus** by day due to his singular sharpness of vision.

->Note to No. 7.<-

Regarding **Halos**, of which **Sundogs** <note>original: *Parelia*</note> are certain parts of circles, as are **Moondogs** <note>original: *Paraselenæ*</note>, I wanted to advise those studious of these matters of the following. **First**, the colors of Halos around the Sun and of Sundogs are the same as those in **Rainbows** <note>original: *Iridibus*</note>, though darker because of the brightness of the sun shining nearby; and they are quite thin in Halos around the moon and in Moondogs. Therefore, they are the offspring of refractions, just like Rainbows. See below in Chapter 5 regarding experiments using water globes and <term>triangular glass</term> <note>Kepler is referring to glass prisms, which were used to study the separation of light into colors long before Newton's more famous experiments.</note>.

**Second**, the diameter of a Rainbow when the sun is setting is always 90 degrees; of a Halo, 45 degrees. Therefore, whoever you are who desires to know anything here beyond **Aristotle** <note>Kepler frequently challenges the ancient Greek "Master of those who know," whose meteorological theories were being overturned by the Scientific Revolution.</note>, know that the cause of this must be demonstrated by you.

**Third**, Halos are seen in clouds that are clearly very close, as is evident from their swift flight. And yet, they are seen by all people regardless of where they are positioned, appearing to be 22 1/2 degrees away from the luminary <note>The sun or moon.</note> as if from their own center. Each person, therefore, sees their own individual Halo in clouds so near, no less than they see their own Rainbow, because a different cloud is interposed between the star and each different spectator.

Indeed, often while I remained in the same place, a Halo and Moondog appeared when a cloud stood in the right spot, then vanished as the cloud moved away, and appeared again when another cloud took its place.

It is necessary, therefore, for the rays of the star to be refracted in a place much higher up—yet in a fluid material with a fixed surface and always of the same density and height—and thus to be sent down after being refracted. But they are not seen unless they are caught by a transparent cloud from above, so that the image appears from below through the transparent body of the cloud.

**Fourth**, Sundogs and Moondogs are almost more frequent than the halos themselves, because there are almost always sundogs within a halo. And as often as these appear, they are always seen at an equal altitude with the Sun or Moon.

**Fifth**, for a Rainbow to appear, it is necessary for the place where it can appear to be both clothed in material and in shadow. For that reason, whenever it rains while the sun is shining through, and a cloud appears very close above the sun—namely, where the shadow of the cloud has barely departed—then the brightest Rainbows are seen.

Therefore, the watery material that is between the spectator and the sun—whether it be rain, or a transparent cloud, or a mist <note>original: *nebula*</note> (for I have seen Rainbows even in mist)—this, I say, forms and shapes the refractions of the sun's rays; but that which is behind the spectator receives these refracted rays of the sun.

He acknowledges his debt to professional anatomists before beginning his own description of the organ of sight.</meta>

->ADDITIONS TO WITELO. 159<-
<note>Witelo (Latinized as Vitellio) was a 13th-century friar and philosopher whose work on optics remained the standard textbook until Kepler wrote this "supplement" or "addition" (Paralipomena) to correct and expand upon it.</note>

...should I have been a spectator, or even an assistant? Therefore, let men of accepted authority speak for me concerning a matter most familiar to them, until the business is brought down to the boundaries of my own profession. For then, they will hand over the lamp to me without complaint, insofar as I shall lawfully take the lead in Mathematics <note>Kepler uses the metaphor of a relay race (handing over the lamp) to show where the anatomist's job ends and the mathematician's job begins.</note>, concerning which the judgment will belong to the experts.

I have primarily consulted the tables of Felix Plater <note>Felix Plater (1536–1614) was a Swiss physician famous for his anatomical drawings.</note> regarding the structure and use of the human body, which, having been published in the year 1583, deserved to be reprinted in this year 1603; with these I have compared the *Prague Anatomy* of my friend Lord Johannes Jessenius of Jessen <note>Johannes Jessenius (1566–1621) was a physician and friend of Kepler who performed the first public autopsy in Prague.</note>: because he professes not only to follow Fabricius of Aquapendente <note>Girolamo Fabricius (1533–1619), known as Aquapendente, was a pioneering anatomist who taught William Harvey.</note> above all others, but also because he has spent a great deal of effort on anatomical labors by his own initiative. If I have bypassed anyone of better merit in this field, being myself very occupied with the profession of Mathematics, they will grant me their pardon.

The word "Eye" (Oculus) is derived from the Greek *opē* <note>original: ὀπή</note>, from which come *opteuō* <note>original: ὀπτεύω; "to look at"</note>, *opsis* <note>original: ὄψις; "sight"</note>, *omma* <note>original: ὄμμα; "eye"</note>, and *ophthalmos* <note>original: ὀφθαλμός; "eye"</note>, because these are like chinks or open holes reaching out from the dark head into the clear air; just as, by a contrary reasoning, the "wolf" (lupus) seems to have been named from the Greek *lykos* <note>original: λυκός</note>: it is not named from "hiding" (occulendo) <note>Kepler is dismissing a common but incorrect Latin folk etymology that linked *oculus* (eye) to *occultus* (hidden).</note>, for when closed they are of no use. There are two eyes in animals, positioned in parallel and at a suitable interval—as will be discussed above in Chapter 3 and below in Chapter 9—for the purpose of noting the distances of things, and not truly so that one might compensate for the loss of the other. For Nature intends no such waste. Their placement is in the highest location, so that sight might reach out to places that much more remote. For since the earth, and especially the sea, is spherical, an eye placed at no height could perceive nothing at all of the plain, being hindered on every side by the curvature of the globe. Storks teach us this, and especially Giraffes <term>Camelopardali</term> <note>Literally "camel-leopards," the classical name for giraffes.</note>, with their necks held high to capture a much more distinct sight and sound of remote things; and above all Eagles, which, intending to survey the whole region for the sake of prey, seek the heights. For this reason, Jessenius speaks more clearly than Plater: the former says eyes are high up to see more things, the latter so that they might better perceive individual things from above. For as far as individual things are concerned, they are better inspected from nearby. Indeed, when we are about to contemplate a coin thrown on the ground, or a low-growing plant, we lower our eyes. Regarding man, Ovid wrote ethically and wisely:

*And while other animals look down at the earth,*
*He gave to man an uplifted face, and commanded him*
*To gaze at the heavens.* <note>Kepler quotes Ovid’s *Metamorphoses* (Book I, 84-86). This was a popular Renaissance sentiment—that humans are unique because they are built to look at the stars.</note>

<meta>This page continues Kepler's anatomical and philosophical exploration of the human eye, specifically discussing the positioning of the eyes and their relationship to human nature and the brain.</meta>

->160 JOHANNES KEPLER<-

*[Nature] commanded [man] to lift his upright face toward the stars.* <note>original: "Iussit, & erectos ad sidera tollere vultus." This is a famous line from Ovid’s Metamorphoses, often cited to distinguish humans from prone animals.</note>
But if you consider it physically, the eyes are neither on the crown of the head, nor are the eye sockets hollowed out upward; rather, they open more toward the sides and downward along the nose. Therefore, for the sake of exchanging speech, they seem to be situated this way in man, since man is a <term>social and political animal</term> <note>original: "animal sociabile & politicum." A reference to Aristotle’s definition of humanity.</note>. Thus, human bodies themselves invite social interaction more than those of other animals. Therefore, regarding this opinion of Platter <note>Felix Platter (1536–1614), a Swiss physician whose anatomical work Kepler studied closely.</note>—that the eyes obtained the front position so they might be placed directly opposite things—you may beautifully understand this as one human being placed opposite another. Another reason is sought from the dignity of man. Since other animals must seek their pasture, they keep their eyes cast down toward what is nearest to them. Man, the master of creatures, has his face directed in such a way that he is continually invited to contemplate how far the boundaries of his possession extend; these are the very heavens, which seem to touch the mountains.

But the reason why the eyes and ears turn toward the same side is most correctly sought from motion. Since motion must occur in a straight line, parallel to the horizon, the bending of the limbs and the placement of the necessary senses absolutely had to turn toward the same region of the horizontal circle. And since Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician and philosopher in the Roman Empire whose theories dominated Western medical science for centuries.</note> said the head was placed on high for the sake of the eyes, as the eyes could not be far from the brain, it is also consistent that the neck was made flexible so that the senses could be turned to see and hear those things that are behind. From this, the following reasoning seems to be quite aptly composed, as if from basic principles: the eyes are near the brain because the objects of sight and hearing are the <term>final cause</term> <note>The purpose or goal for which something exists or is done.</note> of local motion, and truly all local motion is situated in the judgment of the brain. Therefore, so that the limbs of the body might be girded for pursuing those things more swiftly than a lightning bolt—the images of which are carried through the senses to the brain—it was necessary for the eyes to be established within the very embrace of the brain.

Each eye lies hidden in its own chamber for the sake of safety; yet they protrude, lest, hindered by the sides of the chamber, they should be unable to look out upon the whole hemisphere in a single glance. But since that total view cannot be distinct except in the center, while it would be blurred at the sides, it was necessary for a very rapid motion to be present in the eyes, so that the gaze might better transfer itself to every individual part of the hemisphere.

### APPENDIX TO VITELLO. 161

Furthermore, because we have two eyes to help us judge the distances of objects, they require constant adjustment or rotation—which is itself a form of movement. However, it would not be practical for this movement to shift the eyes away from their central point. To ensure they rotate around a fixed center, they had to be spherical on the outside—except for those parts inside the head where they are wrapped in oblong muscles and reach into the brain through a long "process" or canal <note>original: "processu seu canali"; Kepler is referring here to the optic nerve.</note>. The necessity of the eyelids also required the front part of the eye to be spherical, even in the areas where it does not rub against the face during movement. 

Because the eye must remain transparent, it would be nearly impossible to maintain that clarity in an organ that stays as warm as the rest of the body. Without constant care, tears, moisture from the air that condenses on the surface <note>Kepler describes this as "air resolved into water," a common way of explaining condensation in the 17th century.</note>, and drifting dust would cloud the surface. The eye also needs to be moistened to prevent it from becoming dry and rough. 

The eyelid seems to perform all these tasks, as is clearly seen when someone cries. At the same time, the eyelid serves the duty of protection—closing when danger threatens or when sleep creeps in. Nature thus averts the risks that would otherwise threaten a person if their eyes remained open while they slept. 

For the purpose of wiping the eye, the inner lining of the eyelid is a soft membrane, made of the same kind of tissue as the surface it cleans. However, the curve at the edge—called the <term>tarsus</term> <note>The tarsal plate is the thick fold of connective tissue that gives the eyelid its shape and firmness.</note>—is smooth and made of a somewhat harder internal substance, like cartilage. It is soft enough to yield to the touch on its surface, yet it provides structural resistance due to its dense mass. Consequently, the upper membrane tends to fold and stretch over the globe of the eye; when the tarsus is lifted, the lid gathers into itself, and when the tarsus is lowered, it fits so snugly that it never gaps away from the eyeball. It is never stretched more in one place than another, since the entire tarsus moves as a single unit. Here, therefore

<margin>However, Jessenius <note>Johannes Jessenius (1566–1621) was a prominent physician and anatomist who performed the first public dissection in Prague; he was a contemporary and friend of Kepler.</note> says that this was denied by those who had a truncated nose.</margin>

...both individually and together, the stretch of the visible horizon. And so that this might be possible, and the breadth of vision might follow this line, the eye socket <note>original: *camera oculi*, literally "chamber of the eye."</note>, between the forehead and the jaw, needed to be somewhat depressed so that nothing there would stand in the way. This, indeed, was not necessary at the nose; rather, a rampart <note>original: *vallum*</note> had to be formed from the nose, lest the vision of each eye be confused. This rampart seems to provide two things: one, that it takes away the sight of one eye from the other, so they are not blinded by mutual brightness arising from reflections; the other, that by its height it prescribes a limit to the proximity of visible things. But what is taken from one eye by the nose, the other eye compensates. For Nature established the perfection of sight in two eyes. Two other such valleys lead down from the eye socket between the jaws and the nose, so that those things which are closest to the mouth and feet might be open to the eyes. Thus the necessity of movement and sustenance <note>Kepler suggests the facial anatomy is designed specifically to help us see where we walk and what we eat.</note> required. But the arch of the forehead protrudes the most, to shut out the light of the sky, by which visible things would be overwhelmed. For this reason, those for whom the brightness of light is troublesome wrinkle the forehead and bring that rampart closer to the eyes. The eyelashes <note>original: *cilia*</note> and eyebrows <note>original: *supercilia*</note> are for almost the same use. For light sent down through them does not suddenly strike the eyes with a full ray; rather, it is partly obscured by the lashes, and the eyes make a trial of the approaching light through the narrow gaps of the lashes, to see if it can be borne. And indeed, against distant light we protect ourselves with the eyebrows and the wrinkling of the forehead, but in directly opposite light we also use the eyelids, the lashes, and a squinting effort. Aristotle thought this should be discussed by him in Section 31, Problem 16 <note>A reference to the *Problemata*, a work traditionally attributed to Aristotle.</note>, but he did so by the absurd emission of rays <note>Referring to the ancient "extramission" theory that the eye sends out light to see, which Kepler worked to disprove by showing the eye is a passive receiver of light.</note>, which he himself rejects elsewhere. This is precisely the reason why eyebrows are curved into an arch, so that they may surround the circular eyes in a circular manner. Now, as an additional point, they catch dust; the lashes seem to serve as little fans for sweeping away flying dust. Finally, just as in the whole body, here too the moist and tender parts seem to be protected against friction by hairs. Especially when the eyelids are wiped and filth is to be rolled out through the valves <note>Meaning the edges of the eyelids.</note> by rubbing; the lashes perform the role of channels, which turn aside the filth across the valves so it is not forced into the eye. For all hairy things, being parched and dry, by their roughness and a certain kind of stiffness, [repel] moisture—

### ADDITIONS TO VITELLO. 163

...they repel with a coldness by which they are not overcome. From this, the reason is also seen why the eyelashes are straight, not tilted back, not bent forward, not too sparse, nor too dense, nor too long, nor too short, and only moderately curved. These are the things which, surrounding the eye itself, assist in the duty of seeing.

In reviewing the globe of the eye itself, it seems I must work only on this: to understand the anatomists correctly and to be a good <term>nomenclator</term> <note>original: nomenclatorem; a person who provides or organizes names for things</note>. Thus the anatomists seem to me to both paint and describe the eye as if the whole form of the eye, as it is born from the brain, represents the figure of an onion. Just as an onion consists of a bulb and a stalk, so the eye consists of a visible globe and a hidden passage reaching into the brain. And indeed, in onions, cores are found, completely hidden in the bulb, which the layers common to the bulb and stalk include and hide. You might not wrongly compare the <term>humors</term> <note>original: humores; the internal fluids of the eye</note> found in the sphere of the eye to those cores; they are enclosed in almost the same way by the <term>tunics</term> <note>original: tunicis; the membranes or layers of the eye</note> that are common to the eye, the passage to the brain, and even the brain itself.

For the substance of the brain itself is surrounded by two membranes, of which they call the thin inner one and the thick outer one the <term>Meninges</term> <note>original: Meningem; the protective layers surrounding the brain, today known as the pia mater and dura mater</note>. Thus in the brain there are three components, from each of which its own membrane extends into the passage of the eye and afterward into the globe of the eye itself. The thick membrane produces the outer tunic of the eye; the thin membrane produces the middle one; but the substance of the brain itself produces the optic nerve, which becomes the innermost tunic, and even this is not a simple structure. Although Platter <note>Felix Platter (1536–1614), an influential Swiss physician whose anatomical work Kepler relied upon</note> asserts that this layer is improperly called a "tunic," perhaps because he establishes that the optic nerves are similar to other nerves and denies they are hollow—which others assert are entirely hollow.

Now let us distinguish the globe of the eye into the visible and the hidden hemispheres; and let us subdivide that which is visible into the white and the "sun" or the iris, to speak more clearly. Therefore, the anatomists say that from the thick membrane arises the outer tunic of the eyeball, which alone encompasses the whole eye, but receives different names and properties according to its different parts. For from the end of the optic nerve through the entire hidden hemisphere and through the white of the eye, it has the name <term>sclera</term> <note>original: σκληρώδης (sklērōdēs); Greek for "hard" or "tough"</note>. This is the "hard tunic," and it is thick, opaque, white, and almost like cartilage. But that part which covers the "sun" of the eye... <note>The text ends mid-sentence as it moves to the next page, where it will likely describe the cornea</note>

And while the *sclera* with its *cornea* constitutes a complete, unbroken tunic, this *uvea* is perforated in the middle; the *aqueous humor* fills this opening and also bathes it from within. Thus, this entire part called the *uvea* floats in the *aqueous humor*, except for that single circle where I said it was bound to the *sclera* and to its own posterior part, which is called the *choroid*. The *choroid* part is said to be black on the inside, yet not as black as the *uvea*, but rather more blue. The *uvea* part is rough and very black on the inside; on the outside—where it represents the so-called "Sun in the eye" through the translucent *cornea*—it is smooth, and together with the exterior surface of the *choroid*, it displays various colors: now brown, now bluish-gray, now tawny, now bright. Representing such a broad circle (in the middle of which is the black of the eye, or the opening), it is called the *Iris* <note>named after the Greek goddess of the rainbow</note>. For truly, just as a spider hangs suspended in the center of its web, so the crystalline humor hangs in the center of the ciliary processes, with fibers drawn from both sides inward toward the center. 

The aqueous humor, however, has no film of its own: it is held in front by the cornea, behind by the "spider-web" <insert>the lens capsule</insert>, the ciliary processes of the uvea, and the underlying hyaloid of the vitreous humor. It is constricted in the middle, and divided as if into two parts by the uvea <note>the iris</note>, which it washes both inside and outside the opening of the pupil. The vitreous has the greatest volume; the crystalline the smallest—its axis is scarcely a fourth part of the axis of the vitreous. The vitreous has a shape very nearly like a sphere that is more than half-complete. The aqueous consists of spherical surfaces, but in the middle, as I said, it is reduced into a narrow neck.

168 BY JOHANNES KEPLER

<note>Johannes Kepler (1571–1630) was a German astronomer and mathematician. This text is from his 1604 work *Ad Vitellionem Paralipomena* (Additions to Witelo), which laid the foundations for modern optics.</note>

the curvatures of the <term>cornea</term> (the clear front window of the eye) and the <term>crystalline humor</term> (the lens) are, for all intents and purposes, spherical. Their diameters relate to each other in a ratio of 4 to 3. The <term>aqueous humor</term> (the fluid in the front of the eye) is the thinnest, while the crystalline lens is the densest. Both are perfectly clear. The <term>vitreous humor</term> (the gel-like substance filling the back of the eye) is slightly more tinted. If an axis is drawn through the center of the opening of the <term>uvea</term> (the pupil) into the optic nerve, the centers of the circles of the lens lie on this axis. Thus, the lens is correctly said to sit in the center of the eye, provided you understand "center" to mean the point where the eye is divided by a plane perpendicular to that axis. However, regarding the entire rounded shape of the eye, the lens is shifted more toward the front along said axis. The lens is furthest from the end of the optic nerve, closer to the opening of the iris, and closest of all to the surface of the cornea.

### 2 *The manner of vision.*

Although the forehead, eyebrows, eyelids, and eye sockets contribute to the process of vision, they do not perform the primary functions. For that reason, I have already discussed their uses and included them in the previous descriptions. However, the parts I have listed here, which belong to the globe of the eye itself, all work together toward the primary task. Therefore, so that the use of each part may be clear, I shall describe the manner of vision—which, to my knowledge, has never been so thoroughly investigated or understood by anyone until now. I therefore ask mathematicians to consider these matters diligently, so that at long last something certain regarding this most noble function may exist in philosophy.

I say that vision occurs when an image <note>original: "idolum"</note> of the entire world-hemisphere that is in front of the eye (and even a little more) is projected onto the white-reddish wall of the hollow surface of the <term>retina</term>. Precisely how this image <note>Kepler uses the word "idolum" or "picture" to describe the retinal image.</note> or "painting" is connected to the visual spirits <note>In the 17th century, "spirits" were thought to be invisible fluids that carried sensory information through the nerves.</note> residing in the retina and the nerve, and whether it is presented to the "judgment seat" of the soul or the visual faculty within the cavities of the brain by these spirits, or whether the visual faculty—like a magistrate sent by the Soul—descends from the brain’s "headquarters" down into the optic nerve and retina themselves as if to the lower benches of a court to meet this image: this, I say, I leave to the Natural Philosophers <note>original: "Physicis"</note> to debate. For the "armor" of the Opticians <note>By "Opticians," Kepler means those who study the mathematics of light.</note> does not extend further than this opaque wall of the retina, which is the first thing the light encounters within the eye. For I do not think we should listen to Witelo regarding his 20th proposition. <note>Witelo was a 13th-century authority on optics; Kepler is famously refuting his older theories here.</note>

<summary>In this landmark passage, Kepler describes the eye's anatomy and proposes for the first time in history that vision is the result of a physical image being projected onto the retina, acting like a screen.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Johannes Kepler’s critique of medieval optical theories, specifically those of Witelo (Vitellio). Having previously discussed the anatomy of the eye, Kepler now addresses the path of light and "species" beyond the retina and into the optic nerves.</meta>

# SUPPLEMENTS TO WITELO, 169

In Proposition 20 of Book 3, he <note>Witelo</note> thinks these <term>images of light</term> <note>original: "idola lucis"; refers to the visual forms or representations of objects</note> proceed further through the nerve, until in the middle of their journey the nerves of both eyes meet in a kind of knot, and then depart again into their individual cavities in the brain. For what can be pronounced by the laws of *optics* concerning this hidden passage? Since it occurs through opaque and therefore dark parts, and is administered by <term>spirits</term> <note>In 17th-century physiology, "animal spirits" were believed to be a subtle fluid that carried sensory information from the sense organs to the brain.</note>—which differ in every way from the [eye's] humors and other transparent things—it has already entirely exempt itself from the laws of Optics. 

Therefore, since Witelo argues thus in Book 3, Proposition 20: *It is necessary for the <term>species</term> <note>The "species" was the Aristotelian concept of the form of an object traveling through space to the eye.</note> to be united: Therefore (Prop. 21) refraction occurs in the back of the vitreous humor, and (Prop. 22) the spirits are transparent:* I invert this: Spirits are not an optical body, and their slender nerve-cavern is not optically straight; and even if it were, it would immediately become winding due to the contortion of the eye, and would present its opaque parts to the very narrow opening or entrance of the passage. 

Therefore, light neither passes through the back surface of the vitreous, nor is it refracted there, but is instead struck against it. And how can a <term>species</term> be refracted if it enters perpendicularly? <note>Light hitting a surface at a 90-degree angle does not bend (refract).</note> It is a wonder that this did not occur to Witelo when he was writing Proposition 31 of the third book. Hence, in Proposition 73 of the third book, he was cast into no small difficulties because of this joining of the species at the meeting-point of the nerves. 

But if something must be said about this joining of the nerves in the middle of their path, let it be done by physical reasons. For it is more certain than certainty itself that no optical image reaches this far. It seems, therefore, that if each nerve had reached its own seat in the brain in a straight, free path, it would have happened that, using two eyes, we would think we saw two things instead of one. Or, this union was made so that if one eye were closed, that particular chamber of the brain would not cease its function of judging. Or perhaps the doubling of the chambers itself is not just for the sake of the eyes, but contributes of itself to correct judgment, just as the partnership of the eyes contributes to [judging] distances. 

Thus, so that visible things might be judged most correctly—both those seen with one eye and those seen with two—it was necessary for this meeting of the passages to occur. This one thing can be said here optically from the conclusion of the first chapter: the spirits are affected by colors and lights, and this affection is a certain, so to speak, coloration and illumination. For the <term>species</term> of stronger colors remain in the vision after the gaze has been made, and they are mixed with colors impressed by a new gaze,

And yet vision occurs through this [passage], from which the word "Optics" descends: therefore, it is indeed unfairly cast out of Optics, because it cannot be tolerated within Optics due to the poverty of our science.

...pressed, and let the color be a mixture of both. This "species" <note>original: "species"; in 17th-century optics, this refers to the visual form or "likeness" of an object traveling through space</note> is separable from the presence of the thing seen; it does not reside in the humors <note>The fluids within the eye</note> or the membranes, as proved above. Therefore, it exists in the spirits <note>Kepler refers to "animal spirits," the subtle fluids then believed to travel through nerves to convey sensation to the brain</note>, and vision occurs through this impression of species into the spirits. This impression itself is not optical, but physical and marvelous. But these things are said in passing. I return to explaining the manner of vision.

Vision, therefore, occurs through a **picture** of the visible object upon the white [surface] of the retina and the wall of the cavity; those things which are outside on the right are depicted on the left side of the wall, the left on the right, the upper on the lower, and the lower on the upper. Furthermore, green things are depicted in the color green, and in general, every object is painted within in its own color. This goes so far that, if it were possible for that picture to remain on the retina after being pulled out into the light—provided the front parts of the eye which formed it were removed—and if someone had a sufficiently sharp gaze, that person would recognize the very image of the hemisphere in that narrow compass of the retina. For the proportion is also preserved: the same angle at which straight lines drawn from individual points of the visible objects would meet at a certain point within the eye's compass, is the same angle at which those individual parts are depicted inside. Thus, not even the smallest points are neglected; and however great the subtlety of sight is in any man, such is the subtlety of this picture within his eye.

Now, to approach this manner of painting more closely and to gradually prepare myself for the demonstration, I say that this picture consists of as many pairs of cones as there are points in the thing seen. These pairs always use the same base, namely the width of the crystalline lens <note>original: "crystallini"; the lens of the eye</note> or a small part of it. Thus, one of the cones is positioned with its vertex at the point seen, <margin>See the diagram for the following Proposition 23.</margin> and its base at the crystalline lens (though it is changed somewhat by refraction upon entering the cornea). The other cone, sharing the same base at the crystalline lens as the first, reaches with its vertex to some point of the picture on the surface of the retina, having itself undergone refraction upon exiting the crystalline lens. Indeed, all the outer limits of these cones meet in the opening of the uvea <note>The pupil within the iris</note>, where the intersection of the cones occurs, and right becomes left.

So that these things may be better understood, I shall repeat them part by part. Let there be some visible point directly opposite the eye, so that a line passing through the opening of the nerve and the center of the hole in the uvea falls upon this visible point.

point. Since, therefore, any given point radiates outward in all directions, it will also radiate into the various parts of that sphere; for this reason, it shines upon the entire small area of the **cornea** <note>The clear, protective outer layer of the eye.</note>, and will illuminate both the **iris** and its black center, which is the **opening of the uvea** <note>The pupil. In early anatomy, the iris was often called the 'uvea'.</note>. And since the iris is opaque and black, it turns away and blocks the surrounding rays, allowing only the middle rays to enter, as much as the opening permits. And since the cornea and the **aqueous humor** beneath it (both of which I treat as having the same density) are a medium denser than air, the rays sent from a point into the curve of the small sphere are **refracted** <term>Refraction: The bending of light as it passes from one material (like air) into another (like water or the eye).</term> toward the perpendicular. Thus, the rays that previously spread out as they traveled through the air are now gathered together upon entering the cornea. This happens to such an extent that, although the widest circle described by these rays as they strike the cornea is broader than the circle of the pupil, these rays are nevertheless so greatly concentrated through that small depth of aqueous humor that by the time they reach the pupil, their outer edges just graze its margins. Furthermore, as they descend, they illuminate a smaller portion on the surface of the **crystalline lens** than the size of the pupil itself.

Now, having entered the anterior surface of the **Crystalline lens** <note>The biological lens of the eye, which Kepler correctly identified as the tool for focusing images.</note>, if the rays originally began from a point at a certain and proportional distance (which is specific to each eye and not exactly the same for everyone), they all strike almost perpendicularly because of the similar convexity of the cornea and the lens. For this reason, for a point directly opposite the sight and at a fitting distance, almost no new refraction occurs at the front surface of the lens, even though the medium of the lens is denser than that of the aqueous humor. Here again, for the sake of calculating refraction, I assign the same density to the **spider-web membrane** <note>original: "araneæ"; likely referring to the lens capsule or the ciliary fibers.</note> and its humor—that is, the crystalline lens—just as I do below for the vitreous humor and the **hyaline membrane** <note>The delicate membrane enclosing the vitreous humor in the back of the eye.</note>.

Therefore, the rays from this single point—as many of them as were admitted through the pupil—descend through the entire depth of the lens, always coming closer and closer together, until they reach the posterior **Hyperbolic** surface of the lens. Indeed, if it were possible for someone to represent the path of these rays by a cross-section of the eye, he would find that from the top of the cornea to the furthest parts of the lens, they form one and the same **conical surface**. The width of this cone is defined by the pupil at that location, while its **vertex** <note>The sharp tip of a cone.</note> would eventually end at a point somewhere behind the eye. Now, however, these rays pass through the posterior conical surface of the lens...

...having exited into the Vitreous <note>The vitreous humor, the clear gel-like substance filling the back of the eye</note>, the medium of which is thinner than the crystalline medium <note>the lens</note>, they are refracted away from the perpendicular lines drawn through the points of refraction in the surface. Because of this, the refracted rays come together toward the axis; thus they are bounded by a shorter and blunter cone than the one through which they had traveled until now. Finally, all these rays from one visible point come together into exactly one point, which is the very center and extremity of the optic nerve where it is connected to the retina. For Nature has measured the space of the vitreous humor between the crystalline lens and the retina according to the density of the crystalline lens and the future magnitude of these refractions.

And this, at last, is the most distinct vision: when the entire light of that same point—however much it was scattered through the width of the cone admitted by the opening of the uvea <note>original: "foramine vueæ"; here referring to the pupil</note>—is forced by two refractions (one in the cornea, the other in the posterior surface of the crystalline lens) to illuminate most strongly a single point of the retina, namely the very orifice of the nerve carrying the visual faculty or spirit. To that point, no rays from any other shining point can glide, thanks to the blackness and opacity of the uvea, the narrowness of the opening, the ciliary processes, and the other parts which will be discussed shortly.

Moreover, what has been proposed to us as "visible" so far was a point, not a body; therefore, it had no parts, nor distinct right from left, nor top from bottom. It was not truly visible but an element, or rather the boundary of a visible thing: just as the vision of a point explained so far is not to be taken as completed vision, but as a certain element of vision. For just as there are many points in a visible thing, so too there are many elements, as it were, of the vision of that thing. Nevertheless, the 19th proposition of Vitello’s <note>Witelo, a 13th-century scholar whose work on optics Kepler is expanding upon</note> third book remains: nothing is seen unless it possesses some proportional magnitude. Let there be, therefore, another point next to the first and directly opposite it, deviating from it to the right. That point, therefore, will also illuminate the cornea itself and will look at the underlying Iris and its opening from an oblique angle. ...illuminated, but a part not illuminated by the previous point, but more to the left; and it becomes almost the same as what we demonstrated above in chapter 2 regarding the <term>closed chamber</term><note>The *camera obscura*, a darkened room or box with a small hole that projects an inverted image of the outside world onto a surface.</note>. For the pupil stands in the place of the window, and the crystalline lens in the place of the opposite board: except that because of the proximity of the pupil and the crystalline lens, a full intersection of rays has not yet occurred here; therefore, everything is still confused. 

Therefore, this "leftward" cone of light, falling upon the front surface of the crystalline lens, is refracted toward the "straight" cone; nevertheless, being oblique, it still passes through the crystalline lens and strikes the hyperbolic surface of the lens more directly, where it is refracted again—though only slightly—toward the first direct cone. Thus, in the <term>vitreous humor</term><note>original: "vitreo"; the clear, gel-like substance that fills the space between the lens and the retina.</note>, the light will deviate less from the first direct cone than it did in the crystalline lens, but it will deviate nonetheless, and so it glides toward the left wall of the retina. 

But lest the ratio of the hemisphere <note>The 180-degree field of vision.</note> be disturbed—if points outside in the air, which are opposite each other relative to the center of the eye, were to deflect from their opposition due to the triple refraction made by the surfaces of the cornea and crystalline lens, and flow into the depth of the eye as if from an angle, and thus collect themselves onto a portion of the retina smaller than a hemisphere—Nature has found an excellent solution. 

This was done by establishing the center of the retina not at the meeting point of the axes of the cones of light traveling through the vitreous humor, but far within, and by bringing the border of the retina closer from the sides. In this way, the longer cones of light, which spread out more, would strike the straight and therefore short parts of the retina; but the shorter cones, which spread out less toward the sides of the retina, would mark out large portions of the retina (which is placed at an angle) with only a small angle of light. Thus, the rays of light coming from opposite sides, even though they are refracted and no longer perfectly "opposite" in path, would nonetheless fall upon opposite points of the <term>net-like membrane</term><note>original: "retiformis"; the retina, so named because of its net-like appearance.</note>, and so a compensation would occur. 

And so, if straight lines were finally drawn from the points of the visible hemisphere through the center of the retina and the vitreous humor, they will mark the points of their own picture on the opposite retina. Unless this happened, the size of things seen indistinctly from the side would always vary as the eye turns, just as happens when <term>spectacles</term><note>original: "perſpicilla"; eye-glasses, which were relatively new technology in 1604.</note> are held to the eyes. For although these glasses stay fixed to the eye, if they move around with it, they make stationary objects appear to move because the apparent size of the field of vision changes at the sides.

...[it] lies between direct and lateral vision. First, the cone of direct vision is constrained only by the uvea <note>original: *vuea*; here referring to the iris which forms the pupil</note>, and therefore it is contained entirely within the cornea; however, some of the oblique <note>side-view</note> cones are abandoned by the cornea itself. For on account of the uvea they could have been wider: thus they admit light to the retina sparingly <note>original: *maligne*, suggesting an "unkind" or insufficient amount of light</note>. The direct cone is circular or "right," while the oblique cones are compressed or scalene <note>tilted or having unequal sides</note>. The axis of the direct cone is not refracted in the cornea, but the axes of the oblique cones are refracted within it. All lines of the direct cone are almost perpendicular to the crystalline lens <term>crystalline lens: the natural lens of the eye, which Kepler correctly identifies as a refractive element rather than the primary sensor</term>; none of the oblique lines are. The direct cone is cut equally by the front surface of the crystalline lens, whereas the oblique ones are cut most unequally, because the more sloping the front surface of the lens is, the deeper it cuts the oblique cone. The direct cone cuts the hyperbolic surface of the lens—or the "boss" <note>original: *umbonem*, the central raised part of a shield, used here to describe the center of the lens</note>—circularly and equally, while the oblique ones do so unequally. All rays of the direct cone are gathered at a single point on the retina, which is the most important point in this whole business; the lines of the oblique cones cannot all be gathered perfectly for the reasons already stated: therefore the picture becomes more blurred. The direct cone aims at the center of the retina, the oblique ones at the sides. The direct cone falls straight upon the retina, the lateral ones obliquely, because, as just said, the center of the retina is below the point of intersection that the axes of the cones (which are in the vitreous humor) would have made.

Finally, the sensory power, or the spirit infused through the nerve <note>Kepler refers to the "animal spirits" thought by Renaissance scientists to carry sensations to the brain</note>, is more concentrated and stronger at that spot where the retina is exposed to the direct cones, both by reason of its source and its circular arrangement. From that point, it spreads out along with the spherical shape of the retina itself and moves away from the source, and is therefore weakened. And just as in a funnel, or in a fishing net with a pouch—which were used as metaphors for the retina above—all the sides deflect either the liquid or the small fish into the channel or the pouch: so the sides of the retina do not use their own measure of sensation for themselves, but refer whatever they can to the perfection of direct vision. That is to say, we only see a thing perfectly when we discern it with all the surrounding circumstances of the hemisphere <note>the full field of view</note>. Therefore, oblique vision does not satisfy the soul at all, but only invites the eyes to be turned in that direction so that the objects may be seen directly.

This is how Proposition 17 of the third book of Witelo <note>Witelo was a 13th-century scholar whose "Perspectiva" was the standard optics text before Kepler</note> must be interpreted. For through a single perpendicular line alone, nothing is discerned distinctly. But through all the radiations of the same point—from which a perpendicular can be drawn through the centers of the pupil and the humors—collected into the very center of the nerve opening (according to Proposition 29 of the third book of Witelo), vision becomes completely direct, unfolded, and distinct.
