The color of the retina is, therefore, neither dark nor black—so that it does not stain the colors of things—nor is it plainly bright white, lest it pour too much brightness into the vitreous humor <note>The clear, gel-like substance that fills the space between the lens and the retina.</note>, and so that white and bright things represented upon it do not overshadow the darker parts with an immoderate proportion of light. See the corollary to propositions 30 and 31 in Chapter 1. The shape of the retina is more than a hemisphere. First, because it needed to be a hemisphere to receive a proportionate picture of things, as has already been said; but the remaining edge is continued all the way to the ciliary processes <note>The structure in the eye that connects the choroid to the iris and controls the shape of the lens.</note>, so that, as if stuffing a glass globe, the retina is kept stretched out, the neck now being made narrower than the belly. For it could not be tied down anywhere because of its tenderness and the delicacy of the <term>visual spirit</term> <note>original: "spiritus visorij"; a contemporary physiological concept suggesting a subtle substance or "spirit" flowed through the nerves to facilitate sight.</note>: which even required a channel in the nerve, contrary to the nature of other nerves, as it does not even support the substance of the nerve itself. For if the retina had not occupied more than a hemisphere, it could easily have wrinkled and shrunk back toward the attachment of the nerve. It was also necessary for the gap to be filled from the hemisphere up to the ciliary processes: this, therefore, had to be provided either by the choroid <note>The vascular layer of the eye between the retina and the sclera.</note> or by the vitreous humor. It is more beautiful, however, for this to be done by the retina. But neither does this edge seem to cease from the function of seeing. For although none of the cones [of light] formed through the <term>crystalline humor</term> <note>The lens of the eye.</note> touch it, nevertheless, the slits of the ciliary processes seem to be formed for this very purpose: so that light might enter to some extent from the sides through the ciliary processes and be received abundantly by that edge of the retina. Indeed, a straight line drawn from the edge of the cornea, through the nearer edge of the opening of the uvea <note>The iris.</note>, almost falls upon the junction of the crystalline lens with the ciliary processes; a line drawn through the opposite edge of the opening almost touches the origin of the ciliary processes from the uvea. And by this mechanism, nature seems to have achieved the result that we see more than a hemisphere with eyes unmoved—altogether as much as is admitted through the <term>corner of the eye</term> <note>original: "hirquum"; referring to the canthus or the corner of the eyelid.</note>, with the eye not turned at all. Indeed, it is not far off that you might even glimpse your own ears, especially if they are longer, with the eye nearest to them. I have often seen and wondered at both the Sun and my shadow [at the same time], as if both were leaning toward the front and were not opposite each other. Nature seems to have applied this precaution for the protection of the eyes, so that things which were not turned away from the "chamber" <note>Kepler treats the eye like a camera obscura or "dark chamber."</note>—where it was necessary for it to be open—might immediately come into sight as they approach, no matter where the eye is focused. For should the organ that guards the whole animal not also diligently guard itself, and devote this duty to the care of its own body?

Furthermore, the vitreous humor <note>The clear, gel-like substance that fills the back of the eye.</note> has obtained a thin membrane so that its moisture does not weaken the nerve or the retina <note>Kepler often refers to the retina as a "nerve-like" expansion.</note> or cause it to become flaccid; and also so that, in its forward-facing part, it does not mix with the primary fluids of the ciliary processes <note>The structures that hold the lens in place.</note> and the aqueous humor <note>The watery fluid in the front of the eye.</note>. It was necessary for the vitreous to differ in density from the crystalline lens <note>The natural lens of the eye.</note>, and also from the aqueous humor, for the sake of **refraction** <note>The bending of light as it passes from one medium to another.</note>. For if it were not less dense than the crystalline lens, the rays of light would not be gathered from their perpendiculars toward the axis of any given cone. But if the vitreous humor is denser than the aqueous, then the denser it is, the more deeply the rays—which enter through the ciliary gaps—can descend, and they will approach the ends of the cones shaped by the crystalline lens.

The crystalline lens has likewise acquired a small tunic <note>The lens capsule.</note> so that, since it is soft, it might not be confused with the aqueous humor. Moreover, the lens is smaller than would be required to touch the sides of the retina, so that across this gap <note>The space within the vitreous humor.</note> the rays of the light-cones might be gathered to a point. For this reason, it had to be both stabilized and connected for the sake of nourishment, joined to the choroid <note>The vascular layer of the eye between the retina and the "white" of the eye.</note> by the ciliary processes. These processes are black on all sides so that they do not create glare by being illuminated; they are crowded together so that the lower chamber of the vitreous humor might be dark, as is fitting. This ensures that the illuminated vitreous does not wash out the "species" <note>Kepler uses "species" to mean the visual images or forms of objects traveling through the eye.</note>. Undoubtedly, these processes possess a motion for the purpose of inflating and swelling themselves in bright light, and thinning out in dim light, just as the uvea <note>The iris.</note> does. 

Indeed, the rear part of the crystalline lens has the shape of a **hyperbola** <note>A specific type of geometric curve.</note> or a related figure, so that the converging rays of the same right cone, which tend downward through the hyperbola, might be gathered at the same point, but at a shorter distance. It will be demonstrated below that this cannot happen with any other shape. The front surface of the crystalline lens, however, is convex <note>Original: "gibba," meaning humped or protuberant.</note>, so that the more obliquely the opening of the uvea <note>The pupil.</note> is presented to a radiating point, the more steeply this surface would be cut by the scalene cone. Thus, an equality of the quantity intercepted by the cone would be preserved as much as possible. And so that it might be positioned perpendicularly to all rays refracted in the cornea (coming from the same certain point) and tending toward the same point after refraction, I determine that this anterior surface of the crystalline lens is perfectly circular or spherical.

in some room, and places a white sheet of paper behind a globe, at a distance of half a diameter <note>original: "semidiametro"; Kepler refers to the radius of the sphere</note> from the edge of the globe, a glass window—with its wooden frames and leaded channels <note>original: "plumbeo canalibus"; the lead cames used to hold small panes of glass in 17th-century windows</note> surrounding the edges of the glass—is most clearly depicted upon the paper, though in an inverted position. And while the picture appears at this single distance (namely, a radius of the paper from the globe), there is confusion <note>blurring</note> both before and after that point; yet the exact opposite happens when the eye is applied. For if the eye is placed behind the glass at the distance of the globe’s radius, where the picture was previously most distinct, there now exists the greatest confusion of things represented through the glass. Indeed, the glass appears either entirely bright, or entirely red, or entirely dark, and so on. If the eye is moved closer to the globe, it perceives the opposite objects as upright and large, where they were blurred on the paper; but if it recedes further from the globe than the radius of the globe, it perceives things as distinct images, in an inverted position, and small, appearing to cling to the very surface of the globe. Previously, however, when the paper was situated there, the picture had completely vanished. All these things happen around the water globe because of the refractions and the shape, and because a certain convexity is inherent in the form.

Since, therefore, the crystalline lens is also made of convex surfaces and is denser than the surrounding humors (just as water in glass is denser than air), it follows that whatever we demonstrate concerning the water globe in this manner, using these means, the same will also be proven concerning the crystalline lens—though its own unique properties are reserved for it due to its specific convex shape, which differs from the convexity of a perfect globe. Let us proceed, then, to the demonstration of those things which occur around a crystalline or glass globe.

Therefore, I considered it no small honor if it should fall to me to untie the knots that were presented, using a sound method and the clarity of mathematical demonstrations.

And to bring the science of optics to such a level of refinement that it might satisfy the requirements of the astronomer. After Your Imperial Majesty <note>original: "C. Maiestas Tua." I have collected and organized into the form of a book those things which I discovered years ago in Styria while I was earning a salary from the provincial estates, as well as those things which finally had to be added to my discoveries—tasks that were, in truth, the most difficult and laborious of all.

There were two matters in particular regarding the science of optics that Tycho Brahe <note>Tycho Brahe (1546–1601) was a famous Danish astronomer whose incredibly accurate data Kepler used to transition from circular to elliptical planetary orbits.</note>, through his painstaking diligence, first brought to light. The first concerns the <term>refraction</term> <note>The bending of light as it passes through the Earth's atmosphere, which makes celestial objects appear in slightly different positions than they truly are.</note> of the light from the stars; the other concerns the apparent shrinking of the Moon’s diameter during <term>solar eclipses</term> <note>original: "Solis deliquiis," literally "failings of the sun."</note>. Although several other passages appear throughout that man’s great works in which he referred and exhorted astronomers to investigate the mysteries of optics, these two topics are the most essential. Brahe diligently investigated the measurement of refractions at every degree of altitude; however, because the physical cause of these measurements had not yet been explained by optical scientists, complicated disputes arose concerning the nature of the world and the elements. It was not yet clear whether these refractions were the same or different at all times and in all places. From this, it follows that an observer might sometimes place too much trust in the diligence and care they applied during an observation, assuming they had identified a star’s location with absolute precision—

->PREFACE<-

**ASTRONOMY**, which deals with the motions of the stars, <margin>The division of Astronomy into its parts.</margin> has two main parts. The first consists of inquiring into and understanding the form of the motions, serving primarily Philosophical contemplation. The other, arising from the first, investigates the locations of the stars at any given moment and adapts itself to practice, laying the foundations for prognosis <note>In this context, "prognosis" refers to the prediction of future planetary positions or astrological effects.</note>. These two parts fly up toward the heavens, supported—as Plato was accustomed to say—by two wings: Geometry and Arithmetic. While both of these serve both parts of astronomy, Geometry is more subservient to the contemplative part, and Arithmetic to the practical part. Thus, the highest peak of Astronomy ends in the Arithmetical part, which encompasses the Tables of motions and the <term>Ephemerides</term> <note>An ephemeride is a table providing the calculated positions of a celestial body at regular intervals.</note> derived from them.

The Geometric part contains many other sub-divisions according to the diversity of the subject matter that Geometric purity adopts in Astronomy. For, to start from the very beginning <note>original: "ut ab ouo rem deducam," literally "to lead the matter from the egg," a Latin idiom meaning to start from the absolute origin.</note>, there are two types of principles in Astronomical demonstrations: one is Observations, and the other is Physical or Metaphysical Axioms. Regarding Observations, three parts of Astronomy arise. The first is Mechanics, which teaches the Instruments suitable for observing celestial motions and the method of using them; that Phoenix <note>A "Phoenix" refers to someone unique and unsurpassed; here it refers to the great Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe.</note> of Astronomers, Tycho Brahe, of pious memory <note>original: "p. m." for "piae memoriae."</note>, published this five years ago. The second is the Historical part, which encompasses the observations themselves. The reader should know that twenty-four books of such exquisite observations, covering nearly the past 40 years, were left by Tycho, which I hope will be brought to light at an appropriate time. Indeed, because every celestial observation occurs by means of light or shadow, and the media between the stars and the eye have distinct properties, and because what we observe in heaven are either motions—the types of which are <term>retrogradation</term>, station, etc.—or arcs,

This work, I believe, I can call the **Key to a Deeper Astronomy**.

<margin>The Status of Tychonic Astronomy.</margin>

You see, friend reader, in what place <term>Tychonic Astronomy</term><note>The system and data produced by Tycho Brahe, which combined aspects of the Earth-centered and Sun-centered models.</note>—that is, the truest and most exquisite version—now stands. He gathered the most abundant material for the future building into his books of observations; he demonstrated the integrity of that material in his *Mechanics*. He laid two very firm foundations for the house, as I have already said: the catalog of the Fixed Stars, described most subtly and truly, which took the place of the best cement and will serve to bond the material of the Observations together; and the established Theory of the Sun, which has the very strength of the foundation and is the central column, supporting all the arches up to the roof, including the entrance with its vaulted ceiling leading to all the rooms. Indeed, he brought the front of the house to completion—I mean the Theory of the Moon, the primary Palace and porch—so that the house is now fit for habitation. To this end, in this small book, windows and stairs are partly added and partly repaired where they were broken. The "cabinet" or Theory of Mars has been constructed; the folding doors, or its publication, will follow shortly. There remains the workshop, the Oratory, the Dining Room with the bedchamber, and the Library: over all of these, a higher story will be built in place of an observatory to capture the prospect of the centuries—the eighth theory and the <term>Apogees</term><note>The points in a planet's orbit where it is furthest from the Earth (or Sun).</note> of the Planets. These are indeed mixed with some rough beams, decayed by rot, from ancient observations; but even these, as much as possible, will be polished and strengthened, so that finally the roof, or the highest peak of the *Rudolphine Tables*, can be placed upon it. So that this may be done at the first possible opportunity—if indeed you love Tychonic Astronomy:

...you love: join me in praying to God, the Best and Greatest, that he might restrain that sworn enemy of the Christian name <note>A reference to the Ottoman Empire, with whom the Habsburgs were at war during this period.</note> by the arms of Emperor Rudolf <note>Rudolf II (1552–1612), Holy Roman Emperor and patron to Johannes Kepler.</note>, and grant victory to his people. For if that should happen, there is no doubt that the most wise Emperor—who does not neglect these matters even amidst these turmoils of war—will then most abundantly supply the necessary funds.

   Those things in astronomy which must be considered optically are either the objects themselves presented to the sight, where the appearances <term>species: In early modern science, 'species' were the formal images or 'likenesses' of objects transmitted through a medium to the eye.</term> of things, or light and shadow, are considered; or the medium through which the light, the vehicle of these appearances, passes, by reason of which some refracted light reaches us; or finally, the seeing instrument, or the Eye. <margin>The classification of astronomical subjects.</margin>

   Again, the objects themselves are either the celestial bodies—of the Sun, the Moon, and the Stars—or the motions, or the positions of the bodies. We rightly begin with the Bodies. However, in these bodies, we consider nothing astronomically now except their appearance, which they send down to us by the benefit of the light with which they are endowed; and of that appearance, especially of the Sun and Moon, and truly the shape and magnitude of the shadow of the Earth.

   For the most noble and ancient part of Astronomy is the eclipse <note>original: *deliquium*, literally a "failing" or "falling away" of light.</note> of the Sun and Moon, a matter which, as Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman naturalist and author of *Natural History*.</note> says, is the most wonderful in the entire contemplation of nature, and similar to a portent. Anyone who considers this diligently will find—even if he should refuse to place faith in the Holy Books—both that God exists as the founder of all nature, and that He has cared for future humanity in the very design of the world's machinery; having so organized this worldly theater that there might exist in it suitable signs, by which the minds of men (the images of God) might not only be invited to contemplate divine works, from which they might estimate the goodness of the creator, but might also be aided in investigating them deeply. <margin>The purpose of solar and lunar eclipses in Nature.</margin>

   For I ask, what is the cause, if not this, that nature performs such games in the bodies of the Sun and Moon? By which not only are men turned toward admiration and amazement (as histories testify) as long as they are ignorant of the causes, but even the four-footed animals themselves, as Pliny witnesses, are commonly terrified?

   Furthermore, all the books of astronomers teach how much men are aided by the Eclipses of the Lights <note>The "Lights" is a traditional term for the Sun and Moon.</note> in the whole of Astronomy. For as far as the motion of the Sun and Moon is concerned, and the spans of years and months: this entire doctrine first arose solely from the observation of Eclipses, nor could it be established otherwise; nor can it even be further refined and polished, unless the Eclipses of the lights are considered more accurately and precisely, which is the goal of this book.

   Now, he who considers how closely all the rest of Astronomy is joined with the motion of the sun, and how much the Moon, sharer of day and night, helps us—

...[when] all other means fail us: one would rightly believe that the whole of Astronomy relies upon these obscurations of the lights <note>In traditional astronomy, "the lights" or "luminaries" refers specifically to the Sun and Moon.</note>, so much so that these shadows are the eyes of Astronomers; these failures <note>original: *defectus*; here meaning eclipses, but playing on the word for "deficiencies."</note> are an abundance of doctrine; these blemishes illuminate the minds of mortals with the most precious pictures. Therefore, the quantity of the appearance <note>original: *speciei*; in 17th-century optics, this refers to the visible form or image of an object transmitted through space.</note> which the Moon or Sun shows us, whether whole or eclipsed, and the shadow which the Earth extends to the Moon, must be diligently investigated by the Astronomer. The diameters of the other stars are sought only so far as ignorance of them would make observations unreliable, and insofar as we strive to know the same things about them as we do concerning the physical mass of the Sun and Moon.

Moreover, those appearances descend to us by the benefit of light—direct and inherent in the Sun, reflected and borrowed in the Moon.

<margin>The occasion for this work.</margin> Although these appearances are obvious to everyone’s eyes, all the master practitioners of Astronomy complain that they are difficult to measure: partly because the bodies are small in appearance, and partly because their extraordinary light dazzles the eyes, preventing them from performing their duty in seeing. But even here Nature has not deserted those eager to learn, having shown a method by which we might achieve in darkness, without harm to the eyes, what is plainly impossible in bright light with the gaze directed straight at the Sun. Since this method is both worthy of admiration and most ingeniously grasped by craftsmen, it is fitting that it not be held cheap or neglected among Astronomers, but rather adorned with geometric demonstrations and illustrated with examples. This was done by me three years ago, on the occasion of the Solar Eclipse of the year 1600, in the manner that will follow shortly, provided I first set down some preliminaries. For because many things concerning not only direct but also reflected and refracted rays were omitted by Witelo <note>Vitellio (Witelo) was a 13th-century Polish scholar whose work was the standard medieval textbook on optics. Kepler wrote this book as a "supplement" or "appendix" to him.</note>, and many things for which the reasoning should have been given from first principles were instead merely fetched from experience and placed in the position of principles: it pleased me to look a little more deeply into the whole nature of light, and to trace those things that appear back to their principles, as far as was possible for the time being—in case there might be future readers whose talents might be more stirred up or even aided by these Disputations to investigate the secrets of light. Although these things are not at all outside my purpose: for the Astronomer has many things to settle through all types of rays.

IOANNES KEPLER, SUPPLEMENTS TO WITELO, 5

# CHAPTER I.

## *On the Nature of Light.*

<note>This work, published in 1604, is Kepler's "Supplements to Witelo" (Ad Vitellionem Paralipomena). Witelo was a 13th-century authority on optics; Kepler uses this book to expand upon and correct medieval optical theories, essentially founding modern optics.</note>

**C**ONCERNING OTHER MATTERS, since we are here diverging at times from Geometry into physical contemplation, our discourse will also be a little more free—not everywhere restricted to letters and diagrams, nor bound by the chains of formal demonstrations. Instead, being more relaxed in its conjectures, it will pursue a certain freedom of philosophizing. I shall, however, take care, if it be possible, that it is divided into Propositions.

In place of common notions, I must first advise on certain small words. That which the Greeks call by the common term "breaking back" <note>original: *ἀνάκλασιν* (anaklasis)</note> of rays, Latin writers divide into two types for the sake of distinction: they establish one type as **Reflected** rays and the other as **Refracted** rays. Yet, if words are to be varied according to the differing natures of things, it is better to choose those in which the nature of each thing is expressed as appropriately as possible according to common usage. Now, it seems to me that this has not been successfully achieved by the Latin writers of Optics.

For as far as I am aware, "to bend" <term>flectere: to curve or bow</term> for the Latins is the same as that which the Greeks call "to curve" <note>original: *κάμπτειν* (kamptein)</note>. The proper use of the word refers to things that are bowed, and which, if the force ceases, are likely to return to their original state; for this reason, the knee is said to be "bent" because the ligaments are stretched and the shape of the limb appears arched. Other uses of the word follow this analogy.

The term that sounds most appropriate to the Greek "to be broken back" <note>original: *ἀνακλᾶσθαι* (anaklasthai)</note> is that which the Latins call "to break" <term>frangere: to break or shatter</term>, which presupposes a dissolution of something continuous (most especially of wood) and a sound. Therefore, a "branch" <note>original: *κλάδος* (klados)</note> for the Greeks is a small twig plucked from a tree. And "to crash" <note>original: *κλάζειν* (klazein)</note> is used for a noise, which the Latins also call a "crash" <term>fragor: a breaking sound</term> from the word for "breaking." If these terms are compared with the behaviors of rays, the word for "bending," if you look at its proper meaning, clearly does not fit. This is because no such thing happens to rays, whether they experience something from mirrors or from water. On the contrary, both of these actions are most correctly called "breaking" by a common term. For each ray is truly broken—one by the surface of a mirror, the other by the surface of water—and the parts of the break constitute a straight-lined angle. Therefore, even if in a broader sense that thing is also said to "diverge" which, though it ought to be a single entity, [is split] into two straight lines...

<summary>Kepler introduces his study of optics by distinguishing between the physical and geometric approach, focusing specifically on the etymology of "reflection" and "refraction." He argues that light "breaks" (forming sharp angles) rather than "bends" (curving like a knee).</summary>

<keywords>Johannes Kepler, optics, refraction, reflection, etymology, geometry, physical philosophy, Witelo</keywords>

->BY JOHANNES KEPLER<-

to the contiguous parts, clearly as rays: yet for the sake of avoiding confusion, the word "bending" should be entirely avoided. For in this sense, "reflection" would apply to both types of rays, just as with the Greek term *to be bent back* <note>original: ἀνακλᾶσθαι (*anaklasthai*), a term used in Greek optics to describe both reflection and refraction</note>. But because rays are affected differently by mirrors than they are by water; (for one rebounds from a mirror back toward the parts from which it came: the other, from the surface of the water into the depths, turns away toward parts opposite to those from which it arrived) let us therefore follow the custom of the Opticians here, and vary the names. Let one be called by the Virgilian and specific term *rebound* <note>original: *repercussus*</note>, and the other by the general name *refracted* <term>refracted: from the Latin *infractus*, meaning "broken." Kepler prefers this to describe light "breaking" into a new medium like water</term>, so that the very prefixes may hint at the nature of the thing.

<margin>Principles and Suppositions for the discussion on the Nature of light.</margin>

To demonstrate properties of this kind, all Philosophers and Opticians establish a certain comparison between physical bodies and their motions, and light; we shall expand upon this comparison a little more broadly.

<margin>The origin of light.</margin>

First of all, the nature of things was bound to represent God the creator, as far as each thing was able by the condition of its own essence. For since the most wise Creator strived to make all things as good, as adorned, and as excellent as possible: he found nothing better or more adorned than himself, nothing more excellent. Therefore, when he was contemplating the corporeal world in his mind, he destined for it a form as similar to himself as possible. From this arose the whole category of quantities, and within it the distinctions between the curved and the straight, and that most excellent figure of all, the 

<margin>The Sphere as an image of the Holy Trinity.</margin>

Spherical surface. For in forming it, the most wise Creator played with the image of his own adorable Trinity. Hence the point of the Center is a kind of origin of the Spherical shape, the surface is the image of the innermost point, and the way to finding it; which is understood to be produced by the infinite outward movement of the point from itself, until it reaches a certain equality of all outward movements. The point communicates itself into this expansion, so that the point and the surface—the ratio of density to expansion being exchanged—are equal. From this arises everywhere between the point and the surface an absolute equality, the closest union, a most beautiful harmony, connection, relation, proportion, and symmetry. And although there are clearly Three—the Center, the Surface, and the Interval—they are nevertheless so much one that none can be conceived as absent, even in thought, without the whole being destroyed.

This

<margin>The spherical form (and thus that of the world) is the <term>archetype</term> <note>original: "archetypus"; an original model or ideal pattern from which things are copied.</note>.</margin>
This, therefore, is the genuine and most fitting image of the corporeal world, which—whether simply or in some specific respect—whatever among corporeal creatures aspires to the highest perfection takes upon itself. For this reason, since physical bodies themselves are contained within the boundaries of their own surfaces and cannot multiply themselves into a sphere, they are endowed with various **virtues** <note>In this context, "virtues" refers to inherent powers or forces, such as magnetism or light.</note>. These virtues, while "nesting" in the bodies, are yet somewhat freer than the bodies themselves and lack physical matter; however, they consist of their own kind of matter which allows for geometric dimensions. They go forth and seek a spherical shape, as appears clearly especially in the **Magnet**, but also in many other things. What wonder is it then,
<margin>In praise of light.</margin>
if that principle of all <term>ornament</term> <note>original: "ornatus"; referring to the Greek "cosmos," meaning the orderly and beautiful arrangement of the universe.</note> in the world—which the divine Moses introduced on the very first day into the barely-created matter as a kind of instrument of the Creator for the shaping and enlivening of all things—if this principle, I say, being the most excellent thing in the whole corporeal world, the matrix of <term>animal faculties</term> <note>original: "animalium facultatum"; here meaning the "soul-like" powers of living things, from the Latin "anima" (soul/life-force).</note>, and the bond between the corporeal and spiritual world, should have passed into those same laws by which the world was to be adorned. The Sun is, therefore, a certain body, and in it resides
<margin>The Sun’s place in the world.</margin>
this faculty of communicating itself to all things, which we call **light**. For this very reason, the middle place and center of the whole world is due to the Sun, so that it might perpetually spread itself equally into the whole Sphere. All other things that partake in light imitate the Sun. From this consideration, certain propositions will be made, which are found among the principles of Euclid, Witelo, and others.

### PROPOSITION I.
*Light possesses the property of outflow or emission from its origin to a distant place.*
For it has been said that it ought to be communicated to all bodies. That communication must occur through the joining of dimensions: for we have said that light falls under the laws of Geometry and is considered in space as a Geometrical body. Therefore, it will be communicated either by the approach of its source to things (which is absurd and provides no communication at all), or, as remains, by a local egress and outflow from its own body.

### PROPOSITION II.
*Any point flows out in an infinite number of lines. Namely, so that the sphere...*

...so that it may illuminate the whole globe all around, which we said ought to happen. The spherical shape, however, possesses infinite lines.

### PROPOSITION III.
***Light is capable of proceeding by itself to infinity.*** For since it partakes of quantity and density (as established above), it cannot vanish into nothingness through any increase in area; for quantity, and likewise density, can be divided infinitely. This concerns its essence. Furthermore, its force of emission <note>original: "vis eiaculatoria." Kepler views light as being "shot out" from a source.</note> is infinite, because light possesses no matter, weight, or resistance, according to the previous points. Therefore, the proportion of its power to its weight is infinite.

### PROPOSITION IV.
***The lines of these emissions are straight; let them be called rays.*** For we have said that light affects the formation of a sphere. The truly geometric origin of a sphere consists in the equality of the intervals through which the central point is spread out <note>original: "diditur." Kepler is describing the radiation of light from a center point to form the surface of a sphere.</note> to the surface. Those intervals are indeed straight lines. If light were to use curved lines, there would be no equality in its spreading, and thus nothing resembling a sphere.

This same point is also proved, or rather declared, in this way: The goals of motion are diverse. For nature seeks either the unity of parts or their separation; both are achieved most directly by straight motion. Because things are understood to be more united the shorter the distance between them, and straight lines are the shortest of all lines between the same points, it follows that the motion which unites things—such as the motion of weights toward the earth, or of steel to a magnet—must necessarily occur in a straight line. Otherwise, not all parts of the motion would tend toward the same goal, but somewhere in the middle of the journey, that which was meant to be united to another would deflect from this seeking of union. The same must be understood regarding the contrary motion of separation, which in natural things is called "violent" motion. <note>In Aristotelian physics, "natural" motion is a thing's inherent tendency (like a rock falling), while "violent" motion is caused by an external force.</note> For a motion contrary to the motion of union is also appropriate to it; therefore, it is straight, because only a straight line is contrary to a straight line.

To light, not union, but something similar to separation is appropriate: a most forceful emission, or a certain flowing out. Therefore, its motion is also straight. Or, if you prefer, call it the union of that light which is in the luminous body with the thing to be illuminated. For the same result will follow.

But a curved line is also not part of the nature of light. For according to Proposition 3, light is capable by itself...

is suitable to be extended to infinity: but curved lines, insofar as they are curved, return into themselves and are terminated. <note>Kepler is contrasting the infinite potential of a straight line—the path of light—with the closed, finite nature of a circle.</note>

## PROPOSITION V.
**The motion of light does not occur in time, but in an instant.** For as has been demonstrated by Aristotle in his books on motion, there is a certain measurement of time corresponding to the proportion that exists between the moving power and the weight or mobile mass, or of the weight to the medium. <note>Kepler is referencing Aristotelian physics, which held that speed is determined by the ratio of force to resistance. If resistance is zero, speed must be infinite.</note> But here, the moving force for moving light has an infinite proportion: because light has no matter, and therefore no weight. Thus, the medium offers no resistance to light, because light lacks the matter through which resistance is created. Therefore, the speed of light is infinite. <note>While we now know light has a finite speed, in 1604 Kepler followed the classical view that light travels instantaneously because it is a non-material "form."</note>

## PROPOSITION VI.
**As light departs from a center, it undergoes a certain thinning in width.** For light goes out in infinite straight lines (according to Propositions 2 and 4): these lines are truly closer together at the center, because there are just as many of them in a narrow place as there are in a larger space further away. But this is the very definition of thinness and density. Therefore, light thins out in width. <note>This is a foundational observation for the "inverse square law"—the idea that light gets dimmer as it spreads out to cover a larger area.</note>

## PROPOSITION VII.
**As a ray of light departs from a center, no thinning occurs along its length.** That is, it is not the case that the longer the ray, the more rare or scattered it becomes simply because of its length. For in the geometric creation of the <term>Spherical</term> <note>original: "Sphærici"; refers here to the spherical expansion of light from a point.</note>, no such thing can be imagined. Light affects that space by its own communication of itself. Furthermore, the proportion of the ejecting power to that which flows out is infinite, since it lacks matter (as said above); and by Proposition 5, the motion occurs in an instant; and by Proposition 3, it extends to infinity. Therefore, the ejecting vigor is equal everywhere to infinity, being the same as it was at the origin. Wherefore, the strength of the ray is also equal along its length.

## PROPOSITION VIII.
**A ray of light is nothing of the light itself as it goes out.** For a ray (by Proposition 4) is nothing other than the motion of light itself. Truly, just as in physical motion, the motion itself is a straight line while the physical "mobile" is a body—so in light, the motion itself is likewise a straight line, but the "mobile" is a certain surface. And just as in the former case the straight line of motion does not belong to the body, so here the straight line of motion does not belong to the surface. <note>Kepler is making a subtle distinction: the "ray" is the mathematical path (a line), whereas the "light" is the thing that exists on the surface of the expanding sphere.</note>

### PROPOSITION IX.
*Just as the areas of spherical surfaces—where the source of light is the center—relate to one another, the larger to the smaller: so the strength or density of the light rays in the smaller surface relates to that in the larger; that is, inversely.* For according to Propositions 6 and 7, there is just as much light in a smaller spherical surface as in a wider one; therefore, it is so much more compressed and dense in the former than in the latter. <note>This is a foundational statement of the Inverse Square Law. Kepler recognizes that as light spreads out from a central point, the same amount of "illumination" must cover an ever-increasing area, meaning the intensity must decrease as the surface area increases.</note> However, if the density of a linear ray were different depending on its position relative to the center (which was denied in Proposition 7), the matter would be otherwise.

### PROPOSITION X.
*Light is not hindered by the solidity of bodies, insofar as they are solid, from being able to pass through them.* For whatever is hindered is hindered or repelled by something of its own kind, as a body is by a body. Solids, insofar as they are solid, have three dimensions. To light, according to Propositions 6 and 7, only two dimensions belong. <note>Kepler conceptualizes light not as a 3D substance, but as a "species" or a 2D surface-like phenomenon that emanates outward. Because it lacks "depth" in the way matter has "solidity," he argues that the three-dimensional nature of an object isn't what stops light.</note> Therefore, light or its rays suffer nothing from solids insofar as they are solid; nor do they affect each other regarding their solidity.

### PROPOSITION XI.
*A transparent <term>pellucidum | a body that allows light to pass through</term> body is one whose geometric consistency, or the arrangement of its internal parts, is established by a certain flow.* For the geometric definition of "fluid" <note>original: "humidum"</note> is found in Aristotle; specifically, that is called fluid which is not limited by its own boundaries. <note>Aristotle, *On Generation and Corruption*. Kepler uses the idea that in a fluid, the parts are so perfectly joined that there are no internal "gaps" or "surfaces" to disrupt the light.</note> Wherefore all the smallest parts are bounded by one another, and the whole is plainly unified by its internal parts, being distinguished by no actual surfaces. Now truly, through Proposition 10, solidity, as solidity, does not hinder light in its passage. Therefore, whatever is "one" <note>meaning a continuous, unified substance</note> is transparent. But if some things were partly liquid and partly not, those things so mixed do not constitute a single transparent body. Moreover, this definition extends itself through all natural bodies to some degree: which Aristotle plainly approved in his book *On the Senses*. <note>original: "de sensilibus"</note> Furthermore, there are transparent things that are also hard and resonant <note>original: "tinnientia," literally "clinking" or "ringing," like glass or crystal</note>. Nor does it hinder things from being colored which ought to be transparent, as will be seen below.

### PROPOSITION XII.
*Light is affected by the surfaces of whatever bodies it encounters.* For things that belong to the same genus are suited to affect one another; <note>The text cuts off here, but Kepler is beginning to explain that while light passes through the "volume" of a transparent solid, it is changed (refracted or reflected) at the "surface" where two different substances meet.</note>

...light <note>original: "lux"</note> (according to Proposition 7) is in the same category as bodies because of the surfaces by which they are bounded; therefore, it is well-suited to act upon them. Motion is a straight line, whose boundary is in some sense a point on the encountering surface; and the boundaries of infinite rays of light are infinite points—that is, the surface, which as it were consists of them.

### PROPOSITION XIII.
***The surfaces of dense bodies—or those in which many parts of matter fill a narrow volume—are also dense in a certain way, specifically in the respect in which light and bodies act upon each other.*** For even if no thickness (which belongs to bodies) occurs in surfaces when viewed as geometric quantities, nevertheless, insofar as they belong to dense bodies due to this material-geometric difference, the surfaces themselves are understood to be "dense," since they are <term>materialized surfaces</term> <note>Kepler is arguing that a surface isn't just a mathematical abstraction; it inherits the physical properties of the object it covers.</note>. More clearly: density is a quality of matter that occupies three dimensions; of these, two dimensions belong to the surface. Therefore, surfaces participate in the density of bodies according to their own measure. To light, indeed, a certain "superficial density" was ascribed above in that same respect.

### PROPOSITION XIV.
***Light passes through the surfaces of dense things with more difficulty, insofar as they are dense.*** Since motion belongs to light according to Proposition 1, the properties of straight motion also belong to it. Therefore, it also encounters hindrance from a denser medium. This is not, however, because the medium is a solid (according to Proposition 10), but insofar as it is bounded by a dense surface. More clearly: the motion of light occurs naturally with <term>extension</term> <note>the spreading out of light from a source</note> according to Proposition 6, because it always moves from a single source into all regions. Therefore, just as a surface resists motion that exists in lines because of its infinite points, so a dense surface resists "thinning" motion, since density and thinning <note>original: "extenuatio," referring to the spreading or rarefaction of light rays</note> are in the same category.

_Corollary on Method_

Since, therefore, light has two aspects—one of essence, by which it is light, and one of quantities, which it receives—it also possesses two energies: the first being local motion, and the second, in the order of nature (which is prior in sense or form), being illumination (which is accompanied by heating). Of these, local motion belongs to light because of its quantities, while illumination belongs to it because of its essence, as light. According to these two energies, it also has two objects: quantities and color, which is accompanied by matter. 

And because local motion also has two types of objects—both the medium through which it passes and the thing toward which it is carried—there also exist two aspects of this energy in light. On account of the medium, light penetrates the medium and is refracted by it if it is denser; on account of the thing, light strikes the surface it encounters and is reflected from it. 

These two aspects are distinguished from each other in another way. For light, by its motion, is both scattered through the medium and strikes against surfaces; in turn, it is either gathered from the surface of a transparent medium or reflected from the surface of a boundary. Finally, as pertains to illumination, which is the primary work of light: colors are diluted by light, and light is tinted and infected by colors. <note>Kepler describes a reciprocal relationship: light makes colors visible (dilutes them), but the light itself takes on the "stain" of the color it hits.</note> On all these things, in order, in the following sections.

_Let the reader note here the origin of the fourth species of light, which other writers on optics treat coldly._ <note>Kepler is likely referring to "illuminated light" or reflected light that carries color, a phenomenon he felt previous opticians ignored in favor of simple geometric rays.</note>

### PROPOSITION XVIII.

_Light having fallen upon a surface is reflected toward the opposite region from whence it came._ 

For motion has been attributed to light by [Proposition] 1; therefore, a species of motion, namely impact <term>pulsus: Kepler uses this term to describe the physical "push" or "strike" light exerts when hitting a surface, treating it almost like a physical projectile</term>, is also attributed. For what hardness is in the physical motion of conflicting objects—which consists in the permanence of surfaces—this, in light, is the naked surface, or the termination and shaping of bodies. For by the very fact that physical bodies are bounded, they are understood as "hard" in this context. Soft and humid things, however, are defined by the lack of their own boundary. <note>Kepler is arguing that light reflects because it "hits" the boundary/shape of a solid object, treating the geometric surface of an object as a physical barrier that causes a bounce.</note>

The reason why reflection <note>original: "repercuſſus"</note> occurs both in physical motion and in light is found in the "violence" <note>Kepler uses "violence" in the Aristotelian sense, meaning motion caused by an external force rather than a natural tendency</note> of the motion. Since the moving force cannot be entirely abolished by the impact, the motion will therefore surpass the boundary of its line—namely, the surface. But it cannot proceed in a straight line, for in the case of physical objects, one body resists another; here, one surface resists another—in the former case it is a solid resistance, in the latter it is partial, as we shall soon hear. It remains, then, that the motion must turn in the opposite direction. Perhaps these matters might be stated more harmoniously thus: A pulse is an action, and it occurs between opposites, but with action there is a mutual "passion" <note>In historical physics, "passion" is the state of being acted upon by an external force; the counterpart to action</note>; therefore, this is also true in a pulse. Indeed, to the strike where light hits a surface from one side, the reflection to the other side is the opposite. For the power <note>original: "virtus"</note>, both that which drove the mobile object and that which repels it from the opposite side, is the same, because the strike is considered as being inflicted at a single point.

*Reflection occurs at equal angles, and for that which falls obliquely, it occurs toward the other side. This is Witelo's 25th proposition <note>Kepler refers to Witelo, a 13th-century authority on optics whose work he is "supplementing" in this book</note>. For an equal power also presupposes an equal motion. But the power at the point of conflict is one and the same; therefore, the motion is also equal. But that which is at equal angles is equal. Therefore, the reflection of moving objects will be at equal angles.*

I say "also toward the other side," away from where the moving object was struck, if this is what happens. For if it were always reflected along the same line, it would always have to have arrived directly <note>meaning perpendicularly, at a 90-degree angle</note> according to the preceding 18th proposition. But for the most part, it falls obliquely; therefore, the region from which it comes is then also opposed to the surface obliquely, and not directly; hence the reflection is also obliquely into the opposite region, and not directly. Or more clearly: When something is moved obliquely toward a surface, that motion is composed of a part perpendicular to the surface and a part parallel to the surface. But the surface only opposes that part which is perpendicular to it, not that which is parallel. Therefore, it does not hinder the part parallel to itself,

Since, therefore, the surface **CD** is assumed not to hinder the motion of **B** toward the parts from **B** toward **AE**, it will not change the angle **CDE**.

**Light falling obliquely onto the surface of a denser medium is refracted toward the perpendicular of that surface.** <note>Kepler is explaining why an object like a straw looks "bent" when placed in water.    I will attempt this same comparison of physical motion with the motion of light using other, more rigorous arguments. For what a denser medium—which nevertheless yields—or a resting weight—which is nevertheless movable by the impact of another—is in physical motion, a denser surface is in this business: one that nevertheless transmits light and, in a certain way, yields to its passage.

   For just as in physical motion a projectile sometimes collides with the object we were aiming at, and they continue along the same path together in a single motion because they cling to one another: so the same thing happens here with light and a denser surface, which the light penetrates, though without the involvement of matter or the dimension of solidity.

   But I see that the matter of physical motion has not been sufficiently explained to this day—specifically, why refraction (or rather *deflection*, a word more appropriate for physical motion) occurs in this case too, moving away from a straight line of motion toward the line perpendicular to the opposing surface whenever the impacting force strikes it obliquely. And because <margin>A demonstration regarding the principle of the balance, by way of digression.</margin> this whole business relies on the principle of the balance <term>Libra<gloss>The beam of a weighing scale or balance</gloss></term>, the explanation must be drawn from its source. Indeed, I do not think I will be given a more convenient opportunity to settle this demonstration elsewhere.

   Aristotle asks in his *Mechanics* <note>Referring to the "Mechanical Problems" traditionally attributed to Aristotle.</note> what the cause is that if the fulcrum <term>Trutina<gloss>The point of suspension or pivot of a scale</gloss></term> is in a higher position than the balance beam, and the pans are emptied, the bar which was previously tilting is now restored to equilibrium; but if the fulcrum is below, the bar remains tilted as it was by the weights and does not return when emptied. Neither Jordanus <note>Jordanus de Nemore, a 13th-century mathematician.</note> repeated Aristotle's demonstration, nor did Cardano <note>Girolamo Cardano, 16th-century polymath; refers to his work "De Subtilitate."</note> approve of it in his book *On Subtlety*—for he would not have substituted another—perhaps because it is obscure.

->SUPPLEMENTS TO WITELO, 19<-

Guidobaldo’s <note>Guidobaldo del Monte (1545–1607) was a pioneer in mechanics whose work influenced Galileo.</note> error was born from a false starting point: he defined **equilibrium** <term>æqueponderantia: the state where weights balance each other</term> as things that would remain still regardless of how they were positioned, provided they were at equal distances from the center.

But let us get closer to the matter. Cardano <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), a famous Italian polymath.</note> claims, following Aristotle, <margin>Sparring with Cardano.</margin> that the weight at $CA$ is "heavier" when it is higher—specifically at the smaller angle $CAB$—and "lighter" at $AD$ when it is lower, at the larger angle $BAD$. He falters, however, in demonstrating this. His argument boils down to the idea that angles add to the force of gravity. He seeks a foundation in mechanics: for the angle $CAB$ is acute, and its "legs" are more easily pulled apart by the weight at $C$ than the legs of the obtuse angle $BAD$ are by the weight at $D$; therefore, the first weight prevails. Truly, if this were the genuine cause, the effect would follow the same proportion as the cause, and the ratio of the weights in an inclined balance would be the same as the ratio of the angles. But this is false. Cardano points to another cause from a distance, but he does not work out the proof: "Although weight $C$ is heavy," he says, "and naturally inclined to be carried toward the center of the earth as closely as the span of $AC$ allows, it does not descend beyond the point of equilibrium because the counterweight $AD$ would be forced to rise against its nature." 

Thus, he <term>begs the question</term> <note>original: "principium petitur"; a logical fallacy where the premise assumes the truth of the conclusion.</note>. Indeed, Cardano, I do not only ask this, but something more: If that which is heavier strives entirely to reach the point closest to the center, then when there are unequal weights on the scales, why does the heavier one not seek the lowest possible point immediately, while the lighter one is raised completely to the top? 

Therefore, the cause is this: exactly the same as in a **steelyard** <term>statera: a type of balance scale with arms of different lengths</term>. With center $A$ and the distance $AC$ and $AD$, let a circle be drawn, and in it the perpendicular line $BAF$. It is manifest that neither of the weights at $C$ and $D$ can descend deeper than point $F$, nor be raised higher than point $B$. And since both are inclined by nature to tend toward the bottom, and they compete with one another, they share the descent of the path $BF$ between them in the same proportion as the weights themselves. Let perpendicular lines $DG$ and $CH$ be drawn from points $D$ and $C$. Through what has been said, the descent of weight $L$ <note>Likely a typo in the original for weight C</note> (represented by $BH$) compared to the descent of weight $D$ (represented by $BG$) will be as weight $C$ is to weight $D$. I say this is the logic of the balance. For since the angles $HAC$ and $GAD$ are equal, and lines $CA$ and $AD$ are equal, and the angles at $H$ and $G$ are right angles, then $AH$ and $AG$ will also be equal. Therefore, the remaining segments of those equal lines, $HB$ and $GF$, are also equal. Thus, as weight $C$ is to $D$, so is $FG$ to $GB$. Let a perpendicular be drawn from $F$ to $CD$, which shall be $FK$. Therefore, because $CAH$... <note>The text cuts off mid-geometric proof.</note>

### PROPOSITION XXI.

**Both reflected and refracted rays are straight after the point of interaction.**<note>Kepler uses the term "passio" (passion), meaning the point where the light is acted upon by a surface.</note> For it is the nature of light to pass through in straight lines, insofar as it suffers nothing from the obstruction of surfaces (by Proposition 4), nor do they suffer anything further from the solidity of the medium after crossing the surface (by Proposition 10). But physical motions are curved into arcs: the reflected motion, because its power is finite; the refracted motion, because the medium also cooperates through its solidity—factors which do not apply to light.

### PROPOSITION XXII.

**Light illuminating colors is reflected in every direction, and the illuminating colors radiate in a sphere, like light itself; yet more strongly in a direct line.** For all things, even those that are colored, are transparent insofar as they exist (by Proposition 10) and light illuminates colors through the solidity of the object (by Proposition 16). Therefore, it happens from every side. Now indeed, color is the <term>correlate</term><note>Kepler views color not as an inherent property of an object alone, but as something activated by its interaction with light.</note> of light for mutual action. Light strikes color, and does so from every side through the solidity of the object. It is therefore reflected as if from surfaces in every direction. But at the same time, it is also "tinted" (by Proposition 16). Therefore, the reflected ray possesses the color of the medium or the object.

22                      JOHANNES KEPLER

Color therefore radiates, etc. Hence those colored things which are smoothed to the highest degree nonetheless radiate in every direction; this would not happen if all light were reflected from that single surface in one direction and nothing penetrated the true seat of color or became tinted. For light exists within the internal disposition of the body's matter, not merely at its naked boundary. If it pleases anyone more, let him say that the potential lights of colors are brought into action and excited by light, just as that heat which is in <term>ginger (original: *Zyngibere*)</term> is stimulated by the arrival of moisture, ignites itself, and begins to communicate itself; all seeds do the same thing. Of this fourth species of light, the <term>Opticians</term> <note>Kepler refers to writers on optics, such as Alhazen or Witelo, whose work he is "supplementing" in this book.</note> say little. Let us call it **communicated light**. For light that is both reflected and refracted is nonetheless the light of that thing from which it fell and suffered this effect. But this light now becomes, in a certain way, the light of that surface which it had illuminated. Its consideration is extremely necessary for the Astronomer.

->**PROPOSITION XXIII.**<-

*Light descending through the substance of colored transparent things is refracted in every direction, and the illuminated colors radiate from the Sun in a circular fashion, yet more strongly in a direct line. For since light illuminates colors through the solidity of the substance (according to Proposition 16), it therefore illuminates from every side. But it passes through at the same time because the things are transparent. Now indeed, color is the correlate of light for mutual action. Therefore, while passing through, the light—by dilating itself—will be contracted by the substance of the colors, which is to be <term>refracted</term> <note>Kepler is developing a theory where the physical "body" of the color causes the light rays to bend or slow down.</note>. For color here also, as before, takes on the nature of a surface. But at the same time, it is tinted (according to Proposition 16). The refracted ray therefore possesses the color of the medium. Thus the color radiates after passing through the medium. And because that which is less refracted is stronger, and that which is closer to the direct path is less refracted, therefore those rays which are closer to the direct path are stronger. In this way, the light becomes the particular property of the colored medium and is communicated to it.*

->**COROLLARY.**<-

A reason had to be given why, although the Sun illuminates the air everywhere equally, everyone nevertheless perceives the greatest brightness in that part of the air through which the Sun radiates most closely. Thus, one and the same region of air is very bright to one person, but less bright to another for whom the Sun introduces itself elsewhere; for the air has its own <term>whiteness</term> or color. If the cause were not clearly enough...

### PROPOSITION 24.
***Light reflected from the surface of a body, insofar as the body is not colored.***
For according to Proposition 15, color exists within bodies by way of matter, which has three dimensions; a surface, however, has only two. Therefore, color is not present in the surface itself. But where some color is mixed in, the body to which the surface belongs adds this from its own substance, scattering it not only into that specific place but all around.

### PROPOSITION 25.
***Light passing through a colored medium becomes more and more colored, and it emerges redder the deeper it has traversed the medium.*** This is evident from Proposition 16. Because color is brought out by the presence of light not only on the surface but also within the body. <note>original: "color obiectu lucis nō tantùm in superficie, sed & in corpore est." Kepler argues that the "redness" increases with depth because light interacts with more of the material's internal color.</note>

### PROPOSITION 26.
***Rays of light neither color, nor illuminate, nor impede each other in any way.*** For according to Proposition 4, rays are nothing other than the motion of light and color themselves, and the light is not "in" them (as per Prop. 8) but has already passed through. This is surely the same as in physical motion, where one motion does not move another.

### PROPOSITION 27.
***Light in the same medium is partly reflected, partly refracted, and partly adheres to the color of the medium, or is vibrated back by the color, and is thus divided into "thinner" lights.*** <note>Kepler uses the term "thinner" (tenuiores) to describe light that has lost intensity because its power has been split or shared across different paths.</note> For insofar as it strikes the surface, it is reflected (according to Prop. 18); but insofar as that surface belongs to a transparent body (according to Prop. 10), it passes through and is refracted (according to Prop. 20). Therefore, while it illuminates two objects—one by reflection, the other by refraction—each is equal to that which it would have illuminated directly; specifically one of them, because this is the definition of "thinness." The dual nature of the medium itself brings this about. The essence of light, which participates in density, assists this; therefore, it can be divided into thinner parts. In physical motion, this is not so evident because those things are all material and hard, whereas here there is nothing of the sort. Vitello <note>Vitello (or Witelo) was a 13th-century friar and philosopher whose work on optics was the standard text until Kepler wrote this "supplement" to it.</note> proves this through experiments.

### PROPOSITION 28.
***Various lights falling upon the same object are both accumulated and mixed, both among themselves and also with the color of the object, each according to the proportion of its own strength or density, from which a new color—or rather, a "generated" light—exists.***

24 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;THE WORKS OF JOHANNES KEPLER

...produced differently from all others. For because they all participate in quantity <note>Kepler treats light and color as physical quantities that can be measured and mathematically manipulated.</note>, just as they have been able to be thinned out up to this point, so now they can also be accumulated. This does not happen in a transparent medium, because they are not truly in it insofar as it is transparent, but have already passed through it; rather, it happens on an object, because it is here that they first come to rest and are fixed after departing from their own body. They are mixed together, however, because (according to Proposition 16) any given thing is affected by the color of the object in turn. And a new radiant color arises, because (according to Proposition 15) colors differ only by degrees of light and darkness; moreover, accumulated lights vary this degree, and therefore change the color itself.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;PROPOSITION XXIX.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*When there is an excessive mutual proportion between lights falling upon the same object, the sense does not distinguish the weaker light.* To distinguish is, in fact, to compare or discern, which is the duty of the visual sense. As it is with proportion, so it is with comparison. Therefore, if all proportions of colors or brightnesses could be distinguished—since they are infinite in their increase of magnitude—the discerning faculty would have to be infinite, which physicists deny. For all sensory faculties have certain prescribed limits to their powers.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;PROPOSITION XXX.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Colored lights appear more clearly on those surfaces that have colors more akin to light, such as white, than they do on black surfaces.* For since the work of light is illumination—by which it makes its <term>subjectum recipient</term> <note>original: "patiens"; refers to the object being acted upon by the light.</note> similar to itself, as all active agents do—and since color or darkness is continuous within that object, illumination becomes more difficult where colors approach closer to darkness, as with black. And through Propositions 28 and 29, blackness prevails in the color that radiates from the illuminated surface. Thus, less light radiates from a black surface than from a white one, and therefore it is less perceived.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;PROPOSITION XXXI.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Given that we can perceive any one color among many just as clearly on black surfaces as on white surfaces—which can be achieved by applying a stronger light to the black surface—the differences between those colors radiating next to each other will then be more accurately noted on the black surface than on the white.* For because a white surface possesses great brightness, radiant colors closer to light will become intensely bright (according to Proposition 28). In this way, they will wash out <note>original: "obliterabunt"</note> the colors closer to black (according to Proposition 29). This does not happen with black surfaces, because they are instead a privation of light <note>Kepler follows the Aristotelian view that black is not a color in itself, but the absence or "privation" of light.</note>.

<summary>Kepler discusses the physics of light accumulation on surfaces and the limits of human perception regarding brightness. He argues that while colors show up better on white surfaces, black surfaces actually allow for better discernment between different shades if the illumination is strong enough, because the white background does not "overpower" the darker hues.</summary>

From here follows, as if a corollary to the 30th and 31st <note>Kepler is referring to his own preceding propositions regarding how the eye perceives light on different backgrounds.</note> propositions, that rays falling upon **black surfaces** are perceived most distinctly, and upon **white surfaces** most evidently; and if a surface should be intermediate between black and white—such as **blue**, **pale red-white**, and the like—it will behave almost equally toward both individual colors and in representing the distinctions between them.

### PROPOSITION XXXII.
### Heat is a property of light.

It could be proven that light is hot based on the principles we have adopted. For if the life of things consists in heat, and light is destined to foster that life, it must therefore provide warmth. Furthermore, every agent strives to assimilate to itself that which it acts upon <note>A common Scholastic principle: *omne agens agit sibi simile*, meaning an active force tries to make the object it touches more like itself.</note>. Thus, as light strives to warm matter, it must be hot itself.

But I shall establish what I have said through experience. For light alone is always and everywhere accompanied by some heat, according to the measure of its brightness. Regarding **Solar light**, this is most clearly evident because it is also the brightest. Regarding the **light of the stars**, the logic of their brightness <margin>All stars provide heat.</margin> testifies that the heat of all of them combined is in a smaller proportion to the heat of the single Sun than can be simultaneously perceived and judged by a human, for whom there is a fixed threshold of heat measurement. Nevertheless, it appears from the effects of the stars that there is a sensitivity to their heat within the bowels of the earth. For no evaporation—whether cold or hot (in comparison to us)—can be stirred up without some heat thinning and sublimating it. Indeed, all the planets are fit to stir up vapors. Therefore, to all belongs their own effect of heat.

Again, the matter is evident regarding **fiery things**. Regarding the very thin little light of **glow-worms**, <margin>Glow-worm.</margin> you cannot deny that it is accompanied by heat. For they live and move, and this is not accomplished without warming. Furthermore, the light of **rotting wood** <margin>Rotting wood.</margin> is not deprived of its own heat; for rot itself is a kind of slow fire. Although Aristotle distinguishes between them, granting that those things *glimmer* <note>original Greek: λάμπειν (*lampein*)</note> but denying that they *produce light* <note>original Greek: φῶς ἐμποιεῖν (*phōs empoiein*)</note>; if you understand this most soundly, it is nothing other than saying that such light is at the most faint degree. If it is true that the **carbuncle** <margin>Carbuncle.</margin> <note>A legendary gemstone, often identified as a deep red garnet, believed in the Renaissance to emit its own light in the dark.</note> shines by itself: certainly, they attribute virtues <note>In this context, "virtues" refers to inherent medicinal or magical powers believed to reside in stones.</note> to it and to all gems, and it is consistent that those virtues in the carbuncle come forth by means of some degree of heat.

Now, it must also be proven conversely that heat in all other things is external and depends upon the heat of light, and therefore is rightly called "passive." This is clear because there is nothing that possesses heat from itself, except...

For I concede that the heart itself is appointed for the service of the whole animal. I concede that these "revenues" are brought into the heart as if into a workshop, so that the things processed here may be distributed elsewhere through the artery into the entire body for the sake of an unavoidable utility.

<margin>Ventilation and Exhalation.</margin>
Meanwhile, the very form of the drawing-in and pushing-out, and nature's mechanism in the valves, cries out with a loud voice that there is an "artisan flame" within the heart. This flame sustains its life from the taxes paid by the ingredients and, through those same works it was destined to perform—namely, the vital spirit—it casts out waste by the same path. Indeed, the nature of the entire body, and the heart within it, is so arranged that the body is most rightly sustained by the heart’s refuse. For unless the necessity of preserving this little flame urged nature on, it could have brought blood into the heart and squeezed it out again more lightly and quietly, as happens in the liver; there would have been no need for the motion of <term>Systole and diastole</term> <note>The rhythmic contraction and expansion of the heart during a heartbeat.</note>. On the other hand, if you ask in what way any fire or flame could be most rightly preserved in a closed vessel—which it was necessary for the heart to be—I respond: in no other way than that in which the heart is both shaped and opened and closed.

<margin><gloss>Is there a little light in the heart?</gloss></margin>
Therefore, I do not doubt that we would even perceive this little light with our eyes, if it were our lot to enter the hidden recesses of the heart, unharmed, with the light of day shut out.

Some things grow hot when moisture is supplied, but at the same time they set themselves on fire, such as hay. In summary: the soul precedes heat; fire or light accompanies it.

->PROPOSITION XXXIII.<-
**The heat of light is immaterial.** For we have made heat the companion of light, and light has no matter, as we are now considering it.

->PROPOSITION XXXIV.<-
**The heat of light acts upon matter.** For all matter is cold (according to Proposition 32) and light is hot; they are therefore under the same genus. Thus, a thing is acted upon by its opposite. This is also due to the essential opposition between the materialized and the non-materialized. Above, in Proposition 10, we dealt with the **geometrical** action and passion <note>In 17th-century physics, "passion" refers to the capacity of an object to be acted upon or to receive an impression.</note> caused by location, where light and surfaces were equal partners. Here, the action is **physical** and not reciprocal; for only matter is acted upon. That which matter seems to do to light in return, it does by a geometrical action: for example, a crystal globe exposed to the Sun for a long time eventually grows hot, yet the ray passing through the globe is no colder than it was at the beginning.

28

## On the Treatment of Animal Bones with Hydrochloric Acid
->(Excerpt from a treatise by Dr. v. Bibra, see *Annals of Pharmacy* <note>original: "Annalen der Pharmacie"</note>, Vol. LVII, Issue 1.)<-

If one wishes to separate the organic components from the inorganic ones, it is well known that the bones are placed in diluted hydrochloric acid, in which the earths <note>In historical chemistry, "earths" referred to non-metallic mineral substances, in this case, primarily calcium phosphate and calcium carbonate.</note> dissolve.

Until now, it was believed that only the earths were extracted in this process, while the organic substance (cartilage) remained behind in a pure state.

Mr. von Bibra has discovered through experiments, however, that the hydrochloric acid also dissolves a portion of the organic substance, and indeed the more so, the more concentrated the acid is, and the longer the bones remain in it.

The least amount of organic substance is dissolved when using very dilute hydrochloric acid and carrying out the reaction at a temperature below 0° C.

He therefore recommends the following procedure:

One pours over the cleanly scraped bones, sawn into small pieces, a mixture of 1 part hydrochloric acid and 12 parts water, and places the vessel in a location where the temperature is below 0° C. (In winter, outdoors; in summer, in a freezing mixture.)

After the earths are dissolved, the remaining cartilage is washed with cold water until the wash water no longer reacts acidicly.

This cartilage obtained in this way is white, translucent, and still retains the shape of the bone. It consists almost entirely of pure chondrin <note>Chondrin is a gelatin-like substance formed by boiling cartilage; in this context, it refers to the protein matrix of the bone.</note>.

During the investigation of bones from various animals, Mr. von Bibra found that the ratio between organic and inorganic substance varies greatly.

For example, the bones of birds contain more inorganic substance than those of mammals; the bones of fish, on the other hand, contain less.

Differences also appear within the same animal class. For instance, the bones of carnivores have more earths than those of ruminants.

<summary>This text describes an improved method by Dr. von Bibra for extracting minerals from bone using cold, diluted hydrochloric acid to better preserve the organic structure. It also notes that mineral content varies significantly across different animal species.</summary>
<keywords>bone chemistry, hydrochloric acid, Dr. von Bibra, organic matter, inorganic matter, chondrin, comparative anatomy, mineral analysis</keywords>
