For this contradicts the nature of transparent things and light, as well as optical principles. Indeed, a species is always positioned alongside its own body—the body to which the species belongs—and if that body is cut off by something opaque, the species is destroyed by the opposing shadow. Thus, the humors <note>original: "humores"; the various fluids within the eye, like the vitreous or aqueous humor</note> of the eye, by the very fact that they are transparent, never "catch" these species, but rather transmit them. Nor does whatever this species is stick to the opaque membranes. For again, no color or opaque surface is stirred up or made radiant unless a luminous body is present and unobstructed. 

It remains, therefore, that what lingers in the eye is not a species of light, but a species of illumination—of action and passion <note>Kepler uses "passion" in the classical sense of "undergoing" or "being affected by" an external force</note>. This is much like how the sensation of pain remains after a blow—which is understood to be a certain "species" of that suffering—or how in violent motion, a certain species of that motion passes into the projectile and carries it forward for some time, even after the hand that gave the motion has been withdrawn. And since all sensation is perfected through the nerves and the spirits <term>animal spirits: believed to be subtle, fluid-like substances that traveled through the nerves to communicate sensation to the brain</term> carried by them, this species of vision resides in the spirits, not in the humors. ### APPENDIX TO THE FIRST CHAPTER: AND AN EXAMINATION OF THE ARGUMENTS OF ARISTOTLE
#### regarding vision from "On the Soul," Book 2, Chapter 7.

The foolish pursuits of men have reached such a point of vanity that no one's work becomes famous unless they either build or burn down the Temple of Diana <note>A reference to Herostratus, who burned the famous Temple of Ephesus solely to ensure his name would be remembered; Kepler is critiquing scholars who seek fame by either blindly defending or needlessly attacking established authorities like Aristotle</note>. Because of this scarcity of optical knowledge, these truths have been unfairly pushed aside by Aristotelian darkness, while Aristotle reigns everywhere, with optical scientists feigning ignorance and remaining content with their own private freedom. 

Therefore, so that opposites may be illuminated by comparison, and so that the Aristotelians may finally be drawn into the school of optics—whether out of a desire to learn or to contradict—I have decided to discuss Aristotle’s comments on vision here in detail. To be sure, this is properly the material of the fifth chapter, if you look at the titles and topics (since the material of the first chapter is light and colors, which are prior by nature to vision and the eye). 30	**JOHANNES KEPLER**

...I shall weave together a series of arguments and then respond to them. These are the principal propositions:

1. Color is properly and by its very nature the subject of sight, and it possesses within itself the cause of why it exists as something visible.

2. Light is the <term>actuality</term> <note>Aristotle's *entelecheia*: the state of being fully realized or active.</note> of the <term>transparent</term> <note>In Latin, *perspicuum*, referring to the 'diaphanous' medium like air or water.</note> insofar as it is transparent.

3. It is, as it were, a kind of proper color of the transparent itself, when that medium is truly transparent.

4. It is not Fire, nor a body, nor a <term>flow</term> <note>The 'corpuscular' or 'efflux' theory where light is made of traveling particles.</note> from a body, but it is the presence of Fire or a luminous thing, etc., in the transparent medium.

5. It is the presence of that quality in a body because of which that body is called "transparent."

6. And these points are to be understood in this way: we must realize that Aristotle is contradicting Empedocles, who had said that light is carried and stretched in straight lines between the earth and that which surrounds and encompasses us (the sky), even if we do not notice it happening.

7. The nature of a body is the same whether it is currently in a state of light or a state of darkness.

8. And when that body is transparent only in <term>potentiality</term> <note>The capacity to be something, as opposed to actually being it.</note>, then darkness holds sway there.

9. Therefore, it is not when it is transparent in actuality, but when it is so in potentiality, that it is both dark and capable of receiving colors—especially since it is only then without color.

10. The same is affirmed regarding things that are completely unseen, and those which are seen with difficulty: that they are capable of receiving color.

11. However, that which is actually transparent must be counted among things that are visible, yet not by itself, but through a color that is foreign and external to it.

12. Vision occurs (or rather, the motion that is naturally prior to vision, which I would call the "illumination of the eye") in this manner: Color moves that which is actually transparent, such as the air; and by this air thus moved—because it is a continuous body—the instrument of sight, or the eye, is in turn moved.

13. And this is one species of vision: namely, when color is seen, specifically in the light; it is never seen separately, because light is the <term>energy</term> <note>The active power or 'energeia' of the medium.</note> of the transparent.

14. Therefore, vision (the motion of the instrument which vision follows) occurs when the sensory instrument undergoes some effect from the intermediate medium.

15. For the eye does not suffer any effect (that is, I mean the wall of the eye is not moved or altered) by the color itself that is seen.

16. To such an extent that if the intermediate space happened to be left as a vacuum, void of any body, nothing could be seen at all.

17. For there is an analogy between sight, hearing, and smell, by reason of the intermediate medium.

18. There is, however, also another species of vision, by which we discern not color but other things. By this name, one and the same certain something exists in fire and the Sun.

19. Not all things are discerned in the light, but some things produce sensation (or this preceding motion of the instrument) even in the darkness.

20. For even by fire, the transparent (in potentiality) becomes transparent (in actuality).

21. And of those things which are discerned at night or in the dark, some of them do indeed shine, but they do not instill light. <note>original Greek: λάμπεσι μὲν ἀλλ' οὐ φῶς ἐμποιεῖ — "they shine indeed, but do not produce light." This refers to phosphorescent objects like certain fungi or fish scales.</note>

From these aphorisms it appears—and I say this for the sake of greater clarity—so that it may become necessary for sight...

...the motion of the instrument of sight; that for color to be seen, Aristotle requires two motions of the air <note>Aristotle's theory of vision involved the "medium" (air or water) being moved by the object and then moving the eye.</note> or of a similar body: one from light, so that it may bring the transparent into a state of actuality (a motion which suffices for seeing a shining body), and another from the color of the thing being seen.

As for what pertains to the first opinion, it is indeed true, provided that a legitimate definition of color is also assumed. For color is capable of moving the visual instrument <note>the eye</note> precisely because it shares in the nature of light. Therefore, it is the role of light, primarily and by its very nature, to alter walls (and thus the eye).

But it is not enough for color to be related to light for this purpose; it must also be actually illuminated by light, and thus have "drunk in" a certain light, which in this chapter is called **communicated light.** <term>Communicated light (lux communicata): A technical term in medieval optics referring to light that has been reflected or absorbed by a colored surface, as opposed to direct light from a source.</term>

In the second Aphorism, Aristotle defines light—not, I think, in its own nature, but insofar as it contributes to the business of seeing. Even if it seems impossible to thoroughly probe the very innermost nature of light, it is nonetheless better to investigate those things which concern the nature of light more closely before proceeding to the function of light. For it is certain that we know most correctly what anything can do in another thing once we have understood what it is in itself.

The same must be said regarding **the transparent**: <term>The transparent (perspicuum): In Aristotelian physics, this is the medium—like air, water, or glass—that allows light to pass through.</term> which Aristotle defines here in no other way than if he were giving the reason for its name. For something is "transparent" <note>original: *perspicuum*</note> when it is seen through <note>original: *perspicitur*</note>, and "clear" <note>original: *pellucidum*</note> when it shines through <note>original: *pellucet*</note> with certain lights. But neither happens except in the presence of light. Yet he who indicates the physical dispositions by which bodies are fit to be clear—whether light is present or absent—approaches much closer to the nature of things. For it is certain that the nature of bodies is not changed by the arrival of light: and yet some bodies remain dark in both cases, while others are dark only when light is absent.

Thus, in the third opinion, violence is done to both light and the transparent. For the words sound as if light exists in nature primarily for the sake of the transparent: which is otherwise. For light is the cause for illuminating colors; whereas the transparent exists for the sake of both, namely, so that colors could be illuminated by a single, distant sun. Therefore, light is not the "act" of the transparent, but rather the "act" of colors, insofar as they are seen or radiate.

In the fourth, I desire to learn: if light (or, if it pleases one to distinguish with Scaliger, *lumen*) <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger, a famous 16th-century scholar, distinguished between *lux* (light at its source) and *lumen* (light traveling through space).</note> is not an outflow from a shining body, how then is it "present" in the transparent? If the Sun is present in the air, and yet fixed in the heavens, it must therefore be present in the air through an efflux. Unless perhaps some "occult philosophy" lies hidden in these wonderful words: which anyone who likes may admire as something unknown; those eager for real learning are not satisfied by empty words. Add to this that according to what has been demonstrated in this chapter, a ray is not *in* the transparent (insofar as it is transparent), but *was* there, or as if it were there. It is truly found only on the colors and surfaces of things.

Thus I deny the fifth point in every respect. For whether we follow the subtleties of the name, the transparent is not truly "active" except when light, having made its transition through it, strikes a wall. At that time, light is not merely the "presence" of that quality, but something more than this presence. For the origin of the name comes not from light itself, but from the motion of light through the body, or of sight through the body. Or rather, if the nature of the transparent is preferred, light and the form of the transparent are so distinct that they cannot even be contained under the same physical genus: since color is denied to the transparent, that is, every...

*...is, light in every way; let surface be denied, which is not denied of light; let density finally be denied, which itself is even left to light.*

*Neither do I feel differently regarding the sixth point, than that truth itself spoke through the persona of Empedocles* <note>Empedocles was a Pre-Socratic philosopher who proposed that light takes time to travel, a view Aristotle famously rejected.</note> *as long as you make this exception: that light thus extended from the Sun all the way to the Earth is present as matter in the intermediate space in proportion to its density and opacity—that is, it is not present in the transparent <term>perspicuum; the medium through which light travels, like air or water</term> insofar as it is transparent. And this is the reason why it is not detected by us.*

*The seventh and eighth points may be judged from what has been said before.*

*But in the ninth, it does not therefore follow that the transparent is capable of color just because it lacks color. For there is no power in the transparent to receive color insofar as it retains this species of bodily nature; and without such power, a simple negation of a thing, as is well known, does not establish a habit* <note>In Aristotelian logic, a "habit" (habitus) is a formal state of being; Kepler argues that just because something is "not-colored" doesn't mean it has the "potential" to be colored.</note>. *Indeed, the more a transparent thing happens to be colored (since nothing is absolutely transparent), the less transparent it will be.*

*The tenth point plainly denies colors to things lying hidden in darkness. Here again is the same complaint as was made about the transparent: as if colors do not exist except when they are seen. The common people (as Aristotle himself admits) are the masters of speech; therefore, the common people do not define colors so narrowly. But if you say that he did not wish to extend the definition of color further here than insofar as they relate to sight, I say again: first, the nature of the thing should be considered in itself; then what it can do to other things will be most rightly investigated. For in this way, things are surely confused and obscured. Color, therefore, exists in things themselves in reality, even if they are not illuminated, and consequently they neither radiate nor are seen. Nor does the illumination of a translucent thing cause the colors to move the translucent medium; rather, the illumination of the colors causes them to pass through the medium, which is then truly called translucent.*

*The eleventh point includes the transparent among visible things, which are conspicuous. However, "conspicuous" and "transparent" are opposites; thus, violence is done to the word. As for the matter itself, color is conspicuous in itself, according to Aristotle’s testimony; but color, insofar as it is actually seen, is an accident of the surface, not of the body, which he also agrees with. Therefore, only surfaces are made conspicuous through color. But a transparent thing is a body, not a surface; therefore, a transparent thing cannot be made conspicuous by color according to Aristotelian principles. Unless you take the word "color" here in another sense, by which method much ambiguity will arise.*

*Now, in the twelfth point, you would surely find much to be desired. For first, if nothing more is required for the movement or alteration of the sensory instrument than that whatever is between the color and the instrument be actually transparent—that is, actually brought into the state of light—then colors will be seen without being illuminated at all. But that can be proven by no experience, such as the air being everywhere open to light, yet vision of a color occurring without the color being illuminated. For a case is given: suppose the Sun alone shines and touches with its forward edge a surface in which there is color, but the Sun's body is behind that surface (if the body is imagined to be continuous). It will therefore not be able to illuminate the surface which it grazes with its outermost ray, but it will illuminate all the air placed in front of it. Nevertheless, vision will not follow, even if the eye is placed in the space of the illuminated air. Experience testifies to the contrary: that the more strongly a color is illuminated, the more clearly it is discerned (that is, it shines back), and that continuously. Therefore, where there is no illumination of color, there is also no vision of it, whatever happens to the transparent medium. So experience also testifies regarding the transparent, that the more light is noticed in it...*

->ADDITIONS TO WITELO. 33<-

it is observed that the more this happens, the more the vision of colors located beyond it is hindered, because the "clinging" of light within a transparent medium destroys the definition of that medium. <note>original: "inhæsio lucis in perspicuo." Kepler is likely referring to glare or the way light reflecting off dust or the air itself makes it harder to see distant objects.</note>

If you were to ask Aristotle what category of motion this belongs to—when color acts upon the transparent medium, and when the medium acts upon the eye—he would, I believe, call it "alteration" (Chapter 5). <note>Aristotle argued that vision wasn't something moving through space, but a near-instantaneous change in the state of the air.</note> If you ask by what quality it is altered, he must answer that it is by color. Therefore, the transparent medium would be changed from colorless to colored, and then again from green to red or black. Thus, the very same part of the medium would be imbued with all colors at once; yet, it would move different eyes not with a confusion of colors (as if everyone saw the same blur), but—as experience testifies—it would make one person see green, another black, and a third red. I ask you, by what logic could a transparent thing perform this? And how, in a single moment, could such a depth of air be altered? Indeed, how could the same part of it sustain so many colors? Therefore, since this fabricated cause is not equal to the effect, and since the medium itself does not take on various modes to match the variety of visions occurring at one and the same moment, this theory is held to be worthless.

Let us therefore embrace the true opinion described in this chapter and established by irrefutable experiments: namely, that from the Sun, and from colors illuminated by the Sun, flow out **similar species** <term>species: in older optics, this refers to the "form" or "image" of an object that radiates outward through space</term>; and that by this very flow they are thinned out until they strike a medium that is in some way opaque, where they **paint** their own source. Vision occurs (as will be said below in Chapter 5) when the opaque wall of the eye is painted in this way. Vision is confused when the pictures of various colors are jumbled together there, and distinct when they are not.

Unless such a "flowing out" and the thinning of that flowing species are accepted, it can never be explained by Aristotelian principles why the eye is affected differently by the vision of a remote thing versus a nearby thing, even when the seen size and the seen color are placed on an equal footing through compensation. <note>Kepler is arguing that if the air just "changes state," distance shouldn't matter; but if "species" are physical things that spread out and weaken, distance explains why things look smaller or fainter.</note> See also Chapter 3 on this.

**Proposition 13** contains this truth: that colors are not seen except in light. But it assigns a false cause when it introduces light for the sake of "activating" the transparent medium; for light, as I have said, rather harms the transparency. Light is required for seeing colors because colors do not radiate or emit a species into the hemisphere unless they are illustrated by the light of the sun or of torches.

Thus, **Proposition 14** must be completely overturned. The more the eye suffers (for the sake of vision) from the intervening medium, the less correctly and clearly will things be seen through it. Therefore, vision becomes most perfect when the eye suffers absolutely nothing from the intervening medium.

And **15**: the eye is clearly altered by the species of color passing through a transparent body without the "help" of that transparent body.

And **16**: if the region between heaven and earth were entirely a vacuum, the vision of those things now seen in the heavens would become the most accurate of all. (Though it would not be as that Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> said—that one could see an ant in the heavens—because the weakness of the instrument <note>the eye</note> would prevent this.)

Therefore, let others see what should be thought of the **analogy of the senses** introduced in **Proposition 17**. For what if the analogy were better formed like this: that once we are certain about sight, we should then dispute about hearing and smell according to its rule? Regarding smell, no one will deny that something of the scent flows out from the very substance of the thing and is received into the nostrils; and that it is felt more strongly as the medium and the distance are reduced. Thus, the medium contributes nothing to informing the 
E sense... <margin>to the sense</margin>

the medium here contributes to the sensation. Rather, this flow is stopped by time, as the substance is emptied and the source dries up. As for the proportion of this outflow to the medium—that is, to the air—the scent of fire has its own logic, and it is driven upward away from the impurities of the air. This has been observed most clearly in the very high and completely bald mountains of Carinthia <note>A region in the Eastern Alps, mostly in modern-day Austria.</note>, as well as elsewhere. For indeed, those walking through them are met by a most sweet and plainly ambrosial scent rising from the flowering valleys below.

Regarding hearing, the logic of the "emanating species of the strike" <note>Kepler refers to the form or image of a sound produced by a physical impact.</note> is indeed more complex than that of smell, yet easier than that of color. For the movement of light is instantaneous. But the species of a strike flows through time; it therefore accommodates itself more to the logic of matter. And as for the medium, I ask again what I asked before: if the medium exists to inform the sense of hearing, why is sound spread more widely through pure air? Is it because matter hinders sound? Yet, the more a medium deserves to be called a "medium," the more "material" it is? Likewise, if the medium forms the hearing, why do we drink in sounds more correctly from nearby than from a distance? For I think it would follow that as the cause increased, the effect should increase. In general, therefore, all senses are made more perceptive when the instrument <note>The sense organ, such as the ear or eye.</note> undergoes an impression. But so that they might receive impressions from absent things, the logic of "outflows" <note>Effluxuum: the idea that physical particles or "forms" flow from an object to the observer.</note> was introduced, so that what could not be achieved by the things themselves might be provided by their <term>species</term> <note>In this context, "species" refers to the non-material form or "image" of an object that travels through a medium to the senses.</note>. Media exist only by the necessity of nature to exclude a vacuum. Since these media would otherwise be an obstacle to the outflows, they have been purified and distributed: that is, they are made transparent (which is to say thinned out, continuous, and colorless) so that light can pass through, and they are constituted as "smellable" and "soundable" in the air so that these species can also be spread.

The following four opinions contain a contradiction, which I leave to the Aristotelians to discuss. In the 18th opinion, I find nothing lacking: that fire and celestial light have something in common. And the 19th opinion is taken from experience. Stars, fire, rotting wood, and such things are seen at night. And what Aristotle attributes to fire in his own way in the 20th opinion, I also attribute in mine. To him, fire "informs" the medium (as discussed above); to me, fire illustrates colors. But Aristotle does this because "it produces light" <note>original Greek: φῶς ἐμποιεῖ</note>, and "light" <note>original Greek: φῶς</note> is the energy of the transparent. However (in the final opinion), rotting wood and salted fish <note>original: "hadina salita," likely referring to the bioluminescent glow sometimes seen on salted fish or skins.</note> do not do this, which only "glow" <note>original Greek: λάμπει</note>. Therefore, these things are seen when the air is not "actually transparent" <note>Aristotle argued that light is the "actuality" of transparency; without light, air is only potentially transparent.</note>; for light is the act of the transparent, and here it is absent. Here, therefore, the eye suffers nothing from the medium. But neither does it suffer from the thing itself, which is distant. Nor from an outflow, which Aristotle denies. Vision therefore occurs with the eye suffering nothing. The same can be objected to the 14th opinion. If vision is not completed at all without an external medium, how is it that someone can see the "nocturnal sparkling" of their own eyes, which is inside the eye? If you say the humor <note>The fluid inside the eyeball.</note> of the eye acts as the medium, I retort that it could also take the place of the medium for seeing an external thing when that thing touches the eye. But Aristotle brings forward a cause for why this is not seen: the lack of an external medium.

It is clear enough from this that the Opticians disagree with Aristotle on almost every opinion. It is necessary, therefore, that there be a flaw in his arguments, which I will now weigh.

The series is this: 1. In every sense, "the sense organ" <note>original Greek: τὸ αἰσθητήριον</note> is moved by some "sensible object" <note>original Greek: αἰσθητῷ</note>. For sensation is a "passion" <note>A "passion" in the philosophical sense means the state of being acted upon by an external force.</note>, not indeed one leading to "destruction" <note>original Greek: φθορὰν</note>, but one by which a potential is brought into act, similar to "alteration" <note>original Greek: ἀλλοιώσει</note>, yet not "alteration" <note>original Greek: ἀλλοίωσις</note> itself. ->SUPPLEMENTS TO WITELO. 35<-

I. *Vision is a sense. Therefore, the <term>sensory organ</term> <note>original: "τὸ αἰσθητήριον"</note> is moved toward vision by some <term>sensible object</term> <note>original: "αἰσθητῷ"</note>.*
II. *If color is placed directly against the eye, it is not seen. Therefore, a medium is required to intervene in the act of seeing. This is strengthened by the analogy of the other senses.*
III. *Therefore, it is either the color or the medium that moves the sight. But it is not the color (I understand this because when a medium is placed in between, the color does not touch the sensory organ, and no motion occurs without contact). Thus, the medium remains as the thing that moves the sensory organ.*
IV. *That which does not move of its own accord moves because it was first moved by another. The medium moves the sight, but not by itself, because the medium itself lacks color. Therefore, it moves because it was first moved by something else—namely, by a colored object—or, what is the same thing, Color (an admitted visible thing) moves the medium.*
V. *Color moves the medium toward the sight, which we call "transparent" <note>Kepler uses the term "pellucidum," the Aristotelian term for a medium like air or water that can transmit light.</note>; but color does not move just any medium if it exists in darkness (I understand this because in darkness, no vision follows). Therefore, a dark medium is not transparent; or what is the same thing, air and such things are not yet transparent when in the dark.*
VI. *That of which darkness is the privation, light is the "habit" <note>In Aristotelian logic, a "habit" (habitus) is a positive state or quality, while "privation" is the absence of that quality.</note>, because these <term>seem to be opposites</term> <note>original: "δοκεῖ ἐναντία"</note>. But darkness is the privation of the transparent, as just concluded; therefore, light is the habit or the actualization of the transparent. Response to these arguments.*

*I approve of the first point. I only add this in passing: Aristotle should not have been so carefully anxious to avoid the idea that vision undergoes some <term>corruption</term> <note>original: "φθοράν"; here meaning physical wear or deterioration</note>. It is as if he thought it unworthy to believe this of a sense given to living creatures for their preservation. For indeed, as is shown in this chapter, light carries a deadly enmity toward all matter, especially toward the "family of blacks," which are like materialized darkness. The eye, in fact, consists of matter and is black. Therefore, it is gradually corrupted by light. This is why we feel pain from looking at the sun, and why the eyes age, in part.*

*Regarding point II: A generalization was made regarding the vision of colors. However, an objection is raised concerning the vision of sparks in the eyes; the vision of the <term>species</term> <note>In this context, "species" refers to the visual images or afterimages that linger in the "spirits" of the nervous system.</note> remaining in the spirits after the visible thing is removed; and the vision of impurities in the eye's humors after headaches. Therefore, a conclusion cannot be drawn regarding all vision; the conclusion is not universal. Furthermore, there is more in the conclusion than in the premises. For what does it matter if it is granted that a medium always exists between color and sight? It does not yet follow that a medium is absolutely required to form vision or to move the sight.*

*For there are other reasons why colors are less clearly seen when placed directly against the eye. 1. If color—that is, the surface of the visible thing—touched the eye, the eye would feel pain. 2. At most, only one eye could be used. 3. No more of the color could be seen than what can be contained within the circle of the pupil's opening. 4. Most importantly, through contact between the eye and the surface to be seen, all illumination of color is excluded, without which vision cannot happen (except for the glowing eyes of certain animals). 5. Furthermore, it is clear that there is another underlying cause, beyond what has been said or what Aristotle supposes, as to why a thing touching the eye is not seen, which is that*

36 JOHANNES KEPLER

Even when an object is placed too close to the eye, no matter how much of the external medium <note>the substance between the eye and the object, such as air or water</note> remains, it is perceived confusedly and almost not at all. Instead, it is surrounded by an indistinct and almost shadowy edge, the cause of which is explained below in chapter five. Thus, sheer proximity is harmful to sight, even without considering the medium. This is also proven by the eyes of the elderly, for whom distant things are seen more clearly than those nearby.

Therefore, since these experimental reasons are sufficient, it is not permissible to restrict the conclusion to any one cause, much less to any cause other than these. This is all the more important because the very foundations of how we explain vision are being built here.

**To Argument III:** There is an insufficient list in the major premise. For neither the body of the Sun (nor of color) nor the medium itself moves the eye. Rather, it is the *species* <note>original: "species"; in Kepler's time, this referred to the "emanations" or "likenesses" of an object that travel through space</note> or the lights—the rays of the sun and colors—descending through the medium and vibrating outward in a spherical shape into the hemisphere. For the manner of all vision is one and the same, whether it is of the sun, or of color, or of fire, or of *shining things* <note>original: τῶν λαμπόντων (*tōn lampontōn*)</note>, as far as the physical change to the wall of the eye is concerned. The only difference is this: colors must be illuminated first, while the rest are bright by their own nature. The Sun and fire also make other things bright.

But Aristotle seems to take it for granted that the *species*, being a mere "accident" <note>a philosophical term for a property that cannot exist on its own, like "redness"</note>, cannot cause any motion unless it exists inside a subject like the transparent air. However, this is false, as shown in this chapter. For there are certain "passions" <note>physical properties or ways of being acted upon</note> of light or rays descending from bright things that belong to light itself, not to the transparent air it inhabits. Examples include emission and thinning, and their opposites, reflection and refraction (or condensation). Therefore, nothing prevents light from also having its own actions—namely, as experience witnesses, the illumination and alteration of the walls of the eye. Upon these walls, colors or light are not merely poured, but are actually imprinted, and their opposites are destroyed.

I prove that flowing light undergoes these physical properties without needing a "host" or transparent medium in this way: Reflection occurs in space but without taking any time <note>Kepler believed light traveled instantaneously</note>. Yet, for no material body is movement from place to place possible without time.

What if someone says that Aristotle claims this motion or "affection" of the transparent medium is "analogical" <note>symbolic or metaphorical</note> rather than strictly physical? I respond: Aristotle’s meaning would then match the meaning of the Opticians, though the words differ. But why did he not instead follow the nature of things and state that there is an analogical motion in light itself? For I hear from others: "Light or the *species* is a mere accident and can sustain no motion." I retort using the same Philosophy: "A physical body cannot be moved in an instant." Therefore, just as the "body" of light is without matter, so is its motion without time—both are analogical.

In short, Aristotle seems to distinguish between the *species* of colors and *the light* <note>original: τὸ φῶς (*to phōs*)</note>, even though light is spread from every color when it is seen.

Since the major premise is thus dissolved, the conclusion does not follow either. Therefore, Argument IV is easily answered, as its minor premise was the conclusion of III, which was found to be false. For the medium, moved neither by itself nor by another, does not move the sight. Nor is the conclusion true in any sense (the premise having been destroyed) unless one calls the transition a "passion." However, the more easily the medium is crossed, the less it "suffers" or is changed; indeed, it is not changed in any part except on its two surfaces, and in that respect, it ceases to be a "medium." For Aristotle, in order to lead the *species* of colors all the way to the contact of the eye...

Hence, the fifth argument is also refuted, because it depends on the fourth. Yet even if it were shaped from my own principles, it would not be sound, in this manner: Light passes through the transparent, but does not pass through the dark; therefore, things in darkness are not transparent.

For this is a "begging of the question" <note>A logical fallacy where the conclusion is assumed in the premise.</note>, because this very thing creates darkness when light is absent from the transparent medium. Nor does the transparent <term>pellucidum<gloss>The Latin term for a medium that allows light to pass through, like air or glass.</gloss></term> take its name from the actual state of being lit, as if it were not of that nature simply because it is not currently shining. Now, the sixth argument is indifferent. The minor premise is answered by a distinction. The essence of the transparent, insofar as it is transparent, is not light (whether present or absent), but only the internal disposition of the body. Darkness does not deprive the transparent of this essence, and therefore light does not bestow it. But if "transparent" means the same thing as "shining," then darkness certainly indicates that it is not shining; thus, light wins it the name of "the shining thing." But in this way, light is nothing other than a "species" <note>In this context, "species" refers to the outward form or appearance of an object that travels through the air to the eye.</note> emanating from colors, and it does not serve the intent of Aristotle. Aristotle makes "the light" <note>original Greek: τὸ φῶς</note>—the "act" of the transparent—prior in nature and intellect to the "species" of color. For him, the transparent is first brought into action by the informing "light" <note>original Greek: φωτὶ</note>, and afterward, color moves this activated transparent medium and impresses its own "species" upon it.

I wait to see what the Academics <note>Followers of the traditional university philosophy based on Aristotle.</note> will bring against this, and how they will attempt to prefer the honor of their Master (which he himself never sought) over the truth. ->APPENDICES TO WITELO. 39<-

Neither Witelo <note>Kepler refers to him as "Pisanus," as Witelo was often associated with Pisa in medieval citations.</note>, nor any of his successors as far as I know, understood this. Several years ago, a certain light shone for me out of Witelo’s darkness. Since I could not grasp the meaning of his words—which were so obscure—from a flat diagram, I sought refuge in **direct observation** <note>original Greek: *αυτοψίαν* (*autopsian*), meaning "seeing for oneself."</note> using a solid model. 

I placed a book high up to represent a shining body. Between this book and the floor, I fixed a small tablet with a multi-angled hole. I then let down a thread from one corner of the book, passing it through the hole until it touched the floor. I moved the thread so that it grazed the edges of the hole and traced its path on the floor with chalk; in this way, a shape was created on the floor that was similar to the hole. I did the same by attaching the thread to the second, third, and fourth corners of the book, and eventually to infinite points along its edges. Thus, a series of infinite, tiny shapes of the hole on the floor sketched out the large, rectangular shape of the book. 

It therefore became clear, for the purpose of demonstrating this problem, that the roundness of a projected light comes not from the "visual ray," but from the shape of the sun itself. This happens not because the circle is the most "perfect" figure, but because that is the shape of the shining body in this specific case. This was my first success in this labor. 

Furthermore, both Aristotle and the aforementioned Witelo—by offering a most beautiful experiment for clarifying the argument—noted how the ray of a "failing" <note>An eclipsed sun.</note> sun appears similarly failing when it is received through a narrow hole. This provided the opportunity for Reinhold <note>Erasmus Reinhold, a major astronomer who produced the Prutenic Tables.</note>, Gemma <note>Gemma Frisius, a Dutch mathematician and instrument maker.</note>, and my teacher Maestlin <note>Michael Maestlin, who taught Kepler at Tübingen.</note> to adapt this theorem to a no less noble use. For these authors I have named taught astronomers how to use a compass to measure the magnitudes of solar eclipses, the proportions of the diameters of the sun and moon, and the inclinations of the circle passing through the centers of the lights toward the vertical. They could do this without damage to their eyes and without the errors usually committed by estimation with the naked eye. 

From that time on, it is likely that all solar eclipses recorded by excellent mathematicians were observed in the manner just described, since besides this, no other certain method could be established for measuring what happens in the heavens. 

But here it is worthwhile to see how much trouble an unacknowledged demonstration of this theorem causes. For since this escaped certain authors, it happened that by believing the theorem without limitations, they fell into a great error. For how—

However many eclipses were observed in this manner, they all occurred much larger in the sky than they appeared in the ray <note>original: *in radio*; here Kepler refers to the image projected through a pinhole camera</note>; they all showed the diameter of the moon in the heavens to be much larger than in the projected ray. For this reason, that "Phoenix of Astronomers," Tycho Brahe, was wonderingly forced into such a predicament that he declared the diameter of the moon to be always a fifth part smaller in conjunctions <note>the New Moon phase, specifically during a solar eclipse</note> than it appears in oppositions <note>the Full Moon phase</note>, even though it is equally distant from us in both cases. I would not deny, however, that other causes also exist as to why the moon's diameter truly appears somewhat smaller in conjunctions, which I will discuss below.

I hope to remove these great difficulties—which wall off our access to the foreknowledge of eclipses and the exact restoration of the moon's motion—in these few pages. I will do so by a straightforward demonstration of a theorem and by revealing the sources of errors which revealed themselves to me from a careful consideration of the solar eclipse <term>deliquium solaris|an older term for a solar eclipse, literally a "failing" of the sun</term> that occurred in the year 1600.

->DEFINITION<-

*All points, whether of the same or of different surfaces, are said to be on one shining surface if straight lines can be drawn from them to a single remote point to form a pyramid, because that pyramid is understood to be cut by a single perpendicular plane.*

->POSTULATE<-

*Let it be granted that two illuminating lines originating from the same shining point, even if they actually meet at this source, are to be considered perceptibly parallel if they have an immense proportion <note>meaning a very large ratio of distance</note> to the base by which both are connected.*

->PROPOSITION I<-

*If there were a single point (to our senses) from which light was spread, the ray on a wall positioned directly opposite would have a shape similar to the window through which it entered by a straight path; and the ratio of the diameters of the illuminated wall and the window would be the same as the ratio of their distances from the shining point.*

This is the 99th and 100th [propositions] of the first book of Vitello <note>Erasmus Witelo was a 13th-century Polish scholar whose work on optics was the standard text until Kepler wrote this "Supplement to Witelo."</note>.

### LEMMA I. For the following proposition.

*Triangles that intercept equal or the same portions of two parallel lines with their legs have their vertices terminating on a third parallel line.*

[A geometric diagram consisting of two parallel horizontal lines. The top line is labeled n, e, p. The middle line is labeled f, o, g. Various lines intersect these, meeting at points k and i on a third lower horizontal level. Lines include n-f-i, p-g-i, e-o-i, p-o-k, and e-f-k.]

Let the straight line **N E P** be divided into equal parts at **E**. And let **F O G** be parallel to it, similarly divided into equal parts at **O**. Let the straight lines **P O** and **E F** be drawn until they meet at **K**. In the same way, let **E O** and **N F** (or **P G**) be drawn until they meet at **I**; and let **K I** be connected. I say that **K I** is parallel to the bases **N E P** and **F O G**. For in triangles **N E I** and **F O I**, the angles **N E I** and **F O I** are equal, by the 29th proposition of the first book <note>referring to Euclid's *Elements*, which was the standard textbook for geometry</note>. So too are **E N I** and **O F I**, and the angle at **I** is common to both. Therefore, the triangles are equiangular <note>having the same angles</note>, and by the 4th proposition of the sixth book, their sides are proportional. Therefore, as **N E** is to **F O**, so **E I** is to **O I**. In the same way, it is proved in triangles **E P K** and **F O K** that as **E P** is to **F O**, so **P K** is to **O K**. But **E P** and **E N** are equal. Therefore, just as **N E** is to **F O**, so **P K** is to **O K**. But previously, **E I** was also to **O I** in that same ratio; therefore, as **P K** is to **O K**, so **E I** is to **O I**. And by the fifth proposition of the fifth book, as **P O** is to **O K**, so **E O** is to **O I**; and by permutation, as **P O** is to **E O**, so **K O** is to **O I**. Moreover, the angle **E O P** is equal to the angle **I O K**, being vertical angles. Therefore, triangles **E O P** and **I O K**, by the 6th proposition of the sixth book, are equiangular, and the angles **O K I** (or **P K I**) and **O P E** (or **K P E**) are equal. Therefore, by the 28th proposition of the first book, **E P** and **K I** are parallel. The same is also true for **E P K** and **E P I**; which indeed intercept the same common base, and equal portions of the parallel line **F G**. The proposition is therefore clear.

For as many other similar and nearly equal shapes surround this one as there are points of the window surrounding its center, because such a section <note>A "section" here refers to the intersection of light rays in space.</note> occurs in each individual point. Now, let a point be chosen according to the preceding problem that is a smaller number of "window diameters" (**FG**) away from point **O** than it is "light source diameters" (**NP**) away from point **E**. Let this point be **X**. Through this point, a line is drawn parallel to the aforementioned diameters, which will cut the rays at points **H**, **M**, **T**, and **V**. Therefore, the segment **MT** will represent the diameter of the inverted shape of the light source as it falls upon location **X**. However, **HV** is the diameter of the shape produced by the window. Thus, the window's shape (**HV**) will be larger than the light source's shape (**MT**). Consequently, the edges of the window's shape will strike the eyes more than the edges of the light source's shape. 

Conversely, let a point be chosen through the same problem that is a greater number of window diameters away from **O** than it is light source diameters away from **E**. Let that point be **Y**. A line drawn through **Y**, parallel to the others as before, will cut the rays at **A**, **B**, **C**, and **D**. But because the intersection of the rays occurred previously at **K** and **L**, those rays which were on the inside are now on the outside. Thus, **AD**, representing

## PROPOSITION VII. A Problem.

*In a closed room, to represent on a designated wall whatever is outside the room in that direction, whether it is a fixed object or an action, provided it is something visible to the eyes.*

This art was first taught, as far as I know, by Giambattista della Porta <note>Giambattista della Porta (1535–1615) was an Italian scholar famous for his work *Magia Naturalis* (Natural Magic), which described the camera obscura.</note>, and he made it a significant part of "natural magic." However, being content with the experience of the effect, he did not provide a geometric demonstration. Yet, by this single experiment alone, astronomers could have determined the true nature of the image of a solar eclipse.

Therefore, let all the cracks of the room be closed so that not even the tiniest bit of light can enter. Opposite the window that has a view of the things to be represented, let there be a white wall, while the other walls are black. Let a very narrow <term>aperture<note>Latin: *foramen*. A small hole through which light passes to form an image.</note></term> be opened in the window, as small as is sufficient for the strength of vision. However, if the wall or window is thick, the parts surrounding the hole should be cut away into a slope until a clear view through the hole is open to all the objects placed outside that you wish to represent. 

And let the eyes of the spectator be kept from the sight of daylight for fifteen or thirty minutes, until the "images" <note>Kepler refers to "species," a term for the visual forms or impressions that the eye perceives.</note> impressed upon the visual spirits <note>In 17th-century physiology, "visual spirits" were thought to be a subtle fluid that carried sensory information from the eye to the mind.</note> in the bright light of day have faded away, according to what was said in the conclusion of the first chapter. Let the things to be represented be placed in the bright light of either the sun, the day, or torches. 

I say that everything seen to exist or happen outside will be represented inside on the opposite white wall, only with the position inverted. For according to Proposition 22 of the first chapter, things illuminated outside by any light "color" the light communicated to them and spread it out in all directions. Therefore, according to the sixth proposition of this chapter, the external things will illuminate the wall opposite them inside, such that the shape of the illuminated wall is indeed blurred by the shape of the window and the things outside; however, since the window is assumed to be very narrow in relation to its distance from the wall, very little of the window's shape will mix with the shape of the objects standing outside. 

This picture will lack only two things: first, that according to the same sixth proposition, things will appear inside in an inverted position; second, that whatever falls outside within the reach of a cone whose <term>vertex<note>The pointed tip of a cone.</note></term> stands at the wall and is shaped or constrained by the hole, the parts of that object will be expressed on the wall in detail...

*To represent in a closed room, and upon a designated wall, whatever is either present or happening outside the room in that direction, provided it is visible to the eyes.*

Unless the chamber were closed so tightly, although there are infinite colored rays on any wall even without the formation of a hole, they could not be seen because of the brightness of the day (according to Proposition 28 of the first chapter). And because as the shape of the **shining hemisphere** <note>original: *hemisphaerii lucentis*; this refers to the visible half of the world or sky visible through the aperture</note> changes, its image on the wall also changes. Indeed, things that happen—that is, movements—constantly change the face of the hemisphere; therefore, the image inside will also change. Thus, the movements of things outside are visible within.

There is, however, a deficiency in representing colors: according to Proposition 29 of the first chapter and the inverse of Proposition 30, the differences between colors are not well perceived by the eyes because of the brightness of the white rays radiating onto the white surface. Indeed, the nature of black objects is not perceived except as shadows. If you wished to change the color of the surface, the radiation of colors would indeed be made distinct according to Proposition 30 of the first chapter, but it would be stained by the common color of that surface and would be so weak that it could hardly be captured by the eyes.

### PROPOSITION VIII.

The shape of a ray of the sun or the full moon entering through an angular window <note>an aperture or opening</note>—to the extent that the proportion of the window to its distance from the wall is smaller than that of the sun to its own distance—gradually approaches a circular shape more and more, the further it travels from the window.

### PROPOSITION XI.
**The diameter of the moon appears smaller in a projected image of this kind than it does outside in the sky.**

Maintaining the previous figure, let segment **DAC** be continued, and let the center of its circle, **L**, be connected with **C. A. D.** Let segment **DEC** also be continued through **N**, and let the center of its circle, **A**, be connected with points **C. E. D.** and extended to **KGI.** Since, therefore, **DECA** is the exact figure of the remaining part of the sun during an eclipse (according to the third corollary), just as it truly appears in the sky, then the ratio of **LA** to **AE**, or **LD** to **DA**, or **LC** to **CA**, is the true proportion of the diameters of the sun and the moon.

But in fact, since **IGKFBH** is enlarged on all sides by the semi-diameter of the window **EG** or **CK**, two things happen at once. First, the semi-diameters of the sun **AD, AE, AC** are increased and become **AI, AG, AK.** Therefore (by the eighth proposition of the fifth book <note>Referring to Euclid's Elements.</note>), the ratio of **AI** to **AL** is greater than **AD** to **AL.** Second, the semi-diameters of the moon **LD, LA, LC** are decreased, and **LA, LB, LF** likewise become equal, because equal amounts are taken away. Therefore, by the same logic, the ratio of **AD** to **BL** is greater than **AD** to **AL.** Since the ratio of **AI** to **AL** was already greater than **AD** to **AL**, it follows that the ratio of **AI** (the semi-diameter of the sun in the projected image) to **BL** (the semi-diameter of the moon in the projected image) is much greater than the ratio of **AD** (the semi-diameter of the sun in the sky) to **AL** (the semi-diameter of the moon in the sky). This inequality is quite noticeable, because the window is usually assumed to be quite large.

### PROPOSITION XII.
**The Ecliptic Digits appear fewer in the projected image than in the sky.**

In the previous diagram, let the segment **IGK** be continued through **M.** Since the ratio of **EN** to **NA** is the ratio of the solar diameter to the eclipsed part, and **GM** is larger than **EN** by two semi-diameters of the window (**EG** and **NM**), the ratio of **NA** to **MO** is therefore smaller than **NA** to **NE.** But **NA** is equal to **MB**, because **AB** and **MN** are equal. Therefore, the ratio of **MB** (the part of the ray representing the eclipse) to **MG** (the diameter of the projected image) is smaller...

### CHAPTER III.
### On the foundations of Catoptrics & the location of the image.
#### I. Refutation of Euclid, Witelo & Alhazen.

**I**n the very foundation of Catoptrics <term>Catoptrics: the branch of optics dealing with the behavior of reflected light and mirrors</term>, the demonstrations of the optical writers are even now obscure, as they seek from perception that which itself ought to have been proven. Nor does any small error originate from there. In these optical studies, we investigate refractions <note>Kepler is preparing to discuss how light bends, but feels he must first fix the errors in the theory of reflection.</note> more diligently for the sake of eclipses and observations of the stars; but for the sake of refractions, we had to cross through this gap. Therefore, this place must also be filled, and the clouds dispelled, so that the Sun of truth may shine more clearly.

Euclid, in Theorems 16, 17, and 18 of his *Catoptrics*, in order to prove that each of those things which fall under our sight is seen along its perpendicular line to the surface of the mirror, assumes a falsehood. Let the mirror be CD, the sight B, and the visible object A. Let the perpendicular be AC. He thus proves that the location of the image of object A is in AC—specifically at E. For, he says, if the location on the mirror C, upon which the perpendicular AC falls, is "taken up" <note>original: *assumpto*</note>, the visible object A is no longer seen. If you understand "taken up" to mean occupied or covered at point C, this axiom is false—even though Euclid recorded this at the front of his book among his postulates borrowed from experience (or whatever else he calls by the name "phenomenon" <note>original: φαινόμενον</note> in this little book). For even if C is covered or entirely removed, as long as D remains, A is nonetheless seen at E by the eye at B.

<margin>
Above, chapter 1, proposition 20: the same diagram.
</margin>

[Diagram: A geometric figure consisting of a vertical line on the left with points labeled 'a', 'e', and 'c' from top to bottom. A horizontal line 'ef' intersects a diagonal line 'bc' at point 'd'. Another diagonal line 'ad' connects point 'a' to the intersection 'd'.]

Furthermore, this axiom seems to smack of a false belief concerning the true and real ascent of the image along the line CE, which does not differ much from the opinion of certain ancients regarding the emission of visual rays from the eye <note>A reference to "extramission theory," the ancient belief that eyes see by shooting out rays of light like a flashlight.</note>. For Euclid supports this in his first postulate, defining sight (in Greek, *opsis* <note>original: ὄψιν</note>) as a straight line; and so he uses it commonly in his work on mirrors. ->SUPPLEMENTS TO WITELO. 37<-

Euclid indeed speaks *with technical skill* <note>original: ἐντέχνως; meaning with a calculated or systematic method</note>, and assumes things that—even if they are not easily granted—if you do grant them, do not contradict themselves as they progress. Yet, the truth suffers violence from this manner of philosophizing; false beliefs arise, which certainly seem to cling to Aristotle when he speaks of his *visual rays* <note>original: ὄψεσιν</note>. These ideas appear to stem from this Euclidean school, which was not well understood; ultimately, ignorance establishes a kind of tyranny under the guise of technical expertise. Let us grant for now that Euclid’s axiom should be understood differently—suppose he had said this: if, with the eye positioned at point A, point C is covered, then A is not seen. In that case, the axiom is indeed true, but the conclusion does not follow from it, except in the case of perpendicular vision <note>vision looking straight down a line</note>. However, an argument does not hold when moving from straight vision to oblique <note>angled</note> vision.

Alhazen <note>The 11th-century Arabic scholar Ibn al-Haytham, the "father of modern optics"</note> and Vitellio <note>A 13th-century Polish friar and physicist whose work "Perspectiva" was the standard textbook on optics</note> seem to have sensed this. For while they diligently reported what they had found in Euclid, they omitted this particular point as absurd. However, they say something similar regarding refractions <note>the bending of light as it passes through different materials like water or glass</note>.

Vitellio strives to demonstrate the same thing in Book 5, proposition 36; but the "barbarity" of his age <note>Kepler’s dismissive term for the Middle Ages</note> and his familiarity with the Arabs hindered this most diligent author, preventing him from being understood today; indeed, the obscurity of the matter even brought hallucinations <note>errors or delusions in reasoning</note> upon him.

First, I say that he does not argue well from the placement of the seen object to the placement of the image—namely, fearing that if the image does not correspond to the object in position, it might cease to be an "image." Yet in this way, he would easily overturn the whole of <term>Catoptrics</term> <note>The mathematical study of mirrors and reflected light</note>. For many things of this kind appear differently in the image than they do in the physical object.

Next, I truly do not understand the postulate <note>a claim assumed to be true</note> which he repeats from the beginning of the book, except for how much light Alhazen the Arab provides here in Book 5, numbers 9 and 10, from which Vitellio transferred his own work.

Alhazen initially proves at length through experience that the location of the image is always on the perpendicular line drawn from the object to the surface of the mirror. Then, in numbers 9 and 10, he strives to provide the causes for this. For the rest, I do not understand anything better here either, except for this last sentence: *The state of natural things,* he says, *respects the positions of their principles, and the principles of natural things are hidden.* With these words he says two things: first, he repeats that very thing which was proposed...

-># APPENDIX TO WITELO. 59<-

"If," he says, "a point on the surface of a transparent medium <term>diaphanum; any substance like water or glass that allows light to pass through</term>, upon which a perpendicular line from the object being viewed falls, happens to be hidden by the placement of an opaque body between the eye and that point, then that object will not be seen." This is false, I say. For as long as there remains a free point from which a ray from the viewed object can be refracted toward the eye, the image of the object radiating from the depths will certainly be seen. And indeed, a first and more evident image of the opaque body will occur—which, as we have already said, is partly submerged in the water and placed in between—formed by a reflection <note>original: "ex repercussu," referring to the light bouncing back</note> (a thing which perhaps deceived Witelo). But a second and less evident image of the object radiating from the depths, formed by refraction, will appear in the same location, confused with the previous image of the opaque body, or perhaps a little beyond it.

From this passage, that point which we just mentioned Alhazen <note>Ibn al-Haytham (c. 965–1040), the medieval Arabic scholar whose "Book of Optics" was the standard text for centuries</note> used regarding the consideration of plane mirrors is also refuted: that the location of the image follows from the size of the image. A great objection is therefore raised by the business of refractions. In convex mirrors, the image appears both smaller and closer; in plane mirrors, it is equal in both size and distance to the object itself; in concave mirrors, it is both larger and more distant. Thus, here, distance generally follows size. But in refractions, where the image is equal to or larger than its object, it appears closer; when the size of the image is diminished, the image itself moves further away, as can be seen in spectacles <term>perspicillis; early lenses or eyeglasses</term> that diminish the appearance of things if you look through them from a distance.

## 2 TRUE DEMONSTRATION.

Therefore, so that I may reveal the true cause of the location of images—the ignorance of which is a **foul stain** on this most beautiful science—I would wish the principal nerve of the demonstration to be placed before your eyes from the beginning. This is that in plane mirrors, the angles by which things are seen are not changed by reflection; but in convex and concave mirrors, and in denser media, they are changed entirely. For a convex surface reflects the rays that it receives (which were coming together at a wide angle) into a narrower angle; a concave surface reflects those rays hastening toward a meeting with a slight inclination into a shorter pyramid <term>pyramida; the "cone of vision" or the triangle formed by the light rays entering the pupil</term>. A denser medium, once refraction has occurred, changes almost nothing in width for those rays about to meet, yet it makes them meet slightly more acutely; but in height, it acts in a plainly contrary way, forcing them into a large angu- <note>The text cuts off mid-word "angulum" (angle) at the bottom of the page.</note>

   First, from Catoptrics <term>Catoptrics: The branch of optics dealing with reflected light, such as from mirrors.</term>, which we are now entering, I place a definition of the **Image** in the entrance-hall. ### PROPOSITION IV.

It is also immediately evident that *it is necessary for vision to fall into error when determining the region of the world or the position of an object, whenever the forms <note>original: "species"; in Kepler's time, these were the "likenesses" or "images" emitted by objects that allow them to be seen</note> or rays originating from objects, having fallen upon a polished surface, are reflected back to the sight in the opposite direction.* For since in the diagram above, the eye at B is turned toward the direction BD, and cannot perceive that the reflection of the ray ADB occurred at D (according to Proposition 2 of this chapter), it therefore imagines the position of the object at A to be in the direction BD—specifically at E. Thus, the image is separated from its actual object because of its location. The same judgment applies to refraction; for although the directions are not swapped for their opposites here, they still differ perceptibly.

### PROPOSITION V.

Again, since vision is a passion <note>original: "passio"; here meaning a passive reception or an effect produced in the eye by an external agent</note>, and a passion occurs between opposites that belong to the same genus, it follows that *whatever qualities of visible things are shared by the eye by virtue of belonging to the same genus, all of these are to some extent perceived by the eye, with the aid of the visual faculties and through the mediation of that quality.*

### PROPOSITION VI.

First, *the eye consists of transparent humors <note>the fluids within the eye, such as the vitreous or aqueous humor</note>; in this respect, therefore, it is capable of receiving light and colors.* See page 59 of Book III of Vitello <note>Vitello, or Witelo, was a 13th-century Polish friar and physicist whose work on optics Kepler is "supplementing" here</note>.

### PROPOSITION VII.

Next, its shape is round, and this varies across the different tunics <note>the membranes or layers of the eye</note> and humors, both inside and out. Indeed, this visible world is itself concave and round, and whatever we behold of the hemisphere (or even more) in a single glance is a part of this roundness. It is therefore consistent that *the proportion of individual objects to the entire hemisphere is estimated by sight through the proportion of the form that has entered the hemisphere of the eye.* And this is what is commonly called the visual angle, or the vertex <term>the point or tip</term> of the visual pyramid within the eye, the base of which is in the object itself. For in any single glance, the eye becomes the center of the visible hemisphere. Relying, therefore, on this surface of its own instrument (whether it be internal or external will be discussed below in the consideration of the eye), sight measures the angles of vision. For although all solid angles <note>three-dimensional angles, like the point of a cone</note> exist at a point—which is the center of either the eye or one of its specific tunics—they cannot be distinguished at a single point. Therefore, a surface is required by which the solid angle may be measured, as is evident from geometry.

Therefore the round shape of the eye itself is sufficient for us to know, in a general sense <note>original: "crassiori minerua" – a Latin idiom meaning "with a rougher wisdom" or "plainly/without refinement"</note>, that *the eye possesses within itself a sense of the angles formed there.*

          ## PROPOSITION VIII.
  *Thirdly, since nature has given each living creature two eyes separated by a certain distance, the sense of sight uses this aid most correctly to judge the distances of visible things—provided that the distance has a sensible proportion to the distance between the eyes. For if the distance is immensely greater, it is perceived no differently than any other distance that is infinitely larger. Indeed, this is purely a matter of the geometry of triangles, as will be discussed more fully below regarding parallaxes <term>parallaxes|The apparent displacement of an object when viewed from two different points, used by astronomers to calculate distance</term>.*
  *For when two angles of a triangle are given, along with the side between them, the remaining sides are determined.* In vision, the "common sense" <note>In historical psychology, the "common sense" was the faculty that integrated information from the different senses into a single perception</note> knows the distance of its own eyes from habituation; it notes the angles relative to that distance from the sensation of the "contortion" <note>original: "contortio" – Kepler refers to the muscular effort of turning the eyes inward to focus on a near object, a process we now call convergence</note> of the eyes. Indeed, when a thing is so far away that the distance between the two eyes disappears by comparison, the axes of the eyes are directed almost in parallel. However, the closer an object is, the more the eyes will be turned inward.
  Therefore, although in Catoptrics <term>Catoptrics|The branch of optics dealing with the reflection of light, such as in mirrors</term> we do not only determine the location of an image when using two eyes, but also when we use only one: nevertheless, this faculty of distinguishing distances first arose from this partnership between the two eyes, and was afterwards derived into individual eyes through other sensations of the eye.
  For just as I said before that the *proportion of a thing to the hemisphere* <note>meaning the proportion of an object relative to the entire visible field of view</note> is perceived by the eye (by a rougher and more common imagination, which I will explain below in Chapter 5) through a solid pyramid, whose vertex is at the point of the eye and whose base is at the thing seen: so, when we estimate the *distance of a thing*, an isosceles triangle is formed for the most part, whose point or vertex is, conversely, at some point of the thing seen, and whose base is the distance between the eyes. For proportion pertains to all dimensions of the surface seen, but distance is considered only in a straight line; hence there a solid pyramid is required, and here a plane triangle.

Indeed, experience confirms that an image remains on the <term>perpendicular</term><note>original: "perpendiculari"; in 17th-century optics, this refers to the cathetus or the line drawn from an object point directly to the surface of a mirror or lens.</note>, even when we use only one eye; thus, it is necessary that the distances of points are grasped even by a single eye. ### PROPOSITION IX.

*Indeed, that <term>measuring triangle of distance</term><note>Kepler’s "triangulum distantiae mensorium" is the geometric basis for depth perception, usually formed by the two eyes and the object. Here, he proposes a miniature version within a single eye.</note> can be considered even in a single eye, such that the vertex is at the point of the object seen, and the base is the width of the pupil, specifically that diameter of the pupil which coincides with the line connecting the points of both pupils. Thus, a single eye may have learned the business of establishing this triangle through habituation from the pair of eyes. This occurs in such a proportion that if, due to the distance between the two eyes, the vision can discern the distance of objects a hundred paces away, it may aspire to judge distances of ten paces or less through the width of the pupil. There are also other reasons why a single eye measures distances through that diameter of width rather than through the diameter of height. For although the eye is circular everywhere on the inside, on the outside, the <term>valves of the eyelids</term><note>The eyelids.</note> are drawn apart into a line matching the distance between the two eyes, parallel to the horizon. For nature willed both the distance of the eyes themselves and also this opening of the eyelids to be equidistant to the horizon; it is not the case that one eye is higher than the other, or one corner of the eyelids higher than the other (at least in animals of the most perfect sight). This is because the plane of the horizon—meeting the eyes with its own color—contributes greatly to the imagination of the measuring triangle (that is, of the plane), provided that one eye is parallel to the other at the base. For this reason, when we look at things with the head turned upside down or tilted, we use a more confused faculty of discernment.*

## PROPOSITION XII.

But we shall direct more arguments gathered from the air toward the light. Although the eye—also using the argument of a wider illuminated surface at depth—can determine the thinning of light that has occurred within the eye: because above in Proposition 7 of this chapter, we attributed to the eye a sense of the quantity of the surface touched by the light.***

### PROPOSITION XIV.

With these things thus proven through the four preceding points, I will now show by geometric demonstration (what was only established as probable in Proposition 9) how, by a single eye, with the help of the higher faculties, and through the <term>affections</term><note>In this context, "affections" means the physical changes or impacts light has on the eye's fluids.</note> of the eye's humors caused by the density of light as if by an instrument, ***the distances of the points of the seen object (up to where the diameter of the eye is perceptible) are perceived and compared.*** For first, every point radiates in a sphere, according to Proposition 3 of the first chapter: therefore it also radiates into the width of the eye, which width—whether of the whole eye or the opening of the <term>uvea</term><note>The "foramen vueae" refers here to the pupil.</note>—is not imperceptible by our hypothesis.

...thesis. Next, sight perceives both the density and thinness of the **forms** <note>original: "specierum"; Kepler uses this term to describe the visual information or "images" emitted by an object</note> or light arriving from a point through rays, according to Chapter 12 of this book, and the amount of thinning of those same rays within the depth of the eye, according to Chapter 13. By habit, the eye maintains a sense of the depth of its own **humors** <note>The fluids within the eye, such as the vitreous or aqueous humor</note>. Let $\alpha \beta$ be the diameter of the pupil, and $\gamma \delta$ be parallel to it, separated by as much distance as the depth of the eye allows. Therefore, from the edges $\alpha \beta$, let rays $\alpha \gamma, \beta \delta$ be spread at a smaller inclination, and $\alpha \epsilon, \beta \zeta$ at a larger one. Thus, $\gamma \alpha$ and $\delta \beta$ will meet at a more remote source $\theta$, while $\epsilon \alpha$ and $\zeta \beta$ will meet at a nearer source $\eta$. Since the interior angles $\alpha \gamma \delta$ and $\beta \delta \gamma$ are greater than the exterior angles $\alpha \epsilon \zeta$ and $\beta \zeta \epsilon$, when subtracted from two right angles (according to Proposition 32 of the first book <note>referring to Euclid’s Elements</note>), they will leave a smaller angle at $\gamma \theta \delta$ and a larger one at $\epsilon \eta \zeta$. Wherefore, by Proposition 21 of the first book, $\gamma \alpha$ and $\delta \beta$ will meet at the more remote point $\theta$, and $\alpha \theta$ (or $\beta \theta$) will be greater than $\alpha \eta$ (or $\beta \eta$). Since the eye therefore maintains the diameter $\alpha \beta$ and the depth $\alpha \gamma$, and it is sufficient to observe the proportion of $\delta \gamma$ to $\zeta \epsilon$, and of both to $\alpha \beta$—whether from the thinning of the light or from the small portions of the internal surface that are illuminated—it will therefore also observe $\alpha \eta$ and $\alpha \theta$. It does this not by actual calculation, of course, but by comparing the distances of things through this habit, as it were, to the powers of its own body and the reach of its hands and strides.

->**DEFINITION II.**<-

Opticians speak of a **surface of reflection or refraction**, which is defined by three points (for a unique plane is always established by three points not positioned on the same straight line): the center of vision, the point of the object being seen, and the point of reflection (or refraction). In Diagram No. 1 above, these are points D, A, and B.

->**PROPOSITION XVI.**<-

**They demonstrate that a surface of this kind must necessarily be erected perpendicularly over the reflecting or refracting surface.** <note>original: "Huiuſmodi ſuperficiem demonſtrant neceſſariò perpendiculariter erigi ſuper ſuperficiem repercutientem ſeu refringentem."</note> Witelo <note>A 13th-century Polish natural philosopher whose work "Perspectiva" was the standard textbook on optics before Kepler.</note> Book 5, p. 25; Alhazen <note>The Latinized name of Ibn al-Haytham (c. 965–1040), the medieval Arab "father of optics."</note> Book 4, n. 14. The former executes the demonstration through proposition 20, the latter through number 10 of their respective works: namely, that the angles of incidence and reflection are equal. From this, they eventually derive the cause: that nature acts through the shortest lines, an idea they drew from Euclid and Ptolemy.

Yet these effects are not the work of a <term>form: In the philosophy of Kepler's time, "form" referred to the guiding soul or purposeful design of a thing.</term> employing a plan or looking toward an end-goal, but of **matter** bound by its own geometric necessities. Furthermore, we see the images of stars in lakes according to these same laws of reflection, where any comparison of the lengths of lines <note>The argument that light "chooses" the shortest path.</note> completely vanishes. Finally, if this were a genuine demonstration, it would also apply to the business of refraction. However, Witelo (Book 10, p. 1. 2.) and Alhazen (Book 7, n. 9.) change their method of demonstration here; for it is not so easy to argue from the "shortest lines" in the case of refraction.

For us, it is enough to establish that reflection occurs toward the opposite side, and refraction occurs toward the **perpendicular** line which is drawn from the radiating point to the refracting surface. We deduced the former from Proposition 19 of Chapter 1, and the latter from Proposition 20 of the first chapter. We derived both from their own proper causes, from which the equality of the angles of incidence and reflection also followed at the same time. From here, we will now apply the argument in a general sense that Witelo uses specifically for refractions, as far as can be gathered from that obscurity.
