### SUPPLEMENTS TO VITELLO. [PAGE] 69

<note>Johannes Kepler’s *Ad Vitellionem Paralipomena* (1604) is a foundational text in modern optics. Here, he is refining the theories of the 13th-century scholar Witelo.</note>

...[proceed] with the same inclination or angle, even those rays which first glide from a radiant point to the points of reflection or refraction corresponding to the eye, according to propositions 2 and 7 of this third chapter. The genuine location of an **image** is that point in which the <term>visual rays</term><note>Kepler defines the "visual ray" not as light coming *from* the eye, but as the straight line the mind imagines extending from the eye through the point where light was bent or reflected.</note> projected from both eyes meet through their respective points of refraction or reflection, according to proposition 8 of this third chapter. 

However, the visual ray of each eye (a bright line led out from the eye through the point of reflection or refraction, continued through the imagination) exists in the same plane as the "surface of refraction" or reflection, according to definition 2. And for each eye, there is its own surface of reflection or refraction. Therefore, where the visual rays of both eyes meet, there also meet the surfaces of refraction or reflection passing through each respective eye. 

Therefore, since the location of the image is at the meeting point of the visual rays (by the first definition), it will also be at the meeting point of the surfaces of refraction or reflection for both eyes. Indeed, those surfaces meet at the visible point, according to definition 2. And since both of these surfaces of refraction or reflection are perpendicular to the refracting or reflecting surface (by proposition 10 of this third chapter) and they cut one another, their common section will first of all be a straight line (according to the 3rd proposition of the 11th book <note>This refers to Euclid’s *Elements*, the standard geometry textbook of the era.</note>); for which reason both the thing seen and all its images will be on the same straight line, since they all exist in that common section. 

Furthermore, according to the 19th proposition of the 11th book [of Euclid], this common section will be perpendicular to that same refracting or reflecting surface. *For which reason, again, all images of a thing seen will be on the perpendicular line drawn from the object to the surface—whether it be refracting or reflecting. This holds true insofar as the distance between the points of the thing seen is perceived in the said manner, whether by two eyes or by the width of the diameter of a single eye.* 

And since (specifically) a surface that cuts a sphere perpendicularly passes through its center, it follows that the common section of two such surfaces—that is, the line of the images and the visible object—will also pass through the center.

It is not, therefore, some hidden nature of light, nor the ingenuity of "Universal Nature," but solely the **width of vision** that acts as the cause for why vision places the image on the perpendicular.

From these points, therefore, it appears that it is not universally true that the location of an image must be on the perpendicular, unless this limitation is added: that the sight must be positioned relative to the mirror in the specific way that nature demonstrates.

In concave mirrors, the same principle is demonstrated in reverse. For the judgment of opposite things is the same, <note>original: "ceteris paribus"</note> all other things being equal.

I should also add that whatever can be noticed of this effect with only a single eye is either imperceptible—since the arc of the circle of reflections, which changes the visual angle, is always smaller than the <term>pupil<note>original: "pupilla"</note></term> of the eye itself, and therefore the difference between the two reflections is extremely slight—or, if both eyes are brought so close to the mirror and inclined so much that a large arc lies between the points of reflection, the vision is hindered (as previously stated) and even strained. Let the straight line A B cut the circle E D A B at points A and B. Connect these points with D and E, which are any points on the circumference located on one side. Thus, by Proposition 31 of the third book <note>Reference to Euclid’s *Elements*, Book III, Proposition 31, concerning angles in a segment of a circle.</note>, the angles A D B and A E B will be equal; likewise, the vertical angles D H A and E H B are equal. [A geometric diagram showing a circular arc and several intersecting lines. Points are labeled with lowercase letters: f, k, i, g, b, a, d, e.] 

Since the points on the circumference moving toward A are always closer to the perpendicular line drawn from A over A B (provided they are between A and the point on the circumference where the perpendicular to A B touches the circle), point D will always be closer than E. Therefore, assuming that the refractions at A and B are equal, the image in the denser medium approaches the eye from the perpendicular line drawn from the visible point E to the surface B A; this occurs near the horizon, when the angle F A B is small.

Furthermore, because the obliquity of the incidence <term>obliquity of incidence: the angle at which a ray of light hits a surface; the more "tilted" the ray, the greater the refraction</term> of E A upon A B is the cause of refraction (according to Proposition 20 of the first chapter), as the cause increases, the effect will increase, and vice versa. For this reason, the refraction at A will be smaller, because E A deviates less from the perpendicular; at B, the refraction will be greater, because E B is more inclined. Therefore, since K A F is smaller than I B G, D A H is also smaller than H B E. Consequently, A D H is greater than H E B. Thus, A D H and the location of the image D pull back within the circumference and approach A more than point D on the circumference does, by Proposition 21 of Euclid’s first book. Previously, however, D itself approached the perpendicular from A more than the visible point E did with its own perpendicular.

But consider the ratio of the curvature which the cross-section has at the point of reflection $\beta$ (for these types of mixed lines have various ratios). Let the quantity be $\varkappa \beta$, and let a line $\beta \varkappa$ be drawn from $\beta$ perpendicular to $\epsilon \delta$. The location of the image will be where the continuation of $\zeta \beta$ intersects $\varkappa \mu$, namely at $\mu$. Here you can easily see that even if the point of reflection $\beta$ remains the same—and thus also the curvature ratio $\varkappa \beta$ and the location of the eye at $\zeta$—if the visible object $\eta$ moves further away along the line $\beta \eta$, the perpendicular from $\eta$ will always strike a point further from $\gamma$. Consequently, the location of the image will always move further from $\varkappa$ toward the outside. Thus, this difference eventually stretches out toward infinity. It is of great importance to the principles of <term>catoptrics</term> <note>The branch of optics dealing with reflection and mirrors.</note> not to be held in doubt here. 

But enough regarding the location of the image; this consideration was clearly necessary for what follows. Forgive me, Reader, if in some places I have been more concerned with my *Supplements to Witelo* <note>Kepler is referring to his book title, *Ad Vitellionem Paralipomena*, where he "supplements" the work of the 13th-century optical scientist Witelo (Vitello).</note> than with astronomy itself. I know that a natural method would require treating the nature of light and its properties—reflection and refraction—at the beginning; second, the Eye, which operates by refraction; and finally, Catoptrics or the Image, which is the "offspring" of our visual faculties. Had I followed this order, I could have bypassed many crude points and "previewed" knowledge in this chapter; the context of the propositions themselves would have stood with tighter bonds and a more geometric form. 

But to ensure the Reader’s trust, it seemed better to me to follow the actual sequence of my own discoveries. At the same time, I chose to bring these catoptric "supplements" under the yoke <note>A Roman metaphor for subjugation; Kepler is making the study of mirrors serve the higher purpose of explaining refraction.</note> of explaining refractions, and thus pull them, to some extent, into astronomical service. This was to prevent them from being placed on a "royal folio" <note>original: "folium regium"; a term for a large, high-quality sheet of paper, implying a separate grand publication.</note> contrary to the purpose of this book, which might make them seem to encompass the entire goal of the work. This is exactly what would have happened had I followed the "natural method."

...not useless to see if anything certain lies beneath this matter, so that we might dare to pronounce with more confidence whether the **refractions** are the same in all places. ### I. On the skirmish between Tycho and Rothmann concerning the business of Refractions.

Long ago, the Arab Alhazen <note>original: "Alhazen Arabs"; referring to Ibn al-Haytham (c. 965–1040), a foundational figure in optics.</note> and, following him, Witelo <note>original: "Vitellio"; Erazmus Ciołek Witelo (c. 1230–1300), a Polish natural philosopher whose work Kepler is here "supplementing."</note> began to explain the subject of **refractions** <term>Refraction: the bending of light as it passes from one medium (like air) into another (like water or glass).</term> more diligently than the ancients were accustomed to do. And since all our knowledge first proceeds from experience, they first explored with instruments the sizes of those angles by which rays are refracted when entering from air into water; then also those from air into glass, and from water into glass. And since the substance of the heavens was believed, according to the opinion of the ancients, to be almost glass-like—that is, crystalline—while the air was thought to be related to water, these authors were carried away by their boldness to inquire into the secrets of the heavens with the help of refractions. Experience favored their efforts; some principle of refraction was also detected even in the stars, and of such a nature that, through those experiments already proven in water and glass, the **ether** <term>Ether: the substance once believed to fill the space of the universe above the Earth's atmosphere.</term> seemed to be not denser than air, but much thinner than it. 

This care was neglected for a long time, until after several centuries it struck Tycho Brahe <note>The famous Danish nobleman and astronomer (1546–1601) known for his incredibly precise celestial observations.</note>, who set out to measure the angles of refraction in the air with very subtle instruments—a task which Witelo had neglected. Tycho and Rothmann <note>Christoph Rothmann (died c. 1600), the court mathematician to the Landgrave of Hesse and a frequent correspondent of Tycho.</note>, the mathematician to the Landgrave of Hesse, competed over this and many other discoveries. The controversy regarding refractions is extensive in Volume 1 of the *Astronomical Epistles*, which Tycho published in the year [15]97; let anyone who wishes seek it there. For the present, I will write down the summary: Tycho first warned that one must be careful of refractions when taking the altitudes of the Sun. He attributed the cause in passing, as he had read in Witelo, to the differences between the air and the ether. Rothmann, seizing the opportunity, denied for that very reason that there was any difference between the air and the ether, because no refraction occurs which could indeed be attributed to this cause. For the spheres are joined to the circle <margin>since indeed</margin>

The logic of twilights <note>The period of partial light after sunset or before sunrise</note> aided this investigation, as they accompany the sun's descent to a depth of 18 and 24 degrees. He concluded, then, that the rays of the stars are broken <note>original: *infringi*; here meaning refracted or bent</note> in that matter which causes twilights, which Physicists demonstrate by geometric art does not exceed a height of twelve German miles <note>A "German mile" at this time was roughly 7.5 kilometers, making this atmospheric height about 90km</note>.

Tycho did not fail to defend his own case; first, he cautioned that he also saw a dual cause for refractions: the first from the difference between the media of the denser air and the thinner <term>ether</term> <note>The substance once believed to fill the upper regions of space beyond the atmosphere</note>; the second, which so greatly accelerates refractions near the horizon, resides surely in the vapors near the horizon. Nor is it enough to dismiss the differences between air and ether by demonstrating that no refractions of rays happen near the <term>zenith</term> <note>original: *verticem*; the point directly overhead</note> that can be perceived by the senses; for there could be some refractions, but they are imperceptible, and would even be very small at the horizon itself unless aided by another cause. 

They increase suddenly, however, when the stars approach the horizon because of the vapors, which hold the primary role in this cause. Indeed, from what Rothmann himself had pointed out, it appears that the path for rays of setting stars through air 12 miles high is six times longer than for stars at an altitude of 30 degrees. Thus, he conceded that the depth and the doubling <note>original: *conduplicationem*</note> of the vapors, lying at an angle to the stars, combine to measure the angles of refraction. He repeats this in his *Progymnasmata* <note>Tycho Brahe's *Astronomiae Instauratae Progymnasmata*, a foundational work of early modern astronomy</note> on pages 92 and 95, though adding a correction; there he also believes that due to the extreme distance of the heavens, tiny refractions are hidden from view—though this is somewhat irrelevant to the matter of refraction itself.

### PROPOSITION II.
***Vision looks upon very near things with greater difficulty than upon more distant things.*** For it has been said that in the vision of near objects, the eyes must be strained <note>original: *contorquendos*, literally "twisted" or "wrenched," referring to the muscular effort required for the eyes to converge on a close point</note>. This straining is contrary to nature, which granted the eyes a parallel position. Therefore, fatigue follows, and from a lesser strain comes lesser fatigue. From this, those deep in thought <margin>The gestures of those deep in thought.</margin> are easily recognized by everyone; yet no one understands the sign of it. It is this: that they relax the muscles of the eyes, so that they are less strained toward nearby things. Then, therefore, they return to a parallel position. <note>Kepler is describing what we now call the "thousand-yard stare," where the eyes cease to focus on nearby objects and drift toward a parallel, distant focus as the mind withdraws from its surroundings.</note>

### PROPOSITION III.
***Vision is seized by obvious things, but is poorly attracted by faint and vanishing things.*** What experience testifies, the nature of vision proves. For vision was given for this reason: that it might be moved by light; therefore, it will be moved strongly by a strong light. But to be moved by light is to see. Wherefore one who had previously looked at a weak light will, when a stronger light rises from the same region, pursue the latter and lose the former. Or, according to the 28th [proposition] of the first chapter: when strong things illuminate the eye excessively, a weaker illumination will be hidden beneath them. Indeed, vision follows the logic of illumination <note>original: *colluſtrationis rationem*, meaning the way light interacts with and fills a space</note>.

Erazmus Ciołek Witelo (c. 1230–1280/1314) was a medieval natural philosopher whose work on optics was the standard text Kepler was updating here.</note>, the angles of refraction are equal, whether the light travels from water into air, or from air into water, along the same line.

Finally, because refractions are not proportional to the angles of incidence <term>incidence</term> <note>The angle at which a ray of light hits a surface.</note>, but the angles of refraction are much larger in those rays that are more inclined than the degree of incidence warrants: Therefore, a new cause is again added, which gathers the radiations more distant from the perpendicular closer to the sphere than before, while making the radiations closer to the axis meet the axis further from the sphere than before.

### PROPOSITION XI
***It is impossible for the same refracted ray, in a medium that is not extremely dense, to result from several simultaneous radiations falling from a thinner medium onto the same point of a denser surface.*** <note>original: "Impoſſibile eſt eundem refractum in medio non denſiſſimo à pluribus unà radiationibus ex medio rariore in idem punctum ſuperficiei denſioris concidentibus deſcendere." Kepler is arguing that every unique angle of incidence produces a unique angle of refraction; two different incoming rays cannot merge into one path inside the water.</note>

For by Proposition 8 of the fourth chapter <note>Kepler refers to his earlier discussion on the mathematical rules of refraction</note>, the refracted angles are established for all inclinations in this way: first, a certain portion of the angle of refraction increases along with the inclinations; then, once this portion is subtracted from the inclination, the <term>secant</term> <note>a trigonometric function representing the ratio of the hypotenuse to the adjacent side of a right triangle</note> of the remainder repeatedly multiplies that portion. Since, therefore, the basic elements differ in quantity across various inclinations, it is necessary that the composites—that is, the angles of refraction—also differ. Therefore, from different inclinations (which is to say, from different radiations hitting the same point of a denser surface), the refracted rays are different, and in no way are they the same.

### PROPOSITION XII
***Rays coming from different points to the same point on a denser surface intersect one another at that point, and the refracted ray of the higher radiation becomes the lower one.*** <note>original: "Radii à diuerſis ad idem denſioris ſuperficiei punctum venientes, ſecant ſeſe in illo, & ſuperioris radiationis refractus fit inferior."</note>

If this were not so: then let **OH** be a radiation higher than **IH**, and let its refracted ray be **HP**, which cannot coincide with **HG** according to the preceding proposition. Therefore, let **HP** also be higher than **HG**. In this scenario, **IH** is refracted into **HG**, and **OH** into **HP**. Let the perpendicular also be extended to some point **Q**. For it is certain that **QH**, while entering the water, is not refracted but continues toward **HA**. Therefore, while **QH**, having moved through an inclination, arrives at **OH**, the ray which arrives at **HA** under the water [now] arrives at **HP**. Thus, while the former ray moves somewhere between **Q** and **O**, the latter will move between **A** and **P**, and will eventually coincide with **HG**. But previously, **HG** was the refracted ray of **IH**, which was lower than **OH**; now it would be the refracted ray of something higher than **OH**, which is impossible by the preceding proposition. Therefore, **OH** is not refracted into **HP** above **HG**, but into some path below **HG**, and the intersection occurs at point **H**.

**Alternatively.** If **OH** does not descend below **IHG** after the intersection is made at **H**: then all rays higher than **IH** will have refracted rays that are also higher. Because the logic is the same for all—since it has been proven that refractions increase with inclinations—the higher each ray is, the higher its refracted ray will be. Let **GH** be continued for some distance to **R**...

ADDITIONS TO VITELLO, PAGE 195

...through what was demonstrated above. The reason why the image is not found at the boundary $\omega$ of the nearest intersection <note>Kepler is referring to a diagram in the original text where $\omega$ and $\alpha$ represent points where light rays first cross.</note> is because the nearest intersection $\alpha$ is produced by the rays $\alpha$, $\nu$, $\sigma$, $\omega$ falling more weakly from the sides, due to the great refraction. In fact, other rays from that same glowing point—which have passed through the sphere but not yet intersected—occupy the place of section $\alpha$ on the paper. These rays are gathered and bright, and thus they obscure those already gathered at section $\alpha$. Furthermore, the cones of light coming from other points of the glowing object are still wider here, such as $\iota$ and $\kappa$ in this case, and they occupy one another's space, producing confusion <note>Kepler uses "confusion" to mean what we would call a "blurred" or "unfocused" image.</note>.

On the other hand, at the final intersection $\psi$, many rays from the same glowing point—those standing most closely around the strongest perpendicular ray $\psi$ $\omega$—come together at a single point according to the 15th preceding proposition. Because these cones have been thinned into sharp points, they occupy no territory belonging to another; thus, individual points are painted separately and distinctly. Only a few rays from other points of the visible object fall there, but they have already intersected and are weaker (for instance, if another cone ended at $\upsilon$, the vertex of the new cone and the intersected part $\eta$ $\upsilon$ of the old cone would be in the same place). If there is any confusion in this "painting," these rays are what produce it.

The image is indeed inverted, not because of the boundaries of intersections explained so far (which occur before the glass), but because every point of the visible object, radiating perpendicularly into the sphere, paints itself with the strongest cone behind the glass. From this it follows that the axes of the cones $\psi$ $\omega$ intersect each other in the center of the sphere, having suffered no refraction. This is the genuine cause of the inversion of the "painting" <note>original: "picturae"; Kepler refers to the projected image as a "painting" or "depiction" of the object.</note> which is created by a dense sphere when it is not covered by some solid object with a hole left open <note>Kepler is distinguishing a lens-formed image from a pinhole camera (camera obscura) image.</note>.

It is evident through the 2nd corollary of the 16th preceding proposition, and through the 20th proposition. <margin>Suitable for mechanics and optical craftsmen.</margin> This is something a certain engineer might note, as with many other things in this book. You can even prove this during the day using a lighted candle, which will appear to burn upon the paper if it is positioned correctly. What I said above regarding Porta <note>Giambattista della Porta (1535–1615), an Italian scholar famous for his work on the camera obscura.</note> is true in this matter of the "painting"—though not in the matter of the "Image" <note>Kepler distinguishes between a "pictura" (a real image projected on a surface) and an "imago" (an optical illusion or virtual image seen in the air or a mirror).</note>, nor in the air, but upon a wall.

### PROPOSITION 23.

***When a board with a small open window is placed before a globe, positioned between the limits of parallel sections, and the window is narrower than the globe: a picture of the greater part of a hemisphere is projected onto a paper placed behind the globe at the limit of the final intersection of the rays from a luminous point. The picture is inverted, but it is very pure and distinct in the center.***

<margin>Therefore, let us seek some light from "Metholus." <note>Kepler likely refers to Francesco Maurolico (1494–1575), a mathematician whose work on the optics of the sphere preceded Kepler's. The name "Metholus" is a common contemporary corruption of "Maurolycus."</note> One form of the globe's refractions is that by which the sight is deceived into imagining phantoms <note>original: *simulachra*</note> that do not truly exist (we call these "images"), which were discussed in the first 7 propositions and in propositions 17 and 18. Another form of refractions is that by which real pictures of things are formed; and these are indeed of two kinds: some are painted by a naked globe, discussed in propositions 19, 20, 21, and 22; and some by a globe covered except for a small window <note>an aperture or "pinhole"</note>, discussed in proposition 23. For the apparatus of these refractions is different. Those refractions from Proposition 8 to 16 are common to all Refractions of the globe.</margin>

So great is the variety of these matters, and something new appears so often, that unless one is most attentive, they may easily be confused. Indeed, I myself was stuck for a very long time, as I tried to persuade myself that the explanation for these different phenomena was the same.

Let there be a globe of water **BC** with center **A**. Let an opaque board **DG** be placed before it, with an opening **EF** that is narrower than the globe. Let the visible object be **HI**. Let the paper be at **K**, where the final intersection of the radiations from **H** occurs. 

If the board were absent, then according to the preceding Proposition 20, point **I** would paint itself at the final intersection of its radiations at **L**, and point **H** at point **K**. However, the lateral rays of the intersected cones would project each into the other’s place of intersection <note>In a lens without a screen, rays from different points overlap, causing a blurry image unless the screen is perfectly placed.</note>. Now, with the board in place, no more rays from **H** flow into the sphere than what can pass through the opening **EF**, and nearly all of these converge at **K**. This cone of light is reduced by a sort of "pruning" <note>original: *putatio*</note>, so that it cannot throw any intersected rays toward **L**, and thus cannot create confusion there. 

Conversely, the cone of radiations from **I**, which should end at **L**, is clearly "cut off" <note>original: *castratus*. Kepler uses this strong term to describe the blocking of the primary central rays of the light cone.</note> by the obstruction of the board **DE**. It is deprived of its most noble part—namely, the radiation passing through the center **A** and its clearest point **L**. It is so far from scattering anything toward **K** that it could not cause any confusion there. Thus, nothing remains for the radiations from **I** except what can enter through the opening **EF**. 

Whatever rays those are, they intersect each other successively through the width **MN** (according to the preceding Proposition 19), and once the intersection is made, the light passes through **AL** and falls upon the paper placed at **K**, closer than **L**. This does not happen at a single point, but scatteringly, because the intersection has already occurred in the space **MN**. Therefore, the picture is dark and blurred at the sides. If you move the paper closer to the side, the edges will be painted more correctly, but never perfectly, because the intersections are scattered not only in depth **MN** (which would matter little) but also in width.

<summary>Kepler explains Proposition 23, demonstrating how a screen with a small aperture (pinhole) placed in front of a water-filled globe creates a clear, inverted image by "pruning" away the peripheral rays that cause optical blur. He distinguishes between optical illusions (images) and real projected pictures.</summary>
<keywords>optics, refraction, water globe, aperture, pinhole camera, light cones, image inversion, Maurolico, Johannes Kepler</keywords>

### PROPOSITION 24.

**A hyperbolic conical surface bounding a denser medium collects rays that were converging toward a single point within that medium into a new single point, closer than the original one.**

Let there be a globe of a denser medium <note>original: "densius medium," meaning a material like glass or water where light travels more slowly than in air</note> centered at **A**, marked **βζ** <note>beta-zeta</note>, in which the rays **βλ, γκ, δι, εθ, ζη** <note>beta-lambda, gamma-kappa, delta-iota, epsilon-theta, zeta-eta</note> converge toward point **π** <note>pi</note>. And let **β α π** <note>beta-alpha-pi</note> be the axis. Therefore, according to the previous propositions, ray **ζη** will be refracted <note>term: refracted <gloss>the bending of light as it passes from one material into another</gloss></note> toward **η ο**, **εθ** toward **θ ξ**, **δι** toward **ι ι**, and **γκ** toward **κ μ**. I desire to collect all these rays into a single point. To do this, I will need a greater refraction at point **κ** so that **κ μ** and **ν** meet the axis **α π** sooner; however, at points **θ** and **η**, I need a smaller refraction so that **η ο** and **θ ξ** meet the axis **α π** further away. In this way, the points **ο, ξ, ν, μ** would become a single point. Furthermore, the refraction will be greater at **κ** if the ray **γ κ** strikes the surface more obliquely <note>at a sharper angle</note>, and it will be smaller at **η** if **ζ η** strikes the surface more directly. But because the paths of the rays **γ κ** and **ζ η** are fixed, the surface **η θ ι κ** must therefore be changed, so that at **η** it is not so sloped toward **ζ η**, and at **κ** it is more sloped toward **γ κ**.

<margin>a</margin> This change is achieved not by using different circles, but by using **conic sections**. For any of those sections can intersect a circle at four points. See Apollonius <note>original: "Apollonii lib. 4. prop. 25." Referring to Apollonius of Perga, the ancient Greek mathematician known as "The Great Geometer" for his work on conic sections.</note>, Book 4, Proposition 25. Thus, it intersects twice in this semicircle, and twice in the other. Therefore, by intersecting at **η** in such a way that it enters the circle there, it will be presented more directly to the ray **ζ η**; by intersecting that same circle again at **κ** as it exits, it will be presented more obliquely to the ray **γ κ**. Furthermore, among the conic sections, only the **hyperbola** <note>term: hyperbola <gloss>a specific type of smooth curve, one of the four conic sections</gloss></note>—or a line very close to it—measures refractions correctly, as was shown in Chapter Four, number 5. Indeed, it was demonstrated there that a surface which forces all parallel radiations to a single point is a conical surface, and none other than a **hyperbolic** one.

### COROLLARY.

Specifically, nature intended to collect all the radiations of any visible thing that have entered the opening of the **uvea** <note>term: uvea <gloss>here referring to the pupil or the iris opening</gloss></note> into a single point on the **retina**, both so that the point of the picture would be that much clearer, and so that the other points of the picture would not be confused—

### PROPOSITION 25.

**How rays converging to the same point are forced into a closer point has already been explained.** We must now take care to teach how this happens: how those rays which are within a denser medium converge more toward the same point, though they originally flowed from that same point. For example, if in the previous figure the rays α β, κ γ, ι δ, θ ε, η ζ coming from the same point π are to be collected into the same point υ. Since, however, as has often been said, there is no difference in refractions whether we say rays are entering or exiting a denser medium, the demonstration will be the same—with this one exception: the surface which is to collect rays that are diverging within the medium into a point outside it must be sharper than the one we investigated in Chapter 4, Number 5. This is because that surface was meant to collect parallel rays (that is, rays neither converging nor diverging). On the contrary, therefore, the surface which is to collect rays that are already converging and "nodding toward each other" <note>Kepler uses "annuentes" (nodding together) to describe the angle of convergence.</note> within a denser medium more quickly into a point outside it, will be blunter than that surface in Chapter 4. Furthermore, these surfaces cannot be distinguished from one another by the senses in such great thinness (especially if they exist around the base or the "keel" of a hyperbola or an ellipse); nor do they produce any sensible difference even if neither of them departs at all from a perfect roundness. If, therefore, an elliptical conoid <note>A three-dimensional shape formed by rotating an ellipse; Kepler is arguing the cornea has this specific mathematical curve.</note> is present, it must be in the cornea; but the surface of the crystalline lens must be perfectly round so that it may directly receive the incoming rays converging to the same point. Indeed, this roundness must be quite "pressed" <note>Meaning a shallow or flat curvature.</note>, as its center will be far behind the eye.

Therefore, the "pencil" is thick, and not clear and...

### PROPOSITION XXVII.
***When a visible object is located beyond the point naturally assigned to any eye, from which all radiations would be collected onto a point of the retina; that object appears blurred.***

This is evident by the opposite reasoning. For, according to the second corollary of the sixteenth proposition previously discussed, the point where radiations from a distant object are collected is not the same as the point for a near object. However, in any given human, there is one and the same perpetual position of the retina relative to the humors <note>The "humors" refer to the fluids within the eye: the aqueous, vitreous, and crystalline humors.</note>. Yet it was not suitable to provide a human with the most distinct vision for the most distant things, for in that way, the things immediately present would have escaped him. Nor should he have seen only the nearest things distinctly, lest distant things be too greatly confused for him. Therefore, a balance <note>Kepler uses "libramento," suggesting a middle ground or equilibrium in the eye's focal range.</note> was necessary. 

As this balance has its own breadth, it varies among individuals. Perhaps the position of the crystalline lens <note>The natural lens of the eye.</note> relative to the retina is the same in everyone, but the density of the humors is not. Therefore, when the point of a visible object is too remote, its radiant cone is terminated <note>reaches its focal point</note> before it reaches the retina, according to the earlier corollary. Having reached that point of intersection, the light begins to spread out again and strikes the retina as a widened shape. 

This is why those who suffer from this defect see double or triple images for a single, small, and distant object. For this reason, ten or more Moons are presented to me <note>Kepler famously suffered from poor eyesight and polyopia, likely due to a combination of myopia and astigmatism.</note> instead of one. Indeed, for confusion to follow this cross-section of the cone of light, a sensitivity of sight must be added, so that the eye is moved strongly by powerful radiations both at the point of the retina where vision is distinct and around it, across the width of the radiant cone (which has arisen from the defect). Because of this, the cones of radiation from celestial bodies are widened for everyone, but not everyone sees them as blurred.

### PROPOSITION XXVIII.
***Those who see distant objects distinctly, but near objects blurred, are helped by convex spectacles. Those who see distant objects blurred, but near objects distinctly, are assisted by concave spectacles.***

How wonderful it is that the use of such a great thing has been so widely spread, and yet the cause of it has remained unknown until now; so much so that I pronounce this haltingly, even though very clear demonstrations have been discovered. Giambattista della Porta <note>original: "Baptista Porta"; an Italian scholar (1535–1615) who wrote extensively on optics but failed to fully explain how lenses corrected vision.</note> alone professed...

...[he] confessed he was unable to provide a logical explanation in the field of optics; a reason which I have sought in vain from booksellers until now. Receive at last, O man most loving of letters, arts, and professors—and even of me among the least of them—and likewise most discerning (let the Austrian Princes and the most noble Provinces praise your other qualities), receive, I say, an answer; if not sufficiently clear and certain, then certainly delayed enough. 

The cause is not located in this: that nearby things are rendered larger by convex <term>spectacles<note>original: "specillis". Kepler uses this term for lenses or eyeglasses.</note></term>, which was indeed the only answer I formerly had to give. Giambattista della Porta <note>An Italian scholar (1535–1615) whose work "Magia Naturalis" discussed optics but failed to explain the geometry of lenses correctly.</note>, following this, says in vain that nearby things are rendered larger by convex lenses, but blurred. Truly, they are larger for everyone, but not blurred for everyone; just as, conversely, concave lenses represent things smaller for everyone, but blurred to those who see distant things correctly, and distinct to those who see them blurred. For if things were seen more distinctly simply because they were larger, then concave lenses should help no one, for they shrink things. You recognize, most Noble man, your own strong objection. 

Others establish the cause of improved vision solely in the plurality of refractions. In vain: for then everyone would be helped equally, and no one would complain about their spectacles as if they were still in the dark. Therefore, we must not look at whole objects, but at the **individual points of objects**, as we have always done until now. 

For those, then, to whom a very distant point of distinct vision has been assigned by nature <note>This describes farsightedness (presbyopia or hyperopia), where the eye cannot focus on close objects.</note>, when they use convex spectacles, they alter the cone of rays from a nearby point so that it seems to arrive from a distance and enter the eye. Thus the cone is corrected so that it terminates exactly at the **retina**; for unless it is corrected by spectacles, what happens is what we said in the preceding Proposition 26: because of the proximity of the radiating point, the cone—which ought to terminate behind the retina—is cut off by the retina; and thus the cones of radiating points, having acquired some width, blur into one another.

Conversely, for those to whom a very short and near point or distance of distinct vision has been naturally assigned <note>This describes nearsightedness (myopia), where the eye cannot focus on distant objects.</note>, when they use concave spectacles, they alter the cone of rays coming from a distant point so that it seems to arise from nearby and enter the eye...

### 4. *Consideration of what Opticians and Anatomists*
### *have said concerning the mode of vision.*

We shall not examine every single detail, but only the most important ones; nor shall we look at the opinions of everyone, lest the reader be confused. Vitellio, <note>Witelo (c. 1230–1280 or 1314), a Polish friar whose work on optics was the standard text for centuries.</note> and following him Jessenius, <note>Johannes Jessenius (1566–1621), a famous physician and anatomist who performed the first public dissection in Prague.</note> having linked the arachnoid membrane <gloss>original: "araneam"</gloss> and the crystalline humor within it to the retiform tunic <term>retiform tunic: the retina, so named because it resembles a net (*rete* in Latin).</term> and the nerve, they attribute the primary power of sensation to this humor. For they claim that sensation or vision occurs when rays from visible things pass through the tunics, and most especially through the fabric of the crystalline humor, and that the "species" <note>In medieval optics, a "species" was a likeness or image emitted by an object that traveled through the air to the eye.</note> is imprinted upon the crystalline humor so much that it sticks to it; they argue that this humor was made somewhat thick for this very purpose. However, so that vision may be distinct, they claim the rays must be perpendicular to the front surface of the crystalline humor. For perpendicular rays are organized just as the points are organized in the object itself. Unless vision occurs by perpendicular rays alone, they argue vision would be confused, just as perpendicular radiations would be confused by oblique ones. And yet, experience—by which he is most strongly convinced—attributes something to oblique rays as well, since more than a single hemisphere is seen...

enters the eye perpendicularly. Now Vitello says that the **vitreous humor** is the nourishment for the **crystalline humor** <note>The "crystalline humor" is the term used by Kepler and his predecessors for the lens of the eye.</note>, while the **aqueous humor** is actually its excrement. In this, he perhaps follows the Physicians, for Jean Fernel says the same. He considers these parts transparent: the first so that the visual forms <term>species: the "images" or "likenesses" of objects that were thought to travel through the air into the eye</term> can enter; the second so that the forms already perceived by the crystalline may reach the junction of the nerve through the vitreous and the substance of the spirits, where they are recognized by the faculty or **common sense** <note>In the psychology of the time, the "common sense" (sensus communis) was the part of the mind that integrated data from all five senses.</note>. Therefore, he assigns a flat surface to the back of the crystalline (Book 3, Proposition 23) and denies that the rays of things ought to converge, lest the right and left sides be swapped in the image. Indeed, he thinks that a perfect form of the thing seen reaches all the way to the junction of the nerve.

This entire opinion—even though he boasts that his authority is **Aristotle**, who says in Chapter 2 of *On Sense and the Sensible* that <note>original: "τὸ ὄμμα, τὸ ὁρατικὸν ὕδατος"</note> "the eye, the organ of sight, consists of water"—is overthrown by the fact that the crystalline is separated from the nerve and the retina, and is instead joined with the **uvea** <note>The pigmented layer of the eye, including the iris.</note>, as was shown above from the work of **Felix Platter**. Furthermore, as to what should be thought regarding this introduced idea of "nutrition and excretion," let the Physicians argue it; certainly, if no sense is more wonderful and subtle than sight, these explanations for how vision is established are unworthy. Moreover, he assigns the sensing of light to the membranes of the eye based on the model of **touch**. I might believe this if it were a matter of sensing heat, and if vision were not completed in an instant. But as it stands, light and colors—which do not heat in the slightest and enter the eye in a moment—are far too subtle to be perceived by a physical membrane under the logic of touch. See what we argued in the first chapter regarding the **immaterial motion of light**. Therefore, it is not the membrane, nor even the nerve, but the **spirit**—or perhaps something even more divine—that receives and perceives the light, which I denied above could be investigated by Opticians. For in that same place, this idea was also refuted: that visual forms "stick" to or are imprinted upon the humors <note>The fluids within the eye.</note>.

Now, as for the fact that Vitello forms his image using only perpendicular rays of the sun, it is shocking how subtly he distinguishes between perpendicular rays and those very close to them. If light acts upon a sense, and the sense is affected by this action, then the sense will be heavily affected in proportion to the strength of the action. And yet, there is almost no difference in illumination between perpendicular rays and those nearest to them, because the latter are refracted almost not at all. Therefore, the "affection"—that is, the **sensation**—of perpendicular rays and those closest to them is nearly equal.

of the senses. Thus, sensation is confused, and Witelo labored in vain. But there is no need for words. It has been demonstrated by the most certain reasons and experiments that the picture of an object—or of a whole hemisphere—is established upon the concave wall of the **retiform coat** <note>original: *retiformis*; what we now call the retina, named for its "net-like" appearance</note>, with all confusion of rays entirely removed. Next, it is certain that rays from many points of the visible hemisphere converge into a single point of the **crystalline lens**. Finally, it is clear to the senses that a "ghost" or image of the opposite object appears in the black of the eye. Therefore, in ancient times, Democritus—as recorded in Aristotle’s *On the Senses*, chapter 2—said that vision occurs through this image or "idol." Witelo said that vision occurs through a confused illumination of the crystalline lens. I say that vision occurs through this acknowledged and unbeatably demonstrated "picture." All three suppositions are certain; if you are uncertain by which of these vision is completed, follow whichever you like, provided you have heard the reasons. Aristotle indeed refuted Democritus, warning that this "idol" is not an actual thing, but a **reflection** <note>original: ἔμφασιν (*emphaseon*); a Greek term used in optics for images seen in mirrors</note>—an image, as in the study of mirrors—and not a **condition** <note>original: πάθος (*pathos*); an affection or physiological state</note> of the eye in which it is thought to reside, but rather an effect of an eye placed opposite this eye and looking at itself in it. In the same way, I refute Witelo by the very confusion of the rays. For as he says, oblique things are also seen insofar as oblique radiations converge with perpendicular ones; therefore, the oblique and direct radiation are received at the same point. Consequently, two things would be judged to be in one place. I, however, am confirmed by a most universal argument, one used by Witelo himself: the experience of vision follows the action of illumination in both manner and proportion. The **retina**, however, is illuminated distinctly, point by point, from the individual points of things, and most strongly through individual points. Therefore, in the retina—and not elsewhere—the most distinct and evident vision can occur. This is all the more true because the defects of seeing follow the disturbed logic of the picture, as has been demonstrated. And I do not know whether Democritus, under the name of his "idol" by which vision occurs, celebrated this "picture" rather than that mirror-like **reflection**. It often happened to the ancients that they were undeservedly refuted by Aristotle under a fictional version of their own opinions.

For the eye that is your right is the left of your image. This is not to mention that the hollow of the picture would verge inward into the head, while the hollow of the actual object would verge in the opposite direction.

Therefore, if the inversion of this picture disturbs you, and you fear that an inverted vision follows from this inverted image, I would wish you to weigh the matter thus. Just as vision is not an "action" simply because illumination is an action, but is rather a passive reception <note>original: "passio," a philosophical term meaning the state of being acted upon, the opposite of "actio"</note> contrary to action: so also, for the locations to correspond, the things receiving the light must be opposite the agents <note>The objects reflecting light</note> from that region. Furthermore, locations are perfectly opposite when the same center mediates in all lines of opposition; this would not have happened if the picture had been upright. 

Therefore, in the inverted picture, although universally and with respect to some common line rights are exchanged with lefts: nevertheless, the right of the object is perfectly opposed to the right of the picture, and the top of the object to the top of the picture (relative to itself), just as a hollow is to a hollow. Nor is there fear that sight will err in its direction. For someone looking at a high thing clearly turns the eyes upward, or toward low seats, as the location of the object requires. Sight would have erred rather if the picture were upright. For in that case, in some places the inner wall of the eye would be presented directly to the object, and in others not, such as from the sides: for it would decline from the opposition. Nothing absurd is committed, therefore, by the inverted picture—a thing which Vitello so greatly fled, and which Jessenius <note>Johannes Jessenius (1566–1621), a famous physician and anatomist who wrote on the soul and the eye</note> also followed, thinking that refraction in the cornea provides for this correction.

<summary>In this passage, Kepler argues that the image projected onto the retina is naturally inverted, refuting earlier optical theories that attempted to keep the image upright. <meta>This page continues Kepler's investigation into the geometry of vision, specifically focusing on how the physical structure of the eye introduces errors when using astronomical instruments like the sextant or triquetrum.</meta>

# 212 JOHANNES KEPLER

In this business, they require a single center from which the angle may be measured. For this reason, they isolate one eye, imitating craftsmen who, when checking the straightness of a rule, use only one eye. Those who aim scorpions <note>original: "scorpiones"; ancient Roman engines used for firing bolts</note> and those who direct muskets at a target do the same. For in all these cases—though for different reasons—using both eyes at once is a hindrance. Aristotle deemed this a subject worthy of a philosopher’s inquiry in his *Problems*, Section 31, problems 2 and 20. 

Yet, even using a single eye does not mean no caution is needed; indeed, it can lead us into error in two ways. For in the image <note>original: "pictura"; Kepler refers to the optical image formed within the eye</note> through which we have said vision occurs, two regions of the eye are chiefly considered: the Center of the eye, and the surface surrounding the center which receives the image. For it has been said that the image is so arranged on the retina <term>retiformi tunica; literally the "net-like cloak," the light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye</term> that straight lines cast from each of its points through that same center of the retina would, if extended, strike the corresponding points of the visible object.

<margin>What is the center of the angles of vision?</margin>

Thus, when the distances between stars must be captured with astronomical instruments, the more diligent astronomers (as has been said) do not trust the eye alone. For they know that even if the eye touches the very center of the instrument—which is difficult to achieve in practice—it only touches it on the surface. In that case, the lines drawn from each star through the upper sights <term>pinnacidia; the aiming vanes or sights found on early astronomical tools</term> do not actually meet there. 

Let **F** and **G** be the stars, and **BAC** be the instrument with its center at **A**. Let **DA** be the surface of the eye, and **E** the center of the eye. Since the straight lines hitting **F** and **G** must be imagined as emerging not from **A**, but from the eye’s center **E**: when the sights **B** and **C** are aligned so that **EBF** and **ECG** form straight lines, the angle **BAC** will measure the distance incorrectly. It will be larger than it should be, because it is an interior angle compared to **BEC** on the same base; therefore, the arc **BC** is larger than is right, because the depth of the eye **EA** does not allow the Center of the Instrument (**A**) and the Center of the Eye (**E**) to be joined as one.

->[Diagram: A geometric proof showing how the depth of the eyeball (point E) creates a wider angle on an instrument's arc (points B and C) than the true angle between two stars (F and G).]<-

One must be even more cautious of this when very small quantities are measured by angles, such as when we seek the diameters of the sun and moon <note>original: "luminarium"; literally 'the luminaries'</note>—a task that must serve as a foundation for everyone undertaking the restoration of astronomy. 

Archimedes, therefore, in his book *The Sand-Reckoner*, added this caution—

# SUPPLEMENTS TO VITELLO. 213

Archimedes used this [method]: first, having adopted a certain method, he investigated a quantity not smaller than the sight <note>original: *non minorem viſu*; Kepler is discussing Archimedes' *The Sand Reckoner* where Archimedes attempted to measure the angular diameter of the sun using a small cylinder to block its disk.</note>. He placed a cylinder equal to it at center **A** of the instrument, and drew lines from the sight-holes <term>pinnacidia: the small plates with holes or slits used on astronomical instruments for sighting</term> **B** and **C**, touching this cylinder and meeting at a point; let these be **BE** and **CE**. Thus, he determined that the angle **BEC** was very nearly smaller than that angle by which the distance **FG** was perceived. But the angle **BAC** was very nearly larger.

Furthermore, what quantity is "not smaller than the sight" should be determined as follows. Let **AB** be the surface of the cornea, and from the visible point **E**, let the outermost rays that are admitted through the opening of the uvea <term>the pupil; Kepler uses the term for the iris/opening of the eye</term> be **EA** and **EB**. Once refracted at **AB**, let these meet at point **F** of the retiform <term>the retina; the net-like light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye</term>, or very near its surface. Now, let **CD** be a quantity smaller than that which passes through **EA** and **EB**, and closer to the eye **AB** than **E** is. You see that even if **CD** is placed directly in front of point **E**, not all the rays of **E** itself are blocked; instead, they enter from the sides all around and meet at the place **F** destined for them all. When these rays are gathered into one, the vision of point **E** occurs, but it is mixed with the vision of the object **CD**. For the right edge **D** will paint the left part **N** of the retina relative to **F**, and the left edge **C** will paint the right part **M**. Therefore, the middle of object **CD** will paint **F** itself, which **E** was also painting before. Thus, two things will be seen in one place, yet with this difference: that **E** will be thought to be seen more distinctly, while **CD** will be like a shadow or a spiderweb. This is not surprising. For as was said above, because **C** is so close, the rays of point **C** into the eye are gathered far behind **F**; they strike the retina at **F** before they have converged. And in this very way, **CD** will be smaller than the width of the sight. Archimedes proceeds in much the same way; he places a more distant cylinder **GH** equal to **CD**, and orders it to be white for the sake of distinct vision. If the whole cylinder **GH** is seen, with the cylinder **CD** not hindering it at all, he declares them to be much smaller than the sight; but if some part of **GH** is missing, they are a little smaller. If the whole of **GH** is hidden (the two always being equal to each other), they are reckoned larger than the sight...

To me, a more efficient method of sighting <term>collimandi ratio: the method of aligning an instrument with a star</term> has appeared, after long use, than by using two parallel lines directed at any star with two observers employed for the two stars. This method allows the "single eye"—which is treacherous for so many reasons—to be completely retired. This technique was first utilized by Tycho <note>Tycho Brahe (1546–1601), the preeminent Danish astronomer known for his accurate celestial observations.</note> and was eagerly adopted by the Landgrave's staff <note>The astronomers working for William IV, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel, who maintained a major observatory.</note> with great benefit to their observations (see Book 1 of the *Epistles*, page 3). Tycho feared for the design of the Landgrave's instrument (page 8), worrying it might be too similar to the first Sextant he had built; however, its accuracy is defended by the Landgrave on page 22. On page 28, Rothmann <note>Christoph Rothmann, the Landgrave’s court astronomer.</note> reports back to Tycho on the genuine form of the others, which in practice is equivalent to Tycho's version. It differs only in this: in Tycho's Sextant, each of the observers uses the parallel slits of his <term>pinnacidium: a sighting vane or plate on an astronomical instrument</term> to sight the same cylinder at the center of the instrument. In the Landgrave's version, each observer has his own sighting vane, slightly removed from the center, in place of a single cylinder. Therefore, Tycho, in his letters to the Landgrave (page 38) and to Rothmann (pages 61 and 62), highly praises both the design and their industry. These passages should be consulted by anyone desiring more specific details on the method of observation. See also Tycho’s *Mechanics* <note>original: "Mechanica Tychonis"</note> at page H 5. And so, this center of vision has reminded us of these astronomical observations.

We must note this phenomenon of vision much more carefully: why is it that for all people, objects that are bright appear larger in proportion than less luminous objects placed next to them? <margin>Various errors of vision regarding the light of the Moon and Sun.</margin> Indeed, in the first or last phase of the Moon, the bright horn <note>The crescent</note> seems to be enclosed in a much wider circle than the rest of the body, which is illuminated by "earthlight" <note>original: "lumine telluris," now commonly called earthshine—light reflected from Earth that dimly illuminates the dark part of the moon</note> and is very clearly visible. The same occurred on May 15/25 in the year 1603, during an eclipse of the Moon: some observers were able to perceive the edge of the darkened part with their vision, even though more than a third remained; they claimed, therefore, that the circle of the dark part was narrower. On August 7/17 in the year 1600, in the evening, I saw the Moon one hour before its setting joined with the "Heart of the Scorpion" <note>The star Antares</note>. It was entering over the "Heart" on the northern side, so that about a third part of the "terminator" <note>original: "τῆς τομῆς" (tēs tomēs) — the line dividing the light and dark parts of the moon</note> projected above the "Heart." Since the section differed very little from a straight line (the Sun being at 25° Leo), the width of the bright part at that location nevertheless seemed much wider than the distance of the star from the line of the section. These observations were made on the borders of Styria and Hungary, at a polar altitude of 47 2/3°.

<meta>This page continues Kepler's groundbreaking investigation into how light enters the eye and forms an image on the retina, building on his previous demonstrations of how light behaves when passing through small apertures (the "pinhole camera" effect).</meta>

# SUPPLEMENTS TO WITELO, PAGE 219
<note>original: "PARALIPOM. IN VITELLIONEM" — This refers to Kepler's 1604 work "Ad Vitellionem Paralipomena," which serves as a critique and expansion of Witelo’s 13th-century treatise on optics.</note>

Therefore, the things that are painted there <note>referring to the image formed on the retina</note> are less clear where they have extended beyond their own boundaries. This happens either because the objects are too remote, with the <term>intersection</term> <note>the focal point</note> being made before reaching the retina; or because they are too close, so that the retina cuts through the cone of light before it can reach its point (see propositions 26, 27, and 28 of this chapter). Consequently, these boundaries are completely hidden and give way to the white light. Thus, almost the same thing happens in the eye as what I demonstrated above in Chapter 2 regarding the way light rays form a shape on a wall.

However, the appearance of a shining object is not simply enlarged, but rather seems to be multiplied, with one larger, blurred shape being formed out of many distinct ones. This seems to occur either because of the wrinkles of the <term>uvea</term> <note>The pigmented layer of the eye, including the iris. Kepler suggests its texture affects the light.</note>, which dilates at night when we gaze at the Moon and contracts into itself and its wrinkles, or because of the gaps in the <term>ciliary processes</term> <note>The fringe-like structure behind the iris that supports the lens.</note>. Indeed, by squinting the eyelids and wrinkling the brow, many of these false images are wiped away—though not from every direction, because the eye is not covered equally on all sides by the contraction of the eyelids. Instead, it is left exposed horizontally as long as the eyelids are opened only slightly.

For this reason, the "visual picture" <note>the image on the retina</note> is flawed, and it is inevitable that flawed vision follows. If all things were of equal brightness, vision would simply be confused; but as it is, because bright things are so much more powerful, they are distorted in their size. And although the "pictorial cone" <note>the cone of light rays forming the image</note> is perhaps dilated in everyone, not everyone possesses such a delicate visual faculty that they perceive every single stray ray. Those who are affected by all these radiations are the only ones who imagine bright objects to be larger than they are. This is why those with significantly weak vision see not only bright things, but even dark, slender things as doubled, if they are excessively remote.

A related question is found in Aristotle, Section 31, Problem 28: <margin>Why, because of the brightness of the Moon, or Jupiter, or Venus, smaller stars within a few degrees cannot be seen.</margin> why light radiating into the eyes takes away the sight of nearby objects, which returns once the light is turned away from the eyes. For just as has been said so far, some parts of the <term>retiform</term> <note>The "net-like" or retina layer of the eye.</note> are illuminated very strongly, and thus the sensation is very strong; meanwhile, the radiation from the other parts (which correspond to the surrounding visible objects) is of no proportion compared to that strong light. Therefore, there is almost no sensation of them. For just as a distinct picture on the retina leads to distinct vision, so does a strong illumination of the picture lead to a strong sensation, in which the <term>spirits</term> <note>In 17th-century physiology, "visual spirits" were thought to be the fluid or energy in the nerves that transmitted sensation to the brain.</note> are greatly affected. Perhaps this relates more to the second flaw of vision, which follows next.

Therefore, from this chapter, astronomers will consider that ocular intuition or estimation—no matter how carefully considered—is not always to be trusted regarding the size of the diameter of the full Moon, or the extent of the deficit in an eclipse. For this reason, not only should other more certain methods <note>Kepler suggests using instruments like the camera obscura rather than the naked eye.</note> be consulted, but one should not rashly disagree with them based on confidence in sight, if ever it happens that they disagree with sight. For it has been demonstrated most evidently, from the very configuration of sight, that it frequently happens that an error occurs to the sight when it judges bright things to be too large.

_It also seems to belong to this place to state the cause why stars appear more confused to the dim-sighted in the deep of night, but more distinct when the dawn is first rising?_ <margin>Why the stars appear more distinct when dawn is rising.</margin> _And yet, if much light hinders them, they ought to have been hindered more when cumulative with the light of dawn._
_The cause, therefore, is this: that in the nocturnal darkness the opening of the pupil is dilated by natural motion; in the light of dawn, it is closed more tightly. But the cone of the radiating point enters more strongly through a wider opening and makes a strong impression; the same cone, constricted by a narrower opening, moves the eye more weakly. Up to this point, we have always maintained this: that by the exceptional sensation of one thing, the weaker sensations of others are suppressed. And also in the second chapter, it was a fundamental point that distinct lights on a wall, having entered through a wider opening, are more weakly hidden by the stronger; but with the opening narrowed, they do not become proportional; so that although all lights are weakened, more is taken away from the brightness of the stronger, and the weaker light emerges._

...for all motion, life, preservation, and the beauty of both celestial and terrestrial things <note>Kepler is arguing that the Sun is the primary source of all vitality and order in the universe</note> depend upon it; so much so that the more closely you contemplate it, the more miracles you find in that one thing. Whether, therefore, from the beginning the whole body of the Sun is inflamed equally on all sides by its soul, or more so in the center: there is always more of this inestimable fire in the center. Because the rarer medium occurring outside does not prevent something from being reflected back inside—a suspicion I removed above in Chapter 4, Number 9, using the example of a mirror.

## 2. On the Illumination of the Moon.

This was the most ancient part of Astronomy, as men sought the causes in a matter obvious to everyone; namely, how it should happen that the Moon is born and vanishes in its monthly circuit, and takes on various appearances.

Berosus the Chaldean <note>A Babylonian writer and astronomer from the 3rd century BCE.</note>, as reported by Diogenes Laertius, taught that the Moon was bright on one half—or as Cleomedes reports, half-fiery—and deprived of all light on the remaining part: and that it happened by the rotation of the globe that the bright part, after being hidden behind the body, gradually emerges more and more.

Thales of Miletus <note>Often cited as the first Greek philosopher.</note> improved upon this opinion, and was the first to state the reality: that this entire hemisphere is illuminated by the Sun, and he said the Moon shines from no part of itself. Plutarch attributes this view to Anaxagoras. Berosus could have gathered this even from what is evident to the eye: that the same parts of the Moon do not always shine. For that "face" which we imagine in the Moon from the arrangement of its spots <term>maculae</term> <note>original: "macularum" — Kepler refers to the dark lunar plains (maria) that form the "Man in the Moon."</note>, emerges into the light successively, and it is always turned downward toward us, remaining immobile, while the light passes over it

On the western edge of the Moon, a little above the "eye" <note>Kepler often used anatomical metaphors for lunar features; the "eye" likely refers to one of the large dark plains or *maria*.</note> and toward the top, there is a very black spot, like a dot, situated in the midst of very bright light. For this reason, it is not always the same parts of the Moon that are in the light, as **Berosus** <note>original: "Berosus"; a Babylonian priest and astronomer (3rd century BCE) who believed the Moon was a sphere half-filled with fire.</note> used to think.    This opinion regarding the illumination of the Moon is as certain and beyond all risk of doubt as any can be. Nevertheless, there have been those who took it upon themselves to challenge it using optical arguments. Their view is fully debated in **Plutarch’s** *On the Face in the Moon* <note>original: "de facie Lunæ"</note> and repeated by **Cleomedes** in Book 2 (although **Scaliger** attributes this same objection to a certain Arab, the **son of Amram**). They say: If the Sun communicates its light to the Moon, that light will be derived to us through reflection. Thus, we would not see the "light of the Moon" itself, but rather, with our eyes directed at the Moon, we would receive the rays of the Sun itself. If this were granted, it would follow that the Moon is a convex mirror. Therefore, we would see an image of the Sun in the Moon. Furthermore, it would not be possible for us to see the Sun's rays all around the Moon’s body, whether it is full or halved. For the law of reflection <note>original: "Lex enim repercusšus"</note> is this: reflection happens from that single point on a body where the angles formed by the incoming and the reflected rays with the sphere can be equal. Since we neither see an image of the Sun in the Moon, nor is the Moon illuminated in only one certain spot where the equality of angles can exist—but rather it appears sometimes with its whole body lit, sometimes half, and sometimes crescent-shaped at the very edges—they believe it follows that the Moon does not shine by rays coming from the Sun.

<meta>This page continues Kepler's investigation into the nature of light and how it interacts with celestial bodies, specifically the Moon. He is distinguishing between simple reflection and a more complex scattering of light he calls "communicated light."</meta>

...[the previous text] distributes light entirely into direct, reflected, and refracted; it does not recognize a fourth. Hence it is that Cleomedes <note>Cleomedes was a Greek astronomer (c. 1st century AD) known for his work *On the Circular Motions of the Celestial Bodies*.</note>, as if driven into a corner, wrongly concludes that the Moon also has its own light, which is "excited" by the Sun's light where it is touched by it. Kepler uses this term to describe light that is absorbed and then re-radiated or scattered by a surface, rather than bouncing off like a mirror.</note>

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Therefore, even though it is most truly proven by these already explained reasons that the Moon does not use light simply reflected from the Sun, this fourth species of **communicated light** still remains to be attributed to the Moon. For there is no other explanation for that light which descends to us from the Moon—originating from the Sun—than the explanation for the light which, descending from the same Sun onto any wall in its path, radiates into the whole hemisphere; and whatever dark chamber <note>original: "Camera". This is a reference to the *camera obscura* or "dark room" principle where light enters a small hole to project an image.</note> is placed before it, the light enters through a small open window and depicts itself with its own color on the opposite white wall, as was demonstrated above in Chapter 2, proposition 7. To this end, I refer to those words of Plutarch, which he finally attaches to his other useless excuses: *The Moon,* he says, *has many roughnesses and many inequalities, so that the brilliance occurring from a great body can shine back from heights that are not small, and be conveniently reflected, entangled, and continue the radiance among themselves, as if it were brought to us by many mirrors.* By these words, he described almost exactly what I am accustomed to call **communicated light**. Yet Cleomedes did better; he adds this necessary condition: that solar light is not only reflected by the Moon but also altered in the Moon, like the glow of fire in iron, and thus becomes its own.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And from this it is now proven that the body of the Moon is both dense, as the Earth is (which Plutarch contends at length in his often-mentioned booklet), and intensely colored (without which, according to p. 22, Chapter 1, **communicated light** has no place), and with a rough surface, so that it is not transparent. For all experiences sought from every side testify that the body of the Moon is opaque.

->OPTICAL PART OF ASTRONOMY. 229<-

[Folio 164] mentions this. He correctly attributed the same matter to the Moon as that which the Earth possesses (which indeed seems to have been the very ancient opinion of the Pythagoreans <note>A school of Greek philosophers who believed numbers were the essence of all things and held advanced views on the motion of the Earth</note>). Perhaps they intended nothing else by that "Counter-Earth" <margin>Counter-Earth <note>original: "Ἀντίχθονα" (Antichthona)</note></margin>—a concept fruitlessly rejected by Aristotle as a cause of eclipses—than the Moon itself. However, he wished the Moon to differ from the earthly globe in this: that the Moon, like a mirror, sends back the light received from the Sun, whereas the Earth, though bathed in the Sun's rays, only brightens but does not reflect light back. 

But in truth, the nature of both Earth and Moon is the same. For the Moon is not a mirror (as Plutarch, that Arab <note>Kepler refers here to Alhazen (Ibn al-Haytham), the medieval pioneer of optics</note>, and Cleomedes have rightly refuted above), nor is it true that the Earth does not shine with shared light. This was abundantly proven in Chapter 2, Proposition 7, using the examples of all kinds of walls; Plutarch even suggests the example of clothing. 

If Cleomedes allows what he himself celebrates—the "proper light" of the Moon—to be called a color (which I defined above as "light buried in matter" <note>Kepler’s theory that color is light that has been absorbed or "trapped" by a physical substance</note>), then he speaks plainly with me. He concludes with me, and finally, against Poseidonius <note>A Stoic philosopher and scientist who studied the tides and the Sun</note>, he attributes to both the Moon and the Earth their own colors. These colors, when excited by the light of the Sun, radiate into half the sphere, so that in this cause of reflection, the Earth and Moon are equal. Therefore, astronomers are most certain about this illumination of the Moon: that it comes from the Sun, and that here the body of the Moon itself behaves no differently than any wall you might encounter.

Having laid this foundation, astronomers now derive various modes of this illumination from it. First, they argue that since the Sun is spherical in shape, and the Moon is likewise spherical but smaller, the Moon must therefore be illuminated on more than half of its surface. They state that the boundary of illumination is a circle, yet one smaller than the "great circle" <note>The largest possible circle that can be drawn around a sphere, like the equator on Earth</note> described on the spherical body of the Moon, according to the 27th proposition of the second book of Witelo <note>A 13th-century natural philosopher whose work on optics Kepler is commenting on and expanding</note>. From this, having already taken care to know the distance and diameters of both celestial bodies, they teach how to investigate the size of the circle of illumination.

Furthermore, it is obscure upon what other foundations the calculation of this most learned man rests. Therefore, by removing the common angle CDH, the remaining angle FDC is equal to the remaining angle CHD; for this reason, the arc FC is 15' 40''. The arc GB is likewise equal, and the sum of both is 31' 20'', and FAG is a semicircle or 180°. Therefore, the arc CAB is 180° 31' 20'', and the remainder CEB is 179° 28' 40''. 

This is the greatest possible quantity of the arc CAB, specifically when the Moon is both at its apogee <note>Apogee: The point in the Moon's orbit where it is furthest from the Earth.</note> and new. And since the shadow of the same globe becomes longer and sharper if the globe to be illuminated moves further away from the larger illuminating globe: therefore, when the Moon has moved further from the Sun along a straight line, the tip of the shadow there will be sharper than the angle of vision in apogee, which is 31' 20''. 

Wherefore the new Moon in perigee <note>Perigee: The point in the Moon's orbit where it is closest to the Earth.</note>—when, according to the meaning of the word, it has approached the Earth and consequently moved away from the Sun—will terminate its shadow at a sharper angle. Again, the full Moon, when it is nearly 60 terrestrial semidiameters further from the Sun than the Earth is (whereas at the new moon it was just as many semidiameters closer to the Sun than the Earth), will close its shadow with a much sharper tip. Therefore, the arc FC will be much smaller than 15' 40'', and this is according to the opinions of Ptolemy, which we have followed here according to Reinhold's judgment.
